en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Middle Fifty Discourses in the Majjhima Nikāya.
1. The Chapter on Householders (Gahapativagga) 1. Commentary on the Kandarakasutta 1.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Kandarakasutta. Therein, “at Campā” means in the city of that name. For that—
In various places within the city, such as the parks and lotus ponds, *campaka* trees alone were abundant;

therefore, it came to be known by the name Campā. On the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, not far from that city of Campā, there was a lotus pond called Gaggarā, so named because it had been dug by the royal consort named Gaggarā.
It exists. On its banks, all around, is a vast grove of *campaka* trees adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue and others.
In that *campaka* grove, fragrant with the scent of blossoms, the Blessed One dwells. It is with reference to this that it is said:
"on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond. "Together with a great community of monks" means with a number for which no specific limit has been shown.
"Together with a great community of bhikkhus. "Pessa" is his name. "Hatthārohaputta" means the son of a master of elephant-riders.
"Kandarako ca paribbājako" refers to a wandering ascetic named Kandara who lived under a canopy.
"Having paid homage" means having entered between the six-colored, dense rays of the Buddha, as if immersing himself in a clear lacquer solution.

The meaning is: having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One—which were adorned with the mark of the wheel (*cakralakṣaṇa*) and as beautiful as full-blown lotuses the color of lac—just like one spreading out a choice cloth the color of refined gold and covering oneself head and shoulders, or like one receiving with the head campaka flowers endowed with excellent color and fragrance, or like the full moon approaching the base of Mount Sineru;
he sat down to one side, free from the six faults of sitting.
He sat down in one place.
"Silent, silent"—the meaning is that wherever he looked, it was indeed silent;
for there was not even a single monk who had fidgeting with his hands or fidgeting with his feet; everyone [was focused] on the Blessed One.
Out of reverence and because they had themselves trained in the training, they were free from mutual conversation, even to the extent of not making the sound of a cough;
like well-planted posts driven into the ground, like the waters of the great ocean in a windless place,
they were motionless in body and undistracted in mind, surrounding the Blessed One on the peak of Sineru like dark clouds.
They sat down. Seeing the assembly thus seated, great joy and gladness arose in the wanderer.
Being unable to contain that which had arisen within his heart, he gave vent to an expression of affection, saying:
"It is wonderful, sir," and so forth.
In this context, it is marvelous (*acchariya*) that it is not constant, like a blind man’s climbing of a mountain.

This, first of all, is the method of etymological derivation (*saddanaya*). However, this is the method of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathānaya*): it is "marvelous" (*acchariya*) because it is worthy of a finger-snap (*accharā*).

The meaning is that it is fit to be struck by a finger-snap. It is "extraordinary" (*abbhuta*) because what had never occurred before has now occurred. Both of these are synonyms for wonder (*vimhaya*). Furthermore, this...
There are two kinds of wonders: the wonder of censure and the wonder of praise. Among these, "It is a wonder, Moggallāna;
it is marvelous, Moggallāna, that this foolish man will wait even until he is seized by the arm"—this is called the wonder of censure.
"It is a wonder, Mother Nanda; it is marvelous, Mother Nanda, that you will purify even a single thought-impulse"—this is the wonder of praise.
This is what is called the "marvel of praise. Here too, this very thing is intended; for he spoke thus while praising him.
In the phrase *yāvañcidaṃ*, *idaṃ* here is merely a particle. *Yāva* signifies a limit of measure:
as far as [he] was correctly established, by whatever measure he was correctly established—it is impossible to fully describe his praise; rather, it is simply marvelous.
"It is indeed wonderful" is what is meant. "This is the very limit" means: this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, being thus correctly established, is the supreme among that Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
thus it is "this is the very limit. Having established it in such a way as this [Saṅgha] was established, they established it;
the meaning is that there is nothing beyond this. In the second method, they will establish it in this way.

"It should be understood that there is nothing more than this. In this context, "established" means having been joined to the practice of non-opposition, beginning with the conduct of higher morality (*ābhisamācārika-vatta*).
Now, why does this wanderer point to the Buddhas of the past and future?
Is it because he possesses knowledge of the three times? No, he does not; rather, standing upon the method of grasping principles (*nayaggāha*), [he says] "in whatever manner this..."
Thinking, "The community of monks is seated together—tamed, disciplined, and calmed;
even the Buddhas of the past, having made this very thing the limit, caused others to practice it; the Buddhas of the future will also cause others to practice it;
there is no practice beyond this," he spoke thus out of partiality.
2. Thus, "Kandaraka," this is a separate connection. It is said that when the Blessed One heard this, he thought:
"Kandaraka, you say that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is tranquil; however, the reason for this tranquility of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is not known to you.
For you have not fulfilled the thirty perfections, nor have you ripened the roots of merit at the seat of enlightenment."

He began this teaching to demonstrate: "The All-knowing Knowledge was penetrated [by him] alone; however, after I had fulfilled the perfections and brought to their ultimate consummation the conduct for the benefit of relatives, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood, I penetrated the All-knowing Knowledge upon the seat of enlightenment.
For me, the cause of their pacification is manifest."
“There are indeed caves” (*santi hi kandarā*)—this too is a separate connection. It is said that this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
“This wanderer says that this Saṅgha of bhikkhus is ‘calm,’ yet this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, having fashioned and contrived it, maintains its deportment through a state of hypocrisy;
it is not inwardly calm, nor does it manifest the appearance of being calm.”
[The Blessed One] shows this. Herein, there are both those among the community of monks who are fulfilling the practice and those who, having fulfilled the practice, stand at its culmination.
Among them, those who have fulfilled the practice and reached the culmination are calmed by the very qualities they have personally realized;
those fulfilling the practice are calmed by the insight (vipassanā) pertaining to the higher path; but those released from this [world]...
"The remainder have been stilled by means of the four foundations of mindfulness. I shall show you the cause of their being stilled.
To demonstrate that "for this reason and for that reason this community of bhikkhus is stilled," he said, "For there are those in the mountain caves," and so forth.
Regarding what should be said about the phrases "arahants whose taints are destroyed" and so on, that has already been explained in the commentary to the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*.
It has been stated. The practice of the trainee (sekha-paṭipadā) is also explained in detail in that very same place.

"Of constant virtue" (santata-sīla) means of perpetual virtue, of uninterrupted virtue. "Of constant conduct" (santata-vutti) is a synonym for that same term, or it may also mean "of constant livelihood.
The meaning is that they maintain their livelihood by standing firm in that constant virtue; they do not reach death with immorality.
“Nipaka” means endowed with discernment (*nepakka*), being possessed of wisdom (*paññavanta*). “Those of prudent conduct” (*nipakavuttino*) means those who live by means of wisdom;

they maintain their livelihood while standing firm in wisdom. This is unlike someone who, though having gone forth in the Dispensation, wanders among the six improper resorts for the sake of a livelihood—becoming one who frequents prostitutes, widows, young girls, eunuchs, taverns, or nuns.
He dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and disciples of other sects— engaging in improper lay contact;
he performs medical treatments, acts as a messenger, carries errands, lances abscesses, applies ointments to wounds,
administers emetics, administers purgatives, and applies nasal oils.

He cooks; he cooks oil for drinking; he gives gifts of bamboo, gifts of bowls, gifts of flowers, gifts of fruits, gifts of bathing requisites, gifts of tooth-sticks, gifts of water for rinsing the mouth, and gifts of powder and clay;
he acts as a flatterer, he acts as a bean-soup maker, he acts as a servant, and he acts as a messenger on foot—thus maintaining his livelihood by means of these twenty-one kinds of improper search.
He is called one of unstable conduct; he does not maintain his livelihood by standing firm in wisdom.
Consequently, after death, having become what is known as a "monk-yakkha," he experiences great suffering in the manner described: "Even his outer robe is burning and blazing.
Rather than being such a person, even for the sake of life, one who does not transgress the training rules [abides] in the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
Having established himself and mastered the word of the Buddha according to his strength, he fulfilled these noble practices— the practice of the Chariot-Breaker,
the practice of the Great Gosiṅga, the practice of Great Emptiness, the practice of Freedom from Defilement, the practice of the Heirs of the Dhamma,

the practice of Nālaka, the practice of Tuvaṭṭaka, and the practice of the Moon Simile— while abiding in the conduct of the Noble Lineage characterized by contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation.

The meaning is that, having become body-witnesses (*kāyasakkhin*), they dwell with their energy directed toward attaining Arahantship day by day, having established insight (*vipassanā*) and dwelling alone in going and other activities—like elephants that have left the herd, like lions that have let go of the pride, and like great ships that have no following.
"With well-established minds" means having properly established the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). The rest is the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness.
These have already been explained in detail below. Here, however, the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) mixed with both mundane and supramundane aspects are discussed;
by this much, the cause for the tranquility of the Saṅgha of monks has been explained.
3. "As well as well-laid out" means as well-established and well-taught. By the words "We too, venerable sir," he [the Buddha] refers to himself.
He demonstrates his status as an agent and elevates the community of monks. This is the intended meaning here:
"Venerable sir, we too, though householders... [as before] ...dwell with minds well-established;

yet for the community of monks, this alone is the ploughing, the seed, the yoke, the pole, the ploughshare, and the goad. Therefore, the community of monks must at all times be devoted to the foundations of mindfulness."
"But we, having obtained an opportunity from time to time, attend to this [meditation]; we too are practitioners, not those who have entirely abandoned their meditation subject.
"In the dense forest of humans" means they are dense by virtue of the density of human inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*);
it should be understood that their inclinations are also dense by virtue of the density of their defilements (*kilesa*). "In the thicket of coarseness and deceit" as well...
The same method applies here. In this context, "dregs" (kasaṭa) should be understood in the sense of impurity, and "deceitfulness" (sāṭheyya) in the sense of craftiness (kerāṭiya).

"He knows the welfare and harm of beings" means that the Blessed One thoroughly understands the course of conduct regarding welfare and harm for those people who are characterized by grasping, dregs, and craftiness.
Regarding the phrase "all that is born," here "the born" (pasava) refers to all species of four-footed creatures.
"Intended. "I am able" means "I can. "Within whatever interval" means "within whatever moment.
"He will go and return to Campā" means he will perform the act of going from the precincts of the hermitage as far as the gates of the city of Campā, and the act of returning.
"Deceits" means states of being deceitful. "Frauds" means states of being fraudulent. "Crookednesses" means states of being crooked. "Wrinkles" means states of being wrinkled.
"Pātukarissati" means he will manifest or show himself. For it is not possible for him to show those [forms] within such a short interval.

In this regard, when someone wishes to stand in a certain place, if there were no thought, "I shall go ahead and deceive [them] by standing in that place which is dangerous to men," then in that very place where one wishes to stand, a pillar would be firmly planted.
One who stands with his four legs made motionless as if they were fixed is called a *saṭha*. However, one who,
wishing to cut something down in a certain place and let it fall upon a person's body,
does not go ahead to that place which is dangerous to people with the intent to deceive them by saying "I will let it fall," but instead cuts it down right there where it is, is a *kūṭa*.

...named "crooked" (vaṅka). When someone, at a certain point on the road, wishing to turn off the path and return to the opposite way, does not think, "There is a place here where people are in danger;
I will go ahead, deceive them, and do it," but instead turns off the path and returns to the opposite way right there—this is what is called "crooked. For one who...
But just as one who wishes to go at times to the left, at times to the right, and at times by a straight path,
has no thought of going ahead to deceive people at a place where they are in danger,
thinking "I will act thus," but instead goes at times to the left, at times to the right, and at times by the straight path; so too with excrement or urine.
Or, for one who wishes to discharge [semen], thinking: "This place is well-swept, crowded with people, and delightful;
it is not proper to do such a thing in this spot; I shall go further on and do it in a secluded place," he does it right there—this is called crooked (*jimha*).
Thus, this was said with reference to these four kinds of action.
"All those deceptions, frauds, crookednesses, and perversities he will reveal"—even while acting in such ways, those who are deceitful and the like are said to "reveal" those deceptions and so forth.
Having thus shown the exposed nature of animals, [the Buddha] now shows the hidden nature of humans, saying: "Of us..."

He said, "But, venerable sir," and so forth. In that context, "slaves" (dāsā) are those born in the house, those purchased with wealth, those brought as captives, or those who have entered into slavery of their own accord.
"Servants" (pesā) are those who perform errands. "Laborers" (kammakarā) are those supported by food and wages.
"In one way indeed with the body" means they behave toward them with the body in one manner, with speech in another manner, and in yet another manner toward them.
This shows that the mind remains steady through its mode of behavior.

In this regard, those who, upon seeing their master face-to-face, go out to meet him, take goods from his hand, and—relinquishing one thing while taking up another—perform all the remaining duties such as preparing seats, fanning with palm-leaf fans, and washing his feet;
yet at a time when he is out of sight, they do not even look at the oil being poured, nor do they notice even a hundred-fold value [of what is lost].
Even when a task worth a thousand pieces of money was being neglected, they did not wish to turn back and look at it;
these are said to behave otherwise with the body. But those who praise them in their presence, saying, "Our master! Our noble sir!
and so forth—for them there is nothing that cannot be said behind their backs; they say whatever they desire. These are said to behave otherwise...
They address one another with such words.
4. "There are these four types of persons who are like messengers" (*pessapuggala*)—this too is a separate connection. For this messenger (*pessa*) [thought]:
"To what extent, venerable sir, while such grasping for people, such deception of people, and such fraudulence among people are occurring..."

“He knows the welfare and non-welfare of beings,” he said. He began this teaching to show: “The first three persons have entered upon a way of practice that leads to non-welfare, while the fourth above them has entered upon a way of practice that leads to welfare; thus I know the welfare and non-welfare of beings.
It is also appropriate to connect this with the previous discussion regarding Kandaraka. Therefore it was said:
“How well the Blessed Gotama has guided the Saṅgha of bhikkhus!
Then the Blessed One began this teaching, showing that “having set aside the first three types of persons, I guide [them] only in the practice for the benefit of the fourth type of person.
“Peaceful” (santa) is a synonym for the word “existing” (saṃvijjamāna). “They are peaceful...”
In the phrase "calmed and stilled," it is said that they have ceased and are peaceful. In the phrase "These dwellings are called 'peaceful' in the discipline of the Noble One," it means extinguished.
In the phrase "The peaceful indeed proclaim [the truth] among the virtuous," it means wise.
But here, the meaning is "existing" or "being found."

Among those who torment themselves: one who torments and afflicts oneself is a "self-tormentor" (*attantapa*). Devotion to the practice of tormenting oneself is "devotion to the practice of self-torment" (*attaparitāpanānuyoga*).

One who torments and afflicts another is a "tormentor of others" (*parantapa*). Devotion to the practice of tormenting others is "devotion to the practice of tormenting others" (*paraparitāpanānuyoga*).

"In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Starved" (*nicchāto*): "starvation" (*chāta*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*); that [craving] belongs to him.
"Non-existent" means he is free from desire. Because all defilements have been extinguished, he is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*).

Because of the absence of the defilements that burn within, he has become cool, thus he is "become cool" (*sītibhūto*). He experiences the bliss of the jhānas, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna, thus he is "one who experiences bliss.
"By himself, having become sublime" means by himself, having become the most excellent. "He satisfies the mind" means he brings the mind to fulfillment.
"Brings to fulfillment," "takes up," and "gladdens"—this is the meaning.
5. "Repulsive to suffering": it is repulsive to suffering; the meaning is that it stands as an adversary to suffering and does not desire suffering.
6. "Wise": here, one should not be called wise on account of four reasons; rather, it is through the application of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) that one performs the work.

It is appropriate to say that he is "wise" because he acts [in this way]. He should not be called "of great wisdom" (mahāpañña) according to the definition of great wisdom such as "grasping a vast meaning," but rather it is appropriate to call him "of great wisdom" because he is endowed with the wisdom that grasps the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
He will go "endowed with a great purpose" means he will go joined with a great goal.
The meaning is: having sacrificed, he would have gone [to heaven], and he would have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).
But is it the case that for those who possess the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits, an obstacle arises even when Buddhas are present before them? Yes, it does;
yet it is not on account of the Buddha, but rather due to negligence in one's duties or association with evil friends (*pāpamittatā*). In that regard:

There is what is called "decline through non-action": for if the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), having known the disposition of the brahmin Dhanañjāni, had taught him the Dhamma, that brahmin would have become a stream-enterer; thus, first of all, there is decline through non-action.
There is what is called "decline through evil friendship": for if Ajātasattu, having accepted the word of Devadatta, had not committed the deed of parricide...

If he had not done so, on the very day the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* was preached, he would have become a stream-enterer. However, because he accepted his [the king's] words and committed the act of patricide, it did not happen;
thus it occurs through association with evil friends. This lay follower also suffered a decline in his practice;
he rose and departed while the teaching was not yet concluded. Furthermore, monks...
"In this way, too, Pessa, the son of a charioteer, was endowed with great benefit. With what great benefit? With two advantages.
It is said that this lay follower gained confidence in the Saṅgha, and a new method arose in him for the purpose of grasping the foundations of mindfulness.
Therefore it is said: "endowed with great benefit. But as for Kandarako...
He gained confidence in the Saṅgha alone. "This is the time for the Blessed One" means this is the time for the teaching of the Dhamma, or for the classification of the four types of persons.

8. Regarding the sheep-slaughterers and others: "urabbhā" refers to rams (sheep); one who kills a ram (*urabbha*) is an *orabbhika* (sheep-slaughterer). This also applies to the pig-slaughterers and others.
The same method applies here. "Ludda" means cruel and harsh. "Macchaghātaka" refers to a fisherman or one who kills fish.
"Bandhanāgārika" refers to a jailer. "Kururakammantā" means cruel occupations. 9.
"Muddhāvasitta" means one who has been sprinkled on the head with the consecration of a Kṣatriya. "Puratthimena nagarassa" means from the eastern side of the city.
To the east of the city. "Assembly hall" means a sacrificial hall. "Having put on a rough antelope skin" means having put on an antelope hide complete with its hooves.
"With ghee and oil": indeed, setting aside ghee, any other kind of unctuous substance is called "oil.
"Scratching himself" refers to the time when he ought to scratch because his nails had been cut short.
"Scratching with that [horn]. "Not separated by an interval" means not covered by a rug or blanket.
"With a calf of similar appearance" means with a calf of like form. If the cow is white, the calf is also white;

if the cow is brindled or red, the calf is likewise—thus it is "with a calf of similar appearance. "He spoke thus" means the king spoke in this manner. "Calves" refers to the state of being young calves.
The powerful heifers have passed away. The same method applies to the heifers as well.

"For the sake of sacrificial grass" means both for the purpose of making the enclosure and for the purpose of spreading it upon the sacrificial ground. The rest is self-evident, as it has already been explained in detail in various places below.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Kandarakasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgarasutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Aṭṭhakanāgarasutta. Therein, "at Beluvagāmaka" means on the southern side of Vesālī.
"Not far away" means there is a village named Beluva; the sense is that he made that his alms-resort village. "The Tenth" (Dasama):

for he is counted in the tenth place both by way of birth and clan, and by way of the number of families that have attained prosperity; therefore, his name became "The Tenth. "A resident of Aṭṭhakanagara":
one who dwells in the city of Aṭṭhakanagara. "Kukkuṭa Monastery": a monastery established by the merchant Kukkuṭa.
18. Regarding the phrase "proclaimed by that Blessed One...": this is the summary of the meaning.
That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
by that Blessed One, who knows the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions of various beings as clearly as an amalaka fruit placed in the palm of his hand.
By seeing all knowable phenomena; furthermore, by knowing through the recollection of past lives and so forth, by seeing with the divine eye,
by knowing through the three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) or the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), by seeing with the unimpeded universal eye (*samantacakkhu*),
by knowing with the wisdom capable of knowing all phenomena, and [seeing] those things beyond the range of the eyes of all sentient beings.
To one who sees even forms situated beyond a wall or other obstructions with the extremely purified flesh-eye;

who knows through the wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*) which has concentration as its proximate cause for accomplishing one's own welfare; who sees through the wisdom of teaching (*desanā-paññā*) which has compassion as its proximate cause for accomplishing the welfare of others;
who is an *arahant* because of having slain the enemies and because of being worthy of requisites and so forth; and who [knows] correctly and personally—
"By the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), because of his awakening to the truths;
by the Worthy One (Arahat), because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements, knowing the obstructive states and seeing the states leading to liberation;

and by the Perfectly Enlightened One, because of his personal awakening to all phenomena"—thus praised for four reasons by way of the four grounds of self-confidence. "Is there indeed even a single state that has not been declared? [he asked.]
19. *Abhisaṅkhataṃ* means made or produced. *Abhisañcetayitaṃ* means intended or planned.
*So tattha ṭhito* means he is established in that—namely, in those states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
By the two phrases *dhammarāgena* and *dhammanandiyā*, desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) for serenity and insight are expressed; for [in these] serenity and insight, in every respect...
One who is able to eradicate desire and lust becomes an Arahant; one who is unable becomes a Non-returner (Anāgāmī).

Because desire and lust for serenity and insight have not been abandoned, he is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) through the volition of the fourth jhāna; this is the common consensus among the teachers.
However, the caviller says: "Because of the statement 'by that very passion for the Dhamma,' he is reborn in the Pure Abodes by means of an unwholesome state."
He should be told, "Bring a sutta. Certainly, seeing nothing else, he will bring this very one.
Then he should be asked, "But is this sutta of interpretable meaning (neyyattha) or of definitive meaning (nītattha)? Certainly, he will say it is of definitive meaning. Then he should be told:
"If that is so, then one who desires the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) would have to cultivate desire and lust for serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)."
“Once desire and lust have arisen, the fruit of non-returning will be penetrated; let not my discourse be lost!”—thus you should illuminate this or that point.
For when speaking on a question, it is proper to speak after having learned it in the presence of a teacher and having penetrated the flavor of its meaning;
for through unwholesomeness there is rebirth in hell, and through wholesomeness there is rebirth in heaven.
There is no such thing. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, it is not through action born of greed, action born of hatred, or action born of delusion that gods are known, nor are humans known, nor indeed any other happy destinies; rather, monks, it is through action born of greed..."
“Hell is made known by action born of hatred, by action born of delusion, and by action;
the animal realm is made known; the sphere of hungry ghosts is made known; or whatever other miserable destinies there may be.

Thus it should be explained. If he perceives [the truth], let him perceive it; if he does not perceive it, he should be dismissed with the words: “Go, enter the monastery early in the morning and drink some conjey.”

Just as in this sutta, so too in the Mahā-Māluṅkyaputta Sutta, the Mahā-Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, and the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are taught. Therein, in this sutta, whether one proceeds by way of serenity or by way of insight, the primary burden is that of serenity;
in the Mahā-Māluṅkyaputta Sutta, insight alone is the burden; and in the Mahā-Satipaṭṭhāna [Sutta], [both are the burden].
However, the *Kāyagatāsati-sutta* is called "insight-preeminent," while [the *Dhammadāyāda-sutta*] is "tranquility-preeminent.

Thus, householder... [as before] ... "this one dhamma has been declared"—because this was spoken by way of a question from one who asked about a single dhamma, these eleven dhammas came to be known as "one dhamma. For in the *Mahāsakuludāyi-sutta*:
The nineteen sections are called "single states" (*ekadhamma*) by way of their respective practices; here, however, they are presented as "single states" by way of the eleven questions.
Alternatively, it is appropriate to call them all "single states" in the sense that they lead to the attainment of the Deathless (*amatuppatti*).
21. "Seeking the entrance to a treasure" means searching for a treasure. "All at once" means by a single effort. But how?
"By a single stroke of fortune, there is the acquisition of eleven treasures.
Here, a certain person wanders about in the forest searching for treasure. A certain benefactor sees him and asks, "Sir, what are you doing?
He replies, "I am seeking a means of livelihood. The other says, "In that case, my friend, come; turn over this stone. He does so.
Having set it in motion, one might see eleven jars either placed one above another or standing touching each other belly-to-belly;
in this way, by a single effort, there is the acquisition of eleven treasures.
Regarding the phrase "they will seek the teacher’s fee": for those belonging to other sects, in whose presence they learn a craft, to him [they must pay].
They give wealth after bringing it out from their homes, either before learning a craft, after it, or at intervals during its practice.
Those who have nothing in their homes seek it from among their kinsmen; failing to find it there, they even go out for alms and still give it away.
It is with reference to this that it was said.
"How much more so, then, for me?"—this means that even outsiders seek wealth from one who merely imparts a craft in a teaching that does not lead to liberation;

how then shall I not offer worship to my teacher, who teaches this elevenfold path leading to the arising of the Deathless in such a liberating teaching? "I shall certainly do so," he said. He covered him with a pair of fine cloths.
The meaning is that he gave a pair of cloths to each individual bhikkhu. Here, however, the expression used is a formal term of address;
therefore, it is said "he clothed them. "A monastery worth five hundred" means he had a leaf-hut built at a cost of five hundred [kahāpaṇas].
The rest is entirely plain in every respect.
The commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 3.
Commentary on the Sekha Sutta.
22. *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* (Thus have I heard): this is the *Sekha-sutta*. Therein, "a new assembly hall" (*navaṃ saṇṭhāgāraṃ*) refers to an assembly hall recently constructed;
the meaning is that it was a large hall (*mahāsālā*). For on occasions such as the time of departure, kings would stand there [and give orders]:
"So many should go in front, so many behind, so many on both sides, so many should mount the elephants, so many the horses..."
"Let so many stay in the chariots"—thus they arrange themselves and establish a boundary;

therefore, that place is called a *santhāgāra*. Furthermore, it is a *santhāgāra* because those kings, having arrived from their departure points, remain there for two or three days while performing tasks such as plastering the floors with fresh cow dung in their dwellings. For them...

The assembly hall (*santhāgāra*) is so called because it is a hall where kings together provide instruction on matters of state; for they are republican (*gaṇa-rāja*) kings. Therefore, a matter that has arisen cannot be settled by one person alone;
it is necessary to obtain the consent of all. Consequently, everyone assembles there and provides instruction. Hence it is said:
"The assembly hall is so called because it is a hall where kings together provide instruction on matters of state. Furthermore, because these...
Having gathered there, they deliberate upon the duties of household life according to such methods as, "It is appropriate to plow at this time; it is appropriate to sow at this time.
Therefore, because they settle their household affairs there, even in every detail, it is called a *santhāgāra*.
It was newly built means it was well-furnished with woodwork, stonework, painting, and so forth.
It has now been completed like a celestial mansion (*devavimāna*). Regarding the phrase "by a recluse" (*samaṇena vā*):

since deities take possession of their own dwelling place at the very time the site for the house is acquired, it is therefore stated as "by a deity" (*devena vā*) instead of saying "by a recluse, a brahmin, or anyone who is human."
“They approached the Blessed One”: having heard that the assembly hall was finished, thinking, “Let us go;
we shall see it,” they went there. Having surveyed everything starting from the gateway, they said:
“By whom has this assembly hall—which resembles a celestial mansion, being exceedingly delightful and magnificent—been used first for our long-term welfare?”
Thinking, "May it be for their happiness," he considered: "Even if it were given first to our foremost kinsman, it would be more appropriate for the Teacher;

even if it were given on account of his being worthy of offerings, it would be more appropriate for the Teacher. Therefore, we shall first cause the Teacher to partake of it, and we shall summon the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus;
when the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus has arrived, [we shall offer] the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas."
"He will surely come; we shall cause the Teacher to discourse on the Dhamma to us throughout the three watches of the night.
Thus, we shall later enjoy what has been used by the Three Jewels, and this will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time.
Having thus resolved, they approached him.

"They approached the assembly hall" means that on that day, although the assembly hall was well-adorned and well-maintained like a celestial mansion for the purpose of receiving royal families, it had not been prepared or designated as a place worthy of a Buddha.
For Buddhas, by their very nature, have a disposition for the forest and delight in the forest; whether they dwell within a village or not, it is simply according to their inclination.
Thinking, "Therefore, we shall announce [the time] only after knowing the Blessed One’s intention," they approached the Blessed One.
But now, having obtained his permission and desiring to announce it, they went to the assembly hall.
"Having spread the entire assembly hall" means that they spread it in such a way that the whole of it was indeed covered.
Having had it spread out: first of all, thinking "cow dung is suitable for all auspicious occasions," one should have even ground already prepared with plaster smeared with fresh cow dung;

then, once it is known to be completely dry, having had it anointed with the four kinds of fragrant scents so that no footprint remains visible where one has stepped, and having spread various colored mats upon it.

Upon those, beginning with large back-covers and blankets, they had all the available space strewn with various colored rugs suitable for covering, such as elephant-hide rugs, horse-hide rugs, lion-hide rugs, tiger-hide rugs, moon-patterned rugs, sun-patterned rugs, and variegated rugs. Therefore it is said:
"having strewn the assembly hall with a complete carpeting."
"Having prepared the seats": first, having prepared a magnificent Buddha-seat near the auspicious pillar in the central area,

and having spread upon it whatever coverings were soft and beautiful, and having placed for the Blessed One a red, pleasing-looking pillow, he [spread] over it [a cloth] variegated with gold and silver stars.
Having erected a canopy and adorned it with coverings of fragrant garlands, flower garlands, leaf garlands, and so forth;

having created a lattice of flowers in an area twelve cubits on all sides; and having had the space measuring thirty cubits enclosed with a curtain, he arranged for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha seats with cross-frames, backrests, and headrests against the western wall.
Having prepared them and had them covered above with white rugs,
they arranged large back-rest cushions against each eastern wall and placed pillows filled with swan’s down and other materials,
thinking, "In this way, we shall listen to the Dhamma all night without fatigue. It is with reference to this that it is said, "having prepared seats."
"A water-jar" (*udakamaṇika*) refers to a large-mouthed water vessel. "Having set it out" means:

thinking, "In this way the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus will wash their hands or feet, or rinse their mouths as they please," he filled it in those various places with water the color of jewels and placed various flowers and scented powders for the purpose of perfuming it.
Having placed [the oil] inside and covered it with plantain leaves, they set it up. It is with reference to this that it is said, "having established.

"Having lit an oil lamp" means having kindled an oil lamp in lanterns made of silver, gold, and so forth, held in the hands of figures such as Yonakas, Kirātas, and others, or in small vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "They approached the Blessed One": here, those Śākya kings did not merely clean the assembly hall alone;

rather, they had the streets of the city of Kapilavatthu—which extended for a league—swept, banners raised, full water-jars and plantain trees placed at the doors of the houses, and the entire city strewn with garlands of lamps like scattered stars.
Having made such arrangements, they caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming: "Give milk to the infants who drink milk; feed the young children quickly and put them to sleep; do not make a loud noise.
Today the Teacher will dwell within the village for one night;
indeed, Buddhas are those who desire little noise. Then, taking torches in their hands, they approached the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached the new assembly hall together with the community of monks.
When it was announced that it was time, saying, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One may now do as he deems fit," the Blessed One [took] a red double-layered cloth,
the color of a *koviḷāra* flower soaked in lac juice, and a lotus made of scissors...
Having arranged his three-fold robe as if measuring it out and covering himself with the lower garment,
he fastened his waistband, which possessed the splendor of a flash of lightning, as if encircling a cluster of lotuses with a golden sash; then,

having wrapped his upper robe around him like crimson wool draped over the frontal globe of an elephant, he stood upon a golden shrine a hundred cubits high, appearing like one casting a net of coral over it.
As if putting on a cloak of red woolen cloth, as if veiling the full moon with a crimson-colored cloud,
as if sprinkling well-ripened lac juice upon the summit of the Golden Mountain,
and as if encircling the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa with streaks of lightning, [the thunderbolt] struck the entire world-system, including Sineru and Yugandhara.
Having caused the great earth to tremble, he donned the excellent, choice rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*)— which was the color of a *nigrodha* sprout—
and emerged from the door of the Perfumed Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*), like a lion from a golden cave or like the full moon from the peak of Mount Udaya.
Having emerged, he stood at the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber.

Then, from his body, rays of light issued forth like clusters of lightning from the mouths of clouds, and they made the trees of the grove appear as if their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were being drenched by streams of molten gold.
At that very moment, the great community of monks, each taking up his own bowl and robe, surrounded the Blessed One.
And those monks who stood surrounding him were such as these: they were of few desires.
They were contented, secluded, unassociated, energetic, eloquent, patient with speech, reprovers, censurers of evil,
endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by them,
the Blessed One was like a mass of gold encircled by red woolen cloth, or like one standing in the midst of a thicket of red lotuses.
The golden palace shone forth, as if surrounded by a coral railing; likewise,
the great elders such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, having donned that cloud-colored rag-robe, surrounded him like great elephants clad in jeweled armor—
those whose passions had been vomited out, whose defilements were shattered, whose matted locks were disentangled, whose bonds were severed, and who were unattached to family or faction.

Thus the Blessed One—himself free from passion, surrounded by those free from passion; free from hatred, surrounded by those free from hatred; free from delusion, surrounded by those free from delusion;
free from craving, surrounded by those free from craving; free from defilement, surrounded by those free from defilement;

himself a Buddha, surrounded by those who are learned and awakened—was like a filament surrounded by petals, like a pericarp surrounded by filaments, or like one surrounded by eight thousand elephants.
Like the elephant king Chaddanta; like Dhataraṭṭha, the king of swans, surrounded by ninety thousand swans;
like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) surrounded by his military divisions; like Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of devas;
like the Great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by a host of Brahmas; like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars—[he appeared] with the peerless appearance of a Buddha, immeasurable...
With the playful grace of a Buddha, he set out upon the road leading to Kapilavatthu.
Then, from his front body, a golden-hued ray of light arose and reached a distance of eighty cubits.
From his back, his right hand, and his left hand, golden-hued rays of light likewise arose and reached a distance of eighty cubits.
He grasped it. From the upper limit of his hair upwards, rays the color of a peacock’s neck rose from every pore of his hair and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky.
From the soles of his feet downwards, rays the color of coral rose and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth.
Thus, a space measuring eighty cubits all around was [illuminated].
The six-colored rays of the Buddha, shining and quivering, issued forth from golden-staffed torches and spread abroad like nets leaping into the sky,
like streaks of lightning emerging from a great cloud covering the four continents.
All the quarters of space were as if strewn with golden campaka flowers, by streams of liquid gold pouring from golden jars.
They scattered about like water being sprinkled, like a spread-out golden cloth, or like a cloud of *kiṃsuka* and *kaṇikāra* flower pollen stirred up by the *verambha* wind.
And the Blessed One’s body— resplendent with the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura, and the thirty-two excellent major marks—
was like the vault of heaven with its stars risen, like a bed of lotuses in full bloom, or like a *pāricchattaka* tree a hundred leagues high in its entirety covered with blossoms.
He shone as if surpassing the splendor of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two universal monarchs, thirty-two kings of the gods, and thirty-two great Brahmās arranged in succession,
because he had perfectly fulfilled the ten perfections, the ten intermediate perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections.

It was adorned with the thirty pāramīs. The merit consisting of the gifts given, the virtue guarded, and the wholesome deeds performed over four incalculable aeons plus a hundred thousand kappas, finding no place within a single individual existence (attabhāva) to yield its fruit, became as if crowded together.
It was like the time when the goods of a thousand ships must be loaded onto a single ship, or the goods of a thousand carts...
It was like the time when a single cart is loaded, and like the time when the floods of twenty-five rivers break through and form a single mass at the mouth of a river;
and before the Blessed One, who was radiating with this glory of a Buddha, there were many thousands of torches.
They scattered [flowers] behind him; likewise on his left side and right side.

Flowers such as jasmine, campaka, forest jasmine, white jasmine, red lotus, blue lotus, *makula*, and *sinduvāra*, as well as fragrant perfumed powders of blue, yellow, and other colors, were strewn about like showers of water released from clouds over the four continents.
And the sounds of fivefold musical instruments, associated with the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, [resounded].
And the sound of "Thuti" filled all directions. The eyes of gods, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and others felt as if they had obtained the drink of the Deathless (amata).
Now, it is fitting to speak in praise of his journey by means of a thousand verses while standing at this spot.
Herein, this is merely the beginning:
“Thus, endowed with all his limbs, shaking the earth while not harming living beings, the Guide of the World proceeds.
Raising his right foot first, the Bull among Men— ”
Walking, endowed with glory, the Supreme among Bipeds shines forth.
As the Best of Buddhas walks, the soles of his feet are soft;
they touch the ground evenly, and he is not defiled by dust.
When the Leader of the World approaches, the low-lying places rise up;
though the earth is insentient, that which was elevated becomes level.
Stones, pebbles, gravel, stumps, and thorns [disappear].
All paths avoid him as the Leader of the World proceeds.
He lifts [his foot] not too far and sets it down not too close;
he walks without clattering, with both knees and ankles aligned.
The sage of perfected conduct does not set out too quickly,
nor does he walk too slowly; moving with a concentrated mind,
he proceeds upward, downward, across, and likewise toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.
He does not walk looking about, but gazes only as far as a yoke’s length.
With the majestic stride of an elephant, the Conqueror shines in his gait;
the Foremost One in the world walks with grace, bringing joy to all, including the gods.
“Resplendent like the moon-king, like a lion walking with a graceful fourfold gait, gladdening many beings, he approached the excellent city.
This, it is said, is called the “time of praise”; at such times, [the Buddha] would speak in praise of the Buddha’s physical beauty or his qualities, or a preacher of the Dhamma would do so.
One's own capacity alone is the measure; whether in prose or in verse, one should say as much as one is able.
It should not be said that it is "ill-spoken. For the Buddhas possess immeasurable praise;
even the Buddhas themselves are unable to describe their virtues in their entirety, let alone other beings. By this splendor and majesty, the city of the Sakyans was adorned and prepared.
Having entered, the Blessed One, while being honored by the people with clear minds with perfumes, incense, scents, powders, and so forth, went into the assembly hall.
Therefore it was said: "Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, approached that very assembly hall together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"Placing the Blessed One at the very front" means having the Blessed One in front. Therein, the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the monks and laymen;

having bathed him with scented water, having removed the water with a *dukūla* cloth pillow, and having rubbed him with vermilion (*jātihiṅgulaka*), he was like a solid golden image placed upon a seat covered with red woolen cloth.
shone exceedingly. Herein, this is the manner of the ancient eulogies:
"Having gone to the circular pavilion, he whose gait was like that of an elephant sat upon the excellent seat, illuminating [the world], the foremost of the world."
Seated there, the charioteer who tames men,
the god beyond gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits,
shines forth as he occupies the Buddha’s throne.
Like a golden necklace upon a pale woolen cloth,
like a necklace of Jambu-river gold placed upon a pale woolen cloth,
it shines, free from stain, like the radiant Maṇi-ve-rocana gem.
Like a great sal tree in full bloom, adorned like the king of *neru* flowers;
resembling a golden sacrificial pillar, like a red lotus (*paduma*) or a *kokanada*.
Blazing like a lamp-tree, like a fire upon a mountain peak.
“Like the Pāricchattaka tree of the gods, you shine forth in full bloom.

Regarding the phrase “for most of the night with a discourse on the Dhamma” addressed to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu: here, the discourse on the Dhamma should be understood as an incidental talk connected with the expression of appreciation for the assembly hall.
For at that time, the Blessed One was like one pouring down the celestial Ganges, drawing up the very essence of the earth.

As if shaking a great rose-apple tree by its trunk, or as if pressing a jar of honey a league in size with a press-wheel and drinking the honey-liquor, he delivered a miscellaneous discourse bringing welfare and happiness to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu:
"Great King, this gift of a dwelling place is indeed a great thing; your dwelling has been enjoyed by me and by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"It has been enjoyed by me and by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; furthermore, it has indeed been enjoyed by the Jewel of the Dhamma.
Thus, it is said to have been enjoyed by the Three Jewels. For when a gift of a dwelling place is given, every kind of gift is effectively given.
Indeed, the merit of a ground-built leaf hut or even a pavilion of branches cannot be measured."
Having delivered a manifold and diverse discourse on the Dhamma, he said:
“It wards off cold and heat, as well as wild beasts;
And snakes, mosquitoes, the chill, and even the rains.”
Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, one encounters them;
[the gift of a monastery] is for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and for the purpose of meditating and practicing insight.
The gift of a dwelling to the Saṅgha has been praised as supreme by the Buddha.
Therefore, a wise person, clearly perceiving their own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those learned in the Dhamma to dwell there,
providing them with food, drink, clothing, and lodgings.
One should give with a serene mind to those who have become upright;
they will teach him the Dhamma that removes all suffering,
by knowing which Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
"In this way, this too is a benefit of the residence, this too is a benefit"—thus he spoke on the benefits of the residence for much of the night, for more than one and a half watches.

Among these, only these verses were included in the compilation; however, the miscellaneous discourses on the Dhamma were not included in the compilation. The meanings of "he pointed out," and so forth, have already been explained.
"He addressed the Venerable Ānanda" means that, desiring to have him deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, he made it known [to him].

Now, why did the Blessed One entrust this task to the Venerable Ānanda when the eighty great elders, such as Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and Mahākassapa, were present? It was because of the disposition of the assembly.
For the Venerable Ānanda was the foremost among those of great learning (*bahussuta*), and he was capable of delivering a sweet discourse on the Dhamma with perfectly rounded words and phrases.

"He is able to speak" means he is renowned and famous throughout the Śākya circle. Although those Śākya kings had previously heard Dhamma discourses from him after visiting his monastery, their female attendants were not permitted to go to the monastery as they pleased; therefore, it occurred to them:
"Oh, if only the Blessed One would deliver even a brief Dhamma discourse for our most excellent kinsman, Ānanda..."
“...should take up the burden. According to their inclinations, the Blessed One made that very [burden] his own.
“A trainee, one who has entered the path” means a practitioner who is a trainee-monk (*sekha-śramaṇa*).
“May he occur to you, may he appear to you”—this indicates that by specifying the person, one should teach the path for him. But why did the Blessed One [teach] this path?
Why did he restrict it? For many reasons. First, these Sakyans were seeking blessings and desiring prosperity in their auspicious hall;
furthermore, this "path of training" (*sekhapaṭipadā*) is a path of blessings and a path of growth within my teaching—thus he restricted it to this path.
And in that assembly, many who were still in training (*sekha*) were seated; they [were established] in the state they had themselves realized.

He established this method of practice thinking: "They will perceive it without becoming weary while it is being explained. Furthermore, he established this method of practice thinking: "The Venerable Ānanda has attained the analytical knowledges of one still in training;

thus, when speaking on a matter he has personally realized through direct experience, he will be able to make himself understood without weariness. And in the path of training, there are the three trainings.
When [the teaching] has been delivered there, by speaking of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the entire Vinaya Piṭaka has indeed been spoken;
by speaking of the training in higher consciousness (adhicitta-sikkhā), the entire Sutta Piṭaka has been spoken;
and by speaking of the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā), the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka has been spoken. Moreover, Ānanda is learned and a bearer of the Three Piṭakas.
He was thus able to explain the three trainings according to the Three Pitakas;
he established this method with the thought, "When this is explained, there will be only prosperity and growth for the Sakyans. [The Elder asked:
"My back aches—why does it ache? [The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Because the Blessed One exerted himself in striving for six years."
There was great physical suffering, and subsequently, in his old age, a back ailment arose in him.
Or rather, this is no reason [for his passing], for the Blessed One would have been able to suppress that arisen pain and remain seated cross-legged for even one or two weeks.
However, he desired to make use of the Santhāgāra hall through all four postures.
He went from the place for washing his feet as far as the Dhamma-seat; the walking was accomplished over that distance.
Having reached the Dhamma-seat, he stood for a short while and then sat down; that was the standing and sitting distance. He sat on the Dhamma-seat for one and a half watches;
the sitting was accomplished over that duration. Now, having lain down for a short while on his right side, the reclining will be accomplished.
Thus he desired to enjoy [the meal] through the four postures. Now, it cannot be said that "this acquired body does not become weary";
therefore, taking into account even the slight weariness produced by sitting for a long time, he spoke thus.
"Having spread out the outer robe" (saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvā): it is said that on one side of the assembly hall, those kings had a fine cloth screen (paṭṭasāṇi) erected.
Having prepared a lawful couch, spread it with a lawful coverlet, and hung above it a canopy adorned with golden stars, perfumes, garlands, and wreaths, they lit lamps of scented oil, thinking:
"Perhaps the Teacher, rising from his Dhamma seat, might lie down here for a short while to rest; thus this assembly hall will be used by the Blessed One. For four...
“Used in these postures, it will lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time.
The Teacher, intending that very thing, spread out his outer robe there and lay down.
“Having fixed his mind on the perception of rising” means having established in his mind the perception of rising, thinking, “After this much time has passed, I shall get up.”
23. "He addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan": it is said that at that time he was the eldest and the leader in that assembly;
since when he is won over, the rest of the assembly is likewise won over, the Elder addressed him alone.

"Endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanna*) means endowed with virtue; the meaning is one whose virtue is accomplished, whose virtue is fulfilled. "By the true Dhammas" (*saddhammehi*) means by the beautiful Dhammas.
"Or by means of the qualities of the virtuous and true persons.

(24) And as for the words "How, Mahānāma," with this much he has established the outline of the training-path for those in training (*sekha-paṭipadā*) and, wishing to elaborate it in sequence, spoke thus.
Therein, the phrases beginning with "endowed with virtue" (*sīla-sampanno*) refer to [the passage]: "Monks, dwell endowed with virtue."
These should be understood according to the method explained in the *Ākaṅkheyya-sutta* and other such texts.
In the passage beginning with "by bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccaritena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative;

the meaning is that one feels shame and loathing for those things which ought to be shunned, namely, bodily misconduct and so forth. In the description of moral dread (*ottappa*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the causal; [it means] by means of bodily misconduct and so forth.
The meaning is that one feels shame and fear because of the causes of moral dread (*ottappa*). "One who has aroused energy" means one whose energy is exerted and whose mind is free from despondency.
"For the sake of abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing. "For the sake of attainment" means for the purpose of acquisition.

"Possessing strength" means endowed with the strength of energy. "Firm in effort" means having steadfast perseverance. "One who does not cast off the burden" refers to those things that are wholesome (*kusala*).
"Regarding phenomena" means regarding wholesome phenomena; one who has not laid down the yoke and whose energy is not slackened. "By the supreme" means by the highest.
"By mindfulness and circumspection" means by means of mindfulness and by means of the state of being prudent. But why is wisdom included in the section on mindfulness?
It is for the purpose of illustrating the strength of mindfulness. For mindfulness dissociated from wisdom is weak, whereas when associated with it, it is powerful.

"Long performed" means that either by oneself or by another, through the body, one has long performed such acts as the duties of the shrine courtyard (*cetiyangaṇa-vatta*) and so forth, fulfilling the eighty great observances (*mahāvatta*).

"Long spoken" means that either by oneself or by another, through speech, one has long spoken—verbal action (*vacīkamma*) set in motion by way of careful recitation, causing others to recite, exhorting to the Dhamma, teaching the Dhamma, informal discourses, expressions of gratitude, and so forth.
"Recalled" means remembered; regarding that long-performed act by body, [one reflects]: "Body is indeed bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*)."
Speech uttered long ago is called vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). Both of these are material form (*rūpa*);
the mind and mental factors that originate them are immaterial (*arūpa*). Thus, he both remembers and recollects:

"These material and immaterial phenomena have arisen and ceased in this way"—this is the meaning of "he arouses the mindfulness enlightenment factor" (*satisambojjhaṅga*). For it is mindfulness that arouses the enlightenment factors which is intended here.
By that mindfulness, it should be understood that this [mind] was remembered once by way of recollection (*saraṇa*), and repeatedly remembered by way of constant recollection (*anussaraṇa*).
"Leading to arising and passing away" means leading to the rise and fall of the five aggregates, and being capable of penetrating both their arising and their passing away.
"Noble" (*ariyā*) means standing far removed from the defilements (*kilesa*) by way of suppression and by way of eradication.
"By means of purified wisdom": he is one who possesses both insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) and path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*).
"Penetrating": that very [wisdom] is called "penetrating" because it penetrates; the meaning is that he is endowed with it.
Therein, by way of complete eradication, the mass of greed—which had never before been pierced or shattered—[is destroyed] by means of path-wisdom.
It is called "penetrative" (nibbedhikā) because it pierces and shatters the mass of hatred and the mass of delusion;

and because, by way of its factor of "factor-of-the-same-order" (tadaṅga), it leads to the acquisition of path-wisdom which is penetrative through insight-wisdom. Thus, it is appropriate to say that insight is "penetrative.

Regarding the phrase "rightly leading to the destruction of suffering," here too, path-wisdom [is meant], for by means of the right cause and method, it [leads to] the suffering of the round of existence...

It is called "leading rightly to the destruction of suffering" because it proceeds by exhausting [suffering]. Insight (vipassanā) is "leading to the destruction of suffering" because it proceeds by exhausting both the suffering of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭadukkha) and the suffering of the defilements (kilesadukkha) through its function of "overcoming by means of that factor" (tadaṅgavasena).
Alternatively, it should be understood as "leading to the destruction of suffering" because it conduces to the acquisition of the path-wisdom (maggapaññā) which leads to the destruction of suffering.
"Of those based on the higher consciousness" means of those based on, dependent upon, the higher consciousness, which is the supreme consciousness.
"Of the dwellings in happiness in this very life" means of the causes for obtaining happiness at every moment of absorption.

"One who obtains at will" means one who enters [attainment] at whatever moment he desires. "One who obtains without difficulty" means one who obtains it without hardship. "One who obtains without trouble" means one who obtains it in abundance. By virtue of its proficiency, [he can enter] alone at whatever moment he desires.
He is able to attain [jhāna], yet he is unable to suppress the factors that obstruct concentration without becoming weary;

he emerges very quickly even against his own will and is unable to maintain the attainment for the duration of the time-limit he has set—this is called one who gains with difficulty and gains with ease. Another, at whatever moment he desires, and...

He is able to attain [the jhāna], and without wearying himself, he suppresses those states that are obstacles to concentration; he is able to emerge from it exactly according to his predetermined limit.
This one is called "one who attains without difficulty, one who attains without trouble.
27. "Mahānāma, this noble disciple is called a trainee (sekha) practicing the way. Thus, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is a trainee.
This shows that he is said to be "endowed with the practice of progressive growth for the womb of insight" on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*).

"Freedom from rottenness" (*apuccaṇḍatā*) means freedom from putridity. "Capable of breaking out" (*abhinibbidāya*) means capable of the various types of knowledge beginning with insight (*vipassanā*).
"For supreme enlightenment" (*sambodhāya*) means for the Noble Path. "For the unsurpassed security from bondage" (*anuttarassa yogakkhemassa*) refers to Arahantship as the unsurpassed.
This shows that he is capable of attaining what is called "the security from bondage" (*yogakkhema*).
As for the simile brought forward here to illustrate the meaning, it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Cetokhila Sutta*. For in that [sutta], it is stated:
"Just as that hen performs the threefold act upon her eggs, so too does this bhikkhu possess the state of being endowed with the fifteen factors of exertion."
That which has thus come down as a correlation of similes should be understood here by connecting it in this way:
"Just as that hen performed the threefold action upon her eggs, so too does this bhikkhu possess the fifteen qualities beginning with the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampanna*).
Having made this application, it should be known; the rest is exactly as stated everywhere else.

28. "This very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" refers to this supreme purity of mindfulness due to equanimity belonging to the fourth jhāna, which is unlike the first jhānas and so forth. "The first breakthrough" means the first breaking through by means of knowledge;
the same method applies to the second and subsequent ones. As for a chicken chick, however, it emerges once from the mother's womb and once from the shell of the egg.
One is born twice. A noble disciple is born thrice by means of the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*).
Having dispelled the darkness that obscures past lives, he is first born through the knowledge of past abodes;

having dispelled the darkness that obscures the passing away and rebirth of beings, he is secondly born through the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*); and having dispelled the darkness that obscures the Four Noble Truths...
Through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, the third [type of conduct] arises.
"This too is his conduct" means that this virtue (sīla) is called the conduct (caraṇa) of that bhikkhu.
Conduct is manifold and of many kinds; there are fifteen factors beginning with virtue. Among these, this too is one kind of conduct.
This is the meaning. As for the word-meaning (*padattha*): one goes by means of it to a direction not previously traveled; thus it is "going" (*caraṇa*). This method applies everywhere.
"And this is his science (*vijjā*)" means that this knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) is called his science.
Science is indeed manifold and of many kinds—the eight knowledges beginning with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*); among these, this knowledge is also one science.
This is the meaning. As for the word-meaning: one knows by piercing through [ignorance] with this, thus it is "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*). This method applies everywhere.

"Possessed of clear knowledge" (*vijjāsampanno*) means possessed of clear knowledge by means of the three kinds of clear knowledge. "Possessed of conduct" (*caraṇasampanno*) means possessed of conduct by means of fifteen factors.
And "possessed of both clear knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*) means possessed of both of those together.
30. "By Sanaṅkumāra" means by the ancient youth, who has been known as a youth from long ago.

It is said that while still a young boy with five tufts of hair on his head, he attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*) in the human realm; having not fallen away from that absorption, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
That physical form of his was dear and pleasing to him, and therefore he moved about in exactly such a form.
Therefore, they recognize him as Sanaṅkumāra. "Janetasmin" means "among people"; the sense is "in the world.
"Those who follow after clan" refers to those among people who refer to their clan, saying, "I am a Gotama," "I am a Kassapa. Among those in the world who follow after clan, the Khattiya is the best.
"Approved by the Blessed One" means it was taught in accordance with my own explanation of the questions.
In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the Buddha, the Blessed One, said: “I too, Ambaṭṭha, say this:
‘Among those who rely on lineage, the kshatriya is the best in this world;
but one endowed with true knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.’”

By speaking thus, [Ānanda] was authorized and his words were approved. "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!"—it is said that the Blessed One, having heard this sutta from beginning to end without even descending from his sleep, realized that Ānanda had grasped the core of the path of training (*śaikṣa-pratipad*).
Rising up, he sat cross-legged and gave his approval. And at this point, this sutta...
Thus it became known as "Spoken by the Victor" (*jinabhāsita*). The remainder is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Sekha-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is hereby concluded.
4. Commentary on the Potaliya Sutta. 31.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Potaliya Sutta. Therein, “among the Aṅguttarāpas”: that very country is Aṅga;
however, because it is not far from the waters (āpo) to the north of Mahi, it is also called Uttarāpa. Of which Mahi?
"Northward lies the water," [referring to] the great ocean. Herein is the explanation for its manifestation: it is said that this Jambudīpa is ten thousand *yojanas* in extent.
Of that, a region measuring four thousand *yojanas* is submerged by water and is known as the ocean.
Three thousand *yojanas* are inhabited by humans. Three thousand *yojanas* are occupied by the Himavat mountain range.
Five hundred yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and variegated by five hundred rivers flowing from all sides—
therein lies Lake Anotatta, fifty-five yojanas in length and breadth and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference,
as well as Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Chaddanta, Lake Kuṇāla, and Lake Mandākinī.
There are seven great lakes situated there, including the Sīhapapāta lake.
Among them, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountains: Sudassana Peak, Citrakūṭa, Kāḷakūṭa, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak.
Therein, Sudassana Peak is made of gold, two hundred yojanas in height, inwardly curved, and shaped like a crow’s beak.
It stood concealing that very lake. Citrakūṭa was composed entirely of all kinds of jewels; Kāḷakūṭa was composed of collyrium;
and the peak of Gandhamādana was composed of sandalwood, being green like a mung bean within.

It possessed the fragrance of the root, the fragrance of the heartwood, the fragrance of the sapwood, the fragrance of the bark, the fragrance of the inner bark, the fragrance of the pith, the fragrance of the juice, the fragrance of the leaf, the fragrance of the flower, the fragrance of the fruit, and the fragrance of the scent itself.
Abounding with these ten fragrances and covered with various kinds of medicinal herbs, it stands burning like a glowing ember on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight. Kelāsakūṭa is made of silver.
All of them are equal to Sudassana in height and shape, standing so as to cover that very lake. All of them [stand] by the power of the devas.
By the power of the Nāgas, rain falls and rivers flow into them; all that water enters only the Anotatta.

When the moon and sun travel south or north, they cast their radiance upon it through the mountain range, but when traveling directly overhead, they do not; for this very reason, the designation "Anotatta" (Unheated) arose for it.
There, bathing pools were well-prepared with enchanting stone slabs, free of fish and turtles, and filled with water as pure as crystal;
in these, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants whose taints were exhausted, as well as sages possessed of psychic power,
would bathe, while devas, yakkhas, and others would sport in garden games.
On its four sides there are four mouths—a lion’s mouth, an elephant’s mouth, a horse’s mouth, and a bull’s mouth—from which four rivers flow.
On the bank of the river issuing from the lion’s mouth, lions are more numerous;
from the elephant’s mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls [respectively]. The river issuing from the eastern direction is the Anotatta.
Having circumambulated [Mount Sineru] three times from left to right and without approaching the other three rivers,
it enters the great ocean by way of the eastern Himalayas, traveling through a path frequented by non-humans.

Likewise, the rivers issuing from the western and northern directions also circumambulate [the mountain] three times from left to right and enter the great ocean by way of the western Himalayas and the northern Himalayas respectively, traveling through paths frequented by non-humans.

Having gone, they enter the great ocean. But the river that issues from the southern direction, having circumambulated it three times clockwise, proceeds sixty yojanas straight to the south along the rocky surface;
then, striking a mountain, it rises up and becomes a stream of water sixty yojanas wide in its circumference, flowing through the sky.
Having gone forth, it fell upon a rock named Tiyaṅgaḷa; the rock was split by the force of the stream of water.
There, a lotus pond named Tiyaṅgaḷā, measuring fifty yojanas in extent, was formed. Breaking through the bank of the pond and entering the rock, it traveled sixty yojanas.
Then, breaking through the solid earth and traveling sixty yojanas through a subterranean passage, it reached the mountain of the animals named Viñjhu.
Having struck [the rock], it flows forth as five streams resembling the five fingers on the palm of a hand.
Having circled Anotatta three times clockwise, at the place where it has gone, it is called the Āvaṭṭagaṅgā.

At the place where it has gone straight along the surface of the rocks for sixty yojanas, it is called the Kaṇhagaṅgā; at the place where it has gone through the air for sixty yojanas, it is called the Ākāsagaṅgā.
In the region of fifty yojanas at Tiyaggaḷa Rock, it is called the Tiyaggaḷa Lotus Pond;
where, having broken through the bank and entered the rock, it has traveled sixty yojanas, it is called the Thick Gaṅgā;
where it has traveled sixty yojanas by way of a subterranean passage (umaṅga), it is called the Umaṅga Gaṅgā. Having struck the mountain named Viñjhu, it becomes five streams.
In its course, however, it comes to be known by five names: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī.
Thus these five great rivers originate from the Himālaya. Among them, this fifth one called the Mahī is intended here as the "Great Mahī" (Mahāmahī).
Because that region is not far from the waters to the north of it, that country is called Aṅguttarāpa.
It should be understood. In that district of Aṅguttarāpa, there was a place called Āpaṇa;
it is said that in that market town there were twenty thousand distinct shop-fronts.
Thus, because of the abundance of shops, it came to be known simply as Āpaṇa. And not far from that market town, on the bank of a river—
There was a delightful area of ground with dense shade, a great forest grove, where the Blessed One was staying.

From this it should be understood that the specific dwelling place was not fixed. "He approached a certain forest grove" means that having sent the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to the dwelling place, he approached alone with reference to the householder Potaliya. And Potaliya...
"The householder named Potaliya" refers to a householder with that name. "Well-provided with lower and upper garments" means possessing complete lower and upper garments;
the meaning is that he was wearing one long-fringed robe as a lower garment (*nivāsana*) and another as an upper garment (*pāvuraṇa*).
"With sunshade and sandals" means having taken a sunshade and having put on sandals. "Seats" refers to couches, stools, straw mats, and so forth, down to even a broken-off branch.
For it is said that one is called [a householder] only insofar as one is seated [in that state]. "By the address 'householder'" means by this word "householder. "He addressed" means he spoke.
"He said this to the Blessed One" means that, being unable to endure the third address of "householder," he said this to the Blessed One:
"This, Master Gotama... and so forth. In that context, "not covered" (*nacchanna*) means not appropriate (*na anucchavika*). "Not fitting" (*nappatirūpa*)...
It is not appropriate. "Characteristics" (*ākāra*) and so forth are all synonyms for causes.

Indeed, all the marks of a householder—such as wearing long garments and cloths, and having hair, beard, and nails trimmed—are called "characteristics" (*ākāra*) because they make his state of being a householder manifest;

they are called "signs" (*liṅga*) because they exist in the form of a householder's appearance; and they are called "indicators" (*nimitta*) because they serve as the basis for recognizing his state of being a householder. "Just as that of a householder" means:
"Just as there might be the forms, signs, and marks of a householder, so it is with you. Therefore, I address you in this way"—thus he shows.
Then, explaining the reason why he does not accept the designation "householder," he said, "For thus indeed to me...
and so forth. "Niyyātanti" means "bestowed. "Anovādī anupavādī" refers to [not saying] such things as, "Dear ones, plow! Sow! Engage in trade! and so on.
One who advises by way of such a method is called an "advisor" (*ovādī*).
However, one who reviles by way of such a method as, "You do not plow, you do not sow, you do not engage in trade; how will you live? How will you support your wife and children?
is called a "reviler" (*upavādī*). But I do neither of these two things. Therefore, I am there "neither an advisor nor a reviler."
He shows this. "I dwell making food and clothing my highest aim" means: he illuminates that he dwells having made merely food and merely clothing his highest aim;
there is nothing beyond that, nor does he aspire for it.
"Greed and covetousness must be abandoned" means: greed in the form of grasping must be abandoned. "Free from blame and anger" means: free from the state of being blamed.
Non-striking. "Censure and reproach" means the striking of censure. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of cutting off worldly discourse":
here, "discourse" (*vohāra*) refers to conventional usage, designation, speech, and volition. In this regard:
"Whoever among men lives by means of discourse..."
“Know this, Vāseṭṭha: he is a merchant, not a brahmin.
This is what is called conventional usage (*vyavahāra-vohāra*). “Number, designation, description, and usage”—this is what is called descriptive usage (*paññatti-vohāra*).
“He speaks in such and such a way without grasping [at them]”—this is what is called verbal usage (*vacana-vohāra*). “The eight noble usages (*ariya-vohārā*)...”
