The eight ignoble modes of speech—this is what is called the “mode of speech as volition,” and it is this that is intended here.
Or rather, because from the time one goes forth, the volition of being a “householder” no longer exists, while the volition of being a “recluse” arises;
the designation of being a “householder” no longer exists, while the designation of being a “recluse” arises; the conventional usage of being a “householder” no longer exists... [and so on].
The conventional designations "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) or "one who has gone forth" (*pabbajita*) exist; therefore, all these [terms] are applicable here.
Regarding the statement, "On account of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) one is a 'taker of life' (*pāṇātipātī*)," in this context, the taking of life itself is the fetter.
Indeed, it is on account of the taking of life—by reason of the taking of life—that one is called a "taker of life. However, as for the takings of life...
For the sake of the majority, it is said: “Of those indeed for whom I... This means: “Of those fetters,” that is, of those bonds consisting of the taking of life.

“I am practicing for their abandoning and eradication” means that by means of this bodily restraint of virtue known as non-killing, I am practicing for the purpose of abandoning and for the purpose of eradicating them.
“Even myself might censure me” refers to even an ant or a termite.
"Having gone forth in a teaching where one must not take life, I am unable to refrain even from the mere taking of life;
what is the use of my going forth?"—in this way, even I myself would reproach him. Furthermore, wise people, having investigated, would censure me, saying:
"Having gone forth in such a teaching as this, he is unable to refrain even from the mere taking of life; what is there in him?"
Regarding "going forth": having thus investigated, weighed, and scrutinized [this matter], other wise and learned people would also censure it.

Furthermore, although this fetter and this hindrance are not actually included among the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), they are spoken of here as "the eight hindrances" by way of the teaching.
For, in the sense of being a bond for the round of existence (*vaṭṭabandhana*),...
In the sense of concealing what is beneficial, they are called both "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) and "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Taints" (*āsava*) means that, due to the commission of killing living beings, one taint arises, which is ignorance (*avijjāsava*). "Afflictions and fevers" (*vighāta-pariḷāha*) means both afflictions and fevers.

Therein, by the mention of "affliction," both the suffering of defilement (*kilesadukkha*) and the suffering of karmic result (*vipākadukkha*) are included; and by the mention of "fever," both the fever of defilement (*kilesapariḷāha*) and the fever of karmic result (*vipākapariḷāha*) are included.
And it is included. By this method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.

34–40. However, this is the distinction: in the phrase "for the abandoning of those fetters," by means of this bodily restraint of virtue known as refraining from taking what is not given, the verbal restraint of virtue known as truthful speech, and the verbal restraint of virtue known as abstaining from malicious speech...
"He has entered upon the practice for the sake of abandoning and for the sake of uprooting by means of restraint of verbal virtue;

by means of restraint of mental virtue consisting of non-greed and non-lobha; by means of restraint of bodily and verbal virtue consisting of non-censure and non-reproach; by means of restraint of mental virtue consisting of non-anger and non-despair;
and by means of restraint of mental virtue consisting of non-conceit"—in this way, the application should be made in all instances.

"Even I myself would reproach me, and the wise, having investigated, would censure me"—regarding these points, even though I have gone forth under the teaching that forbids taking what is not given even as much as a blade of grass, I am unable to refrain from even the slightest act of taking what is not given;
thus, "What is the use of my going forth?"—in this way, even I myself would reproach me. Having gone forth under such a teaching as this...
If one cannot even refrain from taking what is not given, what is the use of his going forth? Even after such investigation, the wise would reproach me.
Having gone forth in a teaching that prohibits lying, would one speak falsehood even out of a desire for laughter or for the sake of sport?
Having gone forth in a teaching that prohibits malicious speech in every respect, would one harbor even the slightest greed or covetousness?

Even though one has gone forth in the teaching of non-doing; even when one’s limbs are being cut with a saw, having gone forth in the teaching of non-doing, one does not harbor blame or resentment toward others;
even when encountering stumps, thorns, and the like, having gone forth in the teaching of non-doing, one does not harbor anger or distress;
and even the slightest conceit—having gone forth in the teaching of non-doing—one does not harbor even the slightest arrogance.
"My self would also reproach me, saying: 'I am unable to abandon [this], so what is the use of my renunciation?
Or, having renounced in such a teaching as this, he is not even able to abandon excessive pride;
'What is the use of his renunciation?'—thus the wise would also censure me after due reflection. In this manner, the application should be made for all instances.

Regarding the term "taints" (*āsava*): in this context, three taints arise by way of taking what is not given—namely, the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
Likewise, they arise by way of false speech and malicious speech; by way of greed and covetousness, the taint of views and the taint of ignorance arise;
by way of disparagement and resentment, only the taint of ignorance arises; and likewise by way of anger and vexation, and by way of excessive conceit.
The arising of the taints (āsava) should be understood thus: only two taints arise, namely the taint of existence (bhavāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava).
Furthermore, for the sake of non-confusion regarding these eight sections, this summary analysis is given again:
regarding the first four, one should say, "I am unable to abstain"; regarding the latter four, one should say, "I am unable to abandon."
Among the censuring of taking life, reviling, anger, and resentment, there is only the single outflow of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).

In the case of taking what is not given, false speech, and malicious speech, there are the outflows of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), views (*diṭṭhāsava*), and ignorance (*avijjāsava*). In greed and avarice, there are the outflows of views and ignorance. In overweening pride, there are the outflows of existence (*bhavāsava*) and ignorance.
Abstaining from taking life and abstaining from taking what is not given constitute bodily virtue (*sīla*); abstaining from false and malicious speech constitutes verbal virtue.
Excluding non-reproachful ill-will (*anindārosa*), the remaining three are mental virtues (*mānasika-sīla*).

However, because one both strikes with the body and provokes anger with speech, non-reproachful ill-will pertains to two bases; it is both bodily virtue (*kāyika-sīla*) and verbal virtue (*vācasika-sīla*).
What has been stated up to this point? It is the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla*). And for one established in the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha...
It should be understood that the cutting off of worldly conventions for a bhikkhu is spoken of by way of abandoning through reflection.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse on the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmādīnava):
in this detailed teaching, the phrase "one will see him" (*tamenaṃ dakkho*) is to be connected with the word "he would press down" (*upasumbheyya*).
This is what is meant: one should throw that dog near it; the meaning is that one should cast it into its vicinity.
"A skeleton" (*aṭṭhikaṅkala*) refers to the breast bone, the backbone, or the skull. For because it is devoid of flesh, it is called a skeleton.
"Well-pierced, pierced" means pierced in such a way that it is well-pierced.
“Scraped away”: the meaning is that whatever flesh remains adhering there has been scraped off entirely until only the bone is left.
For this reason it is said, “fleshless. However, blood remains smeared over it; therefore it is said, “smeared with blood. “Full of suffering, full of despair”:
they are full of suffering through the sufferings pertaining to the present life and the future life; they are full of despair through the corruptions of mental anguish.
There are many ways [of practicing equanimity]. That equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity refers to the equanimity toward the five strands of sensual pleasure;
because it has various natures by way of having the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object, and because it relies upon those very objects, it is called "diversified" and "based on diversity.
Having avoided that, there is the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, which is unified and based on unity; for that remains fixed on a single object even throughout the day.
They are of a single nature because they arise with respect to the same object; they are called "resting on unity" because they depend upon that very same single object.
"Wherein the grasping for worldly material things ceases entirely without remainder" means:

wherein, by relying upon and depending on the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, all material things consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure—which are reckoned as worldly material things—cease entirely and without remainder.
They cease. "The bait of the five strands of sensual pleasure" refers to the desire and lust directed toward the objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure;

in the sense of grasping, these very things are also called "clinging. "He develops that same equanimity" means he increases that very equanimity of the fourth jhāna, which serves as the antidote to the bait of worldly pleasures and to clinging.

43. *Uḍḍīyeyya* means that it would fly up and go away. *Anupatitvā* means having pursued. *Vitaccheyyuṃ* means that, biting with their beaks, they would tear [the flesh]. *Vissajjeyyuṃ* means that, having dragged the piece of flesh with their claws, they would drop it.
47. *Yānaṃ vā poriseyyaṃ* means a vehicle suitable for men. *Pavaramaṇikuṇḍalaṃ* means various kinds of excellent jewels and earrings.
*Sāni haranti* means they take their own belongings. 48. *Sampannaphalaṃ* means having sweet fruit. *Upapannaphalaṃ* means endowed with fruit, having abundant fruit.
49. “Unsurpassed” means supreme, luminous, and free from defilement. 50.
“I am far away, venerable sir,” means that I am very, very far away, like the sky from the earth, or like the further shore of the ocean from this side.
“Not a thoroughbred” means one who does not know the cause for cutting off the worldly conventions of a householder.
"Food for a thoroughbred" (*ājānīyabhojana*) is food that should be eaten by those who understand the reason [for its excellence].
"Food for one who is not a thoroughbred" (*anājānīyabhojana*) is food that should be eaten by those who do not understand the reason. The rest is entirely clear in every respect.
[Thus ends the section] from the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Potaliya Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Jīvaka Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Jīvaka Sutta. Regarding the phrase "in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove," here:

He is called Jīvaka because he lives (*jīvati*). He is called Komārabhacca because he was supported by the prince (*kumāreṇa bhato*). As it is said: "Tell me, what is this that is surrounded by crows?
"It is a child, Your Majesty. "Does it live? "It lives, Your Majesty. "In that case, tell me, take that child to our inner apartments and give him to the nurses to be raised.
They gave him the name Jīvaka because he lives (*jīvati*), and he was called Komārabhacca because he was raised by the prince (*kumāreṇa posāpito*).
They gave him the name “Komārabhacca. This is the summary here; however, the story of Jīvaka is recorded in detail in the Khandhaka.
His legal analysis (*vinicchayakathā*) is also stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
Now, on one occasion, Jīvaka, having purged the Blessed One’s body which was saturated with bile, [gave him] Sīveyyaka...
Having given a pair of garments, at the conclusion of the recitation of the merit of the cloth, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry and thought:
"I should go to attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day; however, this Veḷuvana is too far away.
My own mango grove is closer; what if I were to have a monastery built for the Blessed One there? He...

Having prepared night-stations, day-stations, caves, huts, pavilions, and so forth in that mango grove, and having had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) built for the Blessed One that was worthy of him,
he had the mango grove surrounded by a rampart eighteen cubits high, the color of copper-plate; then,
having satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with robes and alms-food, he offered the water of donation.
Having caused it to be demolished, he had it conveyed to the monastery. It was with reference to this that it was said: "in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove. "They begin" means they kill.
"Dedicated to someone" means prepared specifically for that person. "A deed done on account of oneself" means a deed performed for one's own sake.
Alternatively, "a deed done on account of oneself" is a designation for a causal deed (*nimittakamma*); herein, the deed is performed on account of that [cause].
"It exists" means that "it is dependent on meat" is what is being said;
they hold the view that whoever consumes such meat becomes an heir to that kamma as well, for the act of killing belongs to him just as it does to the killer.
And when they explain "in accordance with the Dhamma," they speak of a reason that conforms to the reason stated by the Blessed One.
And herein, "the reason" refers to the consumption of fish and meat that is pure in three respects; "the secondary reason" refers to the declarations made by the great multitude.

However, because the Blessed One does not consume what is prepared specifically for him, that is not the reason, nor are the declarations of the heretics the secondary reason. This is a legitimate discussion and counter-discussion.

Being thus provided with reasons by the arguments stated by others, does not even the slightest reason for your doctrine—whether it be your own position or a counter-argument—to come under the censure of the wise? This is what is meant:
"Is there not, in every respect, a censurable reason within your doctrine? *Abbhācikkhantī* means they declare [the fault] after having overcome [the opponent].
52. "By grounds" means by reasons. Regarding the seen and so forth: "seen" refers to seeing deer or fish being killed for the sake of monks.
"Heard" refers to hearing that deer or fish were killed for the sake of monks.
"Suspected" is threefold: suspected on account of what was seen, suspected on account of what was heard, and suspected independently of both.
In this regard, the comprehensive analysis is as follows: Here, monks see people with nets, snares, and so forth in their hands, either leaving a village or wandering in the forest.
On the following day, when those monks have entered that village for alms, people bring them alms-food containing fish and meat. Because of what they have seen, the monks become suspicious.
“Was this made for the benefit of the monks?”—this is called "suspected by sight," and it is not permitted to accept it.
That which is not suspected in this way is permitted. But if those people ask, “Why, venerable sir, do you not take it?
and having heard the reason, say, “Venerable sir, this was not made for the benefit of the monks,” [then it is permitted].
If they say, "This was made by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and the like," it is allowable.
Furthermore, even if the monks do not see [the hunters], but hear that "people, it seems,
are leaving the village or wandering in the forest with nets, snares, and so forth in their hands," and on the following day, when they have entered that village for alms—
They bring almsfood with meat cut into even pieces. Because of that meat, they become suspicious, thinking, "Has this been prepared for the sake of the monks?
This is called "suspicion regarding the meat," and it is not permissible to accept it.
However, that which is not suspected in this way is permissible. But if those people ask, "Venerable sir, why do you not take it? and [the monk] says:
Having heard that matter, if they say, "Venerable sir, this was not done for the sake of the bhikkhus;
it was done by us for our own sake or for the sake of the king’s officials and others," it is allowable.
However, if they neither see nor hear [the work being done], but rather [they receive] the bowl of those who have entered their village for alms—
Having taken it, they prepare a bowl of alms-food containing meat of equal portions and offer it. They suspect, "Was this prepared for the sake of the monks?
This is called "suspected by both [the donor and the recipient]"; it is not permitted to accept even this.
That which is not suspected in this way is permitted. But if those people say, "Venerable sir, why..."
Having asked, "Do you not take it? and having heard that matter, if they say, "Venerable sir, this was not made for the sake of the monks;
it was made by us for our own sake or for the sake of those connected to the king and so forth, or it was meat already available;
we have prepared it for the sake of the monks only after obtaining what is allowable (kappiya)," then it is permissible.
The same principle applies even when [food] is prepared for the sake of performing funeral rites for the deceased or for the sake of auspicious ceremonies and the like.
Indeed, whatever has not been prepared specifically for the monks themselves, and regarding which they have no doubt, all that is permissible.
However, if food has been prepared in a certain monastery for the sake of the monks there, and those monks do not know that it was prepared for their own sake, while others...
They know. For those who know, it is not permitted; for others, it is permitted. Others do not know, while they alone know;

for them alone it is not permitted, but for others it is permitted. They also know, "It was made for our sake," and others also know, "It was made for their sake"; for all of them, it is not permitted. None of them know.
It is permissible for all. For among the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika), that which is prepared specifically for the sake of any one of them is not allowable for all.
However, if someone kills an animal for the sake of a single bhikkhu and gives it to him after filling his bowl, he—
If one, knowing full well that [the food] was prepared for oneself, takes it and gives it to another bhikkhu, and that other bhikkhu consumes it out of faith [in the giver], what is the offense?
There is no offense for either of them. For there is no offense for the one for whom it was prepared because he did not eat it;

and for the other because he was unaware [of its origin]. Indeed, there is no offense in the acceptance of allowable meat (*kappiyamaṃsa*). And as for that which was prepared specifically [for someone]:...
There is no requirement to confess an offense for one who has eaten without knowing [the nature of the food] and only later realizes it;

however, even if one has eaten unknowingly, once it is subsequently realized that the meat was unallowable (*akappiya*), the offense must be confessed. For an offense occurs only while eating after having known that the food was prepared specifically for oneself (*uddissakata*);
likewise, there is indeed an offense even for one who ate without knowing the meat was unallowable. Therefore, one who fears offenses should [examine] the form...

Even one who is examining [the meat] must receive it only after asking; or, having taken it with the thought, "I will eat it after asking at the time of consumption," it must be consumed only after asking.
Why? Because it is difficult to discern. For the flesh of a deer is similar to the flesh of a pig, and the flesh of a leopard and so forth is similar to the flesh of a wild animal;
therefore, they say that receiving it only after asking is permissible.
"Unseen" means it was not seen being slaughtered for the sake of the bhikkhus. "Unheard" means it was not heard that it was slaughtered for the sake of the bhikkhus.
"Unsuspected" means it was not suspected by way of the "seen-suspected" and so forth.
"I say it is fit for use": through these three reasons, it is pure and is called "pure in the three respects" (*tikoṭiparisuddha*).
Its consumption is like the consumption of wild-growing vegetables and potherbs;
for a monk dwelling in loving-kindness who consumes such things, there is no fault or blame. Therefore, I say that it should be consumed—this is the meaning. 53.
Now, in order to show that even for one dwelling in loving-kindness there is no blame in consuming such things, [the Blessed One said]: "In this case, Jīvaka..."

He said, "A bhikkhu," and so forth. In this regard, although it was stated as "a bhikkhu" without specific qualification, it should nevertheless be understood that this was said with reference to himself alone.

For the Blessed One delivered his teaching with reference to himself alone on three occasions: in the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, the Caṅkī Sutta, and in this sutta. [The phrase is] "with excellent almsfood."
In the *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta* mentioned below, any alms-food that is expensive or of high quality is intended by the term "exquisite alms-food" (*paṇīta-piṇḍapāta*);
however, here only meat with sauce is intended. "Unattached" (*agathita*) means unattached by way of craving (*taṇhā*). "Uninfatuated" (*amucchita*) means not infatuated by the delusion of craving.
"Not greedily intent" (*anajjhopanna*) means not greedily intent; it refers to one who wishes to swallow everything all at once, as if taking a lump.

The meaning is that he does not act like a crow. "Seeing the danger" means seeing the peril in this way: "Having entered the belly by staying for a single night, it will emerge through the nine openings of wounds," and so forth.
"Consuming with wisdom regarding the escape" means he consumes after delimiting it with wisdom, thinking: "This consumption of food is for this purpose. For the sake of self-affliction...
"Or he intends" means he intends for his own suffering. "I have heard this" shows: "This was heard by me previously; this is merely my hearing.
"If, Jīvaka, you spoke with reference to this," [it is because] Jīvaka, the Great Brahmā has abandoned ill will and the rest through suppression; therefore, he dwells in loving-kindness toward me.
"If this was said by you with reference to abandonment through complete eradication, then that being the case, I grant the validity of these words of yours"—this is the meaning. He accepted it.

Then the Blessed One, further extending his teaching by way of the remaining divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), spoke the passage beginning with "Here, Jīvaka, monks... The meaning of that is self-evident.
55. "O Jīvaka," this is a separate connection. For at this point, the Blessed One closes the door and demonstrates compassion for sentient beings.
For if someone were to think, "By giving even a single morsel of flavored alms-food, one obtains the excellence of heaven for a hundred thousand eons;
therefore, no matter what must be done, one should give even a morsel of flavored alms-food even after killing another," [the Blessed One would prevent this].
In order to refute that [view], he said: “Jīvaka, whoever [should strike] the Tathāgata,” and so forth.
Therein, “by this first ground” means by this very first reason, which is merely the act of commanding.

“By one who pulls by the neck” means by one who has been dragged along after being bound by the neck with a rope, pulling him by the throat. “Being attacked” means being put to death. By an improper [means]...
"He approaches" means that, having caused someone to eat bear meat thinking it was pig meat, or leopard meat thinking it was deer meat, one then reproaches them, saying:
"What kind of ascetic are you? You have eaten unallowable meat. However, those who, during times of famine and the like, or for the sake of curing a disease, [say]:
"Bear meat is like pig meat; leopard meat is like deer meat," [are not at fault].
This was not said with reference to those who, knowing "this is pork" or "this is venison," say so and then cause others to eat it out of a desire for their welfare;

for such people indeed acquire great merit. "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus"—this is the noble disciple who has attained the fruit, who understands the teaching, and who has seen the truth.
But plunging into this teaching of the Dhamma and generating confidence, he spoke thus in praise of the discourse on the Dhamma.
The rest is clear everywhere.
[End of] the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Jīvakasutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Upālisutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Upālisutta. Therein, "at Nāḷandā" means in the city named Nāḷandā.
Having made that city his village for alms-round, [he stayed] in the Ambavana of the cloth-merchant (pāvārika) seṭṭhi.

It is said that this was his pleasure garden; having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained confidence in the Blessed One and, having constructed a monastery for the Blessed One adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, and so forth, in that garden, he dedicated it to him. He...
The monastery came to be known as the Jīvakambavana, just as it was reckoned as the Pāvārikambavana.
The meaning is that he dwelt in that Pāvārikambavana. "Dīghatapassī" means he received this name because of his tall stature. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto" means returned from almsround. One might ask:
"Is there even in external spheres such a conventional expression as 'alms' (piṇḍapāta), as there is in the Teaching? The answer is: no.
"Paññapeti" means he shows or establishes. "He lays down the rods"—this was said by one questioning according to the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.
Regarding "the bodily rod, the verbal rod, and the mental rod," here they maintain that the first two rods are without consciousness (*acittaka*).
For example, it is said that when the wind blows, the branches move and the water moves, yet there is no consciousness therein; even so...

The bodily rod (*kāyadaṇḍa*) is also without mind (*acittaka*). Just as palm leaves and the like make a sound when the wind blows, or as waters make a sound, yet there is no mind present therein, so too the verbal rod (*vacīdaṇḍa*) is without mind;
thus they designate these two rods as being without mind. But they designate the mind itself as the mental rod (*manodaṇḍa*). Then, for him—
The Blessed One, wishing to establish his statement, said, "But what, ascetic," and so forth.
In this context, "in the subject of the discourse" (*kathāvatthusmiṃ*) means that the discourse itself is the subject of the discourse; the sense is that he established it within that discourse.
But why did the Blessed One do so? For the Blessed One saw: "If this person goes away taking up this discourse, [he will bring] his own..."
He will report this to the Teacher, the Great Nigaṇṭha, and to his assembly;

the householder Upāli is sitting in that assembly, and having heard this discourse, he will come to challenge me with a counter-argument. I shall teach him the Dhamma, and he will go for refuge three times.
Then I shall reveal the Four Truths to him, and at the conclusion of the revelation of the Truths, he will [attain] the fruit of stream-entry.
"It will be established; for it was solely for the sake of gathering others that I fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs). Seeing this purpose, he acted in this way. 57. "He prescribed the karmas":
this was said by the Nigaṇṭha while questioning according to the Buddha's system. Regarding "bodily action, verbal action, and mental action":
here, at the door of the body, there are eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions (cetanā) consisting of taking up, grasping, releasing, and touching.
The twenty types of volition consisting of the twelve unwholesome and eight wholesome types are called bodily action (*kāyakamma*).

When those same twenty types of volition arise at the door of speech, having brought about a variety of utterances without reaching physical grasping and so forth, they are called verbal action (*vacīkamma*).

When the twenty-nine wholesome and unwholesome types of volition arise at the door of the mind, without reaching any movement of the two doors, they are called mental action (*manokamma*). Furthermore:
In brief, the threefold misconduct of body is called bodily action; the fourfold misconduct of speech is called verbal action;
and the threefold misconduct of mind is called mental action. In this sutta, action (*kamma*) is the primary focus; likewise, even in the subsequent sutta where it is stated:
"Puṇṇa, these four kinds of action have been realized by me through direct higher knowledge and proclaimed."
Volition (*cetanā*) is the burden. Volition, wherever it occurs, receives such designations as “black with black result,” and so forth.
In the section of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), this is indeed stated in the manner beginning with, “one performs a bodily formation (*kāya-saṅkhāra*) that is afflictive (*sabyābajjha*).
However, what is intended here as “bodily action” (*kāyakamma*) is that which occurs at the door of the body; that which occurs at the door of speech is “verbal action” (*vacīkamma*).
Mental action is that which occurs at the mind-door. Therefore it was said: "In this sutta, action (kamma) is the primary focus;
in the subsequent sutta, volition (cetanā). For the Blessed One designates even action as "action," as in this very sutta;
and he also designates volition as such, as he said: "Bhikkhus, I say that volition is action; having willed, one performs an action. Why?
But why is volition called "kamma"? Because kamma is rooted in volition.

And in this context, one does not become weary by asserting that bodily and verbal kamma are greater when considering unwholesome states, whereas mental kamma is greater when considering wholesome states.
For it is by means of the body alone that one undertakes the four karmas such as matricide and so forth, and completes them by means of the body alone.
He performs [the act]; he performs the deed of schism in the Saṅgha that lasts for an eon in hell by means of the door of speech.
One who says that bodily action and verbal action are "great" after having encountered such unwholesomeness is indeed not weary.

However, a single volition of jhāna brings about the attainment of heaven for eighty-four thousand eons, while a single volition of the Path, having eradicated all unwholesomeness, causes one to attain Arhatship.
Thus, one who says that mental action is great when it pertains to the wholesome does not become weary.
However, in this instance, when the Blessed One says that mental action is greatly blameworthy when it pertains to the unwholesome, he speaks with reference to fixed wrong view.
Therefore he said: "Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that is so..."
“Monks, wrong view is the most blameworthy thing; indeed, monks, there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view.

Now, even though the Nigaṇṭha was following the path taken by the Tathāgata, he saw no accomplishment of his purpose and said, “But what about it, friend Gotama? and so forth. 58. Regarding “Bālakiniyā”:
it is said that Upāli had a village called Bālakaloṇakāra; from there, people took their income...
Having arrived, he said, "Come now, let us go see our teacher, the Great Nigaṇṭha," and went there surrounded by that assembly.
It was with reference to him that it was said, "by the assembly of Bālakini"; the meaning is, "by the assembly of those dwelling in the village of Bālaka.
"With Upāli at their head" means with Upāli as their leader. Furthermore, "of Bālakini" also means of one who possesses fools, or of one whose assembly consists of fools.
The meaning [is as follows]. "With Upāli at their head" means that among them, the householder Upāli alone was somewhat wise;
he was their leader and senior. Therefore it is said, "with Upāli at their head. *Handa* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.
*Chava* means wretched. *Oḷārikassa* means of the great. *Upanidhāya* means having set beside for comparison. This is what is meant: of the bodily rod...
Having placed it nearby, when one examines it thinking, "Is this one great, or is that one great?"—how can such a wretched mental rod (manodaṇḍa) appear splendid?
From where could it ever appear splendid? It does not appear splendid; it is shown to be not even sufficient for mere comparison.
"Excellent, excellent, venerable sir, you ascetic!"—giving his approval to Dīgha-tapas-sī, he addresses Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta as "venerable sir."
"60. 'I do not like this, venerable sir,' means, venerable sir, 'this does not please me. 'A deceiver' means a magician.
'The illusion of enticement' means the illusion of seizing after having enticed. 'Entices' means that having enticed and surrounded [them], he seizes them.
'Go, householder!'—why did the Great Nigaṇṭha send the householder back as many as three times? [This was] Dīgha Tapassī."
But does he indeed prevent it? For even though the Great Nigaṇṭha was living in dependence on the same city as the Blessed One, he had never before seen the Blessed One.
Indeed, one who professes to follow the Teacher’s word is incapable of seeing the Buddha without abandoning that profession.
Therefore, because he had never before obtained a sight of the Buddha, he [failed to obtain] the excellence of beholding the One of Ten Powers.
Not knowing that this was a discourse leading to liberation, he continued to send messengers even up to three times.
But Dīgha Tapassī would approach the Blessed One from time to time; he would stand, sit, and ask questions.
He understood both the excellence of seeing the Tathāgata and the fact that this was a discourse leading to liberation. Then it occurred to him: "This householder..."

“The wise man, having gone into the presence of the ascetic Gotama, might gain confidence even upon seeing him, and he might gain confidence even after hearing his discourse on the way out [of suffering].
After that, he would not come back to us again. Therefore, he refused him up to three times.
“Having paid homage” means having bowed down. For when people see the Tathāgata, whether they are confident or lacking in confidence, they generally pay homage.
"Few do not pay homage. Why? For even one born into an exceedingly high family should indeed be paid homage while living as a householder.
But this householder paid homage out of faith alone; it is said he was inspired by his very appearance. "Has he come here? means "Has he indeed come here?
(61) "Excellent, excellent, venerable sir, ascetic!"—giving this word of praise to Dīgha Tapassī, he addresses the Blessed One as "venerable sir" (*bhante*).
He speaks. "Standing firm in truth" means standing firm in verbal truth, remaining unshakable like a pillar struck into a heap of chaff.
"It might be so" means it could be for us.
62. "In this world" means in this world. "It might be" means it could be. "One who rejects cold water" refers to the Nigaṇṭhas, because of their perception of a living being [in water].
They reject cold water; it is with reference to this that it was said. "Mind-beings" (*manosatta*) means gods who are attached to, clinging to, the mind.

"Bound to the mind" (*manopaṭibaddha*) shows that because one passes away while being bound to the mind, one is reborn among the gods who are mind-beings. For he will suffer from a bile-born disease; therefore, for him—
It is not permitted to bring warm water for the purpose of drinking, or for washing the hands, feet, and so forth, or for bathing the limbs;
the illness becomes more severe. Cold water is permitted, as it pacifies the illness.
However, this person consumes only warm water, and failing to obtain that, he consumes rice-gruel. Yet, in his mind, he [longs for] cold water.
He desires to drink it and desires to consume it. Consequently, his mental punishment (*manodaṇḍa*) is broken right there.

Even though he intends to guard his physical punishment (*kāyadaṇḍa*) and verbal punishment (*vacīdaṇḍa*, thinking, "I shall protect them"), when he desires cold water or wishes to consume it, he is unable to say, "Give me cold water.
Thus, even when his physical and verbal punishments are guarded in this way, at the moment of death or rebirth-linking—
They are unable to pull [the body] back. But the mental rod, even when broken, still pulls along both the death-moment and the rebirth-moment.
Thus the Blessed One caused it to be said that the bodily rod and the verbal rod are weak, wretched, and inferior, whereas the mental rod alone is powerful and great.
This thought occurred to that lay follower as well: "For those beings who have become unconscious through fainting, even for seven days, inhalation and exhalation..."
They do not function; however, they are not called "dead" merely because of the cessation of the continuity of consciousness.
When their consciousness no longer functions, they then come to be designated as "these are dead; take them out and cremate them.
The bodily rod is inactive and devoid of volitional effort, and likewise the verbal rod. Yet, it is by means of the mind alone that there is both their passing away and their rebirth-linking.
"Thus, the mental rod alone is great. Even when broken, it remains great because it drags one along from death to rebirth.

But the discourse of our Great Nigaṇṭha is not conducive to liberation," he observed. Yet, desiring to hear the Blessed One’s diverse insights into questions and answers, he did not yet grant permission [to leave].

"It does not join with yours" means it does not cohere with yours. "The former with the latter" refers to the present statement, "The mental rod is great," in relation to the preceding statement, "The bodily rod is great.
"Or the latter with the former" means that the latter statement does not cohere with that preceding statement.
63. Now, bringing forward other reasons as well, the Blessed One said, "What do you think? and so forth. In that context, "restrained by the restraint of the fourfold vow" means:
he does not take life, he does not cause another to take life, and he does not approve of one who takes life.
He does not take what is not given, he does not cause another to take what is not given, and he does not approve of one who takes what is not given.
He does not speak falsehood, he does not cause another to speak falsehood, and he does not approve of one who speaks falsehood.

He does not long for what has been cultivated, he does not cause another to long for what has been cultivated, and he does not approve of one who longs for what has been cultivated—thus he is restrained by this fourfold restraint.
And herein, "what has been cultivated" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Sabbavārivārito" means one who has warded off all water; the meaning is that he has rejected all cold water.
For he perceives cold water as a living being, and therefore he does not use it. Alternatively, "sabbavārivārito" means one whose evil has been warded off by the warding-off of all evil.
"Sabbavāriyutto" means endowed with the warding-off of all evil. "Sabbavāridhuto" means [purified] by the warding-off of all... by all.
"By warding off evil, he has shaken off evil. "Pervaded by the warding off of all evil" means he is filled with the complete cessation of all unwholesome deeds.
"He brings about the destruction of small living beings" means he inflicts death upon small creatures. It is said that he designates a one-facultied being as a two-facultied being;
he even designates dry twigs, withered leaves, gravel, and pebbles as living beings.
In that regard, one perceives a small drop of water as a small living being, and a large one as a large one;
it was with reference to this that it was said. "In what does he prescribe? means: in which part, in which category, does he prescribe?
"In the mental rod," venerable sir, means: in the category of the mental rod. Furthermore, even as he spoke, this lay follower observed for himself: "Of us..."
The great Nigaṇṭha, having declared that "volitional action is less blameworthy, while non-volitional action is more blameworthy," then declares volition to be the mental rod (*manodaṇḍa*).
His teaching is not conducive to liberation; only the Blessed One’s is conducive to liberation.
64. *Iddhā* means successful. *Phītā* means exceedingly successful, like a tree in full bloom. *Ākiṇṇamanussā* means crowded with people.
"Beings" (*pāṇā*) refers both to animals such as elephants and horses, and to those of human birth such as women, men, and children.

"A single lump of flesh" (*ekaṃ maṃsakhaḷaṃ*) means a single heap of flesh; "a mass" (*puñja*) is a synonym for that same thing. "One possessed of psychic power" (*iddhimā*) means one endowed with majesty.

"One who has attained mastery over the mind" (*cetovasippatta*) means one who has reached mastery in the mind. "I shall turn them to ashes" (*bhasmaṃ karissāmi*) means I shall turn them to cinders. For what indeed...
Even as that householder was saying, "A single corpse shines in Nāḷandā," he thought:

"By means of physical exertion, even people endowed with wisdom cannot turn a single Nāḷandā into a heap of flesh; but one possessed of psychic power is capable of turning it into ashes with a single corruption of mind.
Our Great Nigaṇṭha’s teaching is not conducive to liberation; it is the Blessed One’s alone."
He observed, “This discourse leads to liberation. 65.
“The wilderness has become a wilderness” means that being devoid of villages, it has become a wilderness and has arisen as a wilderness.

“By the mental resentment of the seers” means: because of the mental resentment directed toward the seers, and because those deities, unable to endure that mental resentment, [destroyed] those kingdoms for the sake of the seers.
They were destroyed. However, worldly sages think that they destroyed them by corrupting their minds.
Therefore, it should be understood that this presentation of the argument is made precisely by standing upon this worldly convention.
In this regard, the way in which the Daṇḍaka forest and others became such forests should be understood as follows: [it occurred] through the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga...
When the assembly had thus grown exceedingly large, an ascetic named Kisavaccha, a pupil of the Great Being,

desiring a life of seclusion, left the group and dwelt in the royal park near the city of Kumbhapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga— situated on the banks of the Godhāvarī River— cultivating solitude. His general was his attendant.
At that time, a certain courtesan, having mounted her chariot and accompanied by a retinue of five hundred women, was wandering about, beautifying the city.
The great multitude followed her, surrounding her as they gazed upon her, so that the city streets could not contain them.
The king, standing with the window open, saw her and asked, "Who is this? [The attendant replied: "She is the one who adorns your city."
"O King! she cried. Becoming impatient, he thought, "What is the use of her beauty? The city itself shall be beautiful," and he had that position of hers revoked.

From then on, seeking intimacy with someone and searching for a position [of influence], she one day entered the royal garden and sat upon a stone slab, leaning against a support-board at the end of a walkway.
Seeing the ascetic, she thought: "How defiled indeed is this ascetic; he is neither anointed nor adorned.
His face is covered with grown-out whiskers, his chest is covered with hair, and both his armpits are overgrown.
Then dejection arose in her: "I am going about on some business, and I have seen this ill omen. Bring water!"
Thinking, “I shall wash my eyes,” he had water and a tooth-stick brought;

having chewed the tooth-stick and spat mouthful after mouthful of saliva onto the ascetic’s body, he threw the tooth-stick upon the matted locks on the ascetic’s head, rinsed his mouth, and poured water right over the ascetic’s head, saying: “Those eyes by which I saw Kāḷakaṇṇī—those...”
“Washed away by the flood of the Kali age,” she said as she departed.
On that very day, the king regained his senses and asked, “Sirs, where is Nagarasobhinī?
“Your Majesty, she is in this very city. He had her reinstated in her former position, saying, “Give her back her previous rank. She [performed] the wholesome deeds she had previously done.
He perceived that the high position he had obtained was due to spitting on the body of the ascetic.
Then, after a few days had passed, the king seized the high position of the royal chaplain.
He went to the city courtesan and asked, "Sister, by doing what did you obtain this high position? "What else, Brahmin? [she replied].

“There is something that must be done. In the royal park there is a certain fraudulent matted-hair ascetic who is neither anointed nor black-eared; spit on his body, and in this way you will obtain a position.
He replied, “I shall do so, Sister,” and having gone there, he did everything exactly as she had instructed and then departed. On that very same day, the king regained his mindfulness.
“Where, sir, is the brahmin? he asked. “In this very city, Your Majesty,” they replied. “We acted without due consideration;
grant him that same position,” he commanded, and had it bestowed upon him. Having obtained it through the power of his merit, he perceived:
“I have gained this by spitting on the ascetic’s body.”
Then, after a few days had passed, the king’s frontier region rose in rebellion. Thinking, "I shall pacify the frontier," the king set out with a fourfold army.
The chaplain went before the king, stood in his presence, and having said, "Victory to the Great King!
he asked, "Great King, you are going for the sake of victory, are you not? "Yes, brahmin. "That being so, in the royal park—"
"A certain rogue ascetic with unanointed black ears lives there; spit on his body.
Having accepted his words, the king did everything exactly as the courtesan and he had done, and he also commanded the women of the harem:
"Spit on the body of this rogue ascetic. Then the women of the harem and the guards of the harem did likewise.
They did so. Then the king, having stationed guards at the gate of the park, issued this command:
"No one who departs with the king shall be permitted to leave unless they have spat upon the body of the ascetic.
Thereupon, the entire army and the various companies followed that very same procedure, spitting and throwing tooth-sticks and mouth-wash over the ascetic.
They poured water [over him], and his saliva and tooth-sticks spread all over his body.
Having heard this last of all, the general thought, "They have indeed struck my Teacher, the Blessed One, the field of merit and the stairway to heaven.
With his heart burning with heat and gasping for breath, he rushed to the royal garden and, having approached the Tathāgata in that manner—
Seeing the seer fallen into calamity, he tied up his hair, cleared away the tooth-sticks with both hands,
lifted him up, and had him seated. Having brought water and bathed him, he rubbed his body with all kinds of medicinal herbs and the four-fold fragrant scents,
wiped him dry with a fine cloth, and standing before him with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus:
“Venerable sir, what will become of these men who have done what is improper?
The deities were divided into three factions regarding the general: some said, “We shall destroy the king alone”; some said, “The king together with his retinue”;
and some said, “We shall destroy the king’s entire realm. Having said this, the ascetic, though it was but a trifle—

Without becoming angry, he spoke, explaining the very means for the world’s peace: “An offense indeed occurs, but for one who knows how to confess that transgression, everything returns to its original state.
Having received this method, the general went into the presence of the king, paid homage to him, and said: “By you, O Great King...”
“‘A grave deed has been committed by those who have offended against a faultless ascetic of great psychic power;

indeed, the deities are split into three factions and speak thus,’ having reported all this, he said: ‘It is said, O Great King, that when [the ascetic] is asked for forgiveness, everything returns to normal.
Do not destroy the kingdom; ask the ascetic for forgiveness. Although the king saw the fault committed within himself, he spoke thus.”
He said, "I will not ask him for forgiveness. After the general had entreated him three times, he said to the one who was unwilling, "Great King, I know the power of that ascetic;
he is neither a speaker of falsehood nor is he angry. Rather, out of compassion for living beings, he spoke thus: 'Great King, ask him for forgiveness.
[The king replied: 'I will not ask him for forgiveness. [The general said: 'In that case, let another take the position of general.'"
"Give it back; I will not live in the place where your commands are enforced. "Go wherever you wish; I shall obtain my own commander-in-chief.
Then the commander-in-chief came into the presence of the ascetic, paid homage, and said, "How should I proceed, venerable sir?
[The ascetic replied: "Commander-in-chief, all those who hear your words, along with their requisites..."
"Seizing both bipeds and quadrupeds, go outside the royal boundary within seven days;
the deities are exceedingly angry and will surely turn the kingdom into a non-kingdom. The general did accordingly.
As soon as the king had departed, he crushed his enemies, pacified the countryside, and returned to the site of the victorious camp.
Having sat down and had the city cleaned, he entered the inner city. The deities first sent down a rain of water.
The great multitude was delighted, thinking, "Ever since we dealt with the fraudulent ascetic, there has been only prosperity for our king;
he has crushed his enemies, and on the very day he arrived, the rain fell. Then the deities...
They caused a rain of *sumana* flowers to fall, and the great multitude became even more delighted. The deities again caused a rain of silver coins (*māsaka*) to fall.

Then they caused a rain of gold coins (*kahāpaṇa*) to fall. Then, thinking that people would not go out for the sake of gold coins, they caused a rain of goods such as hand-held items, foot-worn items, and so forth.
Even those standing on seven-storied palaces descended and, putting on ornaments, were filled with joy.
It occurred to them: "Truly, Kūṭajaṭilaka deserves the spitting of phlegm!
From the moment we spat upon him, our king’s prosperity has increased; he has crushed his enemies, and on the very day he arrived, the rain fell.
Following that, four kinds of rains have occurred: a rain of *sumana* flowers, a rain of māsaka coins, a rain of kahāpaṇa coins, and a rain of finished goods."
Having uttered words of satisfaction, he became complacent regarding the evil committed against the king.
At that moment, deities rained down various kinds of weapons—such as single-edged and double-edged blades—upon the heads of the great multitude, like meat being pounded upon a wooden block.
Immediately thereafter, [they fell] upon those whose fires were extinguished and whose smoke had ceased.

They caused rain to fall upon charcoal the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers, followed by stones the size of gabled houses, and then fine sand that would not fit within a closed fist; thus they created dry land eighty cubits high.
In the territory conquered by the king, the ascetic Kisavaccha, the general Rāma, and Mātuposaka—these three alone remained among humans, healthy and unharmed.
[They] were [there]. For the other animals who did not participate in that work, there was no water at the watering places and no grass at the grazing grounds.
As they went searching for water and grass, they reached the boundary of the foreign country on the very seventh day before they had even arrived. Therefore, the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga said:
“Why indeed, Vaccha, does one who wields a staff, having scattered his kin,
with their roots cut off and along with their kingdom,
roast in the hell named Kukkuḷa?”
"Sparks fell upon his body.
In this way, first of all, the state of King Daṇḍaki’s realm having become a wilderness is to be understood.
Furthermore, while Nāḷikira was reigning in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, five hundred ascetics free from the scent of woman (anitthigandha) lived in the Himālaya.

Having spent a long time dwelling in the forest wearing antelope skins, matted hair, and bark garments, and subsisting on roots and fruits, they descended to the path of men for the sake of obtaining salt and sour gruel.
Gradually, they arrived at the city of King Nāḷikira in the kingdom of Kaliṅga.
There, having adjusted their matted hair, antelope skins, and bark garments, they entered the city, displaying the glory of tranquility befitting those who have gone forth.
They entered for alms. When people saw those who had gone forth as ascetics before the appearance of a Buddha, they were inspired with faith;
having prepared a place for them to sit, taken their alms-bowls from their hands, seated them, and provided the alms-food, they gave it to them.
After the ascetics had finished their meal, they recited the words of thanksgiving (*anumodana*). Hearing this, the people, with hearts full of faith, [asked: "Where..."
“Venerable sirs, where are you going? they asked. “To a place that is convenient for us, friends,” they replied.
“Venerable sirs, there is no need to go elsewhere; please stay in the royal park. We shall come after we have eaten our morning meal and listen to the discourse on the Dhamma.
Having consented, the ascetics went to the park. When the citizens had finished their morning meal and were dressed in clean garments, [they went to hear] the discourse on the Dhamma.
“Let us go,” they said; and so the people, forming groups and crowds, set out toward the park.
The king, standing upon the upper terrace of his palace, saw them going in that manner and asked his attendant:

“Tell me, why are these citizens going toward the park dressed in clean garments with their upper robes properly arranged? Is there some festival or theatrical performance there? “There is not, sire.”
“Your Majesty, these people are going into the presence of the ascetics because they wish to hear the Dhamma.
“In that case, my man, I too shall go; let them go together with me. Having gone there, he announced to them: “The king also wishes to go; you must go surrounding the king.
The citizens, who were already pleased by nature, heard this and said: “Our king is faithless and lacks conviction...”

“O ascetics, they are righteous; by their coming, even the king will become righteous. Thus they became even more joyful. The king went out, surrounded by them, and having gone to the park, he exchanged greetings with the ascetics and sat down to one side. When the ascetics saw the king, one ascetic skilled in introductory discourse said to the king: ... [the rest of the passage continues] ... “O Great King, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world... [and so forth]. The king asked: “What, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of being a righteous person? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for a righteous person, in this very life, there is happiness and well-being; after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that a righteous person has such a fruit and such a benefit. But what, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of one who is unrighteous? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for one who is unrighteous, in this very life, there is suffering and ill-being; after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a place of torment, in hell. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that one who is unrighteous has such a fruit and such a benefit. But what, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, in this very life, there is neither happiness nor suffering; after death, he is reborn in the human world. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous has such a fruit and such a benefit. But what, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of one who is both righteous and unrighteous? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for one who is both righteous and unrighteous, in this very life, there is both happiness and suffering; after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a place of torment, in hell. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that one who is both righteous and unrighteous has such a fruit and such a benefit. But what, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the destruction of both merit and demerit? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the destruction of both merit and demerit, in this very life, there is neither happiness nor suffering; after death, he is reborn in the human world. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the destruction of both merit and demerit, has such a fruit and such a benefit. But what, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the complete destruction of both merit and demerit? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the complete destruction of both merit and demerit, in this very life, there is neither happiness nor suffering; after death, he is reborn in the human world. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the complete destruction of both merit and demerit, has such a fruit and such a benefit. But what, venerable sir, is the fruit, what is the benefit of one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the complete destruction of both merit and demerit, and who, through the destruction of craving, becomes free from lust, attains final knowledge, and realizes Nibbāna in this very life? The ascetic replied: “Great King, for one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the complete destruction of both merit and demerit, and who, through the destruction of craving, becomes free from lust, attains final knowledge, and realizes Nibbāna in this very life, in this very life there is the cessation of suffering, the end of the fever, and the attainment of coolness. The king said: “Venerable sir, it is good that one who is neither righteous nor unrighteous, yet performs deeds that lead to the complete destruction of both merit and demerit, and who, through the destruction of craving, becomes free from lust, attains final knowledge, and realizes Nibbāna in this very life, has such a fruit and such a benefit. The king then said: “Venerable sir, I am now going to the city. It would be good if you were to come to the city as well. The ascetics replied: “Great King, we shall go at the proper time. The king, having dismissed the ascetics, entered the city. The ascetics, having stayed there for seven days, departed for the Himalayas. The king, having heard that the ascetics had departed, was deeply moved and thought: “It is truly a loss for me that those virtuous ascetics have departed. If they had remained, I might have been able to attend upon them. Then the king, accompanied by his retinue, went to the park where the ascetics had stayed and, seeing the footprints of the ascetics, he was overcome with grief. He said: “Alas, those virtuous ones have gone! Alas, those virtuous ones have gone! And he lamented: “If only those virtuous ones had remained, I might have been able to attend upon them. The king then returned to the city. There, the king established a monastery for the ascetics and provided them with all requisites. He also sent a messenger to the ascetics in the Himalayas, saying: “Venerable sirs, please come to the city; I wish to see you. The ascetics, having received the message, came to the city. The king, having seen the ascetics arrive, went out to meet them, welcomed them, and led them into the city. There, the king provided the ascetics with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The ascetics, being thus supported, lived in comfort, free from care, and devoted themselves to meditation. The king, having seen the ascetics living in comfort, was filled with joy and said: “It is truly a gain for me that these virtuous ascetics have come back. I shall be able to attend upon them. The king then provided the ascetics with even greater honor and service than before. The ascetics, being thus honored, lived in comfort, free from care, and devoted themselves to meditation. The king, having seen the ascetics living in comfort, was filled with even greater joy and said: “It is truly a great gain for me that these virtuous ascetics have come back and are living in comfort. I shall be able to attend upon them. The king then provided the ascetics with all the requisites they needed. The ascetics, being thus supported, lived in comfort, free from care, and devoted themselves to meditation. The king, having seen the ascetics living in comfort, was filled with supreme joy and said: “It is truly a supreme gain for me that these virtuous ascetics have come back, are living in comfort, and are devoted to meditation. I shall be able to attend upon them. The king then made a great offering to the ascetics. The ascetics, having accepted the offering, preached the Dhamma to the king. The king, having heard the Dhamma, was filled with faith and said: “Venerable sirs, may you remain here for the rains retreat. I shall provide you with all requisites. The ascetics consented. The king, having arranged for the rains retreat, provided the ascetics with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The ascetics, being thus supported, lived in comfort, free from care, and devoted themselves to meditation. The king, having seen the ascetics living in comfort, was filled with supreme joy and said: “It is truly a supreme gain for me that these virtuous ascetics have remained for the rains retreat and are living in comfort. I shall be able to attend upon them. The king then visited the ascetics frequently. The ascetics, being thus honored, lived in comfort, free from care, and devoted themselves to meditation. The king, having seen the ascetics living in comfort, was filled with supreme joy and said: “It is truly a supreme gain for me that these virtuous ascetics have remained for the rains retreat, are living in comfort, and are devoted to meditation. I shall be able to attend upon them. The king then made a great offering to the ascetics at the conclusion of the rains retreat. The ascetics, having accepted the offering, preached the Dhamma to the king. The king, having heard the Dhamma, was filled with faith and said: “Venerable sirs, may you remain here for another rains retreat. I shall provide you with all requisites. The ascetics consented. The king, having arranged for the second
“Preach the Dhamma,” they requested. That ascetic, looking over the assembly, spoke of the danger in the five precepts and the benefit in the five virtues:
“Living beings must not be killed; what is not given must not be taken; sexual misconduct must not be practiced; false speech must not be uttered;”
Intoxicants must not be drunk. Killing living beings leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth in the animal realm, and to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts;

so too do taking what is not given and the other [unwholesome deeds]. Having been cooked in hell for killing living beings, when one returns to the human world, the remaining karmic result leads to a short lifespan. Taking what is not given leads to poverty.
“Sexual misconduct leads to many enemies; false speech leads to being falsely accused;
drinking intoxicants leads to madness”—thus he spoke of this danger regarding the five enmities.
The king was by nature faithless, lacking confidence, and immoral; for an immoral person, a discourse on virtue is indeed a painful discourse, like the piercing of a thorn into the ear.
Therefore, he thought: "I came here thinking, 'I shall support these men,' yet from the moment I arrived, they have been rubbing against and poking at me, speaking thus in the midst of the assembly."
"I shall do for them what ought to be done. At the conclusion of his discourse on the Dhamma, he invited them, saying, "Teachers, please accept almsfood at my house tomorrow," and then departed.
On the second day, he had large jars brought, filled them with excrement, had their openings bound with plantain leaves, and placed them here and there.

Again, having filled the peak of the scaffolding with thick madhuka oil, *nāgabalā* resin, and other slippery substances, he had the great wrestlers stand right there on top of the ladder with their loins girded and holding clubs in their hands, and said:
"The false ascetics have harassed me excessively; as they were descending from the palace, [I shall strike them] with the peaks [of the scaffolding] at the top of the stairs."
“Having dismissed him, beat him on the head with clubs, seize him by the throat, and hurl him down the stairs!
Furthermore, he had fierce dogs tied at the foot of the stairs.
The ascetics also exhorted one another, saying, “Friends, tomorrow we shall eat in the royal palace; the royal palace is indeed—”
"It is full of danger and fear; indeed, those who have gone forth must be restrained regarding the objects of the six sense-doors.
One must not seize upon signs in any object seen, and restraint must be maintained at the eye-door.
On the following day, having observed the time for the alms-round, he put on his bark garment and draped the deerskin over one shoulder.
Having fashioned a mass of matted hair and arranged it, and having taken up his alms-bowl, he ascended the royal palace in due order.
When the king learned that he had ascended, he had a plantain leaf removed from the mouth of a cesspool.
A foul odor struck the nostrils of the ascetics, reaching a point where it seemed as though it would cause their brains to fall out. The great ascetic then looked toward the king.
The King said: “Let your honors eat and take as much as you require; this is worthy of you.
Yesterday I came thinking, ‘I shall honor you,’ yet you spoke in the midst of the assembly, reviling and piercing me.
This is indeed worthy of you! Eat! And he offered a bowl of excrement to the great ascetic.

He offered it. The Great Ascetic, saying "Alas! Alas!", turned back. Thinking, "Will you go with only this much?", he had the steps made slippery by pouring down dung and gave the signal to the Mallas.
The Mallas struck their heads with clubs, seized him by the neck, and hurled him down the stairs;
not a single one was able to remain standing on the steps, and as they tumbled down...
They reached the very base of the steps. As each one arrived, the fierce dogs tore at them with a snapping sound and devoured them.
Even those who rose up and fled fell into a pit; there too, the dogs pursued and devoured them.
Thus, the dogs left nothing of them but skeletons of bones. In this way...
That king caused five hundred ascetics endowed with ascetic power to lose their lives in a single day.

Then, as before, the deities in his kingdom sent down nine new showers of rain. His kingdom was covered over by a bed of sand sixty *yojanas* in height. Regarding this, the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga said:
“He who deceived those who were self-restrained and had gone forth...”
"While the harmless ascetics are preaching the Dhamma,
those dogs gather together and devour that coconut, writhing in agony."
In this way, the state of the Kāliṅga forest having become a wilderness is to be understood.
In the past, however, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a daughter named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā belonging to a merchant of forty million in wealth;
she was beautiful and charming. Because she was endowed with excellence of physical form, enjoyments, and noble lineage, she was sought after by many.

There was [a man] who, seeing each person sent by her for the sake of the wedding, would find some fault—whether in his birth, his hands and feet, or anywhere else—and saying things such as, "Who is this ill-born, ill-formed one?", he would have him led away, saying, "Take him out!", and then say, "I have seen even such a thing! Bring water; I shall wash my eyes."

She washed her eyes. Because she would have whatever was seen [by her] brought out after it had been made to undergo a transformation, the designation "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā" arose for her, and her original name disappeared.
One day, thinking, "I shall play in the water at the Ganges," she prepared a landing-place and a great quantity of hard and soft food.
Having filled carts with many perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and mounting a covered carriage, he departed from his home surrounded by a company of kinsmen.
At that time, the Great Being had been reborn in the womb of a Caṇḍāla and lived in a tanner’s house outside the city;
his name was Mātaṅga. Having reached the age of sixteen, for some reason...
Desiring to enter the city on some business, he put on one blue rag-robe and tied another around his hand;
holding a basket in one hand and a bell in the other, he entered the city with a humble mind, proclaiming for the sake of making himself known, "Make way, sirs!
I am a caṇḍāla," while paying homage to every person he encountered.
Having entered, he set out upon the main road.
Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, hearing the sound of the bell, looked through the opening in the curtain and saw him approaching from afar;
she asked, "What is this? "It is Mātaṅga, my lady. "Alas, what evil deed have we committed? Whose [is this]?"
“Is this the consequence, is this my destruction that has presented itself? While going out for the very purpose of performing auspicious rites, I have seen a caṇḍāla!
Shaking her body and feeling loathing, she spat out phlegm and said to her attendants:
“Bring water quickly! A caṇḍāla has been seen; I shall wash both my eyes and the face I have taken hold of. Having washed them, she—
Having had the chariot turned back and sent all the prepared offerings to the house, he ascended the palace.
His companions, such as the wine-drinkers, and her attendants asked, "Where is Mistress Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā? Why does she not come even at this hour?
Having heard what had happened, they exclaimed, "Oh, how great indeed is this offering of wine, meat, perfumes, garlands, and other honors!"
“Because of that outcaste, we were unable to enjoy [these things]; seize the outcaste!
Having searched for the place where he had gone, they threatened the blameless Mātaṅga Paṇḍita, saying, “Hey, Mātaṅga! Because of you, we were unable to enjoy this and that honor!
Then, seizing him by the hair, they threw him to the ground and [struck him] with knee-joints, stones, and other such objects.
Thinking he was dead, they beat him, seized him by the feet, dragged him along, and threw him onto a heap of refuse.
When the Great Man regained consciousness and felt his hands and feet, he reflected: "Upon what basis has this suffering arisen?
Realizing, "It has not arisen because of anything else, but has arisen because of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā," he thought:
Thinking, "If I am truly a man, I shall fall at her feet," he trembled and went to the door of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house.
He lay down on the courtyard floor, resolving: "If I obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, I shall rise; if I do not obtain her, I shall die right here.
At that time, this was the custom in Jambudīpa: for one who was a caṇḍāla...
Having become angry, he lies down at the door of the womb and dies; whoever dwells in that womb all become outcasts (*caṇḍāla*).
If he dies in the middle of the house, all the inhabitants of the house [become outcasts]; if he dies at the door, the inhabitants of both the adjacent houses [become outcasts];
if he dies in the courtyard, the fourteen inhabitants of the houses—seven on this side and seven on that—become outcasts. Thus spoke the Bodhisatta.
However, he lay down in the courtyard.
They reported to the merchant, "Master, Mātaṅga has fallen in your courtyard. [The merchant] said, "Go, men! For what reason?
Give him one māsaka and make him get up. They went and said, "It is said, take this māsaka and get up."
They said this. He replied, "I did not lie down for the sake of a coin; rather, I lay down because of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.
"What fault is there in Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā? [He asked. "Do you not see her fault?
I am innocent, yet she had me ruined by men. If I obtain [the coin], I shall rise; if I do not obtain it, I shall not rise."
Having gone, they reported this to the merchant. The merchant, realizing his daughter’s fault, sent word: "Go, give him one kahāpaṇa.
He replied: "I do not want a kahāpaṇa; I want her alone. Hearing this, the merchant and the merchant’s wife thought:
"She is our only dear daughter; there is no other child in our lineage, not even a boy."
Filled with a sense of urgency, they said, “Go, dear ones! Someone might be unable to endure us and take his life;
for if he dies, we are all lost. Therefore, provide him with protection.
Having surrounded him and arranged for his guard, they sent him rice gruel, and they sent him food and wealth; in this way, he refused everything.
Thus one day passed; two, three, four, and five days passed.
Then the inhabitants of the seven houses rose up and said: "We cannot become outcasts because of you;
do not destroy us! Give us back your daughter and let this man rise. They [offered] even a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold].
They sent a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], but he refused it. In this way, six days passed.
On the seventh day, fourteen householders from both sides assembled and said, "We cannot become outcasts;
even against our will, we shall give our daughter to him."
The mother and father, struck by the arrow of grief, fell unconscious upon their beds.
Both sets of fourteen householders ascended the palace as if plucking branches of the *kiṃsuka* tree in full bloom;
they removed all her ornaments, parted her hair with their fingernails, tied it up, dressed her in blue garments, and placed a fragment of blue rag in her hand.
Having wrapped her in fine cloth, adorned her ears with earrings, and given her a palmyra-leaf basket, they brought her down from the palace;
then, taking her by both arms, they gave her to the Great Being, saying, "Take your husband and go.
Even the blue lotus was too much of a burden for that delicate young girl, who had never before been lifted up; thus she said, "Rise, my lord, let us go."
He said: "The Bodhisatta, while still lying down, said, 'I will not rise. Then [the woman] asked, 'How then shall I speak?
He replied, 'Say to me thus: "Rise, noble Mātaṅga. She spoke accordingly. He said, 'People have not made me capable of rising for you;
take me by the arm and help me up. She did so. As the Bodhisatta was rising,"
Having rolled over as if in pain and fallen to the ground, she cried out: "Alas, sir!
Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā first had me pounded by men, and now she pounds me herself! "What shall I do, noble lady? [he asked. "Lift her up with both hands," he said.
Having lifted her up in that manner and made her sit down, she said, "Let us go, master. "Let us go," he replied.
“They are in the forest, while we are humans; I have been greatly tormented by these people and am unable to go on foot.
Carry me on your back. She bent down and offered her back. The Bodhisatta climbed up. “Where shall I take you, Master? she asked.
“Take me outside the city,” he replied. Having gone to the eastern gate, she asked, “Is this your dwelling place, Master?”

“Which place is this? “The eastern gate, sir. Since the sons of the Caṇḍālas were not permitted to dwell at the eastern gate, he had her wander past all the gates without revealing her own dwelling place. Why? Thinking, “I shall cause her pride, which has reached the very peak of existence, to fall.
The great multitude raised a shout of acclaim: “Apart from one such as you, there is no one else who can break her pride!”
Having reached the western gate, she asked, "Is this your dwelling place, my lord? "Which place is that?
"The western gate, my lord. "Go out through this gate and proceed while looking for the leather house.
She went there and said, "Is this leather house your dwelling place, my lord? "Yes," he replied from behind her back.
Having descended, he entered the leather-worker’s house.
Staying there for seven or eight days, being steadfast in his quest for omniscience, he did not commit any breach of caste during all those days. [He thought:
"If the daughter of a great family does not attain great glory through me, I am not one of the twenty-four..."
"I am a disciple of the Buddhas. With the water used for washing her feet, I shall perform the consecration ceremony for all the kings throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa.
Having thought this, he reflected again: "Living in the midst of a household, I will not be able to do it; but having gone forth into homelessness, I shall be able to do it.
Having reflected thus, he addressed her: "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, formerly we were wanderers alone..."
"One can live even by not working, as well as by working; but now that we have entered into the state of supporting a wife, it is impossible to live without working.
Therefore, until I return, do not be distressed.
Having said this, he entered the forest, gathered rags from the charnel ground and other places, made them into lower and upper garments, and went forth into the life of a recluse.

Having gone forth, wandering alone and having attained physical seclusion, he performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, realized the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*),
and thinking, "Now I am able to act as a refuge for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā," he set out toward Bārāṇasī;
there, having put on his robe and walking for alms, he went toward the house of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.
Seeing him standing at the gate, she did not recognize him and said, "Pass by, venerable sir; this is the dwelling place of the caṇḍālas.
