The Bodhisatta remained right there. Looking again and again, she recognized him, and beating her breast with her hands and crying out, she fell at his feet and said, "If you have such a mind as this, my lord, why...?"
“Having deprived me of great glory, you have left me without a protector.
Having lamented in various ways, she wiped her eyes, rose up, took her alms-bowl, seated him inside the house, and gave him alms-food.
After the Great Man had finished his meal, he said: “Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, do not grieve, do not lament.”
“I am capable of performing the coronation ceremony for all the kings in the entire Jambudīpa with the water used for washing your feet;
however, you must do this one thing for me: enter the city and wander throughout it, proclaiming, ‘My husband is not a caṇḍāla; Mahābrahmā is my husband.’”
When this was said, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā replied, "Master, even by nature I have met with calamity because of my own mouth;
I cannot speak such words. The Bodhisatta said, "But have you ever heard me utter a falsehood while living in my home?
Even then I did not speak untruth; now that I have gone forth, what would I say?"
Having said, "He is indeed called a man who speaks the truth," she added, "Today is the eighth day of the fortnight;
proclaim throughout the entire city that on the coming Uposatha day, seven days from now, my husband, the Great Brahmā, will break through the moon’s disk and come to me.
Having said this, she departed.
Having believed him, she became joyful and elated; being courageous, she entered the city every evening and morning and proclaimed it in that manner.
People clapped their hands together, laughing and playing, saying, "Look!
Our Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā makes the son of a Caṇḍāla into a Great Brahmā! She did the same on the following day as well, every evening and morning.
Having entered, she proclaimed: “In six days’ time—or in five, four, three, two, or one day’s time—my husband, Mahābrahmā, will pierce the lunar disk and come into my presence!
The brahmins thought: “This Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā speaks with excessive boldness; it might possibly be so.”
"Come, let us repair the dwelling place of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.

Having had the exterior of the hide-house cleared on all sides, they scattered sand over it. On the Uposatha day, she entered the city early in the morning and proclaimed, "Today my husband will come!
The brahmins thought, "Sirs, this one is not far away..."
"It is being proclaimed: 'Today, it is said, Mahābrahmā will arrive; let us prepare a dwelling place for him.

Having thus had the hide-hut swept clean, smeared with green cow dung, and surrounded with new cloths, they spread out a costly couch, tied a cloth canopy above it, and hung down garlands of perfumes and flowers.
While they were still in the process of preparing it, the sun set.
When the moon had risen high, the Great Man entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

Emerging from that state, he performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*) with a sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*), and by means of his supernormal mind (*iddhicitta*), he fashioned a Brahma-body twelve *yojanas* in height.
Rising up into the air, he entered the interior of the lunar mansion; then, as the moon was emerging from the edge of the forest, he split it open and [entered] the lunar mansion.
Leaving his place and coming forward, he made a resolution, thinking, "Let the great multitude see me. When the multitude saw him, they said, "It is true, sirs!
Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s words were true; let us honor the Great Brahmā as he approaches!
Taking perfumes and garlands, they surrounded Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house and stood there. The Great Man [passed] from head to head...

Having wandered around Benares for seven days and knowing that he had been seen by the great multitude, he abandoned his twelve-league body and assumed a form the size of a human being; even as the great multitude looked on, he entered the leather-worker’s house.
When the people saw him, they cried out, "Our Great Brahmā has descended! Bring mats! and they covered the dwelling with a great many mats.
Having surrounded and encircled him, he stood there.
The Great Being sat down in the midst of his bed of glory. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā stood nearby. Then he asked her, "Is the season right for you, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā?
"Yes, noble sir," she replied. "Take the child given by me," [he said], pointing with his thumb.
It did not touch the circle of her navel. By the mere act of touching it, the embryo was established.
The Great Man said, "Maṅgalikā, by this much your water for washing my feet shall become the consecration water for all the kings in the whole of Jambudīpa;
you may stay," and having manifested his Brahma-form, he departed while the great multitude was looking on.
Having ascended into the air, he entered the solar disc itself. From that time forth, she became known as Brahmapajāpatī.
There was no one who could even obtain water for washing her feet.
Thinking, "We shall have Brahmapajāpatī dwell within the city," the brahmins placed her upon a golden palanquin and [carried her] as far as...
Because his lineage was impure for seven generations, they did not allow him to take the palanquin. Sixteen Brahmins of pure birth took it up.
The others, having honored him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, entered the city and said:
"Sirs, it is not possible to dwell in the house of the defiled Brahmā-Pajāpatī; we shall purchase a site and build a house. Until that is completed..."

"Let her dwell in the pavilion for that long," they said, and so they had her reside in the pavilion. From that time on, those who wished to pay homage while standing within the range of his vision could do so by giving a kahāpaṇa;
those wishing to pay homage within the range of hearing could do so by giving a hundred;
those wishing to pay homage nearby in a place where ordinary conversation could be heard could do so by giving five hundred; and [those wishing to pay homage] at the back of his feet...
Those wishing to pay homage by placing their heads [at her feet] obtained it by giving a thousand;

those aspiring for the water used for washing her feet obtained it by giving ten thousand. From the time she departed from outside the city until she reached the pavilion within the city, the wealth she acquired amounted to exactly one hundred crores.

All of Jambudīpa was stirred; consequently, all the kings sent a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], thinking, "We shall perform the consecration with the water for washing the feet of Brahmadattā," and they obtained it. While she was still dwelling in the pavilion, the birth from the womb took place.
The boy obtained through the Great Being was handsome and endowed with the marks of excellence. By the power of Mahābrahmā...
When it was announced, "A son has been born," the entire land of Jambudīpa was filled with a single tumultuous roar.
Thinking, "May there be a source of jewels for the prince's milk," wealth gathered from here and there amounted to a thousand millions (*koṭi*). At this point, even the residence was completed.
Thinking, "We shall perform the naming ceremony for the prince," they prepared the residence, bathed the boy with scented water, and adorned him.
Because he was born in a maṇḍapa, they gave him the name Maṇḍavya.

As the prince grew up in comfort and reached the age for learning crafts, those throughout all of Jambudīpa who were masters of various skills came into his presence and taught him their arts. The prince was intelligent and wise; whatever he heard or perceived...
He learned by taking up [the texts] as if they were being strung together; whatever he grasped remained fixed like oil poured into a golden vessel.
There was no portion of the scriptures that had reached his lips which he did not master.
Brahmins followed him wherever he went, and he maintained them as his dependents. In his home, eighty thousand Brahmins ate their regular meals.
His house had seven great gate-towers. On auspicious days, the wealth sent by the inhabitants of Jambudīpa amounted to a thousand crores.
The Bodhisatta reflected: "Is the prince negligent or diligent? Then, having understood his state, [he considered:]...
Thinking, “He has become one who feeds only brahmins; he does not know that where a gift is given it becomes of great fruit.

I shall go and subdue him,” he put on his robe, took his alms-bowl, and—thinking, “The gateway is too narrow, so it is not possible to enter through the gate”—arrived through the air at the place where eighty thousand brahmins were eating.
He descended into the open space. Prince Maṇḍabya, having had a golden ladle brought, was serving the food, saying, "Give soup here, rice there," when he saw the Bodhisatta.
Enraged like a venomous snake struck by a staff, he spoke this verse:
"Whence have you come, you ill-clad one?"
“Like a dust-demon from the ruins,
wearing a rag from a rubbish heap around his neck—
who are you, indeed, that you are unworthy of offerings?”
Then the Great Being, without becoming angry, spoke to him as he was instructing him:
"O illustrious one, this food has been prepared by you;
let them eat it, consume it, and drink it."
"You know me as one who lives on what is given by others;
arise, you shall receive alms along with your son.
He spoke thus, showing that this was not prepared for those like you.
“This food has been prepared for me by the brahmins;
it is intended for my benefit, and I have faith in this.
Move aside from here! Why do you stand in my way?”
“People like me do not give to you, O low-born one.
Then the Bodhisatta thought: “The gift should indeed be given to anyone—whether virtuous or devoid of virtue.
For just as a seed, when planted in either low ground or on dry land, thrives by means of the essence of the earth and the essence of water,”
To show that there is no such thing as fruitlessness— that what is sown in a fertile field yields great fruit, like seed sown in a good field—
he spoke this verse:
“On dry land and in the lowlands they sow the seed;”
"Reaping the fruit in a fertile field,
give a gift with this same faith,
so that you may perhaps please those worthy of offerings."
Then the prince, overcome with anger, rebuked the gatekeepers and others, saying, "By whom was entrance granted to this shaveling?
and added: "The fields in the world are known to me, wherein I plant my seeds."
“Those brahmins who are endowed with birth—these, indeed, are the most excellent fields in this world.
Having spoken this verse, he said: “Beat this man with a bamboo staff, seize him by the neck, pass him through all seven gate-towers, and then cast him outside! Then the Great Man said to him:
“You would be digging a mountain with your fingernails, chewing iron with your teeth, and treading upon fire, were you to revile a seer.
Having spoken thus, he added: “If this [seer] were to seize me by the hand or the foot and cause me pain...”
“Having spoken this, the seer Mātaṅga, who was resolute in truth, rose into the air out of compassion for living beings and descended into the middle of the street.
The Blessed One, having attained omniscience, spoke this verse to clarify that matter:
“Having said this, the seer Mātaṅga, resolute in truth...”
"He departed into the sky while the brahmins looked on.
At that very moment, the chief king of the deities who protect the city twisted Maṇḍabya’s neck.
His face was turned around until it faced backward; his eyes rolled back, and saliva flowed from his mouth.
He vomited, and his body became rigid as if it had been impaled upon a stake.
Eighty thousand attendant yakkhas and eighty thousand brahmins did exactly the same. Going with great speed, they reported this to Brahman Pajāpati.
She came in great haste, and seeing that calamity, she spoke this verse:
“The head is thrust back,
the arm is stretched out and useless;
the eyes are white like those of the dead.”
“Who made this son for me?
Then they informed her:
“A recluse wearing coarse garments has come here.”
"Like a dust-demon from the ruins,
wearing a rag from a rubbish heap around his neck,
he indeed made this your son."
Upon hearing this, she understood: "The noble one who bestows honor upon me must have come out of compassion, having perceived that my son was negligent. Then she asked her attendants:
"To which direction did he of vast wisdom go?
Young men, tell me this matter."
"Having gone there, let us confess our transgression,
so that we might perhaps regain our son's life.
They said:
“He of vast wisdom went through the air,
like the full moon on the fifteenth day;
yet he also proceeded toward the eastern direction.”
“The seer is true to his word and of noble character.
Then the Great Man, from the moment he stepped onto the street, made this resolution:
“Let no tracks of my footsteps be obscured by elephants, horses, and the like; let only Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā see them, and no others.”

Having wandered for alms and taken enough mixed rice to sustain him, he sat down in the retiring hall, ate, and when he had finished eating a little, he placed the remainder of his food back in the alms bowl.
Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, descending from her palace and entering the street, saw the footprints and thought:
"These belong to my husband, the noble one who bestows honor."
Having approached by following his footprints, he paid homage and said: "Venerable sir, forgive the offense committed against you by my servant;
for you are not known to be subject to anger. Grant life to my son.
Having spoken thus—
“The head is thrust back,
the arm is stretched out and useless;
the eyes are white like those of a dead man.”

“Who has done this to my son? he asked, and spoke this verse. The Great Being said: “We do not do such a thing; rather, having seen [someone] harming a renunciant, it must have been done by spirits, yakṣas, or deities who have respect for renunciants.
“Venerable sir, let there be no ill-will in your mind; let it be the work of deities. May you live in happiness, venerable sir.”
"O deity, furthermore, Venerable Sir, how should I proceed? "In that case, I shall tell you the remedy.

There is some food remaining from what was eaten in my alms-bowl; pour a little water into it, take a small portion, and place it in your son's mouth. As for the remainder, stir it into the water-vessel for the eighty thousand brahmins."
She placed it in his mouth. Thinking, "I shall do so," she took the food, paid homage to the Great Man, and having gone, did exactly that.
As soon as it was placed in his mouth, the elder brother-king thought, "While my sister-in-law is preparing the medicine herself, we can do nothing," and he released the prince.
He too spat it out, having never before experienced any suffering.
He appeared as if he were his natural self. Then his mother said to him: "See, dear son, the misfortune that has befallen your family preceptors who are devoid of shame and moral dread;
but ascetics are not like this, dear son—feed an ascetic!
Thereupon, she had the leftovers stirred into a water-bowl and made the brahmins swallow them. At that very moment, the yakkhas released [the boy].
They fled. The brahmins, repeatedly spitting and rising up, asked, "What was put into our mouths?
[The answer was: "It is the leftover food of the Mātaṅga seer. They thought, "We have been made to eat the leavings of a caṇḍāla;
we are now born as non-brahmins. From now on, other brahmins will not share [in common] with us, thinking, 'These are impure brahmins.'"
Then, having fled and gone to the kingdom of Majjha, they were called "Brahmins of the Chief Seat" because they ate in the royal palace.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was wandering about, suppressing evil and humbling those of arrogant nature. Then one...
"The ascetic named Jātimanta thinks, 'There is no one equal to me,' and he does not even acknowledge others.
Seeing that ascetic living on the banks of the Ganges, the Bodhisatta went there, thinking, "I shall humble his pride.
The ascetic Jātimanta asked him, "What is your caste, sir? "I am a caṇḍāla, teacher," he replied. "Begone, caṇḍāla! he said.
“Go away, outcaste! Dwell below the Ganges; do not make the water of the upper Ganges impure by your spittle.
The Bodhisatta said, “Very well, teacher; I shall dwell in the place you have indicated,” and while dwelling below the Ganges, he resolved:
“May the water of the Ganges flow upstream! Early in the morning, the ascetic Jātimanta went down to the Ganges.

He rinsed his mouth with water and washed his matted locks. While chewing his tooth-stick, the Bodhisatta let drop morsel after morsel of saliva into the water. He even washed the remnants of the tooth-stick right there.
He made a resolution such that it would not stick elsewhere but would adhere only to the matted locks of the ascetic; thus he disposed of both the saliva and the tooth-stick upon the ascetic.
It settled right back into his matted locks.
The ascetic, feeling remorseful and thinking, "This must be the work of a caṇḍāla," went and asked:
"Sir caṇḍāla, was this water of the Gaṅgā made to flow upstream by you? "Yes, teacher. "In that case, you..."
"Do not dwell below the Ganges; dwell above the Ganges. "Very well, Teacher," he replied, "I shall dwell in the place you have indicated.
While dwelling there, his supernormal power subsided, and the water returned to its natural course.
Once again, the ascetic met with that same calamity. He went back once more and asked the Bodhisatta, "O Caṇḍāla, this..."
“Do you make the water of the Ganges flow against the current at one time and with the current at another? “Yes, teacher. “Outcaste!
Since you do not allow those who have gone forth and dwell in happiness to live in peace, may your head split into seven pieces on the seventh day!
“Very well, teacher; but I shall not allow the sun to rise.”
Then the Great Being thought, "This curse will fall upon him alone; I shall protect him.
Out of compassion for living beings, on the following day he used his supernormal power to prevent the sun from rising. The range of a possessor of supernormal power is indeed inconceivable;
from that time forth, the dawn was no longer seen, and there was no distinction between night and day.
There was no one to employ him in occupations such as farming or trading.
People, thinking, "Is this a spirit-possessed man, or one possessed by a bhūta, a devatā, a nāga, or a supaṇṇa? became distressed and wondered, "What should be done?
Then they thought, "The royal court is indeed possessed of great wisdom; it will consider what is for the welfare of the world."
“We can; let us go there. Having gone to the royal palace, they reported the matter to the king.
Although the king was terrified upon hearing it, he assumed an air of fearlessness and said, “Do not be afraid, dear ones.

An ascetic possessing the power of birth (jātimantatāpasa) who dwells on the banks of the Ganges will know this matter. Having questioned him, we shall be free from doubt. With just a few attendants, he sent men...
Having approached the ascetic together and exchanged greetings, he asked him about that matter. The ascetic said:
"Yes, Great King, there is a certain caṇḍāla who makes this water of the Gaṅgā flow downstream at times and upstream at times;
I have said something regarding that matter, so ask him—he will know."
The king went to the presence of the ascetic Mātaṅga and asked, “Venerable sir, did you not allow the sun to rise?
“Yes, Great King. “For what reason, venerable sir? “Because of the ascetic Jātimanta, Great King;
I shall let it rise when the ascetic Jātimanta comes, pays homage to me, and asks for forgiveness. The king went and said, “Come, Teacher!”
“Beg the ascetic’s forgiveness,” he said. “Great King, I do not pay homage to a caṇḍāla,” he replied.
“Do not act thus, teacher; look upon the face of the land! But he refused once again.
The king approached the Bodhisatta and said, “The teacher does not wish to grant forgiveness. “Until he has been forgiven, I will not release the sun,” he declared.
The king thought, “This man does not wish to ask for forgiveness; as long as he has not asked for forgiveness, he will not release the sun.
What use have we for that ascetic? We shall look after the world. He said, “Go, sirs, to the presence of the ascetic;
seize him by his hands and feet, lead him to the feet of the Mātaṅga seer, make him prostrate there, and cause him to ask for forgiveness.”

"Out of compassion for the people," he said. Those royal officers went, did as they were told, and having brought him back, they made him lie down at the feet of the seer Mātaṅga and asked for his forgiveness.
"I am one who forgives what ought to be forgiven; however, this matter will rest upon him alone."
"When I release the sun, its rays shall strike his head, and then his head will split into seven pieces.
However, let him not suffer that calamity; come now, lower him into water reaching up to his neck and place a large lump of clay upon his head. Then I shall release the sun."
"The sun’s rays, having fallen upon this lump of clay, will shatter it into seven pieces.
Now, if he were to abandon this lump of clay, dive in, and emerge through another landing place—if you tell him this, his safety will be ensured.
Those people said, "We shall do so," and they acted accordingly. For him too, his safety was secured in that very same way. From there...
From that time on, thinking, "Birth is no cause; within those who have gone forth, only virtue is the cause," he abandoned pride regarding birth and lineage and became free from conceit.
Thus, when the ascetic Jātimanta had been subdued, the great multitude recognized the Bodhisatta’s power, and a great clamor arose.
The king requested the Bodhisatta to go to his own city.
Having given his promise, the Great Being thought, "I shall tame those eighty thousand brahmins and release them from their vow," and he went to the city of Majjharāja.
Upon seeing the Bodhisatta, the brahmins exclaimed, "Sirs, here comes that great thief! Now indeed—"
“Having eaten the leftovers of all these people, they have become non-Brahmins,” he will make us public;
thus our residence here will not be possible, so we shall kill him beforehand. Having approached the king again, they said:
“Great King, do not think that this outcaste ascetic is a person of good character; he possesses a powerful spell.”
He knows how to take the earth and turn it into space, and space into earth; he takes what is distant and makes it near, and what is near he makes distant;
having turned back the Ganges, he makes it flow upwards; if he so desires, he can seemingly lift up the earth and cast it down.
Furthermore, the mind of another cannot be grasped at all times; this [is the case] here.
“If he gains a foothold, he might destroy even your kingdom, create a threat to your life, or bring about the extinction of your lineage.
Do as we say, Great King; it is fitting to have him executed this very day.
Kings, indeed, rely on the trust of others; thus, by means of the words of many, he reached a conclusion. The Bodhisatta—
Having wandered for alms in the city and eaten mixed rice at a place convenient for drinking water,
he went to the royal garden and sat down on the auspicious stone slab, free from fear due to his innocence. Because of the non-application of his knowledge—
which was capable of recollecting eighty eons, forty in the past and forty in the future— for only a mere moment, [he did not immediately recall his previous births].

When the time came, he was unable to act; without informing anyone else, the king went there himself and, out of negligence while the Great Man sat in a state of non-restraint, struck him with a sword and divided him into two parts.
In this king’s realm, the eighth rain fell as a shower of iron lumps, and the ninth as a shower of mud. Thus, nine showers fell upon this kingdom as well.
And so the king, together with his retinue, was reborn in the Great Hell. Therefore the wise Saṅkicca said:
“Having struck down Majjha, the illustrious Mātaṅga, he, along with his followers, was destroyed; then the Majjha forest became [desolate].”
In this way, the state of being a forest for the "Middle-Forest" (Majjhārañña) is to be understood. However, by virtue of the seer Mātaṅga, that very same place is called the "Mātaṅga Forest.

66. "Responses to questions" (*pañhapaṭibhānāni*) means explanations of questions. "An adverse [response] should be made" (*paccanīkaṃ kātabbaṃ*) means an adverse response ought to be performed. "They would not think so" (*amaññissanti*) means they would be as if they had taken a contrary part; such is the meaning. 67.
"After having investigated" (*anuviccakāraṃ*) means after having examined, reflected upon, and weighed; it is said, "perform what ought to be done."
“Sādhu hoti” means he is beautiful. For if people like you were to see me and go for refuge to me, while seeing a Nigaṇṭha and going for refuge to the Nigaṇṭha, they would think:
“Why does this Upāli go for refuge only to what he has already seen?
Thus, censure would arise; therefore, he shows that careful investigation is appropriate for those like you. “They would carry a banner” means...

It is said that having obtained such a disciple, they would raise a banner and wander through the city proclaiming, "A certain king, or royal minister, or merchant has gone for refuge to us and become our disciple. Why?
Because they thought, "In this way, our greatness will be made manifest," and [they wondered], "If he were to ask, 'Am I their refuge...'"

"...has gone," remorse might arise; yet, having dispelled that by thinking, "Many know my state of having gone for refuge to them, it would now be painful to turn back," he will not retreat. Therefore it is said: "They would carry a banner. 68.
"Like a well" means standing like a prepared water-pit. "Family" means your residence. It should be given...
"You might think" means that previously, when he saw ten, twenty, or even sixty people arrive, he would give without saying "there is nothing.
Now, he instructs him: "Do not cut off these gifts for them merely because of my having gone for refuge; indeed, one must give to those who have arrived.
"This has been heard by me, Bhante"—from whom was it heard? From the presence of the Nigaṇṭhas; they say...

In noble families they proclaim thus: "We say that a gift should be given to anyone who has arrived, yet the ascetic Gotama says, 'A gift should be given to me alone... [etc. ...what is given to other disciples does not bear great fruit.
It was with reference to this that the householder said, "I have heard this."
69. "Graduated discourse" (*anupubbikathā*) means the sequential teaching as follows: after giving comes virtue; after virtue, heaven; and after heaven, the Path.

In this context, "discourse on giving" means: this so-called giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, the foundation of wealth, a refuge, a shelter, and the ultimate resort for one who has fallen into adversity—in both this world and the next.
There is no shelter, foundation, object, refuge, cave, destination, or ultimate resort equal to giving.

For in the sense of being a shelter, this is like a lion-throne made of jewels; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth; in the sense of being a support, it is like a supporting rope.
Indeed, in the sense of crossing over suffering, it is a boat; in the sense of providing consolation, it is a hero in battle.
In the sense of providing protection from fear, it is a well-constructed city; in the sense of being unstained by the impurity of stinginess and the like, it is a lotus;

in the sense of burning them up, it is fire; in the sense of being difficult to approach, it is a venomous snake. In the sense of being fearless, it is a lion; in the sense of possessing great strength, it is an elephant;
in the sense of being esteemed as highly auspicious, it is a white bull; in the sense of bringing one to the land of safety, it is a cloud.
The King of Horses. This gift was indeed my path; this is my own lineage. While fulfilling the ten perfections, I performed many great sacrifices:
the Velāma Great Sacrifice, the Mahāgovinda Great Sacrifice, the Mahāsudassana Great Sacrifice, and the Vessantara Great Sacrifice.
When I was a deer, I offered myself up into the blazing mass of fire for the sake of those who had come as supplicants.
The mind was captured. For he delivered a discourse connected with the virtues of giving, such as: "Giving indeed bestows the attainment of Sakka in the world;

it bestows the attainment of Māra; it bestows the attainment of Brahmā; it bestows the attainment of a Wheel-turning Monarch; it bestows the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple; it bestows the knowledge of Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
it bestows the knowledge of supreme enlightenment," and so forth.

However, because one who gives a gift is able to undertake moral discipline (*sīla*), he spoke on the discourse of moral discipline immediately thereafter. Regarding the "discourse on moral discipline":
this moral discipline is indeed a support, a foundation, an object of focus, a refuge, a shelter, a destination, and the ultimate resort;
this moral discipline is my lineage—[I was present] during the time of the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, during the time of the Naga King Bhūridatta, and during the time of the Naga King Campeyya.

In my infinite successive existences—during the time of the elephant king Sīlavā, during the time of the elephant king Mātuposaka, and during the time of the elephant king Chaddanta—I fulfilled my virtue (sīla).
Indeed, there is no support equal to virtue for the attainments of this world and the next;
there is no foundation, no object of focus, no refuge, no shelter, no destination, and no ultimate resort equal to virtue; there is nothing like the ornament of virtue.
There is no ornament; there is no flower like the flower of virtue; there is no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue.

For even the world with its devas never tires of beholding one adorned with the ornament of virtue, bedecked with the blossoms of virtue, and anointed with the perfume of virtue—such is the discourse connected with the qualities of virtue.
However, in order to show that this heaven is obtained by relying upon this virtue, he spoke on the subject of heaven immediately after the discourse on virtue. Regarding the "discourse on heaven":
this so-called heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; here there is constant play and constant attainment of prosperity.
The gods of the Four Great Kings enjoy divine pleasure and divine prosperity for nine million years.
They experience [these pleasures] for thirty-three koṭis and six hundred thousand years—such is the discourse connected with the qualities of heaven.
Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas are never exhausted when speaking of the excellence of heaven.
For it has been said: "In many ways, monks, I might speak a discourse on heaven," and so forth.
Having thus enticed him with talk of heaven, he then decorated the elephant and, as if cutting off its trunk, spoke in the manner beginning with,

"Sensual pleasures have been described by me as having little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger therein is even greater," in order to show that even this heaven is impermanent and unstable, and that no desire or passion should be directed toward it.
He spoke of the danger (*ādīnava*), the degradation (*okāra*), and the defilement (*saṃkilesa*). In this context, "danger" means fault (*dosa*). "Degradation" means a low state or base condition.
"Defilement" means the defiling of beings within *saṃsāra* by those [faults], as it is said: "Alas, beings are indeed being defiled!
Having thus stirred them with the danger of sensual pleasures, he proclaimed the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) in renunciation (*nekkhamma*). "A fit mind" (*kallacitta*) means a healthy mind.
"Sāmukkaṃsikā" means drawn out by oneself, grasped and extracted by one's own self;
it is seen through self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), meaning it is not shared with others. And what is this? It is the teaching of the Noble Truths. For that very reason he said:
"Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."

"Stainless and free from impurity": it is stainless (*viraja*) due to the absence of the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; it is free from impurity (*vītamala*) because of the departure of the stains of passion and so forth.
"The eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*): in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*, this is a name for the three higher paths, and in the *Cūḷarāhulovāda*, it is a name for the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).
Here, however, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is intended. To show the manner of its arising, [it says]: "Whatever..."
"Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation," he said.
For it arises by taking cessation as its object, thus penetrating all conditioned things by way of its function.
It is "one who has seen the Dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammo*) because the Noble Truths have been seen by him; this same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Doubt has been crossed.
"By this" means one who has crossed over doubt. "One whose perplexity has departed" means one from whom uncertainty has vanished.

"Attained to intrepidity" means having reached fearlessness. Where? In the Teacher’s dispensation. "Not dependent on another" means that he does not rely on others as a condition, nor does he act here according to the faith of another.

70. Having received it with the mind, having rejoiced in it, and having praised it with speech, he gave his approval. "I shut" means I block or cover. "Unshut" means not blocked, opened, or uncovered. 71. Dīgha Tapassī heard:
It is said that from the time he had departed, [Dīgha Tapassī thought]: "The householder is wise;
the ascetic Gotama is accomplished in vision and speaks of the way out. He will have confidence upon seeing him, and also in his discourse on the Dhamma."

"He will have confidence; having gained confidence, he will go for refuge. Has the householder already gone for refuge, or has he not yet gone?"—thus he wandered about with his ears strained to listen. Therefore, he heard it first.

"Very well, sir," [said the doorkeeper]. Overwhelmed by intense grief, even though he had heard the words "Stop right there," he did not perceive their meaning and continued to converse with the doorkeeper.
"In the middle gate-hall" means: for a house that has seven gate-towers, the fourth gate-tower starting from either the very innermost or the very outermost; for one with five, the third;
for one with three, the second gate-tower is called the "middle gate-hall. However, in the case of one with only a single gate-tower...
In the middle of the house, there was a central hall with a middle door, supported by an auspicious pillar.
Furthermore, it is said that this house had seven gate-towers, or even five.
73. All terms such as "the foremost" (*aggam*) and so forth are synonyms for one another. Regarding the phrase *yaṃ su dā*, here *yaṃ* refers to Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta.
*Sudanti* is merely a particle. *Pariggahetvā* means having taken hold of him while encircling his belly with that very upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
*Nisīdāpeti* means he makes him sit down slowly, as if setting down a large oil jar, saying, "Slowly, teacher! Slowly, teacher!
*Dattosi* means "Are you born dull-witted? *Paṭimukko* means taken hold of by being wrapped around the head.

Even though such words as "Aṇḍahārakoṭi" and so forth are indeed coarse speech, he speaks them because, due to the intense grief arising from the changed state of his attendant, he speaks without even noticing that he is saying this. 74.
"Bhaddikā, bhante, āvaṭṭanī," the Nigaṇṭha says, referring specifically to his own deception; the lay follower [speaks] by himself...
The path of stream-entry has been penetrated. "Therefore indeed" (*tena hi*) is merely a particle; the meaning is simply, "Venerable sir, I shall give you a simile.

Or it is a statement of reason: "For the reason that your teaching is not conducive to liberation, whereas my Teacher’s teaching is conducive to liberation, for that reason I shall give you a simile"—this is what is meant.
75. "Upavijaññā" means one who has reached the time of giving birth. "Makkaṭacchāpakaṃ" means a young monkey.
"Having bought it, bring it here" means: bring it after paying the price. For in marketplaces, they sell playthings such as monkeys, whether animate or inanimate.
It is with reference to this that he said this. "Dyed" means having taken a thick, heavy coating of yellow dye.
The meaning is: "I desire this which has been dyed and given.

*Ākoṭitapaccākoṭitaṃ* means both polished and, having been turned over, polished again and again. *Ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ* means well-polished on both sides with a gem-stone, having its surface produced by rubbing.
"Indeed, it is 'capable of taking dye' because it takes up dye whether animate or inanimate; therefore he said this.
It is 'not capable of being pounded' because, when an animate [object] is placed upon a pounding board and pounded in its belly, the belly breaks and excrement comes out;
when the rest [of the body] is pounded, the head breaks and the brain comes out."
It comes out. Being without consciousness, it goes away in pieces. Therefore he spoke thus.
"Not capable of being rubbed" means that when a conscious object is rubbed with a gem-stone, it becomes hairless and skinless; even an unconscious object reaches the state of being reduced to powder.
Therefore he spoke thus. "But capable of being dyed by fools" means by those who are foolish, that is, those of dull intelligence.
One who is fond of colors produces mere passion and becomes beloved.
However, to the wise, the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas or any other path of useless discourse, such as the *Bhārata*, *Rāmāyaṇa*, or the abduction of Sītā, is indeed disagreeable.

"Not capable of inquiry" (*anuyogakkhamo*) and "not capable of investigation" (*vimajjanakkhamo*) mean that one does not tolerate either inquiry or examination; it is like threshing husks while seeking rice grains.
Like a plantain tree, it is empty and hollow when one searches for its core. "It is pleasing to the wise" means that the discourse on the Four Noble Truths is dear to the wise;
even if one listens to it for a hundred years, one never reaches satiety.
Therefore he spoke thus. But as for the word of the Buddha, however much one delves into it, it remains as deep as the great ocean.

"He becomes" means "capable of inquiry and capable of analysis"; thus he spoke. "Listen, you who are my disciple"—he began to speak in praise of the Blessed One, meaning "listen to the virtues of him [who is your teacher].
76. "Of the wise one": "wisdom" (dhīra) refers to sagacity; that which is wisdom, understanding... [and so on] ...right view; by that—
"I am the disciple of the wise one who is endowed with skill regarding the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the possible and impossible;
he is my Teacher"—thus the connection should be understood for all the following phrases. "Of one whose heart-thorns are shattered" means one whose five heart-thorns have been destroyed.

They are called "victors" (vijayā) because they have conquered, are conquering, or will conquer all worldlings. Who are they? They are the Māra of Death, the Māra of Defilements, and the Māra of the Son of a Deva.
He is "Vijitavijaya" because he has conquered those who are themselves conquerors; [this is] the Blessed One (Bhagavā) of that Vijitavijaya.

"Of the one without distress" (anīghassa) means of one who is free from suffering both through the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha) and the suffering of karmic results (vipāka-dukkha). "Of the one with a perfectly even mind" (susamacittassa) means of one whose mind is perfectly equanimous even toward Devadatta, Dhanapālaka, the Elder Aṅgulimāla, the Elder Rāhula, and others among gods and humans.
"Of the one with mature virtue" (vuddhasīlassa) means of one whose conduct has increased. "Of the one with excellent wisdom" (sādhupaññassa)...
Of one possessed of beautiful wisdom. Of one who has crossed over the unevenness: of one who stands having crossed over and transcended the unevenness of passion and so forth.

Of one who is stainless: of one whose stains of passion and so forth have been removed. Of one who is contented: of one whose mind is satisfied. Of one who has vomited out worldly bait: of one who has cast off the strands of sensual pleasure. Of one who is gladdened: by way of abiding in gladness (*muditā*).
"Of one who rejoices"—this may be a repetition, for one speaks of even a single quality again and again by way of serene confidence (*pasāda*).

"Of one who has performed the ascetic life" (*katasamaṇassa*) means of one who has performed the state of an ascetic (*sāmañña*), that is, one who has reached the pinnacle of the ascetic's duty (*samaṇadhamma*).
"Of a man" (*manujassa*) refers to a single being according to worldly convention; "of a person" (*narassa*) is a repetition. If it were stated otherwise, each verse would [lack its proper sense].
The ten qualities are not sufficient.
"Of the Venayika" means of the leader of beings. "Of the one with delightful Dhamma" means of the one with pure Dhamma. "Of the illuminator" means of the one who sheds light.
"Of the Hero" means of the one endowed with vigor. "Of the Bull" (nisabha) [applies] to all [terms]: usabha, vasabha, and nisabha.
In the sense of being peerless, he is "the bull" (*nisabha*). "Profound" (*gambhīra*) means possessing profound qualities, or profound by virtue of his qualities.
"Attained to silence" (*monappatta*) means attained to knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Possessing the Veda" (*vedasampanna*)—here "Veda" is said to be knowledge; thus, it means one endowed with that.
"Established in the Dhamma" (*dhammaṭṭha*) means established in the Dhamma. "Restrained" (*saṃvuta*) means one whose [senses] are closed off.
"Of the Naga" means because of four reasons he is a naga. "Of the secluded forest-dweller" means of one who has a secluded dwelling place.
"Of the respondent" means of one endowed with the wisdom of responding. "Of the sage" (mona): "mone" is said to be knowledge;
thus, it refers to one endowed with that, or to one whose defilements have been shaken off. "Of the tamed" means of one who is free from deceit.
"Of the seventh sage" means of the seventh counting from the six sages beginning with Vipassī. "Of the one who has attained the Brahma-state" means of the one who has attained the supreme state.
"Of the bathed one" means of the one whose defilements have been washed away. "Of the one skilled in verses" means of the one skilled in composing verse-lines by combining syllables and so forth.
"Of the one who has known the Vedas" means of the one who has realized knowledge. "Of the first-giver" means of the giver of the gift of Dhamma for the very first time.
“Of the capable” (sakkassa) means of one who is competent. “Of one who has attained what is to be attained” (pattipattassa) means of one who has attained those qualities that are to be attained.

“Of the expounder” (veyyākaraṇassa) means of one who illuminates the meaning by way of detailed exposition. For there is no textual passage (tanti-pada) called “unexpounded” (abyākata) by the Blessed One;

rather, the meaning of all [passages] has been explained. “Of one possessing insight” (vipassissa) means of one who possesses clear vision. “Of one not drawn forward” (anabhinatassa) means of one who is not attracted. “Not drawn back” (no apanatassa) means of one who is not repelled.
"Of one not followed by others" means of one whose mind is not followed by defilements (*kilesa*).

"Of one who has eaten" means of one who is unbound. "Of one of vast wisdom" (*bhūripañña*): "vast" (*bhūri*) is said to be the earth; the meaning is that he is endowed with wisdom equal to that earth—extensive, great, and wide. "Of one of great wisdom" (*mahāpañña*) means endowed with great wisdom.
"Of one unsmeared" means unsmeared by the defilements of craving and views. "Worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*) means worthy of receiving an offering (*āhuti*).
"Of the Yakkha": the Blessed One is called a "Yakkha" in the sense of manifesting supernatural power (*ānubhāva*) or in the sense of being worthy of praise (*ādissamānaka*).
Therefore he said, "of the Yakkha. "Great" means of great [power]. "I am his disciple" means: "I am the disciple of that Teacher who possesses such various qualities.
Through the very path by which the lay follower attained splendor, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) arrived. Thus, regarding the subject of the analytical knowledges...

Standing there, while praising the abandonment of the defilements by the One of Ten Powers, he answered the meaning of the question, "Householder, whose disciple do you consider me to be? [Sutta 77] "When were they gathered?
means when were they brought together. It occurred to him thus: "This [discourse] was just now [spoken] by the ascetic..."
“Having gone into the presence of Gotama and returned, when were these colors combined by him?”—thus he spoke.

“One might weave a variegated garland”: by one’s own skill and because the flowers themselves are of various colors, one might weave a variegated garland consisting of single-stalked and other such varieties.
“Even so, venerable sir,” [refers to] here, a great heap of various flowers.
The mass of colors belonging to the Blessed One, as large as Mount Sineru, should be seen as being like various kinds of flowers;
the householder Upāli is like a skilled garland-maker; and the householder’s weaving together of those various colors is like the garland-maker’s weaving together of a variegated garland.
"Hot blood gushed from his mouth. For the Blessed One, unable to endure that honor, thought:
"This householder now has no need for us; starting tomorrow, even if I take fifty or sixty people with me, I will not be allowed to enter his house and eat; my pot of rice is broken! Then to him...
Due to the loss of his attendant, a powerful sorrow arose within him. For these beings think only of themselves.

When that sorrow arose in him, there was heat within; his blood melted and, blown out by a great wind, it gushed from his mouth like dye placed in a bowl being stirred by a strong breeze. This was blood that had been stored away.
However, only a few beings were able to survive after vomiting [the poison]. The Nigaṇṭha fell right there on his knees;
then, having carried him out of the city by means of a litter, they took him in a palanquin and went to Pāvā.
Not long after, he passed away in Pāvā. In this sutta, the teaching of the Dhamma is concluded from the perspective of the person who gains knowledge through an exposition (ugghāṭitaññū).
The commentary on the Upāli Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, from the Papañcasūdanī, is completed. 7.
The commentary on the Kukkuravatika Sutta.
78. Thus have I heard: this is the Kukkuravatika Sutta. Therein, "among the Koliyas" means in the country of that name.
For that [place] is so called because it was the residence of the Koliya princes established in the city of Kola.
"Among those Koliyas" refers to that country. "Wearing yellow garments": it is said that at the time when that market town was founded, [the people] were dressed in yellow robes.
The people were celebrating a festival. At the conclusion of the festival, as they were assigning a name to the town, they called it Haliddavasana.
The meaning is that he dwelt there, making that place his alms-resort village.
Although no specific monastery is mentioned here, it should nevertheless be understood that he dwelt in a lodging suitable for Buddhas. "Govatika" means...
The one who has undertaken the cow-vow wanders about like a cow, placing horns on his head and tying a tail to himself while grazing on grass together with the cattle.
"Acela" means naked and without clothes. "Seniya" is his name. "Kukkuravatikā" means one who has undertaken the dog-vow;
he performs every action of a dog. Both of these were companions from their childhood play in the dust.
"Helpers. "Like a dog, having curled up": a dog, when sitting near its master, sits scratching the ground with two paws while making the barking sound of a dog;
this [man] also, thinking "I shall perform the action of a dog," exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, scratching the ground with both hands, [lowered his] head...
Shaking himself and making the sound "bhū," he sat down like a dog with his hands and feet drawn in.
"Cast upon the ground" means placed on the earth. "Fully undertaken" means taken up after having made it complete. "What is the destination? means what is the result.
"What is the future state? means where will one be reborn in the future life? "Enough" means that it will become unpleasant for him.
He resists up to the third time. "The dog-duty" (*kukkuravata*) means the undertaking of the dog-vow.
"Develops" (*bhāveti*) means increases. "Complete" (*paripuṇṇa*) means without deficiency. "Continuous" (*abbokiṇṇa*) means uninterrupted. "Dog-conduct" (*kukkurasīla*) means the behavior of a dog.
"Dog-mind" (*kukkuracitta*) means [the thought]: "From today onwards, I shall do what is to be done by dogs. Thus...

"Arisen mind. "The dog-like mode" means that there is the manner of walking of dogs, the manner of standing, the manner of sitting, the manner of lying down, and the manner of defecating and urinating;
furthermore, there is the manner of baring one's teeth upon seeing other dogs as one walks—this is called the "dog-like mode," and the meaning is that he develops this. By this, I...

In the passage beginning with "by virtue" (*sīlena*), the meaning is: "by means of this conduct, or by the undertaking of vows, or by the practice of difficult austerities, or by the holy life (*brahmacariya*) consisting of abstention from sexual intercourse.
"A god" (*deva*) refers to any one among Sakka, Suyāma, and others. "A certain god" (*devaññatara*) refers to a particular deity among those occupying the second, third, or other celestial stations.
"Holding wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) refers to having arisen by perceiving as a path leading to the world of the gods that which is actually not a path leading to the world of the gods.
That is what is called his wrong view. "I declare he has a certain destination"—for there is no destination for him other than hell or the animal realm;
therefore he spoke thus. "Lying down properly" means lying down without being mixed with [wrong] views.
"Venerable sir, I do not weep over this that the Blessed One says of me"—that which the Blessed One says of me, venerable sir...
The meaning is: "I do not weep, I do not lament, and I do not wail over this declaration of the Blessed One.
Thus, the meaning here should be understood in terms of its transitive function (*sakammaka*), and not merely as the shedding of tears.
"O mother, they weep for one who is dead, or for one who, though living, is not seen."
“O mother, seeing me alive, why do you weep for me, mother?”—this is the application here.
Furthermore, “But this, venerable sir,” means: “But indeed, venerable sir, this dog-vow has been undertaken by me for a long time;
whether it succeeds or fails, there is no growth [in merit]. Thus, “so much... [is said].
"I weep, venerable sir, reflecting upon my own failure, thinking: 'The deed I have done has become fruitless. 80.
"Like cows," and so forth, should be understood in the same manner as explained regarding the dog-vow (kukkuravata) and others. "Gavākappa" means "cow-like conduct" (go-ākappa).
The remainder is exactly the same as what was said regarding the dog-like conduct (kukkura-ākappa). However, just as there, when seeing other dogs, [people] bared their teeth...
The manner of walking; likewise here, having seen other cattle, the manner of walking with ears pricked up is to be understood.

The rest is just the same. 81. Why did he begin this teaching with the words, "Puṇṇa, there are these four kinds of kamma"? For this teaching was introduced by way of the performance of certain types of kamma;
and when this tetrad of kamma is explained, the performance of these [other types] will become clear. Thus he began this teaching.
Furthermore, he began this teaching because he knew that if this very fourfold classification of kamma were taught, they would understand it; then one would go for refuge and another,
having gone forth, would attain arahantship— thus realizing that this alone was suitable for them,
he commenced the discourse.
In this context, "black" refers to the black action consisting of the ten courses of unwholesome kamma. "Black result" refers to the dark result, because it leads to rebirth in the states of misery.
"White" refers to the white action consisting of the ten courses of wholesome kamma. "White result" refers to the bright result, because it leads to rebirth in the heavenly realms.
"Black-and-white" refers to mixed action. "Black-and-white result" refers to a result consisting of both pleasure and pain.

For having performed a mixed deed, one born in the animal realm through unwholesome [kamma] experiences pleasure during the course of existence through wholesome [kamma], such as when reborn as a state-elephant or in similar positions.
Conversely, even though reborn in a royal family through wholesome [kamma], one experiences suffering during the course of existence through unwholesome [kamma].
"Neither black nor white" refers to the volitional action of the four paths, which brings about the exhaustion of kamma.
For if it were black, it would give a black result; if it were white, it would give a white result.
But because it does not give both results, and because its result is neither black nor white, it is called "neither black nor white.
This, first of all, is the meaning in the summary.
In the *Niddesa*, however, "afflictive" (*sabyābajjha*) means accompanied by suffering.

Among the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so forth, the twelve unwholesome volitions (*akusalacetanā*) that have reached the state of impulsion through the act of grasping and so on via the door of the body are called the "afflictive bodily formation. Those same twelve [volitions] which, via the door of speech, bring about the occurrence of vocal utterance through the impulsion of the jaw are called the "vocal formation.
[The mental formation refers to] those not yet reached by either of these two impulsions, occurring when one is thinking in solitude.

The mental formation is that which occurs at the mind-door. Thus, it should be understood that in all three doors, unwholesome volition—classified as bodily misconduct and so forth—is what constitutes "formations" (*saṅkhāra*).
In this sutta, volition (*cetanā*) is the primary focus; in the Upāli-sutta, it is karma (*kamma*).
"Having formed" (*abhisaṅkharitvā*) means having accumulated or having made into a mass. "A world with affliction" (*sabyābajjhaṃ lokaṃ*) means they are reborn into a world accompanied by suffering.
"Afflictive contacts touch them" means that contacts which have suffering as their result touch them. "Entirely suffering" means uninterrupted suffering.
"From what has come to be" (*bhūtā*) is an ablative used in the sense of a cause; from a deed that has come to be, the arising of a being occurs.
This is what is meant: beings perform deeds according to how they are, and by means of such a deed, in accordance with the nature of that deed, [the result arises].
Their rebirth occurs. For this very reason it was said: “By what one does, by that one is reborn.

And here, the word “by that” refers to karma, as if it were stated as such; yet rebirth itself occurs through the result (vipāka). Since karma is the cause of the result, therefore the meaning here is:
“one is produced by that karma which serves as the root cause. “Contacts contact” means by which...
Born through the ripening of karma, they are touched by the contact that is the result of that same karma. "Heirs of karma" means they are the recipients of karma;
I say that karma alone is their inheritance and their possession.
"Unafflicted" means free from suffering. In this section, there are eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions (cetanā) occurring at the door of the body.
That which occurs at the body-door is called bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*). That which occurs at the speech-door by that same [process] is called verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*).

Those eight [mental factors] occurring at the mind-door, together with the three types of volition of the lower jhānas, are called non-afflictive mental formation (*abyābajjhamanosaṅkhāra*). Let it be granted that the volition of the jhānas is so;
but how is it that the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) [volition] has become "non-afflictive mental formation"? At the time of introducing the meditation object (*kasiṇa*)—
And they are obtained at the time of practicing the kasiṇas. Sense-sphere volition is conjoined with first-jhāna volition; fourth-jhāna volition is conjoined with third-jhāna volition.
Thus, in all three doors, it should be understood that wholesome volition alone—classified as bodily good conduct and so forth—is "formations.
The third section should be understood by way of the mixture of both.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as among humans," it should be understood that for humans, pleasure at one time and pain at another is indeed manifest.

Among the gods, however, this applies to the earth-dwelling devas; and among those in the states of misery, it should be understood that pleasure at one time and pain at another occurs for the *vemānika* petas.
This is likewise found even among animals such as elephants and others.
"Therein" means among those three types of kamma. "The volition for its abandonment" means the path-volition for the purpose of abandoning that [kamma].
Indeed, once kamma has been reached, there is no other state more pure than path-volition.

Furthermore, having reached this fourfold classification of kamma, the twelve unwholesome volitions are called "black," the wholesome volitions of the three planes are called "white," and the path-volition—
"Not black, not white" is how it is handed down. 82.

"May I receive it, venerable sir"—this [thought] occurred to him: "For a long time indeed I have exhausted myself by aligning myself with the faction that leads to no liberation, like one who rolls about thinking, 'I shall bathe on the bank of a dry river,' or like one who threshes chaff."
Having thought, "No purpose has been accomplished; well then, let me apply myself to spiritual practice (yoga)," he spoke.
Then the Blessed One established the probation for former members of other sects (tīrthika-parivāsa) in the Khandhaka on the proper method:
"I, venerable sir, [name], a former member of another sect, standing on the level of a novice, desire [to enter] this Dhamma and Vinaya."

Having formally undertaken [the training] in this manner—saying, for example, "Venerable sir, I request four months of probation from the Saṅgha regarding my higher ordination"—he dwells in probation.
It is with reference to him that the Blessed One said, "Seniya, whoever was formerly a member of another sect," and so forth.
In that context, the word "going forth" (pabbajjā) is used merely for the sake of euphony; for indeed, he goes forth even without having completed the probation.

He obtains [the probation]. However, one who seeks full ordination (*upasampadā*) must undergo the period of probation while fulfilling the eight duties, such as entering villages at the proper time and so forth.
"With a mind resolved" means with a mind satisfied by the fulfillment of the eight duties. This is the summary here.
For a detailed account, this probation for those of other sects (*titthiyaparivāsa*) is found in the commentary on the *Pabbajjā-khandhaka* of the *Samantapāsādikā*, the Vinaya commentary.
It should be understood in the manner already stated. Furthermore, *apica me'ttha* means "and moreover, here for me.
*Puggalavemattatā viditā* means "the diversity of individuals is known. This shows that it is clear to him: "This person is worthy of probation;
this one is not worthy of probation. Then Seniya thought: "Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha's teaching, wherein [the truth] is thus tested and scrutinized!"
“They take what is appropriate and discard what is inappropriate. Then, having conceived even greater zeal for the going-forth, he said, “If, venerable sir,” and so forth.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, perceiving his intense aspiration, thought, “Seniya does not deserve probation,” and addressed a certain bhikkhu: “Go, bhikkhu, bathe Seniya, give him the going-forth, and…”
“Bring him here. Having done so, he ordained him and brought him into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, while seated with the community, conferred full ordination upon him.
Thus it is said: “The naked ascetic Seniya received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One;
he received full ordination.”
"Not long after his full ordination" means having become fully ordained, it was not long at all.

"Withdrawn" means withdrawn from both sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements, by way of body and mind. "Diligent" means not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject.
"Ardent" means ardent through the ardor of energy known as both physical and mental. "Resolute" means through lack of regard for body and life.
*Pesitatta* means one whose self has been surrendered. *Yassatthāya* means for the sake of which. *Kulaputtā* refers to sons of good family who possess proper conduct.

*Sammadeva* means precisely by way of cause and reason. *Tadanuttaraṃ* means that unsurpassed [state]. *Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ* refers to the fruit of arahantship, which constitutes the culmination of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Path.
It is indeed for the sake of this that sons of good family go forth.

"In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāve*). "Having realized by direct knowledge for oneself" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having made it manifest through one's own wisdom;
the meaning is that he knew it independently of others. "Having attained and dwelt" (*upasampajja vihāsi*) means that having reached and accomplished it, he lived.
While dwelling thus, he directly knew: "Birth is exhausted... [and so on]... there is no further state of being."

Having thus shown the stage of his reflective review, it was said—"Furthermore, the venerable Seniya became one among the Arahants"—in order to conclude the teaching precisely at the pinnacle of Arahantship. In that context, "one" (*aññatara*) means a single individual.
"Arahant" (*arahanta*) means he became included within the Arahants, the disciples of the Blessed One; this is the intended meaning.
The remainder is clear in all respects.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Kukkuravatika-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
8. Commentary on the *Abhayarājakumārasutta* (Discourse to Prince Abhaya) 83.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Abhayasutta*. In this context, "Abhaya" is his name. "Prince" (*rājakumāra*) means he was the legitimate son of Bimbisāra.
"Bring a charge" means bring an accusation of fault. "A denizen of hell" (*nerayika*) means one who is reborn in hell. "One who remains for an eon" (*kappaṭṭha*) means...
"Enduring for an eon" means that it cannot be cured even by a thousand Buddhas.
"Unable to vomit it up" means that being unable to release both ends and speak [the answer], he will not be able to vomit it up—that is, to bring it out.
"Unable to swallow it down" means that having found fault with the question, being unable to take it back, he will not be able to swallow it down—that is, to make it enter within.
"So be it, venerable sir," the Nigaṇṭha thought: "The ascetic Gotama is dividing my disciples and taking them away;
well then, I shall compose a question such that, when asked, the ascetic Gotama—sitting there squatting on his heels—will not be able to rise.
Having been served his meal from the house of Abhaya, he ate the rich food.
Having formulated many questions—thinking, "In this one the ascetic Gotama will point out such a fault;
in that one, such another"—and having set them all aside, he saw this question at the end of four months. Then it occurred to him:
"Whether in the asking or the answering of this question, it is impossible to find fault with it; this is the very essence of the inner core."
“Who indeed will take this up and refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama?
Then, concluding, “Prince Abhaya is wise; he will be able to do it,” he had him learn it.
Out of a desire for debate, Prince Abhaya accepted his words, saying, “So be it, venerable sir.”
84. "Today is indeed the wrong time"—this question was prepared over four months.

Therein, he thought thus, considering that if he were to take this [point] and provide an answer to it, the portion of the day would not suffice. "Now" (*dāni*) means "tomorrow. "With himself as the fourth" (*attacatuttho*):
why did he not invite many others? It is said that such was his thought: "If many were sitting together..."
If he gives only a little and speaks while bringing forward another sutta, another reason, and another such instance, then there will be either a quarrel or a mere clamor.
Furthermore, if I invite him alone, even then reproach will arise against me, saying:
"This Abhaya is so miserly that he invites the Blessed One day after day..."
“Even though he saw him traveling with a hundred or even a thousand monks, he invited him alone.
“But in this way, there will be no fault,” [the king thought], and so he invited him together with three others, himself being the fourth.
“It is not, Prince, one-sided in this regard; indeed, Prince, in this question it is not one-sided.”
There is an answer. For such speech as this, the Tathāgata might speak it or he might not speak it;
the meaning is that he would speak it if he saw the purpose in speaking it, and he would not speak it if he did not see it.
Thus, with a single word, the Blessed One pulverized the question prepared by Mahānigaṇṭha over four months, like a mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt.
"Anassuṃ nigaṇṭhā" means the Nigaṇṭhas have perished.
"He was sitting on his lap" means he was sitting on his thighs.

For when those who maintain the doctrine of "stains" (lesavādino) set forth their argument, they sit down taking up some fruit, flower, or piece of cloth. When they achieve victory for themselves, they overwhelm the opponent [with it].
When another wins, they display agitation—as if eating fruit, as if plucking flowers, or as if reading from a book.
But he thought: "This is a Perfectly Enlightened One, who has entered the fray and crushes the doctrines of others.
If I win, that is well; but if I do not, I shall pierce the boy and make him cry."
"Therefore, sirs, look! This boy is crying; stand up for now, and we shall know later.

Having said this, he took the boy and sat down. But the Blessed One was a far more excellent debater than the prince—by a factor of a thousand or even a hundred thousand—and thinking, "I shall break his argument by using this very boy as an illustration," he said: "That..."
"What do you think, prince?"—with these words he began.
Therein, "should place in the mouth" means one should put it in the mouth. "I would remove it for him" means I would take it away from him.
"By the very first effort" means by the very first application. "Unreal" means having an unreal meaning. "Not true" means not factual. "Not connected with the goal" means...
It is not connected with welfare, nor is it based on progress. "Unpleasant and disagreeable" means neither pleasant nor agreeable.
In this same manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
Therein, regarding the side of the unpleasant, the first speech is: calling one who is not a thief a thief; calling one who is not a slave a slave; [calling] one who is not improperly engaged...

"Twofold application" refers to speech that proceeds [in this way]: "The Tathāgata does not speak such [words]. "Second speech" refers to speech proceeding by way of [calling] a thief "thief," and so forth;
the Tathāgata does not speak that either. "Third speech" is: "Now, due to a lack of merit, he is miserable, ugly, and of little influence;
even while standing here, you do not perform merit again. During the second mental moment, how [could one say] from the four states of deprivation?

"You shall not be released"—this is the speech to be spoken with the welfare of the great multitude as the primary concern, with the Dhamma as the primary concern, and with instruction as the primary concern.
In that regard, "the Tathāgata knows the proper time" means that for the purpose of explaining those words during that third proclamation, the Tathāgata knows the proper time;
the meaning is that he explains only after knowing the time for the great multitude to receive and grasp it.
In the section on the beloved, the first statement is called the "Discussion on the Non-Foundational. It should be understood as follows:

It seems that several rogues, wishing to deceive an elderly villager who had come to the city and was drinking in a tavern, stood at the place where he was drinking and, while drinking liquor with him, said:
"Even his lower garment and upper cloak, and all the goods in his hand—"
Thinking, "We shall take him," they made an agreement: "Let us each speak a story from our own personal experience;
whoever says it is 'untrue,' or whoever does not believe what has been told, we shall seize him and make him a slave.
They then asked the elder, "Father, do you agree? He replied, "So be it, father."
One rogue said: "Sirs, when I was in my mother's womb, she had a craving for wood-apple fruit (*kapittha*).
Since she could not find anyone else to bring her wood-apples, she sent me.
When I went there and was unable to climb the tree, I took hold of myself by the feet and flung myself over the tree like a club; then—"
Wandering from branch to branch, I was unable to descend after gathering the fruits.
Returning home, I brought a ladder, climbed down, and went to my mother’s side, giving the fruits to her; they were large, the size of buckets.
Then, while sitting on a single seat with me, my mother ate sixty of those fruits. By me—
Of the fruits brought by Ekucchaṅga, the remainder belonged to the village families, both small and large.
Our house was sixteen cubits long; having removed all other household goods, it was filled with wood-apples (kapiṭṭhaphala) up to the roof.
Taking the surplus beyond that, they made a heap at the door of the house, which was eighty cubits high.
"It was like a mountain. How can one believe such a thing, Master Sakka?
The village elder sat in silence, and when questioned at the conclusion of everyone's talk, he said:
"It will be so, dear ones; it is a great kingdom, and because of the greatness of that kingdom, it is possible to believe. And just as he did, so too—
When the others had also spoken such groundless words, he said: "Listen to me too, sirs;
it is not only your families that are noble. Our family is also a great family. Moreover, among all our remaining fields, our cotton field is the largest.
In the midst of that cotton field, which measures many hundreds of karīsa, there stands a single great cotton tree eighty cubits high."
It came into being. It had five branches; among them, the remaining branches did not bear fruit, and on the eastern branch there was only a single fruit, about the size of a large bowl.
It had six sections, and in those six sections six cotton-clusters blossomed.
Having shaved my beard and bathed and anointed myself, I went to the field and saw those cotton-clusters in bloom.
Standing right there, I reached out my hand and caught them. Those six bales of cotton became six slaves endowed with great strength.
They all fled, leaving me alone; I have not seen them for so long a time, but today they are seen—these six persons.
You are named Nanda, you are named Puṇṇa, you are named Vaḍḍhamāna, and you are named Citta.
Having said, "You are named Maṅgala; you are named Poṭṭhiya," he rose up and, while they were still sitting, seized them by their topknots and stood there.

They were unable even to say, "We are not slaves. Then, dragging them away, he brought them before the court of justice, branded them with the mark of slavery, and made them his slaves for life, using them for his own purposes. Such words as these the Tathāgata does not speak.

The second type of speech consists of various forms of praising others—motivated by worldly gain, flattery, and the like—as well as "animal talk" (tiracchānakathā), such as talk about thieves, talk about kings, and so forth. The Tathāgata does not speak that either.
The third type of speech is discourse based on the Noble Truths, which even the wise do not reach satiety with, even if they hear it for a hundred years.
Thus, the Tathāgata speaks neither all unpleasing speech nor all pleasing speech;
rather, he speaks only when the third [occasion] has arrived, without letting the proper time for speaking pass.
In this context, it should be understood that the preceding simile of the young boy was given with reference to unpleasing speech.

87. "Or is it known by way of its basis?"—he asks this to inquire whether that [knowledge] appears to the Tathāgata at that very moment through the knowledge that arises according to the occasion (*ṭhānuppattika-ñāṇa*).
"Known" (*saññāta*) means recognized, understood, and made manifest. "The element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātu*) is the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
this is a designation for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). That has been thoroughly penetrated by the Blessed One; it has come into the possession of the Blessed One.
Therefore, whatever he desires, all that appears to him immediately upon the thought. The rest is clear everywhere.
This teaching of the Dhamma, however, is concluded by way of the person who is to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
Thus ends the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Abhayarājakumārasutta* is finished.
9. The commentary on the *Bahuvedanīyasutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Bahuvedanīyasutta*. Therein, "the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga": *Pañcakaṅga* means...
His name: because he was endowed with the five parts known as the axe, the hatchet, the chisel, the staff, and the black cord, he was known as Pañcaṅga (the Five-Parted).
*Thapati* means a master carpenter. *Udāyī* refers to the wise Elder Udāyī.
89. *Pariyāya* means a reason. *Dve pānandā* means "both, Ānanda. *Pariyāyena* means by way of a reason. Herein—

Furthermore, they should be understood as twofold by way of being bodily and mental; threefold by way of pleasure and so forth; fivefold by way of the faculties, beginning with the faculty of pleasure;
sixfold by way of the doors, beginning with that born of eye-contact; eighteenfold by way of the modes of mental application (*upavicāra*), such as:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one applies oneself to a form that is a basis for joy"; and sixfold as the joys based on the household life.

There are six kinds of joy based on renunciation, six kinds of grief based on the household life, six kinds of grief based on renunciation, six kinds of equanimity based on the household life, and six kinds [of equanimity] based on renunciation; thus there are thirty-six.
These thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present—thus one hundred and eight feelings are to be understood.
90. "Ānanda, these five strands of sensual pleasure"—this is a separate connection.
Not only were feelings described by the Blessed One starting from two, but by way of a method, even a single feeling was spoken of.
Demonstrating this, he began this teaching in order to support the argument of the official Pañcakaṅga.
"More excellent" (*abhikkantatara*) means more beautiful. "More sublime" (*paṇītatarā*) means more satisfying.
And here, from the fourth jhāna onwards, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; that too is called "pleasure" in the sense of being peaceful and in the sense of being sublime.
Six kinds of pleasure based on the household life have been mentioned. Cessation (*nirodha*) is called "pleasure" by way of the pleasure of not being felt.
For there is what is called the "bliss of felt experience" (vedayita-sukha), which arises by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure and by way of the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti).

Cessation (nirodha) is what is called the "bliss of non-felt experience" (avedayita-sukha). Thus, whether it be the bliss of felt experience or the bliss of non-felt experience, it has become exclusively blissful in the sense of bliss defined as the state of being free from suffering.
91. “In whatever place” means in whichever location. “Pleasure is found” means that either felt pleasure (*vedayita-sukha*) or unfelt pleasure (*avedayita-sukha*) is found.
“The Tathāgata designates all that as pleasure” means that the Tathāgata designates all of that state free from suffering as pleasure itself.
Here, the Blessed One, taking the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as the primary example, [speaks] with reference to individuals who are to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
He brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely with the pinnacle of arahantship.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bahuvedanīya Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
10. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta. 92.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Apaṇṇaka Sutta. Therein, "a journey" means a journey not made in haste. 93.
Why did he say, "But do you have [anyone] there, householders"? It is said that the village was situated at the entrance to a forest wilderness (*aṭavi*). Various kinds of...
Ascetics and brahmins, having traveled along the road during the day, arrive at that village in the evening seeking a place to stay.
Those people spread out beds and seats for them, wash their feet, anoint their feet, give them suitable drinks, and invite them for the following day to offer alms.
With hearts full of faith, consulting with them, they speak thus:
They asked, "Householders, do you hold any view? "No, venerable sir," they replied.
"Householders, the world does not proceed without a view; it is fitting to choose one view, accept it, and adopt it.
Adopt the view that 'the world is eternal,'" they said, and then they departed. On another day, others arrived. They too—

They asked the same question. They reported to them, “Yes, venerable sirs, in previous days, ascetics and brahmins like you came, caused us to adopt this view that ‘the world is eternal,’ and then departed.
[The Buddha said: “Those fools, what do they know? ‘This world is annihilated’—adopt such a view of annihilationism! Thus, they too adopted the view of annihilationism.

Having caused them to take it up, they departed. By this means, they caused others to adopt the view of partial-eternalism, others the view of finite-and-infinite, and others the view of the elusiveness of death;
thus they caused the sixty-two views to be taken up. Yet they were unable to remain established even in a single view.
Finally, the Blessed One arrived. For their benefit, he asked, "But do you have [any views], householders? and so forth.
