In this context, "possessing form" (*ākāravatī*) means possessing a cause, having a reason. "Irrefutable" (*apaṇṇaka*) means uncontradicted, leading to non-duality, and characterized by a categorical grasp. 94.
The ten-based wrong view beginning with "there is no giving" has been explained in detail below in the Sāleyyaka Sutta. Likewise is right view, which is its opposite. 95.
"The advantage in renunciation" (*nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ*) refers to the benefit that exists in their state of having emerged from the unwholesome, as well as the side of purification.
The side of purification; the meaning is that they do not see it. "Persuading by means of unrighteous things" means causing others to perceive what is not true. "Exalting oneself" means:
"Who else besides me is able to make others accept their own view?"—thus one elevates oneself. "Contempting another" means:
among all these people, not even a single one is able to make others accept their own view... [the rest of the sentence follows].

"He cannot" means that he thus casts another down below. "But previously indeed" means that even while one is adopting wrong view, good virtue has already been abandoned and a state of immorality has become manifest. "Thus for him these" refers to these seven factors beginning with wrong view.
Furthermore, by way of their arising repeatedly, those very same factors—conditioned by wrong view—are numerous evil unwholesome states.
"Phenomena indeed arise.
In this context, "therein" means among those views held by those ascetics and brahmins. "A misfortune" (*kaliggaha*) means a defeat.
"Poorly grasped and poorly undertaken" means wrongly apprehended and wrongly clung to. "Standing pervading one side" means standing entirely on one part.
Having pervaded and resolved upon one's own position alone, one remains [thinking], "If indeed there is no other world," and in that state, it brings about security.
"Leaves behind" means he avoids. "Instruction in the True Dhamma" means making known the dhamma as it truly is.
"Seizing the opportunity" means seizing victory. "Well-composed and undertaken" means well-grasped and well-attended to.
"Standing pervading both sides" means standing having pervaded and resolved upon both ends—both parts—namely, one's own position and the opponent's position, thinking:
"Even though it may be that 'there is another world,' or even though it may be that 'there is no other world.'"

Even though this is so, it brings about a state of well-being. Furthermore, regarding the "one-sided" (*ekamsa*) and "both-sided" (*ubhayamsa*) [types of action], the meaning should be understood by this same method.
97. "He who acts" (*karoto*) refers to one acting with his own hand. "He who causes to act" (*kārayato*) refers to one causing action through command.

"He who cuts" (*chindato*) refers to one cutting off the hands and other limbs of others. "He who cooks" (*pacato*) refers to one who oppresses with a staff or threatens. "He who causes grief" (*socayato*)...
"Causing grief to another" refers to both causing grief oneself through acts such as stealing another's property and causing others to do so.
"Fatiguing" refers to both fatiguing oneself through acts such as depriving another of food or imprisoning them, and fatiguing others to do the same.
"Trembling and causing to tremble" means trembling oneself at the time of another’s trembling, and causing another to tremble.

"Taking life" means both killing a living being oneself and causing another to kill. In this way, the meaning in all instances should be understood through the dual sense of performing the act and causing it to be performed.
"A breach" means a breach in a house. "Robbery" means a great plundering. "House-breaking" means plundering by surrounding a single house.
"Standing in ambush" means standing on a path for the purpose of seizing those who come along. For one who performs [the act]...
"Evil is not done": even for one who acts with the perception, "I am doing some evil," no evil is done; there is no evil.
However, the meaning is that beings possess such a perception as "we are doing [it]. "With a razor-edge" means with a razor-rim, or with an edge like the blade of a razor.
"A single lump of flesh" means a single mass of flesh. "A heap" refers to that very same thing.
This is a synonym. "On that account" means on account of the making of a single meat offering.

With reference to the people on the southern bank—who are harsh and cruel—it is said, "they kill," and so forth. With reference to those on the northern bank—who possess faith, are confident, and hold the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha as their own—it is said, "they give," and so forth.
In this context, "sacrificing" means performing a great sacrifice. "By self-control" means by the control of the sense faculties and by the observance of the Uposatha.
"By restraint" means by the restraint of moral virtue (*sīla*). "By the speaking of truth" means by truthful speech. "Coming" (*āgama*) means arrival; the meaning is "occurrence.
In every respect, they reject the very performance of both evil and merit. The "white side" (the virtuous path) is also to be understood according to the method already stated. The rest here...
It is exactly the same as what was stated in the previous section. 100.
Regarding the statement "there is no cause, there is no condition": here, "condition" (*paccaya*) is a synonym for "cause" (*hetu*).
By both terms, they negate the very existence of the defilement-condition of bodily misconduct and so forth, as well as the purification-condition of bodily good conduct and so forth. There is none.

"There is no strength, no energy, no human power, no human exertion"—this means there is no strength, energy, human power, or human exertion that can be exercised by a person to defile or purify sentient beings.
"All beings" indicates without exception those such as camels, oxen, and donkeys. "All creatures" refers to those with a single sense-faculty.

They say "living being" (*pāṇa*) by way of [the expression] "a two-facultied living being," and so forth. They say "all beings" (*sabbe bhūtā*) with reference to beings within egg-shells and womb-sheaths.
They say "all creatures" (*sabbe jīvā*) with reference to rice, barley, wheat, and so on; for among these, they possess the notion of a "living soul" (*jīva*) due to their state of growing.
"Without mastery, without power, without vigor" means that they lack any mastery, strength, or vigor of their own.
Regarding the phrase *niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā*: here, *niyati* means necessity (*niyatatā*). *Saṅgati* means the movement of the six classes of beings (*abhijāti*) from one place to another.
*Bhāva* means inherent nature (*sabhāva*) itself. Thus, they are "transformed" (*pariṇatā*) by necessity, by movement, and by nature;
that is, they have reached various states. For whatever is destined to become in whatever manner, it becomes exactly so.
They show that he who ought to exist does not exist. "In the six classes of birth" means that they experience pleasure and pain while remaining within these six classes of birth;
they show that there is no other ground for pleasure and pain.
In this context, the six classes of birth are: the black class of birth, the blue class of birth, the red class of birth, and the yellow class of birth.

“White birth” and “supremely white birth. In this context, the fowler, the pig-killer, the hunter, the fisherman, the thief, the executioner, or whoever else performs cruel deeds—this is called “dark birth.
They say that monks are of “blue birth,” for it is said they consume the four requisites as if they were thorns. “Monks...”
And "those who live on thorns"—for this indeed is their own canonical text (*pāḷi*). Alternatively, they say that some who have gone forth are called "thorn-livers.
For their canonical text also reads: "the ascetics who live on thorns. They say that the Nigaṇṭhas of the blood-lineage are the "single-robed ones" (*ekasāṭaka*).
It is said that these are whiter than the previous two. They are householders who are disciples of the naked ascetics (*acelaka*).
They say that those of the yellow birth-class (*haliddābhijāti*) are even more senior than the Nigaṇṭhas among their own supporters who provide them with requisites.
They say that Nanda, Vaccha, Saṅkicca, and this [monk] belong to the white birth-class (*sukkābhijāti*); it is said that they are whiter than the former four.
But they say that the Ājīvakas belong to the supreme white birth-class (*paramasukkābhijāti*); it is said that they are whiter than all others.
In this regard, their doctrine is as follows: all beings first become bird-catchers and the like; then, becoming purified, they become Śākya-monks;
then, becoming further purified, they become Nigaṇṭhas; then, Ājīvaka disciples; then, Nanda and others; and finally, they become Ājīvakas.
The "white side" (the path of purification) is to be understood by reversing what has been stated. The remainder here is exactly the same as what was stated in the previous section.

Among these three views, however, the view of non-existence (natthikadiṭṭhi) obstructs the result of action (vipāka), the view of non-doing (akiriyadiṭṭhi) obstructs the action (kamma), and the view of causelessness (ahetukadiṭṭhi) obstructs both. In this regard, by one who obstructs the action, the result is also obstructed;
and by one who obstructs the result, the action is also obstructed. Thus, all of these are identical in meaning.
Those who reject both [the existence of the past and the future] are nihilists, as well as proponents of non-causality and proponents of non-action.
As for those who, having adopted their doctrine, sit in night-quarters or day-quarters to recite and investigate it—[thinking], "There is no giving, there is no sacrifice;
no evil is done by the doer; there is no cause, there is no condition"—in that regard:
Wrong mindfulness settles upon the object; the mind becomes one-pointed; the impulsion-moments (javana) rush forth.
In the first impulsion, they are curable; likewise in the second and so on. In the seventh, even for Buddhas, they are incurable and irreversible, like the thorn of Ariṭṭha.
Therein, one person enters one [of these wrong views], another two, and another even three; and when one has entered, two [others] follow.
Even when three [of the four paths] have been entered, one who possesses fixed wrong view has reached an obstruction to both the path to heaven and the path to liberation;
he is incapable of going to heaven immediately after that very existence, let alone to liberation.
This being is indeed a "stump in the cycle of existence" (vaṭṭakhāṇu), a guardian of the earth. But is he fixed only in that single existence, or also in another?
One is fixed in this very life, yet by way of habitual practice, one continues to take pleasure in various views even in future existences.
For such a person, there is generally no emergence from existence (bhava).
Therefore, [shun] an unwholesome person as one would a venomous serpent.
"One who desires prosperity and possesses discernment should avoid [these] from afar.
(103) "There is no formless realm whatsoever" means that what is called the formless Brahma-world does not exist in any way at all.

"Mind-made" means made of meditative consciousness (*jhānacitta*). "Perception-made" means made of the perception of the formless jhānas. For the sake of revulsion toward and dispassion for forms alone...
"One who has entered upon the way for cessation" refers to one who is either an attainer or a reasoner. An "attainer" is one who has attained the fine-material-sphere jhānas.
For such a person, there is no doubt regarding the fine-material sphere, but there is doubt regarding the immaterial-sphere world.
He thinks: "I hear those who say that the immaterial states exist and those who say they do not; yet I do not know whether they exist or not. [The fourth jhāna...]"
“Making this my foundation, I shall produce the immaterial-sphere jhāna. If the immaterial states exist, I shall be reborn there;
if they do not exist, I shall be reborn in the fine-material Brahma-world. In this way, my infallible Dhamma will remain truly infallible and uncontradicted.
Thus he practices. But as for the one who is a mere rationalist and has not yet attained jhāna—his [practice is likewise].
There is no doubt regarding the fine-material jhānas, but there is doubt concerning the immaterial world. He thought:
"I hear those who say 'the immaterial states exist' and those who say 'they do not exist,' yet I do not know for certain whether they exist or not.
Having performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, having produced the fourth jhāna, and making that the proximate cause, I shall produce the immaterial-sphere jhāna."
"If the formless realms exist, I shall be reborn there; if they do not exist, I shall be reborn in the fine-material-sphere Brahma-world.
In this way, my unerring Dhamma will remain truly unerring and unfailing"—thus he practices accordingly.
"The cessation of existence" means Nibbāna. "In the presence of one who is prone to passion" means in the presence of one who is attached to the round of existence (vaṭṭa) by way of lust.
“For the sake of conjunction” means for the purpose of binding by way of craving (*taṇhā*). “For the sake of delighting” means for the sake of delighting by way of craving and views (*diṭṭhi*).

“He is practicing” means that he is either one who has attained [the fruit] or one who relies on reasoning. One who has attained is one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*).
For him there is no doubt regarding the formless realms (*ārūpa*), but there is doubt regarding Nibbāna. He thinks: “I hear that ‘cessation exists’ and also that ‘it does not exist.’”
“I do not know for myself. Having made meditative attainment the basis, I shall develop insight.
If cessation occurs, I will attain Arahantship and attain final Nibbāna; if it does not, I will be reborn in the formless realm. Thus he practices.
But the dialectician, though not even an attainer of a single meditative attainment, has no doubt regarding the formless realm.
There is the cessation of existence. He thought: "I have heard that 'there is cessation' and also that 'there is not,' yet I do not know it for myself.

Having performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas and attained the eight meditative absorptions (aṭṭhasamāpatti), I shall develop insight (vipassanā) which has those absorptions as its proximate cause.
If there is cessation, I will reach Arahantship and attain final Nibbāna; if there is not, [then I shall remain as I am]."
One practices with the thought, "I shall be reborn in the formless realm. Here it may be asked:
"Let it be granted that 'there is what is given' and so forth are indeed infallible; but how are 'there is no gift' and so forth infallible?
It is by way of their apprehension. For they are called "infallible" because they have been apprehended as "infallible, infallible."

105. "Four" is a separate connection. The nihilist, the non-causalist, the non-actionalist, and the two who hold such views as "there are no formless realms, there is no cessation"—these five persons are the same as the three persons mentioned above.
The five beginning with the realist are one and the same as the fourth person. To show this point:
The Blessed One began this teaching. In this regard, the entire meaning is quite clear.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Apaṇṇaka-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Chapter on Monks (Bhikkhu-vagga) 1.
Commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhula Sutta.
107. Thus have I heard: this is the Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhulovāda Sutta.

Therein, "dwelling at Ambalaṭṭhikā" means he dwells cultivating seclusion in a palace named Ambalaṭṭhikā, which was built at the edge of the Veḷuvana monastery as a small meditation hall for those desiring solitude. As for Kaṇṭaka, from the time of his birth...
"He was as sharp-witted as a razor"—in the same way, this venerable one also dwelt there, cultivating seclusion even during his time as a seven-year-old novice.
"Emerging from seclusion" means having emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"The seat": there was only the seat already prepared there; he shook it and set it down. "In the water-vessel" means in the water-bowl. There is also a reading: "in the place for water."
"He addressed the Venerable Rāhula" means he addressed him for the purpose of giving him instruction.
For the Blessed One had given many Dhamma teachings to the Elder Rāhula. The *Sāmaṇerapañha* was spoken specifically to the Elder;
likewise the *Rāhulasaṃyutta*, the *Mahārāhulovādasutta*, the *Cūḷarāhulovādasutta*, and this *Ambaṭṭhikarāhulovādasutta*.

For at the age of seven, this venerable one grasped the hem of the Blessed One’s robe and, requesting his inheritance by saying, “O ascetic, give me my inheritance,” was ordained by the Blessed One after being entrusted to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One, thinking, “Young boys indeed speak what is fitting and unfitting; I shall give him instruction,” [addressed] Prince Rāhula...
Having addressed him, he said: “Rāhula, it is not proper for one who is a novice to engage in frivolous talk;
when you speak, how should you speak? And he taught the ten questions and fifty-five answers that have never been abandoned by any Buddha:
“One question, one summary, one exposition; two questions... [and so on] ...ten questions, ten summaries, ten [expositions].”
"Explanations. [He asked: "What is one? 'All beings subsist on nutriment'... What are ten? One endowed with ten factors is called an Arahant"—thus he spoke this question for the novice.
Then he thought: "Young boys are fond of lying; they will say, 'We have seen what we have not seen,' or 'We have not seen what we have seen.'"

Thinking, "I shall give him this instruction," he first showed the four similes of the water-vessels for the sake of easy comprehension, followed by the two similes of the elephants and the one simile of the mirror; having looked upon him with his eyes, he spoke this Sutta.

Furthermore, regarding the four requisites, he taught the turning away from craving, the abandoning of desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure, and the reliance upon a spiritual friend.
Having demonstrated his greatness, he preached the Rāhula Sutta. He preached the Rāhula Saṃyutta to show that desire and lust for states of existence should not be formed wherever one arrives.

He preached the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta to show that desire and lust based on the household life should not be formed by relying on one’s own personal identity, thinking, "I am beautiful; my sphere of form is clear."
In this regard, it cannot be said that the *Rāhula-sutta* was spoken at this specific time; for it was spoken by way of repeated instruction.
The *Rāhula-saṃyutta* was spoken from the time he was seven years old until the time he became a novice monk (*avassika-bhikkhu*).
The *Mahārāhulovāda-sutta* was spoken when he was eighteen years old as a novice. The *Cūḷarāhulovāda-sutta* was spoken when he was a novice monk.
It has been stated. Both the *Kumārakapañha* and this *Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda-sutta* were spoken when [the Buddha] was a seven-year-old novice monk.
Among those, the *Rāhula-sutta* was for the purpose of repeated instruction; the *Rāhula-saṃyutta* was for the purpose of the Elder’s conception of insight (*vipassanā-gabbha*);

the *Mahārāhulovāda* was for the purpose of dispelling sensual desire and lust based on the household life; and the *Cūḷarāhulovāda* was [spoken] at the time when the Elder’s fifteen factors conducive to liberation had reached maturity.

This was said for the purpose of causing [beings] to attain arahantship. And with reference to this, the Elder Rāhula, while speaking of the Tathāgata’s virtues in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, said this:
“As a hen protects her eggs, or as a yak protects its precious tail-hair;”
“The Tathāgata, wise and perfected in virtue, protected me.
This *Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovāda Sutta* was spoken for the purpose of abandoning improper speech and for the purpose of not committing conscious lying regarding the questions of the novice.

In this context, “Do you see? means “Do you indeed see?”; “slight” means “a little”; “the state of a recluse” (*sāmañña*) means the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*); “having turned upside down” means having placed face downwards; “having turned upright” means having placed face upwards.
108. “Rāhula, just as ‘the king’s elephant’—this simile was spoken for the purpose of illustrating one who lacks restraint in intentional lying.
In this context, ‘with tusks like chariot-poles’ means having tusks resembling the poles of a chariot. ‘Grown large’ means fully developed and endowed with stature.
‘Noble-born’ means well-born and endowed with a noble lineage. ‘A warrior of battle’ means one who has previously entered into combat.”
"He performs an action" means he causes death by driving forward those who have arrived or are arriving. Regarding the front part of the body and so forth:
first, with the front part of the body, he causes the enemy's shields, watchtowers, circular walls, and so on, to fall; likewise with the rear part of the body.
Having determined the action by way of the head, he turns around and looks about, thinking, "I will crush this spot"—by this much alone, even a hundred [enemies may be slain].
Even a thousand [people] may be split in two. "Work with the ears" means striking and felling [the enemy] with arrows that have reached their ears.
"Work with the teeth" means piercing the elephants, horses, elephant-riders, horse-riders, foot-soldiers, and so forth.
"Work with the tail" means cutting and splitting [the enemy] by binding them with the tail or with a long stone-staff or an iron club.
"He protects his trunk" means that he protects it by inserting the trunk into his mouth.
"Therein" refers to that action of the elephant. "Not relinquished" means not let go;
he thinks, "I see the victory of others and my own defeat. "He also performs work with his trunk" means [he uses] this club or the acacia-wood pestle.
Or, having seized it, he tramples the ground for eighteen cubits all around. "Relinquished" means let go;
[the elephant] now does not fear anything from the elephant-warriors and so forth, thinking, "Behold our victory and the defeat of our enemies.
"I shall do no evil to him" refers to his transgressions such as wrong-doings (*dukkaṭa*) and other offenses, or even to deeds such as matricide.

There is no evil whatsoever that should not be committed. Therefore, "in this regard, you": since for one who speaks deliberate falsehood there is no evil that should not be done, therefore you must train yourself thus:
"I will not speak falsely even in jest or out of a desire for amusement.
"For the purpose of reviewing" means for the purpose of looking back; it means for the purpose of seeing whatever fault exists in the mouth.
This is what is meant. "Having reviewed, having reviewed" means having looked upon, having looked upon.
(109) "It should not be done even with effort" means it should by no means be done. "You should withdraw it" means you should turn back;
do not do it. "You should give it repeatedly" means you should give it again and again, you should support it, you should do it over and over.
“Training day and night” means training both by night and by day.
“One should be distressed” means one should be oppressed by distress. “One should feel shame” means one should feel ashamed.
“One should feel disgust” means one should arouse disgust as if seeing excrement. However, because mental action has no basis for confession, it is not mentioned here.
It is not stated that [the offenses] must be confessed. However, in how many instances are bodily and verbal actions to be purified, and in how many is mental action?
First, bodily and verbal actions are to be purified within a single morning meal alone.
For after having performed the duties of the meal, one sitting in the daytime resting place should reflect: "From the time of sunrise until this..."
"In this interval between standing and sitting, have I perhaps committed any bodily or verbal action disagreeable to others?
If he knows that there has been such an action, he should confess what is fit for confession and reveal what is fit for revelation.
If there is none, he should dwell in that very joy and gladness. As for mental action, however, in this matter of seeking almsfood—
It should be purified. How? One should ask: "Is there today, in the course of my search for alms-food, any desire, lust, or aversion toward forms and so forth?
If there is, one should resolve with the mind alone: "I shall not act thus again.
If there is none, one should dwell in that very joy and gladness.
"Whether they be recluses or brahmins" means whether they be Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples of the Tathāgata. "Therefore, indeed" means:
because in the past they purified themselves in this way, in the future they will purify themselves, and in the present they are purifying themselves;
therefore, the meaning is that you too, training in accordance with them, must train in this manner. The rest is entirely clear in every respect.
But the Blessed One brought this teaching to its conclusion by way of the person to be guided (neyya-puggala),
as if grasping the peak of a heap of jewels rising as high as the summit of existence with a yojana-long mass of gems.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovāda Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta: 113.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta. Therein, “he followed closely behind” refers to the act of seeing.
Without abandoning his movement and without interrupting it, he followed closely behind,
tracking the Blessed One’s postures step by step. For at that time, the Blessed One was walking forward with a graceful gait,
placing one foot after another, while the Venerable Rāhula followed the Ten-Powered One, keeping pace with every step behind him.
Therein, the Blessed One shone like a noble elephant that has just emerged from its stall to enter the beautiful forest of blossoming *sāla* trees;
and Rāhula-bhadra was like a young elephant calf emerging behind that noble elephant.
At the time of evening, the Blessed One, having come forth from his jeweled cave and set out for his alms-round, was like a maned lion; and Rāhula-bhadra—
And the Blessed One was like a young lion cub emerging from the forest thicket, resplendent with jewel-like mountains, while following after the lion king;
and Rāhula the Fortunate was like a young tiger cub following after the great tiger, powerful in his fangs.
The Blessed One was like the king of the Supaṇṇas emerging from a *simbali* tree, and Rāhula the Fortunate [was like] the [young] Supaṇṇa [following] the king of the Supaṇṇas.

Like a young garuḍa chick that has emerged from behind; the Blessed One was like a king of golden swans leaping into the sky from Cittakūṭa Mountain, and Rāhula Bhadda was like a young swan chick following after the lord of swans.
The Blessed One was like a great golden ship that had plunged deep into a vast lake, and Rāhula Bhadda was like a small boat following behind that golden ship.
The Blessed One was like a universal monarch (cakravartin) traveling through the sky by the power of the precious wheel-treasure (cakkaratana),
and Rāhula-bhadra was like the precious minister-treasure (pariṇāyakaratana) following after the king. The Blessed One was like the moon, the king of stars, proceeding across a cloudless sky,
and Rāhula-bhadra was like the pure medicinal star following in the path of the lord of the stars.
The Blessed One was born into the lineage of Mahā-Sammata, in the royal dynasty of Okkāka; so too was Rāhula-bhadra.
The Blessed One was born into a most pure kṣatriya clan, like milk poured into a conch shell;

so too was Rāhula-bhadra. The Blessed One renounced his kingdom and went forth into homelessness; so too did Rāhula-bhadra. The body of the Blessed One was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
It was as enchanting as a jeweled arch erected in a royal city, and like a *pāricchattaka* tree in full bloom; so it was for Rāhulabhadda as well.

Thus, both of them were endowed with resolute intent (*abhinīhāra*), both were kings who had gone forth, both were delicate nobles, both were golden-hued, and both were possessed of the [major] marks;
traveling one after the other, they proceeded along the same path.
They shone as if overwhelming the splendor of two moon-disks, two sun-disks, and the majesty of Sakka,
Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti,
Mahābrahmā, and others. There, the Venerable Rāhula, walking right behind the Blessed One, [appeared] from the soles of his feet up to the hair at the crown of his head...
He gazed upon the Tathāgata. Seeing the Blessed One’s graceful splendor in the guise of a Buddha, he thought: "The Blessed One shines, his body variegated with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;

because he is encircled by a fathom-wide aura, he is like one standing amidst scattered golden dust, or like a mountain of gold encircled by streaks of lightning, or like a golden casket variegated with jewels drawn forth by a thread from a loom—even though he is covered by a saffron-colored rag-robe."
Like a golden mountain encircled by red woolen cloths; like a golden pinnacle adorned with coral creepers;
like a golden cetiya sprinkled with Chinese lacquer powder; like a golden sacrificial pillar smeared with liquid lac;
like the full moon suddenly emerging from within a mass of red clouds—oh, [the splendor] of that which has been prepared through the power of the thirty pāramīs!
He thought, "This is the attainment of glory for my person. Then, looking at himself, he reflected: "I too am beautiful.
If the Blessed One had exercised the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch over the four great continents, he would have granted me the position of chief counselor.
If that were so, the surface of Jambudīpa would have shone exceedingly. Thus, based on his own physical form, he conceived a desire for the household life.
He gave rise to desire and lust.
As the Blessed One was walking ahead, he thought: "Rāhula’s physical form is now fully developed in skin, flesh, and blood.
The time has come for his mind to leap toward objects of passion, such as forms and so forth; what need is there for further elaboration?"

“Is Rāhula now passing his time? Then, with the mere act of looking, he saw that thought-arising of Rāhula—like a fish in clear water, or like the reflection of a face in a spotless mirror. Having seen it, [the Buddha said]:
“This Rāhula, though being my own son, as he follows behind me, thinks: ‘I am beautiful; my sphere of beauty—’”
"Confident" means that, based on one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*), one generates desire and lust directed toward the household life;

one leaps across where there is no ford, enters upon a wrong path, and wanders in what is not a proper resort. Like a traveler who has lost his direction, he goes toward a destination that should not be gone to.
Furthermore, this defilement, increasing within him, will not allow him to see even his own welfare as it truly is.

It leads to harm for others and to harm for both. Consequently, it will cause one to take rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, in the sphere of hungry ghosts, in the host of asuras, or even in the cramped womb of a mother—thus casting one down into the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra. For this:
Lobha produces what is harmful; lobha agitates the mind.
Fear born from within, people do not perceive it.
One who is greedy does not know what is beneficial; one who is greedy does not see the Dhamma.
When greed overcomes a person, then there is blinding darkness.
Just as a great ship filled with many treasures, when water enters through a crack in its planks, must not be neglected even for a moment,
but requires that the opening be closed with speed, so too this [defilement] must not be overlooked.
As long as this defilement does not destroy the jewels of virtue and the rest within, right then and there—
“I shall restrain him,” he thought, forming this intention. In such circumstances, however, Buddhas employ what is called the "elephant-like gaze" (nāgavilokana).
Therefore, turning his entire body like a golden statue rotated by a machine, he stood facing Rāhula and addressed him.
With reference to this, it is said: “Then the Blessed One, having looked around,” and so forth.

In that regard, the passages beginning with "whatever form" and so forth have been explained in detail in all their aspects in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the aggregates (*khandha-niddesa*).
The passages beginning with "this is not mine" and so forth were spoken in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta*. Why does he ask, "Is it form alone, Blessed One?
It is said that having heard from him, "All form—this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self," [he wondered]: "The Blessed One..."
The method arose: "If it is said that all form is to be seen thus by means of insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), how then should one proceed regarding feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates?
Therefore, standing upon that method, he asks. For this Venerable Rāhula is skilled in methods (*naya*);
when it is said, "This should not be done," he thinks, "This too should not be done, and that too certainly should not be done."
One penetrates this through a hundred methods and even through a thousand methods. The same principle applies when it is said, "This is what must be done.
For this venerable one desires training; even at dawn, he scatters a mere handful of sand in the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber, thinking:
"Today, from the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One, [I shall receive] such and such instruction, and from the presence of my preceptor, such and such..."

“I receive reproach. The Fully Enlightened One, placing him in this foremost position—“Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are desirous of training, Rāhula is the foremost”—established him as preeminent specifically in regard to training.
And that venerable one, in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, uttered that very lion’s roar:
“Having directly known all this, my father, the King of Dhamma,
placed me in the foremost position before the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
I am the foremost among those who desire training, as praised by the King of Dhamma.”
"My excellent companion is one who has gone forth out of faith;
the King of Dhamma is my father, and the Protector of Dhamma is my grandfather;
Sāriputta is my preceptor—this is the entirety of the Victor’s teaching."
Then the Blessed One said, "Rāhula, form as well... and so forth, because it was not only form that must be viewed in this way, but feeling and the other aggregates as well.
"Who now today? means "Who indeed today? It is said that the Elder thought:
"The Fully Enlightened One, knowing the desire and lust residing in my person, [is saying] 'A recluse should not entertain such a thought.'"
He did not speak to him even by way of indirect discourse; he did not send a messenger, saying, "Go, monk, and tell Rāhula: 'Do not again entertain such a thought.
Instead, standing right before me, he gave the "Advice of the Well-Gone One" (Sugato-vāda) face-to-face, like one seizing a thief with his goods by the topknot.
And this so-called "Advice of the Well-Gone One" [is something that] even in incalculable aeons...
“Rare indeed! What wise person of discerning nature would enter a village for alms today after having received such instruction in the presence of a Buddha like this?

Then that venerable one, abandoning his meal-preparation, turned back from the very spot where he had stood while receiving the instruction and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The Blessed One, too—
Seeing the Venerable One returning, he did not say, "Do not return yet, Rāhula;
it is time for your almsround. Why was that? It was because this thought occurred to him: "Let him first enjoy today the ambrosial food of mindfulness directed to the body.
As for the phrase "the Venerable Sāriputta saw": he saw while walking behind after the Blessed One had departed. Regarding this Venerable One...
The conduct for one living alone is different from that for one living with the Blessed One.
For when the two chief disciples dwell alone, they sweep their lodgings early in the morning, attend to their physical needs, enter into meditative attainments, and sit down;
then, according to their own preference, they go out for alms. When dwelling with the Blessed One, however, it is otherwise.
But the elders do not act in this way. For at that time, the Blessed One goes on his first alms-round surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

When he has gone, the elder emerges from his own lodging and, thinking, "In a place where many people dwell, can they all maintain a pleasing appearance, or cannot they? he goes here and there to see what is untidy.
He sweeps the place. If there is refuse that has not been discarded, he discards it.
In a place where drinking water is to be kept, if there is no water-jar, he sets down a water-pot.
Going to those who are ill, he asks: "Friend, what shall I bring for you? What do you need? He goes to those who are young and unmarried—
"Enjoy yourselves, friends; do not be despondent; the teaching of the Buddha has practice as its essence," he exhorted them.

Having done so, he would go on his alms-round last of all. For just as a wheel-turning monarch, when wishing to go anywhere, sets out first surrounded by his army, while the jewel of the general remains behind after having arranged the divisions of the host; so too did the Teacher.
Just as [the king] goes forth, so too does the Blessed One, the Wheel-turner of the True Dhamma, go forth first, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
following him, the Dhammasenāpati—who is like the Jewel of the General—to having performed this task, goes forth last of all.
Having thus gone forth, on that day he saw the venerable Rāhula sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
He saw him. Therefore it is said: "Going behind, he saw.
Then why did he direct him toward mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*)? Because it was suitable for one sitting down.

It is said that the Elder, without even reflecting on the thought, "The Blessed One has taught this man the meditation subject of the physical form (*rūpakammaṭṭhāna*"), [saw] in what manner this man, being unshakable and unbound...
Having sat down and reflected, "This posture is suitable for him as a meditation subject," he spoke thus.

Therein, "mindfulness of breathing" (ānāpānassati) indicates: "Having discerned the inhalation and exhalation, having produced the fourfold and fivefold jhāna therein, and having developed insight, attain Arahantship."

"It bears great fruit": how great is the fruit it bears? Here, a bhikkhu devoted to mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) attains arahantship while sitting in a single session, having exhausted all taints (āsava).
Failing to do so, he becomes one who reaches the goal simultaneously with his death (samasīṣī).
Failing even that, he is reborn in the world of the gods; there, having heard the Dhamma from a son of the gods who is a preacher of the Dhamma...
One attains arahantship; if one fails to attain it from there, one realizes pratyekabodhi when no Buddha has appeared in the world;
and if one does not realize that either, one becomes one of swift direct knowledge in the presence of Buddhas, like the Elder Bāhiya and others.
Thus, [this practice] is of great fruit. "Of great benefit" (*mahānisaṃsa*) is a synonym for the same thing. And this has also been said:
“Mindfulness of breathing, for one by whom it is fulfilled and well-developed,
cultivated in successive stages as taught by the Buddha—
this illuminates the world like the moon freed from clouds.”
Perceiving this great fruitfulness, the Elder exhorted his co-resident disciple to practice there.
Thus, having both taught their respective meditation subjects—the Blessed One the meditation subject of the body and the Elder Ānāpānasati—they departed;
Rāhulabhadda remained behind at the monastery itself. Although the Blessed One knew of his remaining behind, he did not himself...
Taking hard food and soft food, he departed; he did not place it in the hands of the Venerable Ānanda, nor did he give notice to King Pasenadi, Anāthapiṇḍika, or others.
For had they received even a mere sign, they would have brought a meal of rice-cakes.
And just as the Blessed One, so too the Venerable Sāriputta did nothing at all. The Venerable Rāhula remained without food, his meal cut off.

Furthermore, no such thought even occurred to that venerable one: "Even though the Blessed One knew I was left behind in the monastery, he neither took the almsfood he had received himself and brought it back, nor sent it in the hand of another, nor gave notice to the people;
and even though my preceptor knew my state of being left behind, he likewise did nothing at all. How much less, then, could there have been [any offense] on account of that?

He might give rise to self-conceit or overweening pride. However, having continuously attended to the very meditation subject explained by the Blessed One—both before and after the meal, thinking, "In this way form is impermanent, in this way it is suffering, in this way it is foul, in this way it is non-self"—as if fanning a fire, he reflected in the evening: "I have been taught by my preceptor..."
"‘Cultivate mindfulness of breathing,’ he said; yet I will not do as he says. For one who does not follow the instructions of teachers and preceptors is called ‘difficult to admonish.
And there is no affliction more harsh than the arising of reproach, such as: ‘Rāhula is difficult to admonish;
he does not even follow his preceptor’s word. Thus [the Blessed One] spoke, desiring to ask about the method of cultivation.
He went into his presence. To show this, it is said: "Then the Venerable Rāhula," and so forth. 114.

Therein, "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) means being alone. Why [does the Buddha say], "Whatever there is, Rāhula"? The Blessed One, having been asked about mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), explains a meditation subject on form (*rūpakammaṭṭhāna*).
It is for the purpose of abandoning desire and lust for form (*chandarāga*). For such was his thought:
—“Sensual desire has arisen in Rāhula with reference to his own physical body, and the meditation subject on form was already explained to him briefly below.

Now, by means of forty-two aspects, I shall cause him to become dispassionate toward and to dismantle this physical body, so that the sensual desire dependent upon it will be rendered subject to non-arising. Why, then, did he explain the space element in detail?
It is for the purpose of showing derived matter (upādārūpa). For previously only the four great elements (mahābhūta) were mentioned, not derived matter.
Therefore, he elaborates upon the space element (ākāsadhātu) by way of this [section] in order to demonstrate it.
Moreover, material form delimited by internal space also becomes manifest.
"Form, delimited by space, goes to dissolution;
for the sake of making that very [dissolution] manifest, the Leader revealed it.
Herein, as for what ought to be said regarding the first four elements, that has already been stated in the Great Elephant Footprint Simile.
118. "In the space-element, 'that which has gone into space' means that which has attained the state of space. 'Appropriated' (upādinna) means taken up, grasped, or clung to;
the meaning is that it is the basis for the body. 'The ear-aperture' refers to the opening of the ear that is not touched by flesh, blood, and so forth.
The same method applies to the nostril-apertures and the rest. 'By which' means by which aperture. 'Swallows' means causes to enter within, from the point where it is bound by the tongue."
For as far as the human abdomen, there is a hole four fingerbreadths wide;
it is with reference to this that it was said. "Where" means in whatever place. "Stands still" means it settles.
For humans have an abdomen as large as a cloth water-strainer; it is with reference to this that it was said. "The lower part."
"It emerges" means it emerges from below. That which is about thirty-two finger-breadths long and curved in twenty-one places is called the "intestine";

it is with reference to this that this was said. Or, by the phrase "or whatever else," he indicates the extremely subtle skin and flesh, as well as the space situated within them and existing in the form of the pores of the body. The rest here is also [as explained] previously.
It should be understood in the same manner as described for the earth element and the others.
Now, explaining the characteristic of his state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*), he says: "He is like the earth," and so forth.

For one who does not become attached to or repelled by what is desirable or undesirable is called "equanimous" (*tādī*). Regarding the phrase "pleasant and unpleasant," here [refer to] the eight types of consciousness associated with greed.
"Agreeable" means [objects] associated with two types of minds accompanied by mental joy; "disagreeable" means those associated with two types of minds accompanied by mental grief.

"They will not persist by taking hold of the mind" means that these contacts, having arisen, will not be able to persist by seizing and overwhelming your mind as if squeezing it into a closed fist, thinking, "I am beautiful;
my sphere of color is clear," and thus [re-identifying] with the selfhood.
Depending on this, desire and lust will not arise. In such expressions as "gone to excrement" (*gūthagata*), "excrement" itself is "gone-to-excrement.
This applies everywhere. "Not established anywhere" means it is not established even upon a single thing such as earth, mountains, or trees;
for if it were established upon the earth, it would perish along with the earth when the earth perishes, and likewise upon a mountain...
If the tree falls, he would fall with it; if the tree is cut down, he would be cut down with it.

(120) Why did [the Buddha] begin with "Loving-kindness, Rāhula"? It was for the purpose of showing the cause of the state of being such (tādibhāva). For previously, the characteristic of the state of being such was shown;
and it is not possible to become such without a cause by merely thinking, "I am such," nor is it possible by thinking, "I am born of a high-born family..."
"Because I am learned and a recipient [of offerings], kings, royal ministers, and others attend upon me; I am such a person"—

it is for the purpose of showing the cause of being "such a one" (*tādī*) that the Teacher began this teaching, [demonstrating] that one becomes such a person not merely through these reasons, but through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
In this context, "by developing" means by one who brings [the mind] to access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā). "Ill will" (vyāpāda) is anger toward sentient beings;
that shall be abandoned. "Harm" (vihesā) is the injuring of sentient beings with the hands and so forth.

"Discontent" (arati) is a state of longing for secluded dwellings and for higher wholesome states (adhikusaladhamma). "Repulsion" (paṭigha) is [aversion] toward any sentient beings or conditioned phenomena whatsoever.
And it is the defilement that is struck down. "Foulness" refers to access and absorption concentration regarding the bloated corpse and so forth.
This development of foulness regarding the bloated corpse and so forth has indeed been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Lust" refers to lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"Perception of impermanence" refers to the perception co-nascent with the contemplation of impermanence; or rather, this is simply insight itself, which, though not a [mundane] perception, is called "perception" by way of its function as perception.
...spoken. "The conceit 'I am'" (*asmimāna*) means the conceit "I am" regarding form and so forth. 121.
Now, expanding upon the question asked by the Elder, he said: "Mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*), and so on.

Therein, this meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), the cultivation of the meditation subject, and the meaning of the text—together with the discourse on its benefits—all of it in every aspect [is explained].

This has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the recollections (*anussati*). The Blessed One brought this teaching to its conclusion specifically for the sake of a person who is to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Mahā-Rāhulovāda-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
3. Commentary on the Cūḷamāluṅkyasutta 122.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Māluṅkyasutta. Therein, "of Māluṅkyaputta" means of the elder of that name.
"Set aside and rejected" means that those so-called views were set aside with the instruction that they should not be explained. And thus they were set aside...
"And [the things] rejected. "The Tathāgata" refers to a sentient being (*satta*). "That does not please me" means that this non-explanation does not please me.
"Having renounced the training" means having rejected the training. 125. "Being who are you, and whom do you reject?

For either a petitioner might reject what was requested, or one who has been requested might reject the petitioner. You are neither a petitioner nor one who has been requested; therefore, the meaning is: "Being who are you now, and whom do you reject?"
126. "Pierced" (viddho) means he might be pierced by one standing in the enemy army. "With a thick application" (gāḷhapalepanena) means with a heavy coating.
"Physician" (bhisakka) means a doctor. "Sallakatta" means a surgeon, one who speaks the sutta concerning the extraction of arrows.
"Akkas" refers to those who, taking *akkavāka* fibers, make a bowstring; thus it is said, "of the *akkas*. "Of the smooth" (saṇhassa) refers to the bamboo reed (*veṇuvilīva*).
They prepare it with the stalks of both *maruvā* and *khīrapaṇṇī*. Therefore it is said: "either with *maruvā* or with *khīrapaṇṇī*.
"Grown" means produced on mountains, in thickets, along rivers, and so forth. "Planted" means grown after being planted;
it is made by taking *sara* from a thicket of *sara* grass. "The one with loose jaws" refers to a bird of that name. "The terrifying one" refers to a black lion.
“Semhārassa” means “of the monkey. “Evan no” means that when this view exists, [rebirth] does not occur; such is the meaning.
“Attheva jātī” means that when this view exists, there is no living of the holy life (brahmacariya), yet birth certainly exists.
He shows that aging, death, and so forth are likewise present. “Yesāham” means “of whom I am. “Nighātam” means affliction, injury, or destruction.
The intention is that my disciples, having become disenchanted with these things, attain Nibbāna right here.

(128) “Therefore, Māluṅkyaputta, this has not been left undeclared” means: because this has not been declared, whereas it is only the Four Noble Truths that have been declared by me; therefore is the sense.
“For this, Māluṅkyaputta, is not connected with the goal” refers either to that speculative view or to that declaration which is based on [mere] reasoning.
"It does not exist. "It is not the beginning of the holy life" means that there is not even the mere beginning of the holy life, nor even the mere preliminary virtue.

Regarding the phrases "not for disenchantment," and so forth: it is not for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), nor for the purpose of fading away from passion, nor for the cessation of the round, nor for the pacification of lust and the other defilements, nor for the purpose of directly knowing the phenomena to be known through direct knowledge, nor for the sake of enlightenment consisting of the four paths.
Or it is not for the sake of realizing unconditioned Nibbāna. "This" refers to this exposition of the Four Noble Truths.

"The beginning of the holy life" means that which constitutes the beginning and the preliminary foundation of the holy life (*brahmacariya*). The remainder should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated previously.
The Blessed One concluded this teaching as well with reference to the person who is to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
The commentary on the Cūḷamāluṅkyasutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 4.
The commentary on the Mahāmāluṅkyasutta.

129. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāmāluṅkyasutta. Therein, "fettering to the lower realm" means those belonging to the lower portion which lead to rebirth in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). "Fetters" means bonds. "Whose, pray, are these? means:
whose—whether of a deity or a human—are they taught that you remember; did you alone hear them, and no one else?
"It underlies" means it underlies because it has not been abandoned. When it underlies, it becomes what is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
In this case, the Blessed One asked about a fetter, and the Elder also answered regarding a fetter.
Even so, the Blessed One attributed a fault to his position. Why is that? Because the Elder held such a view. For he—
His view was: "One is called 'bound by defilements' only at the moment of their manifestation; at other moments, one is unbound.
For this reason, the Blessed One attributed fault to him. Then the Venerable Ānanda thought:
"The Blessed One has begun this teaching of the Dhamma according to his own nature, thinking, 'I shall teach the Dhamma to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,' yet it has been misunderstood by this unwise man."
“The bhikkhu has been deceived. Come now, having requested the Blessed One, I shall teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.
Thus he did. To show this, it was said: “When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda,” and so forth.
Therein, *sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitena* means by one who is obsessed with, seized by, or overcome by the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). *Sakkāyadiṭṭhiparetena* means...
“By one who follows the view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). Escape means Nibbāna, which is called the escape from views;
that he does not understand as it really is. “Not relinquished” means not removed, not swept away. “Fetter pertaining to the lower realm” means a fetter belonging to the lower portion.
The same method applies to the remaining phrases. The positive side (*sukkapakkha*) is self-evident. “With underlying tendencies, it is abandoned.”
Regarding this, however, some say on the basis of the wording that "the fetter (saṃyojana) is one thing and the underlying tendency (anusaya) is another.

Their position is that just as when it is said, "rice with sauce," the sauce is something other than the rice, so too, because of the expression "possessing underlying tendencies" (sānusayā), there must be an underlying tendency distinct from the manifest view of a self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). They are to be refuted by such statements as, "having covered [the body] up to the head."
For there is no person other than the head. Yet, it might be argued:
"If that very fetter (saṃyojana) were the underlying tendency (anusaya), then, this being the case, the Blessed One has unfairly leveled a reproach against the Elder by comparing him to a youth.
It is not unfairly leveled. Why? Because he held such a view; this has been explained in detail. Therefore, that same defilement is a fetter in the sense of binding.

It should be understood that the Blessed One said, "It is abandoned together with its underlying tendency," with reference to this meaning: that an underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is so called in the sense of being unabandoned.
Regarding the passage beginning with "having cut the skin," the correlation of the simile is as follows: the attainment (*samāpatti*) should be regarded as like the cutting of the skin.

Insight is like the cutting away of the sapwood; the Path is like the cutting away of the heartwood. However, the practice (paṭipadā) is appropriate as a mixture of both the mundane and the supramundane.
"They are to be seen thus" means that such individuals are to be viewed in this manner. 133.

"By seclusion from acquisitions" (upadhiviveka) means by means of seclusion from acquisitions. By this, seclusion from the five strands of sensual pleasure is expressed. Of the unwholesome [states]...

"By the abandoning of mental states (*dhammānaṃ pahānā*)" refers to the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). "By the subsiding of bodily rigidity (*kāyaduṭṭhullānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā*)" refers to the subsiding of physical sloth.
"Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" means being apart from sensual pleasures by way of seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*).
"Secluded from unwholesome states" means by the abandoning of unwholesome states and by the subsiding of bodily rigidity.
And being devoid of unwholesome states. "Whatever exists therein" means whatever class of phenomena such as matter (rūpa) and so forth exists there at the very moment of entering the attainment.
"Those phenomena" refers to those phenomena, beginning with matter, mentioned in the manner of "the category of matter" and so on.
"As impermanent" means not as permanent. "As suffering" means not as pleasure. Regarding "as a disease," and so forth:
In the sense of being an affliction, it is sickness; in the sense of an internal corruption, it is a tumor; in the sense of being pierced and in the sense of producing suffering, it is a dart;
in the sense of suffering, it is a calamity; in the sense of sickness, it is an affliction; in the sense of not belonging to oneself, it is alien; in the sense of disintegrating, it is perishable;
in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being, it is empty; and in the sense of not being a self, it is non-self. Therein, "perishable" means impermanent.
The characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) is explained by two terms; the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) by the six beginning with "as suffering" (*dukkhato*);
and the characteristic of non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*) by the three beginning from "furthermore, as empty" (*suññato*) and "as non-self" (*anattato*).
"He [sees] those phenomena through them" means that he, having thus applied the three characteristics to those phenomena—the five aggregates within meditative absorption—that have been seen.
"He turns the mind back" means he withdraws, releases, and removes the mind.

"He brings it forward" means that, by way of hearing, praise, mastery, and formal definition, he first brings the insight-mind toward Nibbāna as "this is peace," thus directing it toward the unconditioned, deathless element.
The path-consciousness [brings it forward] toward Nibbāna solely by way of making it its object.
"He does not say, 'This is peaceful, this is sublime,' yet by penetrating it in this manner, he directs his mind toward it"—this is the meaning.
"He stands firm therein" means he stands established in that insight (vipassanā) which has the three characteristics as its object.
"He attains the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya)" means he attains it by gradually developing the four paths. For that very reason...
"By lust for the Dhamma" means by desire-lust for the phenomena of serenity and insight.
For one who is able to completely exhaust desire-lust for serenity and insight attains Arahantship; one who is unable becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
"Whatever there is therein belonging to feeling"—here, however, form (*rūpa*) is not included. Why? Because it has been transcended.
For this person has, by way of serenity (*samatha*), transcended form by first attaining the fine-material-sphere jhāna and then entering the immaterial-sphere attainment;
and by way of insight (*vipassanā*), form has been transcended because, having correctly contemplated form below and transcended it, they now contemplate the formless. In the formless...
However, since there is no material form whatsoever [in that state], it is with reference to this that material form is not included here.
Then, when he asks "What then?", he asks, "What am I asking? For one who proceeds by way of serenity (*samatha*), one-pointedness of mind is the primary factor;
he is called "liberated by mind" (*cetovimutta*). For one who proceeds by way of insight (*vipassanā*), wisdom (*paññā*) is the primary factor; he is "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*).
Regarding the term "name," the Elder has no doubt here. He asks:

"What is the reason why, among those who proceed by way of serenity (samatha) alone, one is called 'liberated in mind' (cetovimutta) while another is called 'liberated by wisdom' (paññāvimutta); and likewise, among those who proceed by way of insight (vipassanā), one is called 'liberated by wisdom' while another is called 'liberated in mind'?
This is because this [person] is indeed a phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma).
"I speak of a difference in faculties" means I speak of a diversity of faculties. This is what is meant:
"Ānanda, you did not penetrate omniscience by fulfilling the ten perfections; therefore, this is not manifest to you. I, however, penetrated it; therefore, it is manifest to me.
For here, the diversity of faculties is the cause. Indeed, among those who proceed by way of serenity alone...
For one bhikkhu, one-pointedness of mind is the primary factor; he is called "liberated by mind. For another, wisdom is the primary factor;
he is called "liberated by wisdom. And among those who proceed by means of insight alone, for one wisdom is the primary factor;
he is called "liberated by wisdom. For another, one-pointedness of mind is the primary factor; he is "liberated by mind."
Thus it is named. The two chief disciples attained Arahantship by taking serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) as their respective primary vehicles.

Among them, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) became one liberated through wisdom (paññāvimutta), while the Elder Mahāmoggallāna became one liberated by mind (cetovimutta). Thus, it should be understood that the difference in their faculties (indriya) is the cause here.
The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Mahāmāluṅkyasutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 5.
The commentary on the Bhaddālisutta.
134. Thus have I heard: this is the Bhaddāli Sutta. Therein, "eating at one sitting" means eating a meal at a single sitting before midday;
the meaning is, food that is to be eaten [at once]. "Freedom from illness," and so forth, are explained in detail in the *Kakacūpama Sutta*. "I am not able" means I am not capable.
"There might be anxiety, there might be remorse"—if one eats in such a manner for as long as life lasts...
The meaning is: "Will I be able to lead the holy life (brahmacariya), or will I not? Might I experience remorse and anxiety?

Regarding the phrase "having eaten a portion": it is said that the ancient elders, having placed food in their bowls and been given ghee, would eat just a little while it was still warm from the ghee;
then, having washed their hands and taken the remainder outside, they would discard it.
They sit down and eat in a place where there is shade, water, and comfort. It was with reference to this that the Teacher said:

"But, Bhaddāli, you thought: 'If I were to eat the food given once after filling my bowl, and then, having washed the bowl again and filled it with rice, take what I have received outside and eat it in a place where there is shade, water, and comfort'—in this way..."
“Otherwise, who would be able? Thus he said, “Therefore, venerable sir, even for this reason I am not able.
It is said that in his immediately preceding birth in the past, he was reborn in the womb of a crow. Crows, it is said, are very gluttonous;
therefore, he was known as the Elder Chātakatthera (the Glutton). While he was still crying out, the Blessed One crushed him.

Having overwhelmed him [with his teaching], he laid down the training rule: "Whatever monk should eat or consume solid or soft food at an improper time, it is an offense entailing expiation. Therefore it was said: "Then the Venerable Bhaddāli...
[as before] ...proclaimed his lack of confidence."
"Just as" means that just as another person who does not fulfill the training would not present himself before the Teacher even while living in the same monastery, so too he did not present himself;

he neither went to attend upon the Blessed One, nor to the place where the Dhamma was being taught, nor to the thought-hall, nor did he set out on even a single alms-round path. In whichever family the Blessed One sat down, [he did not go there either].
He did not even stand at his door. If the Blessed One was going to his dwelling place, he would find out beforehand and go elsewhere.
It is said that this clansman had gone forth out of faith and was of perfectly pure virtue.
Therefore, no other thought occurred to him: "I have indeed, for the sake of my own belly, obstructed the Blessed One’s promulgation of the training rules."

"This was not appropriate for me to do"—this was the very thought that occurred to him. Therefore, even while living in solitude, out of a sense of shame, he did not present himself before the Teacher. 135.
"While performing the work on the robe": people gave the Blessed One a length of cloth for a robe; having taken it, [he began] the robe...
“They do so. “This fault,” means this occasion, this transgression; the meaning is: “Pay close attention to the reason for resisting when the Teacher is laying down a training rule.

“More difficult” means that when monks who have spent the rains retreat and departed for various directions are asked, “Where did you stay? and they reply, “We stayed in Jeta’s Grove,” [the Teacher says], “Friends,…”
They will ask, "During this rains retreat, which Jātaka did the Blessed One tell? Which Suttanta?
Which training rule (sikkhāpada) did he prescribe? Then they will say, "He prescribed the training rule against eating at improper times;
a certain elder named Bhaddāli opposed it. Hearing that, the bhikkhus will think, "Even the Blessed One himself [prescribed] a training rule..."
"They say that for one who is making a formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*), to reject it is improper and without reason.
Thinking, "In this way, this fault of theirs will become manifest among the great multitude and will become difficult to remedy," they spoke thus.

Furthermore, other monks will also come into the presence of the Teacher after having performed the *pavāraṇā*. Then you [will have to say], "Come, friends, while I am asking my Teacher for forgiveness..."
“Be my companions,” you will say, and thus cause the Saṅgha to assemble. There, the visiting monks will ask, “Friends, what has this monk done?
Then, having heard this matter, they will say, “A grave deed has been committed by this monk;
it is improper for him to oppose the One of Ten Powers. In this way, this offense of yours will be known among the great multitude.
Thinking, "Having become public, he will fall into a state that is difficult to remedy," they spoke thus.

Alternatively, the Blessed One, having performed the *pavāraṇā*, will set out on his journey; then, wherever you go, you will convene the Saṅgha for the purpose of asking the Blessed One for forgiveness.
There, the monks residing in various directions will ask, "Friend, what [is this] by him?"
"Done by a bhikkhu," they said... [and so on]... thinking, "He will become difficult to deal with," they spoke thus.

As for the words he spoke, beginning with "Venerable sir, I have transgressed," he said this thinking: "What I have done is improper; yet the Blessed One, without dwelling upon my great faults, will accept my confession of the offense."
In this context, "transgression" (*accaya*) means an offense. "It has passed over me" (*maṃ accagā*) means it occurred having surpassed and overcome me.

"May he accept it" (*paṭiggaṇhātu*) means may he forgive it. "For restraint in the future" (*āyatiṃ saṃvarāya*) means for the sake of restraint in the future, for the purpose of not committing such an offense, fault, or lapse again.
"Truly" (*taggha*) means certainly. "Indeed, Bhaddāli, there is even an occasion for you... (*samayopi kho te, bhaddālīti*).
"Bhaddāli, there is one reason that ought to have been penetrated by you;
it shows that even this was not penetrated or observed by you.

(136) Regarding the passage beginning with "one liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), the two types—the follower of the Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*) and the follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*)—are each momentary of a single consciousness.

These are persons possessing the path. Now, it was not appropriate for the Blessed One to command even these seven noble persons (ariyapuggala) in this way, nor was it appropriate for them to act thus when commanded by the Blessed One.

However, this was said by way of imagining an impossible case, in order to demonstrate the easy-to-instruct nature of noble persons and to demonstrate the difficult-to-instruct nature of the Elder Bhaddāli.
Why did you begin the teaching at that time with the words, "Are you one liberated in both ways"? It was for the purpose of rebuking Bhaddāli.
This is the underlying intention here: "Bhaddāli, these seven noble persons are the ones in the world worthy of offerings, the masters in my dispensation;
when I am laying down a training rule, they are the ones to whom any objection should be addressed if there is a valid reason."
"It is proper to oppose [me]. But you are outside my teaching; while I am laying down the training rules, it is not proper for you to oppose me.
"Empty and hollow" means that he is empty and hollow due to the absence of noble qualities within him; in his words as a lord, there is nothing [of substance].
"It is so. "You make amends in accordance with the Dhamma" means you act exactly as the Dhamma stands;
it is said that you ask for forgiveness. "We accept that from you" means we forgive that offense of yours.
"For this, Bhaddāli, is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline" means, Bhaddāli, this is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Growth" means what? It is the undertaking of restraint for the future after having seen one's transgression as a transgression and having made amends in accordance with the Dhamma.

However, speaking with reference to the individual, he said: "He who, having seen his transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future."

137. The Teacher also reproaches him, thinking upon hearing that "a certain monk named so-and-so, a co-resident of such-and-such a senior elder and a pupil of such-and-such a person, has entered the forest to realize the supramundane Dhamma":
"What is the use of his dwelling in the forest, since he is one who fails to fulfill the training in my teaching?"
In this way they reproach him; the same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
Furthermore, in this case, the deities do not merely reproach him, but also display terrifying objects and cause him to flee. As for the phrase "even by himself":
when he adverts to his own virtue, a defiled spot becomes manifest, his mind runs away, and it does not settle upon the meditation subject. He thinks, "What..."
“By my dwelling in the forest like one such as I,” he says, and being remorseful, he rises and departs.

“He blames himself by himself” means that he has been blamed by himself; or rather, this is simply the reading [of the text]. The white side (the virtuous alternative) is to be understood by the reverse method of what was stated above.
The passage beginning with “Having quite secluded himself from sensual pleasures” is stated for the purpose of showing how he realizes [this state] in such a way.
140. "They act by repeatedly overcoming [the fault]" means that they suppress even a minor offense and cause it to be performed again and again.
"Not so" means that even in the case of a great transgression, they do not act by overcoming [the offender] in the same manner as the other [minor offense].
It is said that he was addressed by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus thus: "Friend Bhaddāli, do not worry; such a thing happens. Come, ask the Teacher for forgiveness."
Having sent a certain bhikkhu to summon him into his presence, he expected favor even from the Teacher, saying, "Bhaddāli, do not worry; such a thing as this does exist.
Then, thinking, "I have been neither consoled by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus nor by the Teacher," he spoke thus.
Then, in order to show that the Blessed One and the community of monks as teachers instruct only those who are worthy of instruction and not others, he said here:
"In this case, Bhaddāli, some... and so forth. In that context, terms such as "with one thing [he answers] another" have been explained in detail in the *Anumāna-sutta*.

"He does not conduct himself rightly" means he does not even conduct himself in what is right. "He does not grow a hair's breadth" means he does not conduct himself in accordance with the conformable practice (*anuloma-vatta*).
He takes it in reverse order. "He does not proceed to deliverance" means he does not proceed in the manner of one who delivers;

he is not one who, being in a hurry and full of zeal, acts with urgency for the sake of emerging from an offense. "In that regard" means in that misconduct of his. "One who frequently commits offenses" means one whose offenses are continuous.
"One who has many offenses" means the time during which he possesses offenses is great, while the time he is pure and without offenses is small.
"Appoti" means "it reaches. "It does not subside quickly" means it does not subside immediately; it becomes a long-drawn-out matter.

When the time for washing the feet has arrived, the holders of the Vinaya say, "Go, friend, it is the proper time. When he returns again, thinking it is still time, they say, "Go, friend, it is now your time for the vihāra;
go, friend, it is now the time for giving the recitation to the novices and others."
Saying things such as, "It is our time for bathing; it is the Elder’s time for attendance;

it is our time for rinsing the mouth," she would dismiss him whenever he arrived, whether during the day or at night. Even when he asked, "Venerable sir, at what time will there be an opportunity?", she would say, "Go, friend;
you know this very place yourself. Such-and-such a Vinaya-master Elder is taking a soothing drink..."
Having said such things as, "He drinks [medicine]; so-and-so is administering a purgative; why are you in such a hurry?", they make it a long-drawn-out matter.
141. *Khippameva vūpasammatīti*: It is quickly settled; it does not become a long-drawn-out matter.
The monks, having become anxious, say: "Friend, this monk is easy to speak with; those who live in the countryside, indeed, [regard] the dwelling, sitting, and so forth in a village monastery..."
"The ribs do not heal, wandering for alms is painful, and we must quickly settle this legal case.
Having assembled, they cause him to emerge from the offense and establish him in purity. 142.

"One who commits offenses occasionally" means he commits an offense now and then. Although he is modest and a regular monk (*pakatatta*), because of his difficult-to-speak-to nature, the monks deal with him in that same way.
144. "He subsists by mere faith and mere affection" means that he maintains himself with a small degree of worldly faith and a small degree of worldly affection toward his teacher and preceptor.
For this so-called going forth is like the taking of rebirth;
a newly ordained person, not yet knowing the virtues of the going forth, maintains himself through mere affection for his teacher and preceptor. Therefore...

Such persons as these should be gathered. For even by receiving a small measure of support, those established in the going-forth will become great ascetics who have attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
By this line of discourse, the Blessed One has demonstrated precisely this point: that "one should exhort those worthy of exhortation, and not others."
145. “Having understood, they stood firm” means they were established in *arahatta* (the state of an Arhat).

“While beings are declining” means that when the practice (*paṭipatti*) declines, beings are said to decline. “While the True Dhamma is disappearing” means while the True Dhamma of practice is disappearing;
for even the True Dhamma of practice is said to disappear when there are no beings who fulfill that practice. “Conducive to the taints” (*āsavaṭṭhānīya*)...

“Cankers” (*āsava*) means those things in which cankers abide; thus they are called “bases for cankers. In these, the cankers consisting of blame from others and remorse regarding the present life and the future life—such as killing, binding, and so forth—as well as the specific sufferings of the states of misery, simply persist.

The meaning is that these serve as their causes. As long as those factors that constitute bases for cankers and lead to transgression do not manifest within the Saṅgha, the Teacher [does not pass away].
"He lays down a training rule for his disciples"—this is the construction here.
Having thus shown what is not the proper time, he spoke the words beginning with "But when, Bhaddāli," in order to show the proper time again. Therein, "when" (*yato*) means "at which time";
the rest should be understood according to what has already been stated. This, then, is the [explanation] here.

The summary meaning is as follows: At whatever time faults consisting of transgressions—known by the designation "states conducive to the taints" (āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā)—become manifest in the Saṅgha, at that time the Teacher prescribes a training rule for his disciples. Why?
For the purpose of warding off those very faults consisting of transgressions known as "states conducive to the taints."

Having thus stated that the non-arising of those things which are the basis for the outflows (*āsava*) is the improper time for the formulation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), and their arising is the proper time, he now spoke the passage beginning with "Not yet, Bhaddāli, here some... in order to show the time of non-arising and the time of arising of those things.
Therein, "greatness" (*mahatta*) means the state of being great. For as long as the Saṅgha...

The Sangha does not reach such magnitude by way of elders, novices, or those of middle standing; at that time, the lodgings are sufficient, and certain conditions conducive to the arising of taints do not appear within the Dispensation.
But when it reaches magnitude, those arise, and then the Teacher lays down a training rule. In this context, the training rules laid down for the Sangha when it has reached magnitude are as follows:
“Whichever bhikkhu should lie down in the same sleeping place for more than two or three nights with one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
