Whichever bhikkhunī should give the full admission every year, there is an offense entailing confession. Whichever bhikkhunī should give the full admission twice in a single year, there is an offense entailing confession.”
These points are to be understood by this method.

"The pinnacle of gain" means the highest point of gain. For as long as the Saṅgha has not reached the pinnacle of gain, taint-producing states do not arise in dependence upon that gain. But when it has been reached, they do arise; then the Teacher lays down a training rule:
"Whosoever, monk, should with his own hand give fresh or cooked food to a naked ascetic, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, there is an offense of expiation."
For this training rule was laid down by the Teacher when the Saṅgha had reached the pinnacle of gain.
"The pinnacle of fame" means the highest point of fame. For as long as the Saṅgha has not reached the pinnacle of fame, taint-producing states do not arise on account of fame;
but when it has reached it, they do arise, and then the Teacher lays down the training rule.
“Drinking fermented liquor and spirits is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). For this training rule was laid down when the Saṅgha had attained great learning (bāhusacca).

“Great learning” means the state of being well-versed in the scriptures. Indeed, as long as the Saṅgha has not attained great learning, the states that are the basis for the taints (āsava) do not arise.
But when it has attained great learning—since [one can master] one Nikāya, two Nikāyas, or even five Nikāyas—...

Having learned [the teachings], those persons who emerge from them with improper reflection, blending one flavor with another, proclaim a doctrine contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, misrepresenting the Teacher’s instruction.
Then the Teacher, following the method beginning with, "Whosoever, monk, should speak thus:
'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One... and so on, down to "even a novice should speak thus," lays down the training rule.
Regarding the phrase "one who has attained seniority" (*rattaññutaṃ patto*): here, those who know the nights are called "knowers of the nights" (*rattaññū*).
Because they know many nights starting from the day of their own going forth, it is said that they are "long-ordained. The state of being such knowers of the nights is "seniority" (*rattaññutaṃ*).
It was with reference to Upasena Vaṅgantaputta within the Saṅgha who had attained such seniority that this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was laid down.

It should be understood thus: When that venerable one saw monks who had been ordained for less than ten years ordaining others, he himself—having been ordained for only one year—ordained a student (saddhivihārika).
Then the Blessed One laid down a training rule: "Monks, one ordained for less than ten years must not ordain another;
whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When this training rule had been thus laid down...
Again, monks ordained foolish and incompetent persons, saying, "We have ten years [of seniority], we have ten years.
Then the Blessed One laid down another training rule: "Monks, one who is foolish and incompetent must not grant full ordination.
Whoever should grant it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Monks, I allow that a monk who is competent and capable [grant full ordination]."
“Let him grant full ordination with ten years of seniority, or with more than ten years of seniority. Thus, two training rules were laid down at the time he attained long-standing seniority.
146. “They shall teach the Dhamma discourse comparable to a thoroughbred colt”: having made the Dhamma comparable to a young thoroughbred colt, they shall teach it.
I taught it. "Therein" means in that state of non-refuge. "Indeed, Bhaddāli, this is not the only cause" means that this state of failing to fulfill the training is not the sole cause.

"He causes the reason for placing the mouth [to be applied]" means he causes the reason for firmly making the neck hold steady when the mouth is placed [on the bit] by means of the bit-fastening and so forth.
By the words "deceptive posturing" and so on, he spoke of deceptive conduct. All of these are synonyms for one another.
"In that place" means in that mode of movement. "He attains final Nibbāna" means he becomes free from such movement;
the meaning is that he abandons that movement. "In the yoke-halter" means in the placing of the yoke, for the purpose of firmly grasping the yoke.
"In the successive step" refers to the lifting and setting down of all four feet simultaneously. For [when facing] an enemy army...
Standing in a pit and seizing his sword, they cut the feet of the horse as it approaches.
At that moment, thinking "it will lift all four feet at once," they perform this maneuver by means of a rope-fastening device.
In the case of the *maṇḍala* (the circular maneuver), it is so arranged that the rider, while remaining seated on the horse, is able to seize a weapon that has fallen to the ground.
In this way, for the purpose of training, he has the horse trained in the arena. "He makes it step with its forehooves" means by touching the ground with the tips of its hooves.

For when entering at night, so that the sound of its footsteps is not heard, they give a signal at a certain spot and train it to go only on the tips of its forehooves; it is with reference to this that this was said. "He makes it run" means in swift driving.

“Dhāve” is also a reading. This cause is made to occur for the purpose of fleeing when one is defeated oneself, and for the purpose of pursuing and seizing another who is fleeing. Regarding “in excitement” (davatte):
by way of excitement; for at the time of battle, when elephants are trumpeting, horses are neighing, chariots are rattling, or warriors are shouting—
Without being afraid of that noise they were making, this reason was made for the purpose of entering the enemy army.
"Royal qualities" (*rājaguṇa*) means the qualities to be known by a king. It is said that King Kūṭakaṇṇa had a horse named Guḷavaṇṇa.
Having departed through the eastern gate with the thought, "I shall go to Cetiyapabbata," the king reached the bank of the Kalamba River. The horse—
Standing on the bank, he did not wish to descend into the water. The king addressed the horse-trainer, saying, "Alas!
The horse has been so well-trained by you that he does not wish to enter the water. The trainer replied, "The horse is indeed well-trained, Your Majesty;
for his mind is thus disposed: 'If I enter the water, my mane will get wet, and if my mane is wet, the king..."
"If water were to fall on his limbs," he said, "then out of fear of water falling upon your body, it would not descend;
therefore, have him seize a hair. The king did so. The horse descended with speed and reached the other side.
This is why this ritual is performed. "In the royal lineage" means in the lineage of the horse-kings. And this lineage of the horse-kings is such that...
Even when their bodies were mangled and pierced by blows, they would not let the cavalrymen of the enemy army fall down, but would indeed carry them outside;
the meaning is that they cause this very purpose to be accomplished.
Regarding "in supreme speed," it means they cause the accomplishment of speed to be achieved, so that there may be supreme speed; the meaning is that they cause this to be accomplished accordingly.
"Regarding 'in the state of a supreme steed' (*uttame haye*): the meaning is that he causes it to be done in such a way that he becomes a supreme steed.
In this regard, by his very nature, only one who is already a supreme steed is worthy of the task of a supreme steed, not anyone else.
And for the sake of the task of a supreme steed, only a horse proceeds with supreme speed, not any other."

In this regard, there is this story: It is said that a certain king, having obtained a young Sindhava horse, gave it to a trainer with the instruction, "Train this one," without knowing its Sindhava breed.
The trainer, likewise unaware of its Sindhava nature, put it to work alongside horses accustomed to eating only grass.
Because the task was unsuitable for him, the horse did not apply itself to the work. [The king] then set out to tame it...
Being unable to do so, he had him released, saying, "This horse is a counterfeit, Great King. Then one day,
a certain young former horse-trainer, while going along carrying his preceptor’s belongings,
saw that [horse] grazing on the bank of the moat and said to the preceptor, "Venerable sir, this is a priceless Sindhava colt."
He spoke. "If the king were to know this, he would consider it a good omen," [the horse-keeper] said. The Elder said, "The king is possessed of wrong view, my son;
nevertheless, speak of it to the king, so that he might perhaps gain faith in the Buddha's teaching.
He went and said, "Great King, there is a priceless colt of the Sindhu breed. "Was it seen by you, my son? "Yes, Great King. "What..."
"Is it right to receive? [The youth replied: "Your golden bowl for eating, your food for eating, the drink you consume, your perfumes, and your garlands.
The king had all of these provided. The youth had them taken up and departed.
Upon smelling the fragrance, the horse thought, "I suppose there is a teacher who recognizes my virtues," and he raised his head.
He stood watching. The young man went over and snapped his fingers, saying, "Eat your meal.
The horse came forward, ate the food from the golden bowl, and drank the broth.
Then, having anointed him with perfumes and adorned him with royal ornaments, [the king] snapped his fingers, saying, "Go on ahead, go on ahead! He went right before the young man.
Having gone, he stood at the auspicious spot. The youth said, "Great King, this is your priceless Sindhava colt;
have him tended according to this very method for a few days," and then he departed.
Then, after a few days had passed, he returned and said, "Great King, you shall see the horse's power. "Very well."
“Teacher, standing where shall we see him? “Go to the park, Great King. The king had his horse saddled and set out.
The youth snapped his fingers and gave the horse the signal, “Circle around this tree.
The horse leaped forward, circled the tree, and returned. The king saw neither the horse going nor the horse coming.
[The King] saw him. "Did you see him, Great King? "I did not see him, dear father.
[The Elder] said, "Place this cleaning stick against that tree," and snapped his fingers, saying, "Go and take the cleaning stick!
The horse leaped forward, took it in its mouth, and returned. "Was he seen, Great King? "He was seen, dear father."
Again he snapped his fingers, saying, "Go along the top of the park wall. The horse did so. "I saw him, Great King," [the man said].
"I did not see him, dear one," [the king replied]. Having had a red blanket brought and bound around the horse's legs, he gave the same command as before.
The horse leaped up and went all around along the top of the wall. By a strong man...
It appeared atop the park wall like the flickering flames of a whirling firebrand. The horse went and stood nearby. "It has been seen, Great King," [the groom] said.
"It has been seen, dear boy," [the king replied]. He gave the signal to go around the perimeter of the Mangala lotus pond.
Again, he gave the signal: "Descend into the lotus pond and walk among the lotus leaves. [He led the horse] to the lotus pond.
Having descended and walked upon every lotus petal, he departed;
not even a single petal was stepped upon, nor torn, nor split, nor cut, nor broken. "Was it seen, Great King? "It was seen, dear one.
Having clapped his hands, he held out that palm. Steadfast in the relics, he leaped and stood upon the palm of the hand.
“Was it seen, Great King? “It was seen, dear one. Thus, the noble horse proceeds with supreme speed for the sake of the supreme goal. Regarding “supreme gentleness”: this refers to soft speech.

For by means of soft speech, he should be made to undergo the training for the sake of becoming a noble horse, [being told]: “Do not worry, dear one; you will become the king’s auspicious horse; you will receive the king’s food and so forth. Therefore it was said:
"Utmost gentleness": "Royal domain" (*rājabhogga*) means the king’s enjoyment. It is reckoned as the king’s very limb;
thus, wherever one goes, one must proceed without obstruction, just as with one's own hand or foot.
Therefore, it is reckoned as a "limb," or else it is one of the four constituents of an army (*senaṅga*).
"By means of the right view of one beyond training" means by means of the right view of the fruit of Arahatship. Right intention and the others associated with it are likewise included.
Right knowledge is simply the right view mentioned previously. However, with the exception of the eight factors of the fruit, the remaining states should be understood as "liberation.
The rest is clear throughout. This teaching, moreover, is intended for a person who gains knowledge through a condensed presentation.
It was brought to completion by taking the pinnacle of Arahantship as the basis.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhaddāli Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
6. Commentary on the Laṭukikopama Sutta (The Simile of the Quail) 148.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Laṭukikopama Sutta. Regarding the phrase "where that grove was":
the Venerable Mahā-Udāyin had entered the town for alms together with the Blessed One and returned together with him. Therefore, it is said: "where [the Blessed One]..."
"Approaching the grove," it should be understood that he approached it. "One who takes away" means a robber; "one who brings near" means a bringer.
"Emerging from seclusion" means emerging from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
149. "At which time the Blessed One": *yasmiṃ samaye bhagavā*. "Come now" (*iṅgha*) is a particle used for an injunction. "Alteration" (*aññathattaṃ*):...
There was a change of heart. This, however, was not on account of the Blessed One;
rather, it should be understood as having occurred on account of the exquisite food, [the monks] thinking, "If we do not obtain such exquisite food, how shall we sustain ourselves?
By the phrase "at one time," he shows that the night meal was of an exquisite nature. "Sūpeyya" refers to fish, meat, lotus stalks, and so forth, which are to be served with soup.
"Let us eat together" means we shall eat from one [place]. "Prepared foods" refers to prepared soft foods (*khādanīya*).
"All those at night" means all those prepared foods exist only at night; by day, however, they are few, limited, and meager.
For people, even when sustaining themselves during the day with rice gruel, bean soup, and so forth, they eat only according to their means and as it is provided at night.
"Once upon a time..."—by this, he shows the disadvantage of eating at improper times during the night.
In that context, "in the thick darkness" means in dense gloom. "By young men" means by thieves. "Who had performed their task" means who had carried out their thieving work.
It is said that when thieves have completed their deed, they kill people for the sake of an offering to the deity from whom they sought assistance to accomplish that deed.
They seize the gall-bladder and other such parts. When other people are being killed, a clamor arises;
thinking, "There is no one seeking an ordained person," they seize monks and kill them—it is with reference to this that it was said.

"By those who have not performed the ritual" means that at the time of coming from the wilderness to the village, a preliminary offering (*balikamma*) is made for the sake of accomplishing the ritual.

"By those desiring passion. "He invites with what is not the true Dhamma" means: "Come, monk! Eat right here for this one night, stay right here, enjoy the pleasures, and you shall depart tomorrow"—thus he invites him by way of sexual intercourse.
"Again, formerly" is said by him to state the reason he himself had seen. "In the interval between lightning flashes" means at the moment when lightning strikes.
"Vissaramakāsī" means he made a great noise. "Abhumme" means "bhū" is growth; "abhū" is non-growth, meaning "my destruction.
"Pisāco vata maṃ" means "Alas, a demon has come to devour me! "Ātumārī mātumārī": here "ātu" means father and "mātu" means mother.
This is what is meant: [he cries out] for one who has a father or a mother.

"Parents, having produced a child—whether by their own means or otherwise—and having given him whatever food or nourishment is available, lay him down in one place. Thus, he does not wander for alms even at night.
But it seems your parents are dead; that is why you wander in this manner."
150. "In this very way" means in exactly this manner, without seeing any benefit whatsoever, and for no reason at all.
"They said thus" means he spoke while censuring them. In that context, "they said" means they speak. "But what indeed [should be said] regarding this? means:
what indeed can be said concerning this trivial matter? Should one not act as if one neither sees nor hears it? "Of something trifling" means of something merely insignificant.

"They are over-refining" means that this ascetic is over-exerting himself; he is practicing excessive refinement (*atisallekhana*), like one churning butter, or like one sawing through the fiber of a lotus stalk.

"Desirous of training" refers to those such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna who are desirous of training, yet they harbor distrust toward him. For it occurs to them: "If these [monks] think, 'This is a mere trifle...'"
"If they were to say, 'Bring it, Blessed One,' would the Teacher not bring it?
But instead of saying that, they sit surrounding the Blessed One, gaining even greater enthusiasm, saying, 'So be it, Blessed One; well done, Blessed One; please explain, Blessed One.
Therefore, they manifest a lack of confidence in them."
"Of those" means of certain of those foolish persons. "That" refers to that trifling thing which ought to be abandoned.
"A large piece of wood" (thūlo kaliṅgaro) is like a great log tied around one's neck. "The little quail" (laṭukikā sakuṇikā) is the *cātaka* bird.
It is said that after crying out a hundred times and dancing a hundred times, it takes its food only once. [It does so] from the sky to the ground.
But seeing it firmly established, cowherds and others bind it with rotting creepers for the sake of play;
it is with reference to this that it was said. "It approaches" means it comes near.
For "that of it" refers to that binding with rotting creepers, which—due to its being a weak body and lacking strength—is called a strong bond, difficult to sever like a large coconut rope.
"Of them": for those foolish men, due to the weakness of their faith and the weakness of their wisdom, there is what is called a powerful bond;
even a matter that is merely a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*) becomes as difficult to abandon as a grave offense involving defeat (*pārājika*). 151.
Regarding "of that which is to be abandoned in the bright side (*sukkapakkha*)," what is the reason for this slight thing that is to be abandoned by the Blessed One?

There is something that must be said: "That which the Blessed One has declared as to be abandoned. Does this not mean that even having understood the Blessed One’s intention in this way, [the conclusion] is that it must indeed be abandoned?
"Appossukka" means "without exertion" (anussukka). "Pannaloma" means "with hair fallen out," not with hair standing on end from the fear of what must be abandoned.
"Paradattavutta" means "those who live on what is given by others," that is, those who subsist on what they have received from others.
"Abiding with a mind that has become like a deer" means they abide having taken their stand on the side of non-expectation.
For a deer, having received a wound, does not harbor the expectation, "I shall go to a human habitation and obtain medicine or ointment for the wound";
rather, having received the wound, it enters a forest devoid of villages, lies down making the site where it was struck its lower part, and remains there.
When it is safe, they rise and depart. Thus deer stand on the side of not looking back.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "They dwell with a mind become like that of a deer.
For that [snare]—namely, that binding of the leather thong—is called a weak bond for that elephant-king because of his great body and great strength. (It is) a rotten creeper.

It is easy to pierce. For those sons of good family, because of the greatness of their faith and the greatness of their wisdom, even a matter involving defeat (*pārājika*) is as easily abandoned as a mere matter of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
152. "Poor" means endowed with poverty. "One who has no property" means one who possesses nothing. "One who has no wealth" means destitute. "A little hut" means...

A small house. "Ruinous and dilapidated" means that the rafters of the house have come loose from the ridgepole and are hanging from the rafters, or have come loose from the rafters and are hanging on the floor.
"Crow-infested" means that when one sits inside thinking, "I will eat something," there is no separate door-function; crows enter from here and there and swarm around.
For when it is time to flee, the *sūrakāka* (crow) flies out from its very position facing [the danger] and escapes.
"Not of supreme beauty" means not having the excellent appearance like the house of those possessed of merit. "Khaṭopikā" refers to a bedstead made of split bamboo.
"Oluggavilugga" means broken down and dilapidated. "Dhaññasamavāpaka" refers to both grain (*dhañña*) and leguminous plants (*samavāpaka*). Therein, "grain" refers to millet (*kudrūsaka*).

*Samavāpakaṃ* refers to the various kinds of seeds, such as gourd seeds, pumpkin seeds, and so forth. *Na paramarūpaṃ* means that it is not of the highest quality, unlike the pure seeds of fragrant *sāli* rice and the like belonging to those with merit. *Jāyikā* means a poor woman.

*Na paramarūpā* means she is not of beautiful form—having a protruding head, long breasts, and a large belly, she is as hideous as a *pisāca*. *Sāmaññaṃ* means the state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*). That...
"O how wonderful! O how marvelous! That man indeed would be truly a man who, having shaved off his hair and beard, would go forth into homelessness.
"He would not be able"—meaning that even after thinking thus, upon returning home, he would think: "Going forth is highly esteemed, yet it is difficult, hard to approach;
one must wander for alms even through seven or eight villages and return with the very same bowl as when one set out."
He reflects: "When I have returned, unable to maintain myself in this way, a place to live must be sought;
materials such as grass, creepers, and wood are indeed difficult to gather. What shall I do? Then that little hut appears to him like the Vejayanta Palace.
Then, looking at his mattress, he thinks: "After I have gone, someone will dismantle this and [use] the embers from the hearth..."
He thought, "They will surely provide things such as rice cakes, fried cakes, and sweetmeats; what shall I do?
Then, that [house] appeared to him like a royal couch. Next, looking at the jar of grain, he thought:
"When I have gone away, this mistress of the house will eat this grain with them [the others]. When I return, how indeed shall my livelihood be sustained?"
He thought, "When I have gone, this elephant-keeper or horse-keeper or whoever it may be will seduce her; when I return, how shall I obtain a woman to cook my food?
Then, as he looked at the woman, she appeared to him like one hundred and twenty-five storehouses. Thereupon, looking at the woman, he thought:
"When I have gone, this elephant-keeper or horse-keeper or whoever it may be will seduce her; when I return, how shall I obtain a woman to cook my food?"
He thinks. Then she appears to him like a goddess possessing form. It is with reference to this that it was said: “He would not be able,” and so forth.
(153) *Nikkhagaṇānaṃ* means of hundreds of gold *nikkhas*. *Cayo* means a collection made by way of accumulation. *Dhaññagaṇānaṃ* means of hundreds of carts of grain.
(154) Regarding the statement, “Udāyi, there are these four persons,” what is shown here? Below [it was said]: “They abandon both that...”
“They do not abandon that very thing”— thus both those who abandon and those who do not abandon are shown by way of a collective heap,
rather than being analyzed individually. Now, just as a man who has gone for the purpose of gathering timber cuts down trees in succession and,
turning back again, sets aside the crooked ones and takes only what is suitable to be employed in his work, even so, regarding those who do not abandon...
He began this teaching to show that there are four types of persons who abandon [the world] after having discarded and rendered things non-conventional (*abbohārika*).

"For the abandoning of acquisitions" (*upadhipahānāya*) means for the abandoning of these acquisitions: the acquisition of the aggregates (*khandha*), the acquisition of defilements (*kilesa*), the acquisition of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the acquisition of sensual pleasures (*kāmaguṇa*).
"Associated with acquisitions" (*upadhipaṭisaṃyutta*) means those who pursue acquisitions. "With memories and intentions" (*sarasaṅkappa*): here, they are called *sara* because they run (*dhāvanti*).
*Sarā* (streams). *Saṅkappentīti saṅkappā*: they intend, thus they are intentions (*saṅkappa*). By both these terms, only applied thoughts (*vitakka*) are expressed.
*Samudācarantīti*: they assail; they proceed by overwhelming and flooding over. *Saṃyuttoti*: bound together with the defilements (*kilesa*). *Indriyavemattatāti*:
diversity of the faculties (*indriya*). *Kadāci karahacīti*: after a long time has passed. *Satisammosāti*: through forgetfulness of mindfulness (*sati*). *Nipātoti*: in a metal ring.
Falling away. To this extent, three groups have been shown: "does not abandon," "abandons," and "abandons quickly.
Among these, four types of persons are said to "not abandon," four are said to "abandon," and four are said to "abandon quickly.

In that regard, the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmī*)—these four types of persons are said to "not abandon."
Let us set aside for now the ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others; how is it that the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) does not abandon [the underlying tendencies]?
For as long as he still possesses greed for existence, he continues to delight in the thought, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! Therefore, it is said that he does not abandon them.
However, these four types of persons indeed abandon them. Let us first consider the stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and so forth; as for the ordinary worldling:

How does one abandon them? When defilements arise suddenly due to a lapse of mindfulness, one who has initiated insight practice feels a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, "Defilement has arisen even in a monk such as myself. Having exerted energy and increased his insight, he eradicates the defilements by means of the Path.
In this way, he is said to abandon them. Those four [types of persons] abandon them quickly.

[This is] the name. In this regard, although the third section is included in these suttas—namely, the *Mahāhatthipadopama* and the one on "the development of the faculties" (*indriyabhāvanā*)—it should be understood that the question is actually addressed by the second section alone.

Regarding the statement "clinging (*upadhi*) is the root of suffering," here the five aggregates (*pañca-khandhā*) are what is called clinging; thus, it means that this [clinging] is the root of suffering.

Having understood [this], one becomes free from the substrate of defilements (*nirupadhi*); the meaning is that one is without grasping (*niggahaṇa*) and without craving (*nitaṇha*). "Liberated through the destruction of the substrate" (*upadhisaṅkhaye vimutta*) means liberated by way of the object in the extinction of craving, which is *nibbāna*. 155.
Having thus explained the four types of persons in detail, those who abandon [defilements] are now described as "these [persons] abandon these many defilements..."

“They abandon them. As for those who do not abandon them, in order to show that “these [beings] do not abandon this many defilements,” he said, “Udāyi, these five strands of sensual pleasure,” and so forth. In that context, *miḷhasukha* means impure pleasure.
*Anariyasukha* means pleasure practiced by the ignoble. It is “to be feared” both in terms of the acquisition of this pleasure and its result.

“Happiness of renunciation” (*nekkhammasukha*) is happiness that has emerged from sensual desire. “Happiness of seclusion” (*pavivekasukha*) is happiness secluded from both the crowd and the defilements.

“Happiness of peace” (*upasamasukha*) is happiness for the purpose of pacifying lust and the other [defilements]. “Happiness of enlightenment” (*sambodhasukha*) is happiness for the purpose of producing enlightenment, which is designated as the Path.
“There is no need to fear” refers to neither the acquisition of this happiness nor its fruition.
One should not fear; rather, this very thing should be developed.
“In the case of movement, I say”: I say that movement is wavering, shaking. And what therein is “in the case of movement”? What therein is movement?
This is what is meant by “in the case of movement”: those thoughts and examinations (*vitakka-vicāra*) which have not yet ceased—this is it.
In this context, "movement" (*iñjita*) refers to that. The same principle applies to the second and third jhānas as well.
When it says, "I say it is unmoving" (*aniñjitasmiṃ vadāmi*), this means I say that the fourth jhāna is unmoving, unshakable, and without fluctuation.
When it says, "I say it is without substrate" (*analanti vadāmi*), it means I say it is without a basis for clinging; it shows that no substrate of craving (*taṇhālayo*) should be produced here.
Or alternatively, "insufficient" means not enough; I say that one should not form the conclusion, "It is sufficient with this much.
"Even of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" means I speak even of the abandoning of such a peaceful attainment.
"Whether subtle or gross" means whether small or large, or whether of slight censure or of great censure. The rest...
Everything is clear throughout. However, the teaching was brought to its conclusion by means of the arahant-peak for the sake of a person who is still to be guided (*neyyapuggala*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Laṭukikopama-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
7. Commentary on the Cātuma Sutta 157.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Cātuma Sutta. Therein, “at Cātumā” means in a village of that name.
“About five hundred bhikkhus” refers to five hundred bhikkhus who had recently gone forth. It is said that the elders thought thus:
"These sons of good family went forth without even having seen the One Possessed of Ten Powers;
we shall show them the Blessed One, and having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, they will each be established according to their respective spiritual potential.
For this reason, they had come bringing those bhikkhus with them. "Paṭisammodamānā" means engaging in friendly greetings such as, "Is it well with you, friend? and so forth.

"Making ready" means: having asked where their respective teachers and preceptors dwell, they open the doors and windows, take out the beds, stools, mattresses, and so forth, shake them down, and arrange them in their proper places.
"Putting away the bowls and robes" means: "Venerable sir, this is my bowl..."
"Set this robe aside, this bowl, this water-pot, and this walking staff"—thus they were guarding their requisites for the ascetic life.
"Loud noise, great noise": it was "loud" because it rose upward, and "great" because it was widespread—an undifferentiated sound.
"Making a noise. This was said with reference to the place where fishermen set out their fish-traps;

there, a great crowd of people gathers and makes a loud clamor and uproar, saying: "Give me another fish here! Give me a fish-hook! You have given this one to him, but a small one to me! It was in this sense that it was said.
Even when the net has been cast for the purpose of catching fish, at that spot the fishermen and others raise a great clamor, saying, "Has it entered or not?
Has it been caught or not? It was with reference to this that he said this. "I dismiss you" means I send you away.
"You must not dwell in my presence" means you must not stay in the dwelling place of a Buddha such as I am.
"Come here and make such a great noise! Living according to your own nature, what propriety could you possibly maintain?
There is no need for people like you to dwell in my presence," he thus indicated.
Among them, not even a single bhikkhu was able to say, "Venerable Sir, you are banishing us merely because of our loud noise," nor could they say anything else; all remained silent.
Accepting the Blessed One’s words, they said, “So be it, Venerable Sir,” and departed. However, this thought occurred to them:
“We came thinking, ‘We shall see the Teacher, we shall hear a discourse on the Dhamma, and we shall dwell in the presence of the Teacher.
Yet, having come into the presence of such a venerable Teacher, we made a great noise; it was indeed our own fault.”

“This is our misfortune! We have been dismissed; we shall not be able to dwell in the presence of the Blessed One, nor behold his golden-hued body, nor hear the Dhamma from his sweet voice. Having become deeply despondent, they departed.
“They approached him”: it is said that even at the time of their arrival, those Sakyans found the monks already seated right there.
They saw them. Then this thought occurred to them: "Why have these bhikkhus returned immediately after entering?
We shall find out the reason for it. Having reflected thus, they approached those bhikkhus. *Handā* is a particle used in the sense of encouragement or exhortation.
"But where are you going? means: having just now arrived, where are you departing? Is there someone... [of yours]?

“Is there some danger, or is it the One Possessed of Ten Powers? Although those monks had this way of speaking as an excuse—saying, “Friends, we have come to see the Blessed One; we have seen the Blessed One;
now let us go to our own dwelling places”—they did not employ such a pretext, but rather reported the matter exactly as it was.
"Friends, the Blessed One has dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," they said. Now those kings were pillars of the Dispensation;
therefore, they thought: "If the Blessed One’s presence at his feet is lost while the two chief disciples depart with five hundred bhikkhus, we shall create a pretext for their return.
Having thought thus, they spoke the words beginning with, "Therefore, venerable sirs..."
Among those monks, not even a single one opposed them, thinking, "We have been dismissed merely because of a great noise; we did not go forth because we were unable to live [otherwise].
Instead, they all accepted it equally, saying, "So be it, friend. 159. *Abhinandatū* means:
may he welcome the arrival of the Saṅgha of monks. *Abhivadatū* means: may he come.
"Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus welcome me," he should say, thus generating such a thought.

"Supported" means supported by both material gifts (*āmisa-anuggaha*) and the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-anuggaha*). "Alteration" would mean an alteration of faith, such as thinking, "I do not obtain a vision of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
"Transformation" would mean an alteration through transformation [of mind] for those who are departing because of that alteration of faith.
“Of young seeds” means of young crops. “There might be a change” means that, at the time for watering, there might be a change due to their withering from not receiving water;
there would be a transformation through reaching a state of withering after having dried up.
However, the drying up of a calf due to thirst is called “change,” while its passing away after having dried up is called “transformation.”
160. It is said that while seated right there, the Elder saw with his divine eye (dibbacakkhu) that Brahmā had arrived;

he heard the sound of the invitation with his divine ear-element (dibbā sotadhātu); and through the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa), he knew the Blessed One’s state of being pleased.
Therefore, [he thought]: "It would not be convenient for them to go if they were summoned by sending some bhikkhu."
Thinking, “We shall go as soon as the Teacher does not send us,” he spoke thus.

“With little concern” means having become free from anxiety regarding other duties. “Devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life” means that the Blessed One, it seems, wishes to dwell intent upon the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*);
[the monk] says, “It occurred to me that he will now dwell according to his own preference.”
"Mayampi dāni" means: "We too, now"—meaning, we who were expelled from the monastery while admonishing others—what use have we for admonishing others?
"Now we too shall dwell only in a dwelling that brings happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra)," he indicates. At this point, the Elder failed;
he did not recognize his own responsibility. For this Saṅgha of bhikkhus [belongs] to both Great Elders.
It is a burden; therefore, in order to prevent him [from taking it], the Blessed One said, "Wait," and so forth. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna, however, recognized his own state as a burden.
Therefore, the Blessed One gave him his approval (*sādhukāra*).
161. Why did he begin with, "Bhikkhus, there are these four"? In this Dispensation, there are four fears. He who—
He is fearless; he is able to establish himself in this teaching, whereas the other is not able.
To demonstrate this, the Teacher began this discourse. In this context, "descending into water" refers to persons who are entering the water.
"Fear of crocodiles" means fear of *suṃsumāra* (crocodiles). "Fear of sharks" means fear of fierce fish.

162. This is a designation for anger and despair (*kodhupāyāsa*). For just as one who has entered the external water might perish by sinking in the waves, so too, having sunk into anger and despair within this Teaching, one falls away from it. Therefore, anger and despair are called the "fear of the waves.
163. This is a designation for gluttony (*odarikatta*). For just as one who has entered the external water might be devoured by a crocodile (*kumbhīla*), [so too...]
He dies; in this same way, one who has been consumed by gluttony departs from this teaching. Therefore, gluttony is called the "danger of the crocodile. 164.

"With an unguarded body" means having become one whose body is unguarded through such acts as shaking the head. "With unguarded speech" means having become one whose speech is unguarded through such things as speaking indecently.
"With unestablished mindfulness" refers to mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).
"Without having established [the mind]. "By those who are unrestrained" means by those who do not close [their senses]. This is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).

For just as one who has entered the external water might die after sinking into a whirlpool, so too one who has gone forth in this teaching might disrobe after sinking into the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called the "danger of the whirlpool."
165. *Anuddhaṃsetīti* means he exhausts or withers [them]. *Rāgānuddhaṃsenā* means by one who has not exhausted passion.

"Woman" (*mātugāma*) is a designation for this; for just as one who has entered external water dies after being struck by a fierce fish, so too in this teaching, one who has fallen in love with a woman through the arising of sensual passion falls away from the faith. Therefore, a woman is called "the fear of the crocodile."
Now, having feared these four fears, just as for one who does not descend into water there is no benefit derived from the water,
and he remains parched by thirst for water and his body is defiled by dust and dirt— even so,
for one who does not go forth into homelessness within this Teaching out of fear of these four fears, there is likewise no benefit derived from this Teaching.
He is parched by the thirst of craving and his mind is defiled by the dust of the mental corruptions (*kilesa*).

Just as there is the aforementioned benefit for one who enters the water without fearing these four fears, so too there is the aforementioned benefit for one who has gone forth in the Dispensation without fearing these [four]. The Elder, however, said: "The four..."
"Just as one who, being afraid, does not descend into the water, is unable to reach the opposite shore by cutting through the current;

whereas one who descends without fear is able [to do so], even so, one who, being afraid, does not go forth into homelessness within the Teaching is unable to cut through the stream of craving and see the further shore of Nibbāna;
but one who goes forth without fear is indeed able [to do so]. The rest is the same everywhere.
This is quite clear. However, this teaching was concluded by way of the person who is to be guided (*neyyapuggala*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Cātuma Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
8. Commentary on the Naḷakapāna Sutta (166).
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Naḷakapāna Sutta. Therein, "at Naḷakapāna" means in a village of that name.
It is said that formerly our Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey as a large-bodied king of monkeys, surrounded by many thousands of monkeys.
He wanders at the foot of a mountain. He is wise and possesses great merit. He exhorts his assembly thus:
"Sirs, at this foot of the mountain there are indeed poisonous fruits; there are indeed lotus ponds presided over by non-human beings.
You should eat only those fruits you have eaten before, and drink only those waters you have drunk before."
"Eat and drink; you have no need to ask me anything regarding this. However, do not eat fruits or drink water that you have never eaten or drunk before without first asking me.
One day, while wandering, they went to another mountain foot, took their food, and were looking for water when—
Seeing a lotus pond possessed by a non-human being, they did not drink immediately; instead, they surrounded it and sat waiting for the arrival of the Great Being.
When the Great Being arrived, he asked, "Why, dear ones, do you not drink water? "We are waiting for your arrival," they replied.
"Very well, dear ones," he said, and while searching all around for footprints, he found only the tracks of those who had already descended.
He saw [the tracks], but not the footprints; having seen them, he knew, "There is danger here.

At that very moment, a water-demon (udakarakkhasa) manifested there, splitting the water in two. He arose with a white face, a blue belly, red hands and feet, large fangs, and crooked tusks—deformed and hideous.
He spoke thus: "Why do you not drink the sweet water?"
“Drink the water; why do you listen to his words? The Great Being asked, “Are you a non-human being dwelling here?
“Yes,” he replied. “Do you have the power over those who enter here? “Yes, I have it; I shall devour you all.
“You will not be able to do so, O Yakkha. “But will you drink the drinking water? “Yes, we shall drink it.”
"If this remains so, not even one of you shall escape. [The monkey thought,] "We shall drink the water, yet we will not fall under his power.
He had a single reed brought, grasped it at both ends, and blew into it; it became entirely perforated with holes. Sitting right on the bank, he drank the water;
then, having had separate reeds brought for the other monkeys and blown into them, he gave them to them. All [the monkeys fell] into the hands of the *yakkha*.
They drank the water as they were passing by. And this has been said:
“Having seen a footprint that has not yet crossed over, and having seen a footprint that has already crossed over, we shall drink the water through a reed; you will not kill me.”
From that time until this very day, the reeds in that place have remained with a single opening throughout.
Along with this, there are four wonders lasting for the duration of an eon (*kappa*) in this world-age: the moon appearing with the image of a hare;
the cessation of the fire’s progress at the site of the Act of Truth in the *Vaṭṭaka-jātaka*; and [the fire] remaining at the dwelling place of Ghaṭīkāra the potter’s parents.
The drying up of the lake was due to the fact that the reeds on its bank had become hollow.
Thus, because water was drunk from it through the reeds, that lotus pond received the name *Naḷakapāna*.
Later on, a village was established dependent upon that pond, and that village also came to be known by the same name, *Naḷakapāna*. It is with reference to this that it is said: "at Naḷakapāna."

"Palāsavana" means in a forest of *kiṃsuka* trees. "Certainly, Bhante," means: "Indeed, Bhante, we are delighted with one accord. They indicate that those others who delight in your teaching do so only by being just like us. Regarding the phrases "not led away by a king" and so forth: suppose one person commits an offense against a king and flees. The king asks, "Sir, where is such-and-such? [The reply is: "He has fled. The king says, "Bring him back. [The reply is: "He cannot be brought back; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him stay there. [The reply is: "He does not stay there either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he wishes. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he wishes either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him remain wherever he is. [The reply is: "He does not remain wherever he is either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he likes. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he likes either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he pleases. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he pleases either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds safety. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds safety either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds security. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds security either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds peace. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds peace either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds refuge. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds refuge either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds shelter. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds shelter either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds rest. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds rest either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds comfort. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds comfort either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds ease. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds ease either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds freedom from fear. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds freedom from fear either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds liberation. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds liberation either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds release. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds release either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds deliverance. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds deliverance either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds safety from danger. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds safety from danger either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds protection. [The reply is: "He does not go wherever he finds protection either; he has gone to a place where he will not be seen again. The king says, "Then let him go wherever he finds security from harm. "Seclusion" (*viveka*) means having become secluded, having separated oneself. This is what is meant: from sensual desires and from unwholesome states...
And by seclusion, the joy and happiness known as the first and second jhānas should be attained; if,

“They persist by seizing hold of the mind. Herein, “discontent” (*arati*) is dissatisfaction with superior wholesome states.

168. *Saṅkhāya* means having known. *Ekaṃ* means a certain one. *Paṭisevati* means he practices that which is fit to be practiced.

9. Commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Goliyāni Sutta. In that context, "conduct of foot" means weak conduct or coarse conduct.
One who is dependent on conditions is like the Elder Mahārakkhita. It is said that while he was sitting in the family of a supporter, the supporter said to him:
"Venerable sir, I have given a robe to a certain elder. [The Elder replied:

"Well done by you for giving a robe to one who dwells constantly thinking only of that very person. [The supporter said: "Venerable sir, I shall give one to you as well. [The Elder replied: "Well done; you will do so."
"Taking hold," he said. This, too, was such coarse conduct. "With deference" means with one who is senior;
one should not dwell having made oneself the senior. "By way of independent living" means by way of living according to one's own will, living without restraint.
"Without encroaching" means without intruding or entering upon [another's space]. In that regard, as for the one between two great elders...
If, while they are seated, he sits down without asking permission, jostling them with his robe or his knee, this is called "sitting encroaching.
Instead of doing so, one should stand near one's own bowl and seat and sit only when told, "Venerable sir, sit.
If they do not say anything, one should ask permission by saying, "I shall sit, venerable sir," and then sit; from the moment of having asked permission...
Whether it has been said, "Sit down starting from this point," or not, it is indeed permissible to sit. Regarding the phrase "I will not obstruct":
here, if someone sits beyond his own allotted seat in a place that would otherwise have reached the junior monks, he is said to "obstruct the junior monks with a seat.
For when he has sat there in such a manner, the junior monks [think], "We cannot sit..."
“They are giving [us]!”—thus they stand grumbling, or they wander about searching for a seat. Therefore, one should sit only on the seat assigned to oneself.
In this way, it is said that one does not refuse [the seat].
“Even the rule of conduct (*ābhisamācārika-dhamma*)” means even the mere performance of duties and observances pertaining to conduct. “Not too late” means...
One should not enter too early, nor should one depart too late; one must enter and depart only together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
For if one enters too early and departs too late, the observances for the shrine courtyard (cetiyaṅgaṇa), the Bodhi-tree courtyard (bodhiyaṅgaṇa), and so forth will be neglected.
Having washed the face at the very early hour, while cutting the "monkey-threads" and letting drops of dew fall, [one should perform the duties].
Having entered the village and sought alms-gruel, one should sit right within the village until the time for alms-round, engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk;
then, having finished the meal, one should depart during the day and return to the monastery at the time for washing the monks' feet.
One must not go among families either before the meal or after the meal.
"But whichever bhikkhu, having been invited and being provided with a meal, should go among families before the meal or after the meal without having informed a bhikkhu who is present—
except on an appropriate occasion— there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
For one observing this training rule, the "going among families" mentioned in its analysis (vibhaṅga) prior to and after the meal must be understood as follows:

One must not fall into [such states]. "He is agitated and fickle" means that he is by nature prone to restlessness (*uddhacca*), and is possessed of the frivolity characteristic of young children—namely, the adorning of robes, the adorning of bowls, the adorning of lodgings, or the fondling and beautifying of this putrid body.

"One must be possessed of wisdom" means being endowed with the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-paññā*) regarding those duties that ought to be performed, such as the work of making robes and so forth.

It must be so. Regarding the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya: one should apply oneself to both the Abhidhamma Piṭaka and the Vinaya Piṭaka by way of the canonical texts (pāḷi) and the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
At the very least, in the Abhidhamma, it is not permissible to omit the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* along with the *Duka* and *Tika* matrices (mātikā).
In the Vinaya, however, [one must study] the determination of what constitutes a formal act (*kamma*) and what does not.
It is not permissible to be without the two Pātimokkhas well-determined together.
By the phrase "the formless," the eight attainments have been stated. However, for one who is unable to accomplish them all entirely, practice should be undertaken in seven, or six...
[and so on] ...or even five. At the very least, one should practice with a single kasiṇa.
Having made the preliminary meditation subject proficient, one should take it up and go about; without this much, it is not possible.
By the phrase "superhuman states" (uttarimanussadhamma), he indicates all supramundane states (lokuttaradhamma). Therefore, one should dwell having become an Arahant;
for one who cannot attain Arahantship, [one should dwell] in the fruit of Non-returning, the fruit of Once-returning, or the fruit of Stream-entry.
Or it should be established. At the very least, one should proceed by taking up and becoming proficient in even a single method of insight (vipassanāmukha) all the way up to Arahantship.

The rest is clear everywhere. However, the Venerable Sāriputta concluded this teaching by means of a person who is "to be led" (neyya-puggala), leading him step by step from the observance of the rules of conduct (ābhisamācārika-vatta) until he attained Arahantship.
The commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 10.
The commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta.
174. Thus have I heard: this is the Kīṭāgiri Sutta. Therein, "among the Kāsīs" means in the country so named.
"Come, monks, you too"—that is, "Come, monks, perceiving these five advantages, eat apart from eating at night.
Thus the Blessed One [forbade] these two types of eating at improper times: eating at night and eating during the day.
Without having caused him to abandon them all at once, he first caused him to abandon eating at improper times during the day.
Then, after some time had passed, while causing him to abandon eating at improper times at night, he spoke thus. Why?

Because these two types of eating, being practiced and thoroughly habitualized within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), have entered [into his nature] like water that has flowed into a river; even in windless places...
Furthermore, noble sons who have grown up delicate after eating fine food in their homes suffer when they must abandon two meals at once.

Therefore, rather than having them abandon them all at once, the Blessed One had them abandon the evening meal during the day in the Bhaddāli Sutta, and here he has them abandon the evening meal at night.
And in having them abandon it, he did not do so by means of intimidation or by means of suppression.
But by showing the benefit in this way—saying, "By means of their abandonment, you will perceive freedom from illness"—he caused them to relinquish it.
*Kīṭāgiri* is the name of that town.
*Assaji-Punabbasuka* refers to Assaji and Punabbasuka, two group-teachers among the six members of the Chabbaggiya group.
Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, Mettiya, Bhummajaka, Assaji, and Punabbasuka—these six persons are known as the Chabbaggiyas (the Group of Six).
Among them, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, taking their own retinue with them, reside in Sāvatthī;
Mettiya and Bhummajaka reside in Rājagaha; these two persons are residents at Kīṭāgiri. "Residents" means those who dwell there permanently, being bound by that [location].
They build dwellings that have not been built; they repair those that are dilapidated; and they exercise authority over what has been built.
"Timely" (*kālika*) refers to the benefit to be obtained at a future time.
178. What does [the Buddha] show here by saying, "And this, monks, by me"? Monks, having eaten three times a day...
One who arouses only pleasant feeling is not called a "doer of what ought to be done" in this Dispensation.
However, this teaching was begun to show the meaning that "only so much feeling is to be cultivated, and so much is not to be cultivated.
The phrase "abandon such pleasant feeling as this" refers to worldly joy (*gehassita-somanassa*), while "having attained, dwell" refers to [the noble joy].

And this is by way of the joy based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*). In the two subsequent sections as well, the meaning should be understood by way of the dejection and equanimity based on the household life and based on renunciation respectively. 181.
Having thus shown the feelings that are to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, [the text now addresses] those for whom the duty must be performed through diligence (*appamāda*).
And in order to show those for whom nothing need be done, he said: "I do not say, monks, of all [of you]," and so forth.
Therein, "what was to be done by them through diligence has been done" means that whatever was to be accomplished by them through diligence has been accomplished.
"Conducive" means favorable to practice, suitable for the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), such that while dwelling there, they are able to attain the paths and fruits.
"To attain. "Balancing the faculties" means making the faculties, beginning with faith, equal.
(182) "Bhikkhus, these seven persons"—what does this show here? It shows this meaning: those for whom there is nothing further to be done through diligence are two;
those for whom there is something to be done are five; thus, all these together constitute the seven persons.

In this context, "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) means liberated by way of two parts: liberated from the body of form (*rūpakāya*) through the immaterial attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*), and liberated from the mental body (*nāmakāya*) through the Path.

This refers, by way of example, to four types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who have attained Arahantship after emerging from each of the four immaterial attainments, having comprehended conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), as well as those who have attained Arahantship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*).
It is fivefold. As for the canonical text here: "And what is the person liberated both ways?
Here, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
Thus it is presented in the Abhidhamma by way of one who has attained the eight liberations.

"Liberated by wisdom" means liberated through wisdom. He is of five kinds: the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*), and the four who have attained Arahantship after emerging from the four jhānas.
However, the text here is presented specifically by way of excluding the eight liberations (*aṭṭha-vimokkha*).
As it is said: "He does not dwell having personally experienced the eight liberations with the body; yet, through wisdom..."
"Having seen [this], the taints (āsava) are completely destroyed. This person is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta).

One who realizes the limit of what has been touched is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī). He who first touches the contact of jhāna and subsequently realizes cessation, Nibbāna—he is of six kinds, beginning from the stage of the fruit of stream-entry up to the stage of the path of arahantship."
...should be understood as existing. For this very reason it was said: "Here, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body;
and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are utterly destroyed. This person is called a 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī).
One who has reached the view is a "view-attainer" (diṭṭhippatto). Herein, this is the brief definition: conditioned phenomena are suffering, [nibbāna] is bliss...
"Cessation" is known, seen, understood, realized, touched, and discerned by wisdom: thus one is "attained to vision.
In detail, however, this person also has six types, just like the body-witness (kāyasakkhin). Therefore it was said: "Here, a certain person understands as it really is:
'This is suffering'... [and so on] ...this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus he is one attained to vision.
...he understands; and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and fully realized by him through wisdom...
[as before] ...this person is called one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*).
"Liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutto*) means liberated by means of faith. He too is of six kinds according to the method already stated. Therefore it was said: "In this case, a certain person..."
“A person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and fully mastered by his wisdom … though not in the same way as one who has attained through vision. This is called a person liberated by faith. For among these:

For one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*), at the moment of the preliminary path, the destruction of the defilements occurs as if he were believing, as if he were placing his confidence, and as if he were resolving.
For one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*), at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off the defilements proceeds unhindered, sharp, and courageous.
Therefore, just as a plantain tree cannot be cut with a sword that is not very sharp—
When one cuts with a blunt axe, the cut surface is not smooth, the axe does not glide swiftly, a sound is heard, and a greater effort must be exerted;
such is the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by faith.
But when one cuts a plantain tree with a well-sharpened sword, the cut surface is smooth, the sword glides swiftly...
The vehicle moves, no sound is heard, and there is no need for strenuous effort; such is to be understood as the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).
"One who recollects the Dhamma" is a follower of the Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*). "Dhamma" here means wisdom; the meaning is that he develops the path preceded by wisdom.
This same method applies to the follower of faith (*saddhānusārī*) as well. Both of these, however, are still at the stage of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*). It has also been said:

It is said: "That person who, practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, possesses a preeminent faculty of wisdom and develops the Noble Path led by wisdom and carried by wisdom—this person is called a 'follower of the Dhamma'.
Likewise: "That person who, practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry..."
The faculty of faith is predominant; he develops the Noble Path, which is carried by faith and preceded by faith.

This person is called a "follower by faith. This is the summary here. However, this discussion on those liberated in both ways and so forth is stated in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein. As for...
This passage has been included here for the purpose of showing their distinction.

In that regard, since there are no formless attainments (ārūpasamāpatti) apart from the form attainments (rūpasamāpatti), it should be understood that when the "formless" are mentioned, the eight liberations (vimokkha) are effectively mentioned as well.
"Having touched with the body" means having touched by means of the co-nascent mental body (nāmakāya). "And having seen with wisdom" means by means of his wisdom.
Having seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths. "Some taints" (*āsavā*) refers to those taints that are to be abandoned by the first path and so forth, which are only partial taints.
"Proclaimed by the Tathāgata" means the Dhamma of the Four Truths proclaimed by the Tathāgata. "Are clearly seen through wisdom" means:
in this place virtue is taught, in this place concentration, in this place insight, in this place the path, and in this place the fruit—thus [it is seen].
Because they have practiced [the path] regarding meaning by means of meaning and regarding cause by means of cause, they are well-seen through the wisdom of the path. "Vocaritā" means "traversed.
"Faith is settled" means that faith as conviction (*okappanā-saddhā*) is established. "They find satisfaction in mere reflection" means they find satisfaction in mere observation.
"The measure of faith" refers to faith itself; the other term is a synonym for that very same thing.
Thus, among these individuals who have duties to perform through diligence, three are trainees (sekha) who have already penetrated the paths and fruits.
Among them, by resorting to favorable lodgings, associating with virtuous friends, and harmonizing their faculties, they gradually attain arahantship.
Therefore, the meaning of the text remains as it stands for them. At the end, however, there are two who possess the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti). By means of them—
For that path, a lodging conducive to it has been frequented, spiritual friends have been associated with, and the faculties have been brought into harmony.

However, for the sake of the three higher paths, those who frequent such lodgings, associate with spiritual friends, and bring their faculties into harmony will, by gradual stages, attain arahantship; this is the meaning of the text in this context.
But the caviller, taking this very scriptural passage, says: "The supramundane path is not of a single moment of consciousness; it is of many moments of consciousness.

He should be asked: "If one uses a lodging with one consciousness, associates with spiritual friends with another, brings the faculties into harmony with another, and [uses] yet another as the path-consciousness—referring to this, you say 'it is not of a single moment of consciousness'."
"If you say that the path consists of many moments of consciousness, then while one is using a lodging, one sees a mountain with a blue luster,
sees a forest, hears the sounds of beasts and birds, smells the fragrance of flowers and fruits,
tastes the flavor of drinking water, and while sitting or lying down, experiences tactile contact. In this way, for you, even one endowed with the fivefold sense-consciousness..."
"One will indeed be a possessor of supramundane states. But if you accept this, you contradict the Teacher.
For the Teacher has stated that the five groups of sensory consciousness are exclusively indeterminate;
he rejected the idea of wholesome or unwholesome states in one who possesses them, whereas the supramundane path is exclusively wholesome. Therefore, abandon this doctrine."
It should be assigned. If he does not accept the assignment, he should be dismissed with the words: "Go, enter the monastery early in the morning and drink rice-gruel.
(183) "I do not say, monks, from the very beginning" means that I, monks, [do not say this] regarding a frog leaping up at the very first.

I do not say that establishing oneself in Arahatship is like going elsewhere to please another. "Gradual training" (*anupubbasikkhā*) is a nominative singular form used in the sense of the instrumental.
The same principle applies to the following two phrases as well. "One who has conceived faith" (*saddhājāto*) means one whose faith has arisen through the faith of conviction (*okappaniyasaddhā*).
"He approaches" (*upasaṅkamati*) means he goes into the presence of the teachers. "He attends upon" (*payirupāsati*) means he sits near them. "He bears in mind" (*dhāreti*)...
Having practiced well, he maintains it. "Zeal arises" means that the wholesome zeal consisting of the desire to act arises.
"He exerts himself" means he applies energy. "He weighs" means he weighs [the aggregates] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

"Having weighed, he strives" means that weighing them thus through the insight of investigation, he strives with the exertion of the path. "One whose self is sent forth" means one whose mind is directed [toward the goal].

"By body indeed" means that by means of the mental body (*nāmakāya*), one realizes the truth of Nibbāna. "And by wisdom" means that one penetrates and sees it by means of the path-wisdom associated with the mental body.
Now, because they did not even go out to meet the Teacher upon hearing of his arrival, therefore for them—
"Even she, monks, was not possessed of faith," he said, beginning with the words "censuring his conduct.
In that context, "how far away? means at what distance; it would be appropriate to say even a hundred yojanas or a thousand yojanas, yet he did not say anything specific.
"The four-footed exposition" is said with reference to the exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
184. “Of that which has been pointed out” means of that which has been indicated. “That teacher, monks,” refers to a non-Buddhist teacher (*bāhiraka*). “Of such a kind” means of such a nature.
“Bargaining and haggling” means both bargaining (*paṇaviyā*) and haggling (*opaṇaviyā*). “It does not apply” means it does not exist.
The meaning is that there is no increasing or decreasing of value, as occurs at the time of buying and selling. “What is this ox? [is the question].
Saying "it is worth twenty" or "it is worth twenty" is called *paṇati*. Saying "it is not worth twenty, it is worth ten" is called *opaṇati*.

Denying this, he said: "The process of bargaining (*paṇopaṇaviyā*) is not applicable. Now, in order to demonstrate that bargaining, [he says]: "If it were so for us, then we would do it; but if it were not so for us, [we would not]."
"I would not do that," he said.

"But what, monks?"—"Monks, when the Tathāgata dwells entirely detached from worldly gains (*āmisa*), how could such bargaining and haggling be appropriate for a Teacher who is thus detached? It would be a matter of mere sophistry."

"Having thoroughly investigated, having lifted up, and having grasped," this refers to one who proceeds [in accordance with the Dhamma]. "This is the *anudhamma*" means this is the natural order (*sabhāva*).
"The Blessed One knows, I do not know": the Blessed One knows the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) in eating at a single sitting, whereas I do not know it;
thus, out of faith in me, he abandons eating three times a day and eats at a single sitting. "*Ruḷahanīyan*" means...
It is to be made to grow. "Nutritious" means possessing essence (*ojas*). By the phrase "even though the skin," he shows the fourfold energy (*caturaṅgavīriya*).
For here, the skin is one factor, the sinew is one, the bone is one, and the flesh and blood are one;
thus, it shows that having resolved upon energy endowed with these four factors, one practices in this way: "I shall not emerge until I have attained Arhatship."

The remainder is clear in every respect. However, the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship for the sake of a person who was still to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Kīṭāgiri-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Chapter on Wanderers (Paribbājakavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Tevijjavacchasutta.
185. Thus have I heard: this is the Tevijja-Vacchagotta Sutta. Therein, "Ekapuṇḍarīka" means that *puṇḍarīka* refers to the white mango tree (*setambara*);
since there was one such tree in that monastery, it is called "Ekapuṇḍarīka. "This occurred to him" means that it occurred to him with the desire to enter there.
"It has been long indeed, venerable sir," is said in reference to the fact that he had previously come there as a regular visitor. Of the Dhamma...

"And in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhamma*): here, "Dhamma" refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), while "in accordance with the Dhamma" refers to the explanation given to the great multitude.
The rest is exactly as stated in the *Jīvaka-sutta*. By saying "Not for me" (*na me te*), he stands in refusal and rejects even what has been permitted.
For this indeed must be admitted: "The Omniscient One, the All-Seeing One, claims a knowledge and vision that is without remainder."
One might think: "While walking... [and so on]... it is present for me"—but this should not be admitted. For he understands by reflecting with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Therefore, standing as one who does not admit it, and rejecting even what has been admitted, he spoke thus.
186. Regarding the phrase "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*): since the taints, once destroyed, have no further need to be destroyed, the phrase "only so far as" (*yāvadeva*) is used.

It was not stated [explicitly]. Herein, the Blessed One demonstrates the quality of knowing the past by means of the knowledge of former existences (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), the quality of knowing the present by means of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), and the supramundane quality (*lokuttara-guṇa*) by means of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).
Thus, having condensed all the qualities of a Buddha within these three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*), he spoke.
“The household-fetter” means the bond of a householder, the attachment to the requisites of a householder.
“There is none, Vaccha,” means that there is no one who makes an end of suffering without having abandoned the household-fetter.

For even those such as the minister Santati, Uggasena the merchant’s son, and the boy Vitasoka, who attained Arahantship while remaining in the outward signs of a householder, they too [attained it] through the Path regarding all conditioned phenomena.
Having dried up their attachment, they attained [the fruit]. But having attained it, they did not remain in that form;

for this layman’s form is inferior and cannot sustain the supreme quality. Therefore, one who remains there, having attained Arahatship, either goes forth on that very day or attains Parinibbāna. However, the earth-deities remain. Why? Because there is a place for them to hide.

In the remaining sensual realm (kāmabhava), among humans, three [types of noble ones]—the stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and so forth—remain; likewise, among the gods of the sensual realm, the stream-enterers and once-returners (sakadāgāmin) remain.
However, non-returners (anāgāmi) and those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) do not remain there. Why? Because that place is the dwelling of frivolous people;
there is no secluded or concealed spot there suitable for their solitude. Thus, the one whose taints are destroyed does not remain there.

He attains final Nibbāna; having passed away, the non-returner is reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heaven. Furthermore, from the gods of the sense-sphere upwards, all four types of noble ones (ariya) abide there.

"He was indeed a proponent of karma" means that he too was a proponent of karma and did not deny the efficacy of action. For he spoke while referring to himself as being at the end of ninety-one aeons ago.
At that time, it is said, the Great Being had gone forth into homelessness for the purpose of investigating various religious sects.
Having understood that this heresy was fruitless, he did not slacken his energy; being a proponent of action, he was reborn in heaven.
Therefore he spoke thus. The rest is clear everywhere.
[From] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the *Tevijja-Vacchagotta Sutta* is finished.
2. The commentary on the *Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta*:
"Thus have I heard... Regarding this, in the first instance, "I do not" means "I am not one who holds the view of eternalism."

He says: "In the second case, I am not one who holds the view of annihilationism. In this way, the rejection [of all views] in every instance—beginning with those concerning the finite and infinite—is to be understood.

Furthermore, "both exists and does not exist" here is the doctrine of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*); "neither exists nor does not exist" is to be understood as the endless equivocating (*amarāvikkhepa*).
189. "With suffering" means it is with suffering both by way of the suffering of defilements (*kilesa-dukkha*) and by way of the suffering of result (*vipāka-dukkha*).
"With vexation" means it is accompanied by affliction by way of those same two. "With despair" means it is accompanied by despair by way of those same two.
"With fever" means it is accompanied by fever by way of those same two.
"Any view whatsoever": he asks this because there exists even a single view that has been accepted, approved, and grasped.
"Set aside" means removed or cast away. "Seen" means seen by wisdom (*paññā*).
"Therefore" means because he saw the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, therefore. "Of all conceivings" means of all three types of conceiving—craving, views, and pride.
"Mathitānaṃ" is a synonym for those very same things. Now, showing them by way of analysis, he said:
"all underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and conceit. For here, "I-making" is view, "mine-making" is craving, and the "underlying tendency of conceit" is conceit itself.
"Liberated through non-clinging" means liberated without clinging to any phenomenon whatsoever by means of the four kinds of clinging.
190. “It does not approach” is not tenable. In this context, one might concede that “it is not reborn”;
