however, if that were said, that wanderer would grasp at annihilationism. But if it is said that “it is reborn,” that is eternalism;
if it is said that “it is both reborn and not reborn,” that is partial eternalism; and if it is said that “it neither is reborn nor is not reborn,” [that is the view of neither-nor].
[This refers to] the "shaking off of the immortals" (*amarāvikkhepa*). Therefore, the Blessed One—without granting permission, thinking, "Let this be without foundation and without support;
let it not find a place for easy entry"—remained standing and rejected even what had been permitted. *Alam* means capable or sufficient.
*Dhamma* here refers to the dhamma of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra-dhamma*). *Aññatrayogena* means by application elsewhere. *Aññatrācariyakena* means...
By living in the presence of other teachers who do not understand the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). 191.

"Therefore, Vaccha," [the Blessed One said], "since you say that I have fallen into confusion, I shall therefore question you right here in return. 'Without nutriment, he is extinguished' means that, being without conditions (*appaccaya*), he is extinguished.
192. "By which form" means by which form one might designate the Tathāgata—who is reckoned as a sentient being—as "possessing form. "Profound" means...
"Profound in qualities. "Immeasurable" means that it is impossible to grasp its measure. "Difficult to fathom" means difficult to enter or difficult to understand.
"Just as the great ocean" means that just as the great ocean is deep, immeasurable, and difficult to understand, so too is one whose taints are destroyed.
With reference to such a person, all [statements] such as "he is reborn" and so forth are not tenable. How so? Just as in the case of one who has attained final Nibbāna...
In this way, everything such as "having set out toward the eastern direction with reference to fire" is not tenable.
"Impermanence" means by way of impermanence. "Established in the essence" means established in the essence of the supramundane Dhamma. The rest is clear in all respects.
[Thus ends] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.
The commentary on the *Agnivacchasutta* is finished.
3. The commentary on the *Mahāvacchasutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Mahāvacchasutta*. In that context, *sahakathī* means one who engages in debate; much has been [discussed] by me.
By reminding him, "Has this not been spoken with you before? he rekindles his memory and fosters friendship. For the previous two discourses were indeed spoken to him;
likewise, in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, that which is called the *Abyākata Saṃyutta* was spoken to him:
"Master Gotama, is it the case that 'the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false'—this has not been declared by you"? Thus [he spoke].
This very same account is also told in the *Ekuttaranikāya*. Therefore, he spoke thus. The Fully Enlightened One, having received him as he arrived, granted him an audience.
Why? Because this man held the view of eternalism (*sassataditthika*), and those who hold the view of eternalism do not readily relinquish their tenets;
they are like a rag soaked in oil and fat, which takes a long time to dry.
They were purified. And the Blessed One foresaw: "As time passes, this wanderer will abandon his wrong views, go forth under me, realize the six direct knowledges, and become a renowned disciple.
Therefore, showing him favor whenever he arrived, the Blessed One granted him an audience. This, however, was his final visit.

For in this sutta, whether it be crossing or not crossing, he had come having made the firm resolve, "I shall go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama and go forth," like one who has descended into the water after letting go of his staff.
Therefore, requesting a teaching on the Dhamma, he said, "It would be well for me, sir Gotama," and so forth. To him, the Blessed One [spoke] by way of the roots...
He taught the concise teaching and the detailed teaching by way of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*). Herein, the teaching by way of the roots is extremely concise;
the teaching by way of the courses of action is concise yet similar to the detailed one. Indeed, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a "detailed teaching" in an absolute sense.
For even the twenty-four *Samanta-paṭṭhānas* are all contained within the seven treatises of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
It is indeed concise. Therefore, it should be understood that he taught it concisely both by way of the roots and by way of the courses of action (kamma-patha).

194. In this context, regarding the sequence beginning with "Abstention from taking life is wholesome," seven factors in that order belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while the three beginning with non-covetousness may also belong to all four planes of existence.

Although the statement, "From the time, Vaccha, that a bhikkhu... was spoken without specific restriction, it should nevertheless be understood that, as in the Jīvaka Sutta and the Caṅkī Sutta, the Blessed One spoke this in this sutta with reference specifically to himself.
195. But when he asks, "Is there, however...? what is it that he is asking? It is said that this is his tenet:
"In each respective dispensation, only the Teacher is an *arahant*; there is no disciple capable of attaining *arahantship*.
And the ascetic Gotama speaks as if addressing only a single bhikkhu when he says, 'Vaccha, when for a bhikkhu...'; is there indeed [anyone else]?"
“I shall ask about this matter: ‘Is there a disciple of the ascetic Gotama who has attained arahantship? Thus he asks, thinking, “I will inquire about this point.
Therein, “Let the venerable Gotama wait” means: let the venerable Gotama wait for now, for the meaning is that the venerable one is well-known in the world as an arahant.
When that had been answered, he asked further questions concerning the bhikkhunīs and others, and the Blessed One answered them as well.
196. "One who accomplishes, one who achieves, one who fulfills. 197.
"That which is to be attained by the knowledge of the trainee (sekha)" refers to the three lower fruits that are to be attained. He says, "All of that has been attained by me.
However, the caviler (vitaṇḍavādī) asks: "Which phenomena are those of the trainee? The four paths not included [in the mundane] and the lower..."
And because of the statement, "and the three fruits of recluseship," the path to arahantship has also been reached by him. However, the fruit has not yet been attained;
therefore, he asks for further instruction regarding the practice for the sake of attaining it. He should be thus informed:
"He who, having abandoned the five defilements..."
One who has fulfilled the training, whose nature is not subject to decline,
who has attained mastery over the mind, and whose faculties are concentrated—
he indeed is called a person of steady mind.
For the non-returner (anāgāmī) is a trainee (sekha) who is entirely perfected. It is with reference to him that it was said: "to be attained by the knowledge of a trainee.
However, because the path (magga) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, there can be no question for one established therein.
If it is argued that, according to this sutta, the path must also consist of many moments of consciousness, this is not the word of the Buddha; [as seen] in the verse cited:

And thus the meaning is not contradicted. Therefore, it should be understood that he causes [the monk] to receive instruction in the insight for the path to Arahatship while remaining in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Furthermore, because this is not only a decisive support (upanissaya) for pure Arahatship itself, but is also a decisive support for the six direct knowledges (abhiññā), the Blessed One said:
"In this way, having performed the work in serenity (samatha), he will produce the five direct knowledges."
"Having performed the work of insight (vipassanā), he will reach Arahantship; thus he will become a great disciple possessing the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiñña).
Thus, without mentioning insight alone, he taught both serenity (samatha) and insight.

198. "Mindfulness is the base of mindfulness": here, "mindfulness" refers to the cause of mindfulness. What is the cause here? It should be understood as either the direct knowledges (abhiññā), or the jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges, or finally, Arahantship itself; or else, insight is the cause of Arahantship.
"200. 'The Blessed One has been served by me'—for it is the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) who are said to serve the Blessed One;
when one whose taints are destroyed serves him, the Blessed One is truly served. Thus, declaring his attainment of Arahatship in brief, the Elder spoke these words.
But those monks did not understand that meaning; failing to understand, they nevertheless accepted his statement [regarding] the Blessed One."
They reported [this]. "Devas" means deities who have attained those qualities. The rest is entirely clear throughout.
The commentary on the Mahāvaccha Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
4. Commentary on the Dīghanakha Sutta 201.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Dīghanakha Sutta. Regarding the phrase “at Sūkarakhatā”: *Sūkarakhatā* is the name of a cave.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, when the earth had been rising during the interval between Buddhas, that cave was [buried].
It was born and remained within the interior of the earth. Then one day, a certain boar dug up soil near the edge of its covering.
When it rained, the edge of the covering was washed clean by the mud and became visible. A forest-dweller, seeing this, thought:
"This must have been a cave used by virtuous ones in the past; I shall restore it," and he [cleared it] on all sides.

Having removed the earth and cleared the cave, he constructed a surrounding wall, fitted it with doors and windows, and made the courtyard of the cave covered with sand as smooth as well-finished plasterwork, painting, or silver plate.
Having prepared beds and seats, he gave it to the Blessed One for his residence.
That cave was deep, such that one had to descend to enter and ascend to leave; it was with reference to this that it was said.
“Dīghanakha” is the name of that wanderer. As for why he approached him:
it is said that he thought to himself regarding the Elder who had gone forth half a month prior, “My maternal uncle went over to another sect and did not remain there long;
yet now, half a month has passed since he went into the presence of the ascetic Gotama. What is his news?”
"I have not heard it; indeed, I shall know whether this teaching possesses vital essence (ojas)," he thought, and became desirous of going. Therefore, he approached.

Regarding the phrase "standing to one side": at that time, it is said, the Elder was standing fanning the Blessed One, while the wanderer, out of shame and moral dread toward his maternal uncle, asked the question while remaining standing. For this reason, it is said, "standing to one side."
“Nothing is acceptable to me” means he speaks with the intention that all my rebirths are unacceptable and all my linkings-on (*paṭisandhi*) are unacceptable.

By this much, it is demonstrated that he thinks, “I am an annihilationist. But the Blessed One, setting aside his underlying intention, spoke the passage beginning with “Even though for you,” pointing out the fault in the literal expression itself. Therein, this...
"This view does not please you"—this means that even this view which you previously accepted, having found it agreeable, and then adopted, does not now please you.
"If this view of mine, Master Gotama, were to please you"—for my view is that "nothing at all pleases me";
of that view of mine, namely "nothing at all pleases me," let this very view please you. As for that [which you said], "nothing at all... [pleases me]"...
It was said, "I do not approve," and for him that is exactly the same.

Just as this view, though included by the term "all," is approved, so too he would have to approve that [other view] as well. Thus, perceiving the fault attributed to his own doctrine, he speaks with the intention, "I am avoiding that";
yet in actual fact, he falls into the position of saying, "This view is not acceptable to me. For one to whom this...
"It is not acceptable, it is not pleasing; because of that view, [he thinks] 'nothing at all is acceptable to me'—this is his accepted view.
Therefore, since one must be unacceptable and displeased by that view, he falls into the position that 'everything is acceptable, everything is pleasing.
Yet he does not actually accept that; he merely grasps at the very annihilation of that annihilationist view as well."
Therefore the Blessed One said: "In this way, Aggivessana, ... pe ... they cling to another view.

In that context, *ato* (from this) is the ablative used in the sense of relinquishing; the meaning is that those who do not relinquish—namely, those who are spoken of as being distinct from those who do relinquish—are more numerous.
In the phrase "for many are more numerous," the particle *hi* is merely a filler (*nipātamatta*); the meaning is simply "many are more numerous."
The same method applies even to the phrase "thinner than thin. "Those who speak thus" means those who say this.
"They do not abandon that very view, but grasp another view" means they do not abandon the fundamental view, but grasp a secondary view.
And herein, having taken up eternalism, one should not—without abandoning even that—take up annihilationism or partial eternalism.
It is impossible to grasp eternalism or partial-eternalism without first grasping annihilationism and not abandoning it;
likewise, it is impossible to grasp eternalism or annihilationism without first grasping partial-eternalism and not abandoning it.
However, it is possible to grasp another form of eternalism without abandoning root-eternalism. How so? For at one time [one might think], "Form is eternal."
Having grasped [the aggregates], at another time one grasps: "Not only form is eternal; feeling also is eternal, and consciousness also is eternal.
The same method applies to annihilationism and partial-eternalism as well. And just as it should be applied to the aggregates, so too should it be applied to the bases (*āyatana*).
It was with reference to this that it was said: "If they do not abandon that very view, and..."
"clinging to views.
In the second instance, *ato* (than this) is the ablative used among those who do not abandon;
the meaning is that those who do not abandon are, compared to those who are said to abandon them, thinner and fewer. They abandon that very view and another view as well.
They do not cling, meaning they abandon that view as their root and do not take up another view. How so?
For at one time, having grasped "form is eternal," and at another time, seeing the danger therein, they abandon it, thinking, "This view of mine is coarse.
And it is not only the view that "form is eternal" [that they abandon].
“Coarse is the view that feeling is eternal... [and so on] ...consciousness is eternal,” he replies.
The same method applies to annihilationism and partial-eternalism as well. And just as it should be applied to the aggregates, so too should it be applied to the sense-bases.
In this way, they abandon that root-view and do not adopt another view.
Why did he begin with the account of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta? This man held the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) but concealed his own view;
however, when the praise of that doctrine was being spoken, he would reveal his own view. Therefore, the Teacher began this teaching in order to analyze and demonstrate three views together.
In passages such as "near to passion" (*sārāgāya santike*), the meaning is: craving is near to the fetter of the round (*vaṭṭa*) because, by way of passion, it is close to the coloring of the round;

and it is near to the fettering of the round by way of the fetters of craving and views. "Near to delighting" (*abhinandanāya*) means it is near to grasping and swallowing up by way of craving and views.
In passages such as "near to non-passion" (*asārāgāya santike*), the meaning is: it is near to the non-coloring of the round, and so forth.
The meaning should be understood according to this method.
And herein, the view of eternalism is slightly blameworthy and slow to fade away, while the view of annihilationism is greatly blameworthy and quick to fade away.
How so? For the proponent of eternalism knows that both this world and the next exist, [and thus he knows] of good and evil deeds...
One knows that there is a fruit [of action]; one performs wholesome deeds; when performing unwholesome deeds, one fears them; one relishes and delights in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).
When in the presence of Buddhas or the disciples of Buddhas, one is unable to quickly abandon one's wrong views.
Therefore, this view of eternalism is said to be "slightly blameworthy" and "slow to fade away. As for the annihilationist (ucchedavādī):
However, one who knows that this world and the next exist, who knows that there is a fruit for good and evil deeds,
yet does not perform wholesome acts, does not fear while performing unwholesome acts, does not find satisfaction in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and does not rejoice in it,

abandons the desire for a swift audience with the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddhas when they are present. Even if such a person is capable of fulfilling the perfections (*pāramitā*), [they cannot reach the goal].
Having become a Buddha, if one is unable [to fulfill the perfections], one makes a resolution and, having become a disciple, attains final Nibbāna.
Therefore, the view of annihilationism is said to be a great offense and quickly fades away.

But that wanderer, failing to perceive this fact, perceived instead: "He praises and extols my doctrine; surely my doctrine is excellent," and so he spoke the words beginning with, "May there be for me... and so forth.

Now, since this wanderer is filled with the view of annihilationism just as a bitter gourd is filled with sour gruel, he is incapable of attaining the paths and fruits without abandoning that adherence;

for just as it is impossible to pour oil, molasses, or other substances into a gourd without first removing the sour gruel—and even if they were poured in, he would not accept them—so too, without abandoning that adherence, he is incapable of attaining the paths and fruits. Therefore, [one must abandon] that adherence.
The passage beginning with "In order to dispel that, Aggivessana... has been commenced. "Vigraha" means quarrel.
"Thus there is the abandoning of these views" means that by seeing the danger of such things as quarrels, there comes to be the abandoning of those views.
For that wanderer, thinking, "What use have I for this quarreling and so forth?", abandons that doctrine of annihilationism.

205. Then, as if pouring ghee, molasses, and other substances into a gourd that had been rinsed with sour gruel, the Blessed One said, “This, Aggivessana, is the body,” and so forth, while teaching insight (vipassanā) with the intention of filling his heart with the medicine of the Deathless.
Its meaning has already been explained in the Vammika Sutta. The terms “impermanence” and so forth have also been detailed below. That which is in the body...

"Desire for the body" (*kāyacchanda*) is that craving (*taṇhā*) which exists toward the body. "Affection" (*sneha*) is precisely the affection of craving. "Subservience to the body" (*kāyanvayatā*) is the state of following after the body;
the meaning is: the defilement (*kilesa*) that pursues the body.

Having thus shown the meditation subject of the material form (*rūpakammaṭṭhāna*), he now spoke the passage beginning with "But three... in order to show the meditation subject of the immaterial (*arūpakammaṭṭhāna*).
Furthermore, showing the unmixed nature of those very feelings, he said: "At whatever time, Aggivessana," and so forth.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: at whatever time one experiences one feeling among the pleasant and so on, at that time there is no other feeling sitting by waiting for its own turn or opportunity; rather, it has simply not yet arisen.
They are like water bubbles that burst and vanish. The passage beginning with "Pleasant indeed... is stated for the purpose of showing the pulverized and scattered nature of those feelings.
"It does not agree with anything" means that, having grasped its essence, even one who is an annihilationist [would not agree] with one who is an eternalist, saying, "I am an eternalist."
It does not accord [with his view]; therefore, having grasped that very [view], he does not dispute with the partial-eternalist, saying, "I am an eternalist.
In this way, these three positions should also be applied by way of permutation. And as for "that which is spoken of in the world":

whatever is said or expressed in the world, by means of that he expresses himself, without misapprehending anything—that is, without grasping at any phenomenon through the grip of misapprehension. And this has also been said:
“If there is a bhikkhu who is an arahant, one who has done what was to be done,
whose taints are destroyed, and who bears his final body—
if he were to say, ‘I am,’ I say that he would be speaking falsely.”
"He might even say, 'They are speaking of me';
for being skilled in the conventional designations known in the world,
he would speak by means of mere worldly usage."

Furthermore, it is said: “These, Citta, are merely worldly designations, worldly expressions, worldly conventions, and worldly descriptions, by which the Tathāgata speaks without misapprehending them.
(206) He spoke of the abandoning of eternalism and so forth after having directly known—that is, understood—the eternity of those respective phenomena;
he spoke of the abandoning of annihilationism and partial-eternalism after having directly known them.
"He speaks. The meaning here should be understood according to the method beginning with: "Having directly known form, he speaks of the abandoning of form," and so forth.

"Reflecting" means while reviewing. "The mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging" means that the mind was liberated by not grasping at the taints, which had been ceased through their non-arising and cessation.
Up to this point, this refers to the meal prepared for another.

Having eaten as if dispelling his hunger, he directed his knowledge toward the Dhamma teaching commenced by another, and by increasing his insight (vipassanā), he attained both Arahantship and the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). Having penetrated the sixteen kinds of wisdom, he remained established therein.
As for Dīghanakha, however, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), he was firmly established in the refuges.
But the Blessed One, having completed this teaching while the sun was still shining, descended from Vulture Peak, went to the Bamboo Grove, and convened an assembly of disciples.
That assembly was endowed with four factors. These are the factors: it was the full-moon Uposatha day conjoined with the Magha constellation;
they had not been invited by anyone else, but [had come] of their own accord.

By way of natural law, twelve hundred and fifty monks had assembled; among them there was not even one who was a worldling (*puthujjana*), nor any who was merely a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, dry-insight practitioner, or arhat—all were indeed possessors of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Furthermore, there was not even one among them who had gone forth by having his hair cut with a blade;
all were indeed those who had been summoned with the words "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*).
The commentary on the Dīghanakha Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 5.
Commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
207. Thus have I heard: this is the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. Therein, "fire-chamber" refers to the hall for the fire-sacrifice (*aggihoma*).
Regarding "the straw mat": there were two Māgaṇḍiyas, an uncle and a nephew. Of these, the uncle had gone forth and attained *arahantship*;
the nephew, too, possessing the necessary potential (*upanissaya*), would before long go forth and attain *arahantship*. Then the Blessed One [perceived] his potential...

Having seen that delightful fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), which resembled the womb of a deity, he left it and, having spread a grass mat in a fire-hut there—though it was defiled by ashes, straw, refuse, and the like—he dwelt for several days for the sake of winning over others.
It is with reference to this that it is said. "He approached him" does not mean only on that very day; rather, because he...
The fire-hall was crowded and not secluded by boys and girls in the vicinity of the village;
therefore, after spending the daytime portion of the day in that grove, the Blessed One would go there in the evening for the purpose of staying overnight.
He saw... [pe] ...a grass mat spread out. On other days, the Blessed One had [seen] a grass mat...
He usually went after gathering [the grass] and making a sign, but on that day he went only after having prepared it.

Why? Because at that time, having looked upon the world at dawn, he saw: "Today Māgaṇḍiya will come here, and seeing this grass mat, he will engage in a conversation and discussion with Bhāradvāja concerning the grass mat; then I..."
“I shall go and teach him the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he will go forth in my presence and attain arahantship.
For it was solely for the sake of gathering others together that I fulfilled the perfections. Having thus prepared a grass mat, he departed, thinking:
“I consider this grass mat to be a ‘resting place befitting a recluse’—a bed suitable for a recluse.”
Nor is this a place where an unrestrained ascetic has dwelt.
For here, no spot is visible where one was dragged by the hand, or dragged by the foot, or struck with the head;
it is unconfused, uncrowded, and undisturbed, appearing as if demarcated by a skilled painter using a brush on a wall. [This is] for a restrained ascetic.
He asks, "Whose dwelling place is this? [The opponent replies,] "It is the dwelling place of the *bhūnahu*.
He says this because [the opponent] has acquired the view of establishing growth at the six sense-doors. For his view is this: "The eye is to be cultivated, it is to be increased;
what has not been seen is to be seen, and what has been seen is to be transcended. [The same applies to] the ear... [and so forth].
It should be cultivated and increased; what has not been heard should be heard, and what has been heard should be transcended. The nose should be cultivated and increased;
what has not been smelled should be smelled, and what has been smelled should be transcended. The tongue should be cultivated and increased;
what has not been tasted should be tasted, and what has been tasted should be transcended. The body should be cultivated and increased.
That which has not been touched should be touched; that which has been touched should be transcended. The mind should be cultivated and increased; that which is not yet known should be known;
that which is already known should be transcended. In this way, he prescribes growth in regard to the six sense doors.
But the Blessed One said: “Restraint of the eye is good; restraint of the ear is good;”
Restraint through the nose is good; restraint through the tongue is good.
Restraint through the body is good; restraint through speech is good.
Restraint through the mind is good; restraint in all things is good.
“A bhikkhu restrained in all respects is liberated from all suffering.
Thus he prescribes restraint at the six sense-doors. Therefore, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is one who destroys growth and establishes boundaries,” he said, “He is a destroyer of beings.
[The phrase] “skilled in the noble way, the Dhamma, the pure, the causal Dhamma, the blameless”—what does this show? Of such a person...
When speaking words over one who is high-born, renowned, and famous, one must speak after having investigated and reflected, and having established a guard over the mouth.
Therefore, he shows: "Do not speak rashly; establish a guard over the mouth.
For it is thus that [this teaching] descends into our Sutta; for it comes down in our Sutta in this way, and we do not [speak] merely out of a desire for what has ascended to the mouth.
"We say this: since we are speaking what has indeed come down in the Sutta, whom should we fear? Therefore, the meaning is that we should speak even in his presence.
"Free from anxiety" (appossukka) means being without concern or preoccupation for the sake of protecting me.
"He should speak only as told by me" means that, having been told by me and without being asked, he should initiate the discussion regarding mangoes, rose-apples, and so forth.
"As if having grasped [the meaning], may the venerable Bhāradvāja speak according to the method I have explained; let him speak"—this is the sense.

"He heard" means that the Teacher, expanding his vision, saw Māgaṇḍiya arriving there with his divine eye, and he also heard the sound of the two people conversing with his divine ear. "Having emerged from seclusion."
He had emerged from the attainment of the fruit. "Agitated" means agitated, moved, and shaken by the agitation of rapture (*pīti*).
It is said that this thought occurred to him: "Neither Māgaṇḍiya informed the ascetic Gotama, nor did I.
Apart from us two, there is no third person here; surely our sound must have been heard by a man with keen hearing."
Then, rapture arose within him and caused his ninety-nine thousand pores of the body to bristle.
Therefore it is said: "Aghast, with hair standing on end. Then, as for the wanderer Māgandiya:
the knowledge of a wanderer has reached its full maturity, like a seed whose mouth has burst open; therefore, being unable to remain seated, he was wandering about.
Having returned again to the presence of the Teacher, he sat down to one side. To show this, it was said: "Then Māgaṇḍiya... and so forth.
The Teacher, without saying, "Is it true, Māgaṇḍiya, that you spoke to me thus?", began his teaching of the Dhamma to the wanderer with the words, "The eye, Māgaṇḍiya.
In this context, form (*rūpa*) is the "pleasure grove" (*ārāma*) of the eye in the sense of being its place of dwelling.

The eye delights in forms; it is "delighting in forms" because it takes pleasure in forms. It is "gladdened and delighted by form" because the eye is made joyful and glad by form; thus it is "exulting in form.
"Tamed" means rendered free from turbulence. "Guarded" means protected. "Protected" means having a guard established. "Restrained" means closed off.
"For the sake of restraint" means for the purpose of closing it off.
210. "Previously enjoyed" means previously delighted in. "The fever of form" means the fever that arises with reference to form.

But regarding this one, Māgaṇḍiya—what would you have to say? What words would you have to speak concerning this one who, having fully mastered form, has attained Arahantship and whose taints are exhausted?
You should say of him: "He is one who has destroyed growth and established the boundary."
"It should not be said" is what he asks. "Nothing at all, Master Gotama"—that is, Master Gotama, there is nothing whatsoever that should be said.
This same method applies to the other doors as well.
211. Now, since you have defined the five aggregates, [tell me] of the one who has attained Arahantship with taints destroyed, is there anything...

There is nothing further to be said. To show that he himself has also nothing to say to him—since he too has attained omniscience after having fully comprehended the five aggregates—he said, "But as for me," and so forth.

In the phrase "To me, Māgaṇḍiya," he spoke thus while pointing out his own prosperity during the time he was a householder. Regarding the terms *vassika* and so on therein, wherever there is happiness...
That which is for dwelling during the rainy season is "rainy-seasonal" (*vassika*). The same method applies to the others as well. Here, however, is the etymological analysis: *vassa* is dwelling;
that which is worthy of *vassa* is "rainy-seasonal. The same method applies to the others as well.
In this regard, a rainy-seasonal palace is neither too high nor too low; its doors and windows are neither too narrow nor too large.
In this case, even floor coverings, rugs, and various kinds of food and drink are permitted as long as they are mixed [with other items].
During the winter, the pillars and walls are low, and the doors and windows are thin with fine lattices.
To allow heat to enter, wall-protrusions are constructed. Furthermore, in this season, floor coverings, rugs, undergarments, and upper robes—
Warm things such as woolen blankets and the like are appropriate. Food and drink should be unctuous and seasoned with pungent spices.
In summer, even the pillars and walls are high; moreover, there are many doors and windows here consisting of extensive lattices.
Ground coverings and such items made of fine linen (dukūla) are appropriate, as are food and drink possessing sweet flavors and cold potency.
Furthermore, having placed nine water-vessels near the Vātapāna pillar and filled them with water, they cover them with blue lotuses and other flowers.
In various locations, they construct water-channels from which streams of water emerge like rain falling from the heavens.
For the Bodhisatta, however, they fill eight hundred golden jars and silver jars with scented water.
They prepared a bed with blue lotus plants and placed it around [the palace].
Having filled large iron cauldrons with fragrant mud and planted blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses, they set them here and there for the sake of capturing the seasons;
the flowers bloom by the rays of the sun. Various swarms of bees enter the palace and [settle] upon the flowers.
They wandered about collecting the juice. The palace became exceedingly fragrant.
Having placed a metal tube between the twin walls, a fine-meshed net was fastened over the jeweled pavilion on the roof-terrace of the nine-storied palace.
In one place, the skin of a dried bull was spread out. At the time of the Bodhisatta’s water-sports—
They threw stone balls at the hide of a wild ox; it sounded like the roar of thunderclouds. Below, they turned the mechanism;
the water rose up and fell upon the surface of the net, like rainwater falling during the monsoon.
At that time, the Bodhisatta dressed in a blue cloth, put on a blue cloak, and adorned himself with blue ornaments. His retinue also consisted of forty thousand dancers.
Clad in blue garments and ornaments, and anointed with blue unguents, they surround the Great Man and proceed to the jeweled pavilion.
Spending a portion of the day sporting in the water, he experiences the pleasant sensation of coolness.
At the four corners of the palace there are four lakes. During the daytime, flocks of birds of various colors [emerge] from the eastern lake...
Emerging and crying out, they go from the top of the palace to the western lake. Emerging from the western lake, they go to the eastern lake;
from the northern lake to the southern lake, and from the southern lake to the northern lake, as if it were the intermediate rainy season.
The winter palace, however, had five stories, while the summer palace had seven stories.
“Devoid of men” means without men. Not only were the musical instruments devoid of men here, but all the places were likewise devoid of men.
Even the doorkeepers were women, and even those who performed services such as bathing were women. It is said that the king thought:
“When I am enjoying such an abundance of sovereign power and pleasure, the sight of a man arouses suspicion.”

“Let her not be for my son,” he said, and he appointed only women to all his duties. “Delighting in that delight” refers to the delight of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*) belonging to the fourth jhāna.
Regarding the phrase “a householder or a householder’s son”: here, because the aspiration of kṣatriyas is directed toward the white parasol (*setacchattra*) alone...

They have great worldly elaboration (*papañca*); the brahmins wander about seeking mantras, never satisfied with their recitation, whereas householders, from the very moment they have mastered mere arithmetic and accounting, enjoy prosperity.
Therefore, excluding the kshatriyas and brahmins, he said, "a householder or a householder’s son. "Would be drawn back" means drawn back for the sake of human sensual pleasures.
The meaning is "it would be. "More excellent" means more distinguished. "More sublime" means more satisfying. And this has also been said:
"If one were to take water on the tip of a blade of kusa grass and measure it against the water of the ocean, such are human sensual pleasures in the presence of divine sensual pleasures."
"He stands having attained" means that having taken up divine bliss, he remains in a state even more distinguished than that.

Furthermore, the application of the simile here should be understood as follows: the time when the householder was endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure is like the Bodhisatta’s time of delighting among forty thousand women in the three palaces; his good conduct...
The time when the Bodhisatta, having gone forth, attained omniscience upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka) is like the time when [the deva] was reborn in heaven after filling [the vessel];

the Tathāgata’s period of transcending the bliss of the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) of the fourth jhāna is like that being’s period of enjoying prosperity in the Nandana Grove; his [period of] five human...

Just as there is a time when one does not long for the strands of sensual pleasure, so too, for the Tathāgata who passes his time in the bliss of the fruit-attainment of the fourth jhāna, there is no longing for the happiness of inferior people. 213.
"Happy" means that he was first miserable and later became happy. "Independent" means that he was formerly accompanied by a physician.

"Afterwards, one may be free and alone. "Master of oneself" means that previously, while living under the physician's control, one sat when told by the physician, "Sit," lay down when told, "Lie down," ate when told, "Eat," and drank when told, "Drink";
afterwards, one becomes master of oneself. "Going wherever one wishes" means that previously one could go to whatever place one desired.
He did not obtain [permission], but later, when his illness had subsided, he became free to go wherever he wished for the purpose of seeing forests, mountains, peaks, and so forth;
wherever he desired to go, there he would go.
Here too, this is the application of the simile: the time of the man’s leprosy is like the Bodhisatta’s dwelling in the midst of the household life.
The time of wearing [the garment] is like a single pan of glowing coals; two objects of sensual pleasure are like two pans of glowing coals;
and for Sakka, the king of the gods, two hundred and fifty million celestial nymphs are like two hundred and fifty million pans of glowing coals.
Scratching the openings of wounds with one's fingernails and then applying them to a pan of glowing coals is like the indulgence in sense-objects; it is a medicine.
Having approached [this state], it is like the time of being free from illness; having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, one goes forth.

At the time of becoming a Buddha, it is the period of transcending the bliss of the attainment of the fruit associated with the fourth jhāna. It is like the time of not desiring anything upon seeing another person afflicted with leprosy;
for one who passes his time with that bliss, it is the time of not desiring the pleasures of inferior people.
214. "With impaired faculties" means one whose physical sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*) has been impaired by a disease called *kimirākuṭṭha* (worm-eruption).

"With impaired faculties" also refers to those whose faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is impaired. Just as that leper with an impaired physical faculty conceived a perverted perception, thinking "this is pleasure" regarding the fire which is actually a painful contact, so too, because their faculty of wisdom is impaired, they conceive "this is pleasure" regarding sensual desires which are actually painful contacts.
They encountered perverted perceptions.
Regarding the phrases "even more impure" and so forth: by their very nature, those things were already impure, foul-smelling, and putrid;
but now they have become even more impure, even more foul-smelling, and even more putrid. "Kāci" refers to that...
For when one is tormented by heat or scratching, insects enter within, and foul blood and pus flow out;
thus there is for him only a mere measure of gratification.
Regarding the verse beginning with "Health is supreme": whatever gains there may be—whether gain of wealth, gain of fame, or gain of children—health is [supreme].
Of these, the highest and most excellent is that there is no gain superior to it; thus, health is the supreme gain.
Whatever happiness there may be—whether the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of the path, or the happiness of the fruit—Nibbāna is the supreme among them;
since there is no happiness superior to it, Nibbāna is the supreme happiness. "Of the paths" refers to the preliminary paths (*pubbabhāga-magga*).
By its very preliminary course, the eightfold path leading to the Deathless is secure; there is no other path more secure than it.
Alternatively, in the phrase "the secure, leading to the Deathless," both "secure" (*khema*) and "Deathless" (*amata*) are names for Nibbāna itself.
This is because all the various recluses and brahmins of other sects have been included under the designation of those who claim to go to security and those who claim to go to the Deathless.
The meaning here is this: among all those paths leading to the attainment of the Deathless, the Eightfold Path is the supreme and the highest.
216. “Of the teachers and the teachers’ teachers”: this refers both to the teachers and to the teachers of the teachers.

“It coincides” means it becomes identical—without any difference—like what has been measured by a single tube or weighed on a single scale. “He does not rub down” means [he does not rub] the hand downward...
As he immersed himself, he rubbed his head at one time and his chest at another, saying: “This, Master Gotama, is that health; this, Master Gotama, is that Nibbāna.
217. *Chekaṃ* means accomplished. *Sāhuḷicīrena* means with a coarse robe made of black sheep’s wool. It may also be called a rag from a rubbish heap (*saṅkāracoḷaka*).
They say: "He should utter speech" means he should utter it by moving through the beginning, the middle, and the end at the proper time;
that is, he should speak. "By those of old" means by those of the past. For the Blessed One Vipassī...
[and so on] ...the Blessed One Kassapa also, while seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly, spoke this verse; thus it is called a "verse dependent on the meaning."
The great multitude memorized it. After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, at a later time, they entered among the wanderers (paribbājakas).
Having committed it to books, they were only able to preserve two lines. Therefore he said: "This has now gradually become the 'Stanzas of the Worldling' (puthujjanagāthā).
218. "Like a disease, like a spirit" means a disease-spirit (*rogabhūta*). The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. "The noble eye" means the completely purified [eye].
Both insight-knowledge and path-knowledge. "Is capable" means he is competent. "Should administer medicine" means he should administer medicine such as emetics, purgatives, and eye-salves.
"He would not restore his eyesight" refers to one whose visual faculty has been obstructed internally by being enveloped in bile, phlegm, and so forth.
One who has been struck by an affliction may, by consulting a skilled physician and using suitable medicine, restore his eyesight.
However, for one born blind, the eyes have perished even within the mother’s womb; therefore, he does not obtain them. Thus it is said:
"He would not restore his eyes."
220. On the second occasion, "blind from birth" means one who has been blind since the time of birth due to being enveloped by bile and other humors.
"In this [case]" refers to what was stated previously. "One might even burn him as an enemy" means one might treat him as an enemy, thinking, "He is my enemy.

The same method applies to the second phrase as well. "By this mind" means by a mind that follows the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "For me, with that as the condition for clinging" (*tassa me upādānapaccayā*)...
The structure of conditions (paccayākāra) has been explained as having a single connection and two summaries, and thus the round of existence (vaṭṭa) has been elucidated.
(221) "In accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhamma) means the practice that is in conformity with the Dhamma, appropriate to it.

"These are diseases, abscesses, and arrows" points to the five aggregates. By saying "with the cessation of clinging," he shows the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa). The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 6.
The commentary on the Sandaka Sutta.
223. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Sandaka Sutta. Therein, "at the Pilakkha Cave": at the entrance of that cave there was a *pilakkha* tree;
therefore, it became known as the Pilakkha Cave. "Emerging from seclusion" means emerging from solitude.
"The rain-pool" (*devakatasobbha*) is a large lake formed in a place where water had been collected by the rains. "For the purpose of seeing the cave."
Here, "cave" refers to a cave of sand. It was situated on a high ground where water had receded;
having cleared away the stumps and sand from one side and driven stakes inside, it was constructed as a small house covered with a flat stone roof, in which those wanderers lived.
During the rainy season it remained filled with water, but in the heat of summer, there—

They dwell there. With reference to this, he said, "for the purpose of seeing the cave. For it is appropriate to go for the purpose of seeing a monastery after reflecting on the *Anamatagga* [Sutta], or even for the purpose of seeing the ocean and mountains.
*Unnādiniyā* means "shouting loudly. And as she was shouting thus, by way of her upward movement, it was high; in all directions—
"Great noise" means a loud clamor due to its pervasive nature; by that loud clamor.

For those wanderers, there was no temple service (*cetiyavatta*), no service at the Bodhi tree (*bodhivatta*), no service toward teachers or preceptors (*ācariyupajjhāyavatta*), nor even proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) to be performed after rising early in the morning.
Therefore, having risen early in the morning, they sat in the morning sun, or in the evening...
Having gathered for the sake of comfort during their discourse, they initiate conversation by taking as their subject one another’s hands, feet, and so forth— such as saying,

“This person’s hand is beautiful,” or “This person’s foot [is beautiful]”— or by discussing the appearance of men, women, boys, and girls, or some other basis for the gratification of sensual desire (*kāmasāda*) or the gratification of existence (*bhavassāda*).
Gradually, they engage in various kinds of worldly chatter (*tiracchānakathā*), beginning with talk about kings and the like.
For that is called "animal talk" (tiracchānakathā) because it is like an animal, being devoid of the path to heaven or liberation.
Among these, "talk about kings" (rājakathā) is discourse concerning kings, proceeding in such a manner as: "Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, Dhammāsoka—such was their great power," and so forth.
The same method applies to talk about thieves and the rest.
Among those, talk concerning the household—such as, “That king was handsome and beautiful to behold,” and so forth—is indeed frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).
However, talk that proceeds thus, “Even he, who possessed such great power, has come to destruction,” remains within the state of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Regarding thieves as well, [talk such as] “Mūladeva had such great power; Meghamāla had such great power,” [is likewise acceptable].
Talk such as "Oh, what a hero! regarding a person based on their deeds is indeed worldly talk (tiracchānakathā).

Even regarding battles such as the Mahābhārata war, talk concerning how "so-and-so was killed by so-and-so" or "was pierced in such a way," when conducted with a craving for sensual pleasure (kāmassāda), is tiracchānakathā.
However, talk occurring in all contexts such as "Even they have indeed come to destruction" is simply a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Furthermore, regarding food and so forth, it is not permissible to speak by way of the gratification of sensual desire (*kāmasāda*), saying:
"Thus we ate, chewed, drank, and enjoyed food that was so beautiful in color, fragrant in scent, delicious in taste, and perfect in texture.
However, having made it purposeful, one may say: "In the past, there was food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, and scents endowed with such beauty and other qualities..."
It is permissible to say, "We gave to those who were virtuous; we made offerings at the cetiya.

However, even in conversations about relatives and the like, it is not permissible to speak out of a sense of attachment, saying, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we traveled in such various vehicles.
But it is permissible to speak for a purposeful reason, saying, "Those relatives of ours..."
Or one may say, "They have perished," or "Previously we gave such sandals to the Saṅgha.

Talk about villages—whether concerning their good or bad location, abundance or scarcity of food, and so forth—or saying things like "The inhabitants of that village are brave and capable" is not permitted if done out of a sense of gratification;
however, it is permissible if done for a purposeful reason, such as when one has faith and confidence.
Or it is permissible to say that they have reached destruction and fall. This same method applies to talk concerning cities, capitals, and provinces.

Regarding talk about women as well, it is not permissible to speak of their beauty, shape, and so forth from the perspective of gratification; however, it is permissible to say, "She has faith, she is confident, she has reached destruction.
The same applies to talk about heroes: one may say, "The warrior named Nandamitta was a hero," but only from the perspective of gratification.
It is not permissible [to say], "The street was well-established; it has come to an end. It is only permissible in this way: "The faithful one was serene; he has come to an end.

Regarding talk about streets as well, such as "This street is well-established," "That street is poorly established," "It is brave," or "It is capable"—it is not permissible by way of gratification alone;
it is only permissible in this way: "The faithful one was serene; he has come to an end."
“Talk about a water-pot stand” (kumbhaṭṭhānakathā) refers either to talk about a bathing place with a water-pot stand or to talk about a female water-carrier.

Even that is not permissible by way of enjoyment—such as thinking, “She is lovely, skilled in dancing and singing”—but it is permissible only in the manner of [thinking], “She has faith, she is confident,” and so forth.
“Talk about deceased relatives” (pubbapetakathā) refers to talk about relatives who have passed away. The determination (vinicchaya) therein is the same as for talk about living relatives.

"Discourse on diversity" refers to all other useless talk of various kinds that is free from both prior and subsequent discourse. "Discourse on worldly speculation" refers to such Lokāyata and sophistical debates as:
"By whom was this world created? "It was created by such-and-such a person"; "Crows are white because their bones are white;
cranes are red because their blood is red," and so forth.
The "discourse on the origin of the ocean" refers to such meaningless talk as: "Why is it called the ocean? It is the sea (sāgara).
It is the 'sea' because it was dug by the god Sāgara; it is the 'ocean' (samudda) because [Sāgara] signaled with a hand-gesture, saying, 'It has been dug by me,'" and so forth.
Thus, the discourse that proceeds by stating various meaningless reasons such as "existence is thus" or "non-existence is thus" is called "discourse on existence and non-existence."
And here, "existence" (*bhava*) means eternalism; "non-existence" (*abhava*) means annihilationism. "Existence" means increase; "non-existence" means decrease.

"Existence" means sensual pleasure; "non-existence" means self-mortification. Thus, together with these sixfold discourses on existence and non-existence, there are what are called the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*). He was sitting while such frivolous talk as this was being spoken.
Then the wanderer Sandaka, having observed those wanderers, thought: "These wanderers show extreme lack of respect and deference toward one another.
Since the appearance of the ascetic Gotama, we have become like glow-worms in the rising of the sun, and our gains and honor have diminished. But if the ascetic Gotama were to come to this place..."
“If either a disciple of Gotama or even a lay supporter of his were to come here, it would be extremely shameful.
For the blame of the assembly falls upon the leader of the assembly.
Looking here and there, he saw the Elder. Thus it was said: “Then the wanderer Sandaka... [and so on] ...became silent.”
Therein, "he composed her" means he instructed her; he concealed her fault. He established her in such a way that she was well-composed.

Just as a man entering the midst of an assembly might adjust his lower garment, adjust his upper robe, and wipe away spots of dust for the purpose of concealing a fault, so too did he act for the purpose of concealing her fault.
“Teach ‘Be quiet, sirs!’”—the meaning is that he established it in such a way as to ensure it was well-established.
“Desiring little noise” means they desire quiet; they sit alone, they stand alone, and they do not live in the company of crowds.
“Disciplined by little noise” means disciplined by the Buddha, who is free from clamor. “Praisers of little noise.”
"A place that is quiet and noiseless. "One who speaks in praise of such a place" means one who thinks, "I should approach him," that is, "I should come here.
But why does he expect to approach the Elder? Because he desires his own advancement.
It is said that when wanderers see Buddhas or disciples of the Buddha coming into their presence, they think: "Today, into our presence..."
"The ascetic Gotama has arrived; Sāriputta has arrived. Yet these two do not go into the presence of just anyone.
Behold our superior status! Thus they exalt themselves before their own attendants, placing themselves in a high position.
They even strive to win over the Blessed One’s own attendants. It is said that regarding the Blessed One’s attendants...
Having seen this, they say: "Your teacher, Master Gotama, and even the disciples of Gotama come to our presence;

we are all in harmony with one another. Yet you do not wish to look at us with your eyes, nor do you perform the proper duties of respect toward us; what wrong have we done to you? Some people, however...
—"Even the Buddhas go to them; what then of us? From that time on, whenever they saw them, they did not become negligent.
"They became silent" means that, having surrounded Sandaka, they sat down without making a sound.
"Welcome to the venerable Ānanda" means a good arrival for the venerable Ānanda, for you have indeed come to us.
"Joy arises" indicates that there is sorrow when he has departed. "After a long time" is a term of affectionate address.
However, because the Elder goes from time to time to the wanderers' park for the purpose of wandering about, [the other monk] spoke thus by referring to his previous departure.
And having spoken thus, he did not sit down stiff with pride, but rather rose from his own seat.
Having cleared the seat, he invited the Elder to sit, saying, "May the venerable Ānanda be seated; this seat is prepared. He asked, "What conversation was left unfinished? by which he inquired:
"From the moment you began until my arrival, what kind of talk was left incomplete in the interval? Because of my arrival, what discussion has not reached its conclusion?
Then the wanderer replied, "This was merely a useless talk, devoid of substance and centered on worldly existence; it was not fit for your presence."
Demonstrating that [the person] is worthy of being addressed, he says, "She stands here, sir," and so forth. By saying, "Not she, sir," he indicates:
"If you, sir, should wish to hear it, this matter will not be difficult to obtain later; however, we have no need for it.
Having obtained your arrival, sir, we are desirous of hearing some other, more excellent reason for your coming."

Then, requesting a teaching on the Dhamma, he said, "It would be well indeed if the venerable one... and so forth. Therein, "in the teacher's doctrine" (*ācariyake*) means in the system of the teacher.
"Lacking consolation" (*anassāsikāni*) means devoid of comfort. "Sasakkaṃ" is a particle used in the sense of "certainly";
the meaning is that a wise person would certainly not dwell [there]. And "dwelling there, he would not succeed" (*vasanto ca nārādheyya*) means he would not achieve it, he would not fulfill it.
This has been said. "The method, the Dhamma, the wholesome" refers to the Dhamma that serves as the cause, which is wholesome in the sense of being blameless.
225. "In this world" means in this world. "There is no giving," and so forth, are stated in the Sāleyyaka Sutta.
"Consisting of the four great elements" means composed of the four great elements. "Earth, the body of earth" means the internal earth element [regarding] the external earth element.
*Anupetīti* means "he follows after. *Anupagacchatīti* is a synonym for that same term; it also means "he goes along with.
By both expressions, he shows that one "approaches" (*upeti*) and "draws near to" (*upagacchati*). The same method applies to the words beginning with *āpa*. *Indriyānīti*:

the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, leap into space. *Āsandipañcamāti*: "with the couch as the fifth" means together with the couch upon which one lies; namely, the couch itself and four [others].
The meaning is that four men stand holding the bedstead. "As far as the cremation ground" (yāvāḷāhana) means up to the cemetery.
"Footprints" (padāni) refers to the words concerning qualities, such as "he was thus virtuous" or "he was thus immoral," which proceed in this manner;

or rather, it is intended here that the physical body itself is what is meant by "footprints. "Dove-colored" (kāpotakāni) means having the color of a dove, that is to say, the color of a pigeon's wing.

*Bhassantā* means ending in ashes; or this is the very same reading (*pāḷi*). *Āhutiyo*: whatever gift has been given, whether in the form of food parcels, honors, and so forth—all that ends in ashes alone;
the meaning is that it does not proceed beyond that as a giver of fruit.
*Dattupaṇṇattaṃ*: established by fools, by ignorant people. This is what is meant: by fools who lack wisdom.
"This gift is prescribed by fools, not by the wise. This shows that it is the fools who give and the wise who receive.
"Those who speak of what exists" means they speak only this doctrine of what exists: that "there is giving, there is the fruit of giving. Their empty words are a false fabrication.
"Both fools and the wise" means both the foolish and the learned.
"By what has not been done by me, here, has my work been done"—by this very ascetic work of mine that remains undone, at this very moment, the work is said to be accomplished;
by this very holy life that remains unfulfilled, it is said to be fulfilled. "Here" means in this duty of an ascetic (*samaṇadhamma*).
"Equal and equal" means exceedingly equal, or equal through equal qualities. "Attained to the state of an ascetic" means attained to the condition of equality.
226. *Karatoti* and so forth are stated in the *Apaṇṇaka-sutta*. Likewise for *natthi hetū* and so forth. 228.
In the fourth dwelling of the holy life (*brahmacariya-vāsa*), *akaṭā* means "unmade. *Akaṭavidhā* means "having an unmade arrangement";

the meaning is that they have not been caused to be made by anyone with the instruction, "Do it thus. *Animmitā* means not even fashioned by supernormal power (*iddhi*). *Animmātā* means not caused to be fashioned.
Some say there is a word "animmitabbā" (uncreated), but that is found neither in the Canon nor in the Commentary.
"Barren" means fruitless, like barren cattle or barren palm trees; the meaning is that they do not produce anything for anyone.

By this, he rejects the notion that the earth-element and so forth are producers of form and other qualities. "Standing like mountain peaks" means they are fixed as peaks (*kūṭaṭṭhā*). "Standing firm like a reed" means... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
They stand like a reed in a clump of muñja grass. Herein, this is the intended meaning:
that which is called "arising" emerges as something already existing, just like a reed from a clump of muñja grass. There is also the reading *esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā*;
the meaning is that they stand firm, like a well-planted pillar of wood that remains motionless. By both [readings], he illustrates their lack of destruction. They do not waver.
Because they stand like a pillar of glass, they do not waver. "They do not undergo transformation" means they do not abandon their intrinsic nature (*pakati*).
"They do not afflict one another" means they do not harm one another. "Not able" (*nāla*) means not capable.

In the phrases "the earth-body" (*pathavīkāya*) and so forth, "earth-body" refers either to earth itself or to a collection of earth. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to those [elements] that have the living being as the seventh.
"In bodies": he illuminates that there is no one capable of killing or causing to kill, hearing or causing to hear, knowing or causing to know.

"But only among the seven bodies": just as a weapon struck against a heap of beans, for example, enters through the gaps between the beans, so too [it enters] through the openings among the seven bodies.
Through an opening, the blade enters. This shows that there is merely a mere perception [in the mind] of the thought: "I am depriving this one of life.
"A hundred thousand principal wombs" means one hundred and fourteen thousand principal wombs—that is, the highest wombs—and another six hundred and sixty.
"And five hundred actions" means five hundred types of kamma.
Furthermore, he merely expounds a useless view based on mere reasoning alone. The same method applies to such statements as "five karmas" and "three karmas.
However, some say that "five karmas" is spoken of by way of the five faculties, while "three" is by way of bodily karma and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in karma and half-karma," his conviction is that both bodily karma and verbal karma constitute "karma."
"Volitional action of mind is half an action. "Sixty-two ways of practice": he says there are sixty-two ways of practice. "Sixty-two intermediate aeons":
in one aeon there are sixty-four intermediate aeons; however, not knowing the other two, he speaks thus.
The six classes of beings are explained in detail in the Apaṇṇaka Sutta.

"The eight stages of man" refers to these eight stages of man: the stage of the infant, the stage of play, the stage of inquiry, the stage of rectitude, the stage of training, the stage of the recluse, the stage of the Conqueror, and the stage of the wise.
In this context, from the day of birth for seven days, beings are dull and deluded because they have just emerged from the cramped place [the womb]. This...
He says, "This is the stage of dullness. However, those who have come from an unhappy destination weep and cry out frequently;
those who have come from a happy destination smile as they repeatedly recollect that [past life]. This is called the stage of play.
Taking hold of a parent’s hand or foot, or a bed or a chair, and placing one's feet on the ground is the stage of testing.

The time when one is capable of walking on foot is called the *ujugata-bhūmi* (the level of straightforwardness). The time of training in the various crafts is called the *sekkha-bhūmi* (the level of the learner).

The time of going forth from the household life into homelessness is called the *samaṇa-bhūmi* (the level of the recluse). The time of knowing [the truth] after serving a teacher is called the *jina-bhūmi* (the level of the Victor).

As it is said, "The bhikkhu is a victor (*jina*) who has laid down his burden and does not take up anything," they call such a non-gainer a *samaṇa* on the *pannabhūmi* (the level of the one who has laid down the burden).
“Forty-nine hundred modes of livelihood” means forty-nine hundred ways of making a living. “A hundred wanderers” means a hundred ascetic orders of wanderers.
“A hundred abodes of nāgas” means a hundred circles of nāgas. “Twenty hundred faculties” means twenty hundred faculties.
“Thirty hundred hells” means thirty hundred hells. “Dust-places” refers to places where dust is scattered, such as the backs of hands, the backs of feet, and so forth.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). He says "seven wombs of percipient beings" (*saññī-gabbha*) with reference to the camel, ox, donkey, goat, sheep, deer, and buffalo.
He says "wombs of non-percipient beings" (*asaññī-gabbha*) with reference to rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, *kaṅgu* millet, *varaka* millet, and *kudrūsa* millet.
He says "wombs of *nigaṇṭhi*" with reference to those born from a *nigaṇṭhi* plant; he speaks with reference to sugarcane, reeds, bamboo, and so forth. Seven...
"Devas" means many gods, yet he calls them "beings" (*satta*). "Humans" are also infinite, yet he calls them "beings.
"Satta pisācā" means great *pisāca* demons; he calls them "beings.
"Sara" means great lakes: the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Siṅhapapāta, Kuḷira, Mucalinda, and Kuṇāla lakes.
Having taken [the water], he speaks. *Pavuṭā* means a knot. *Papātā* means great precipices. *Papātasatāni* means hundreds of small precipices.
*Supinā* means great dreams. *Supinasatāni* means hundreds of small dreams. Regarding *mahākappā*:
here, from a single great aeon (*kappa*), one removes a single drop of water with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass every hundred years, after every hundred years.
He asserts that when a lake has been rendered waterless for seven times, one *mahākappa* (great aeon) is completed.
His doctrine is that after exhausting eight million four hundred thousand such *mahākappas*, both fools and the wise bring an end to suffering.
For it is said that even the wise cannot attain purification in the interim, while even the fool does not go beyond that limit.

"By virtue" means by the virtue of a naked ascetic (*acelaka*) or by any other kind of virtue whatsoever. "By conduct" means by such conduct as that. "By austerity" means by the practice of asceticism (*tapas*).
One who purifies himself prematurely, thinking "I am wise," is said to bring to maturity what is not yet matured.
One who makes what is already matured completely pure by repeatedly encountering it, thinking "I am a fool," is one who does so after the lapse of the time period previously mentioned.

"It goes. "In this way it does not exist" means that it does not exist in such a manner; for he demonstrates that neither of those two can be established. "Measured by a *doṇa*" means as if measured by a *doṇa*.
"Pleasure and pain" (*sukhadukkha*) is a compound of pleasure and pain. "With a fixed limit" (*pariyantakata*) means having its limit determined by the time already mentioned.
"There is no waning or waxing" means there are no instances of decrease or increase. "For the wise man, there is no cycle of existence" (*saṃsāra*); [the wise man] does not wander in saṃsāra.
"It wanes; it does not increase for the fool"—this is the meaning. "In rising and falling" (*ukkaṃsāvakaṃse*) means rising and falling; this is a synonym for decrease and increase.
Now, in order to establish that meaning by way of a simile, he said, "Just as if," and so forth. Therein, "a ball of string" refers to a ball of string made by winding [it].
"It runs away even as it is being unwound" means [as if one were] standing on a mountain or at the top of a tree...

Just as a thread, when unwound according to its measured length, continues until it is exhausted, after which it stops there and does not go further—so too, he shows that [the soul] does not go beyond the time already stated. 229.

When asked, "What is this? What is this ignorance of yours? Are you indeed called 'omniscient'? he replied with the words, "My house is empty," and so forth, thereby casting himself into the doctrine of fatalism (*niyativāda*).

230. "He is one who relies on hearsay" means he is dependent on what has been heard from others. "One who stands by hearsay as truth" means he remains fixed after having taken what was heard to be true. "By the perfection of the Piṭaka" means by the excellence of the textual collection consisting of the *vagga* and *paññāsaka* divisions.
232. "Dull-witted" means one of dull wisdom. "Deluded" means excessively bewildered. "He falls into verbal wrangling" means he engages in a confusion of speech. Of what kind?
It is the wrangling of an immortal (*amarāvikkhepa*), meaning a limitless or endless wrangling. Alternatively, "immortal" (*amarā*) refers to...

The "fish-species" (macchajāti): just as that [fish] cannot be caught while darting about in the water by way of surfacing and diving, even so this doctrine darts hither and thither and does not come to a grasp;
thus it is called "eel-wriggling" (amarāvikkhepa). That eel-wriggling.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Even this is not my view," when asked, "Is this wholesome? he says, "Even this is not my view. Then, when asked, "What is unwholesome?
he says, "Even that is not my view. When asked, "Is it otherwise than both? he says, "Even that is otherwise is not my view.
Then, when asked, "Is your doctrine that it does not exist in any of these three ways? he says, "Even 'it is not' is not my view. Then...
When asked, "Is it not so according to your doctrine?", he resorts to evasion, saying, "It is neither 'not so' nor 'not not so'," and does not stand on either side.
"He departs in disgust" means that since even this teacher is unable to be a refuge for himself, he departs in disillusionment, thinking, "How could he possibly be able to do so for me?
This same method applies to the previous [teachers] who offered no consolation as well.

234. "To enjoy sensual pleasures by means of hoarding" means that just as formerly, when he was a householder, he enjoyed sensual objects by making a hoard, so now he is incapable of enjoying sesame, rice, ghee, butter, and so forth after having made a hoard;
this is the meaning. But surely sesame, rice, and the like are seen in the dwelling place of one whose taints are destroyed?
They are not seen there, yet he does not set them aside for his own sake; rather, he sets them aside for the sake of those who have gone forth into homelessness because they are unwell, and so forth.
"What is the case of the non-returner? Even for him, the five strands of sensual pleasure are entirely abandoned;
however, having acquired what is obtained through the Dhamma, he enjoys it after reflecting upon it.
236. "The sons of one whose son is dead"—it is said that having heard this teaching, he perceived that the Ājīvakas were indeed "dead," and thus he spoke.
This is the meaning here: the Ājīvakas are called "dead"; their mother is one whose son is dead; thus, the Ājīvakas are called "the sons of one whose son is dead.
Regarding "in the recluse Gotama": there is a dwelling in the holy life (brahmacariyavāsa) in the recluse Gotama.
He demonstrates that this is not found elsewhere. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Sandaka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyisutta 237.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāsakuludāyisutta. Regarding that, "at Moranivāpa":
they proclaimed safety for the peacocks at that place and gave them food; therefore, that place became known as Moranivāpa (the Peacock Sanctuary). "Annabhāra" means...
The name of one wandering ascetic was Varadhara; likewise [the name of another].

"And others" means not only these three, but many other well-known wandering ascetics as well. Regarding the phrase "one who speaks in praise of quietude," this was stated here without saying "one disciplined by quietude.
Why? Because the Blessed One was not disciplined by anyone else.
238. "The former" means those belonging to the previous day; beyond that are the "earlier. Regarding "the hall of curiosity":
there is no such thing as a hall for curiosity (*kutūhala-sālā*) existing in isolation;
rather, it is where various recluses and brahmins of different sects engage in all kinds of discourse. To many people, [it is known as] "what does this one say? What does this one..."
Because it is a place where curiosity arises as to what [the ascetics] are saying, it is called the "Hall of Curiosity" (*kutūhalasālā*).

The reading *kotūhalasālā* also occurs. Regarding "gains" (*lābhā*): the meaning is that these are the gains of those from Aṅga and Magadha who obtain the opportunity to see such ascetics and brahmins, to ask them questions, or to hear their discourse on the Dhamma.
In the passage beginning with *saṅghino*, those who possess a *saṅgha*—defined as a community of those gone forth—are called *saṅghino*.
Those who possess that very same group (*gaṇa*) are called *gaṇino*. One who is a teacher (*ācariya*) of that group by way of training them in conduct is a *gaṇācariya*.
They are known, renowned, and famous. Their fame has arisen through both qualities that correspond to reality and qualities that do not correspond to reality.
"They possess these" means they are "glorious. For in the case of Pūraṇa and others, their fame arose in such ways as, "He is of few desires and contented;

out of fewness of desire he does not even wear a cloth," and so forth. In the case of the Tathāgata, it arose through his qualities as they truly are, such as, "Thus indeed is that Blessed One," and so forth.
"Founders of sects" means makers of dogmatic views. "Esteemed as good" means: "These are good, beautiful, and true persons."
Thus they are so esteemed. "By many people" means by both the unlearned, blind, foolish worldling (*puthujjana*) and by the discerning, wise person (*paṇḍita*).
In this regard, the heterodox teachers (*titthiya*) are esteemed thus by the foolish person, while the Tathāgata is esteemed by the wise person.

By this method, the meaning of [the epithets] such as "leader of a community" (*saṅghī*) and so forth regarding Pūraṇa Kassapa should be understood. But as for the Blessed One, because he possesses the thirty-eight objects of meditation...
By analyzing [the Dhamma], he established many fords for crossing over to Nibbāna; therefore, it is appropriate to call him a "founder of a sect" (*titthakara*).
But why did all these [heretics] also enter there? It was for the sake of protecting their patrons and for the sake of gain and honor.
For they thought thus: "Our patrons might go for refuge to the ascetic Gotama, and they..."
“We shall protect [ourselves]. When they see that those who attend upon the ascetic Gotama are being honored, our own attendants will also honor us.
Therefore, wherever the Blessed One goes, there they all go.
“Having raised a dispute” means having attributed a fault to the argument. “Have departed” means they have gone away; some have departed toward a certain direction.
Some have attained the state of householders, while others have entered this teaching.
"Sahitaṃ me" means my word is appropriate, well-connected, meaningful, and reasoned; "asahitaṃ te" means your word is inappropriate.
"Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ" means that which has been long-practiced by you and is thus well-mastered is [reversed] for me.
It stands having been turned back and overturned by that very same single statement; the meaning is that nothing has been produced.
"A charge has been brought against you" means a fault has been attributed to your doctrine by me.

"Go for the sake of escaping the charge" means go about, wander here and there, and train yourself in order to release yourself from the fault. Or, "Unravel it if you are able" means then, yourself...
"You were able; now, release [your speech].
'With a roar of Dhamma' means with a roar of the true nature. 'We shall hear that' means we shall hear that Dhamma taught to us.
'Small honey' means honey made by small flies. 'Unblemished' means faultless, free from the stings of flies. 'He would press out' means he would give."
"Paccāsīsamānarūpo" means: he would stand waiting with a bowl in his hand, hoping, "Perhaps he will give me food after having filled it.
"Sampayojetvā" means: having engaged in some slight dispute. "Itarītarena" means:

by means of something inferior. "Pavivitto": this refers to the wandering ascetic speaking with reference to mere physical seclusion; however, the Blessed One is secluded by means of all three types of seclusion.
242. Regarding "those who eat from a bowl-casket" (*kosakāhārā*): in the houses of donors, there are small bowls intended for setting aside the finest alms-food.
The donors either set aside the best portion of food there and eat it themselves, or when a renunciant arrives, they give that food to him.
That bowl is called a "casket" (*kosa*). Therefore, those who subsist on just a single bowl of food [are so described].
"Those who eat from cocoons. "Those who eat from *beluva* fruits" means those whose food consists of a meal the size of a *beluva* fruit.
"Level to the brim" means level with the lower line of the rim of the mouth. "By this practice" means by this practice of eating little.
However, it cannot be said that the Blessed One was not one who ate much in every respect; for during the six years on the ground of striving, he indeed ate little, as did [the Buddha] at Verañjā.
For three months he sustained himself on nothing but rice-gruel in the Pālileyyaka forest grove; for another three months he sustained himself on nothing but lotus roots.

Here, however, he demonstrates this point: "At one time I was one who took little food, yet my disciples, from the moment they undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), do not break those practices as long as they live. Therefore, if they [the disciples] by this...
"They should honor me with the Dhamma, for they are more distinguished than I. However, he shows that there is yet another Dhamma by which they honor him.
This method of interpretation should be understood to apply to all sections.
