"Paṃsukūlikas" refers to those who have undertaken the practice of wearing rag-robes. "Wearers of coarse robes" refers to robes made from cloth worn out by knives or threads.
"Wearing. "Endless" (*nantaka*) means pieces of cloth devoid of ends; for if they had an end, they would be reckoned as mere rags (*pilotika*).
"Having picked out" means having torn [the cloth] and, discarding the weak parts, taking only the strong parts.
"Fine like the down of a gourd" (*alābulomasa*) indicates that the threads are fine, resembling the down of a gourd. And at this point, the Teacher—
He cannot be said to be "unsatisfied with contentment regarding robes.
For on the day he took the rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*)—which had been cast down after being worn by Puṇṇa-Dāsī at the Atimuttaka cemetery—the great earth shook even to its watery boundaries.
Here, however, he demonstrates this point: "I took the rag-robe at only one time; but my disciples..."
"From the time they undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) until the end of their lives, they do not break those ascetic practices.
"Alms-food eaters" (piṇḍapātika) means those who have undertaken the practice of eating alms-food after rejecting extra gains.

"Those who go for alms in regular order" (sapadānacārin) means those who have undertaken the practice of going for alms in regular order after rejecting the practice of seeking food greedily. "Delighting in the vow of gleaning" (uñchāsake vate rata) means [delighting] in that which is known as the practice of gleaning (uñchācariyā).
The meaning is that they delight in their natural state as monks, standing at the doors of high and low houses and partaking of alms-food collected from various sources.
"Into the interior of a house" (*antaraghara*) refers, in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*, to the area starting from the threshold;
here, however, it is intended to mean starting from the doorpost (*indakhīla*). And up to this point, the Teacher [has spoken] regarding contentment with alms-food.
"He is not to be called 'dissatisfied,'" but rather, everything should be detailed according to the same method already stated for "moderation in food.
Here, however, he shows this meaning: "I did not accept an invitation at more than one time;
but my disciples, from the moment they undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), do not break those practices for as long as they live."
"A tree-root dweller" means one who has rejected a roofed dwelling and undertaken the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree.

"An open-air dweller" means one who has rejected both a roofed dwelling and the foot of a tree and undertaken the practice of dwelling in the open air. "In the eight months" refers to the months of winter and summer;
however, during the rainy season, they enter a roofed dwelling for the sake of protecting their robes. To this extent, the Teacher [praised] contentment with lodgings.

"He is not to be called 'dissatisfied,'" for his contentment with lodgings is to be illustrated by both his six-year Great Struggle and by his stay in the Pālileyyaka forest grove. Here, however, he demonstrates this point:
"At one time I did not enter a roofed dwelling, yet my disciples, from the moment they undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), do not break those practices for as long as they live."

"Forest-dwellers" means those who have undertaken the forest-dweller’s practice by rejecting a monastery within a village. "They enter into the midst of the Saṅgha" refers to what is said regarding an unbounded boundary;
however, those living within a bounded boundary perform the Uposatha right at their own place of residence.
And to this extent, it cannot be said that the Teacher is not secluded, [as he said]: "Bhikkhus, I desire a half-month..."
"‘To dwell in seclusion’—in this way his solitude is made known. But here, he shows this meaning:

‘I dwelt in seclusion at only one such time; however, my disciples, from the moment they undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), do not break those practices for as long as they live. ‘My disciples’ means disciples of me."
244. "With a cause" (*sanidāna*) means with a condition (*sappaccaya*). But why does he not teach the unconditioned (*appaccaya*), Nibbāna? It is not that he does not teach it;
rather, having given that teaching as being accompanied by causes (*sahetuka*), he teaches it, and not as being without cause (*ahetuka*).
"With a demonstration" (*sappāṭihāriya*) is a synonym for the former [term]; the meaning is "with a reason" (*sakāraṇa*). In the phrase "that indeed" (*taṃ vata*), *vata* here is merely a particle.

245. "The path of discourse regarding the future" means setting aside for today the path of discourse concerning when a particular answer will arrive—whether tomorrow, the day after, in half a month, a month, or a year.
"He shall not see it" means that Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha did not perceive [the answer], even though he was speaking while specifying the reason for his coming in order to refute himself.
"It is impossible that he would not see it thus. "By means of the Dhamma" (*sahadhammena*) means with reason.
"They might interpose their talk" means they might interrupt my turn for speaking and insert their own talk in between.
"But I, Udāyī," [means] Udāyī, I [did not do so] because of Ambaṭṭha, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, Saccaka, the Nigaṇṭhas, and others.
Even when a great debate is taking place, I do not expect instruction from my disciples, thinking: "Oh, would that even a single disciple of mine might offer a simile or a reason!
In such circumstances, my disciples expect instruction and advice from me alone.
246. "I win their confidence" means that by answering that question, I capture, satisfy, and fulfill their minds;
I do not answer one thing when asked another, like answering about a jackfruit tree when asked about a mango, or an mango tree when asked about a jackfruit.
And here, in the phrase "honoring [me] in regard to higher virtue," it refers to the Buddha's virtue (*buddhasīla*).
The name has been stated; in the passage where it says, "honoring the advanced knowledge and vision," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);

in the passage where it says, "honoring higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*)," it refers to situational wisdom (*ṭhānuppattikapaññā*); and in the passage where it says, "by means of which suffering," it refers to the wisdom that explains the Truths (*saccabyākaraṇapaññā*).
Among these, setting aside both omniscient knowledge and the wisdom that explains the Truths, the remainder...
Wisdom partakes of higher wisdom.
Now, explaining the path for the attainment of those various specific distinctions, he said, "Furthermore, Udāyī," and so forth.

In that context, "having reached the perfection which is the culmination of direct knowledge" means having attained Arahantship, which is designated both as the culmination of direct knowledge and as the perfection of direct knowledge.
"In right exertion" means in the exertion of skillful means (*upāya*). "Arouses desire" means he arouses the wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
"Exerts himself" means he makes effort. "Arouses energy" means he sets energy in motion.
"Uplifts the mind" means he raises the mind. "Strives" means he performs the exertion of skillful means. "For the fulfillment of development" means for its increase.

For the purpose of fulfillment. Furthermore, it should be understood that here the preceding term is the meaning of the following, and the following is the meaning of the preceding, as follows: “That which is stability is non-confusion... [and so on] ...that which is abundance is the fulfillment of development.
But what is expressed by these right endeavors? By way of the discourse in the Kassapa-saṃyutta, the preliminary practice of a disciple is explained. For this is said there:

“Friends, there are these four right endeavors. What are the four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu arouses ardor so that evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen might not arise; he arouses ardor so that evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen might be abandoned; [he arouses ardor so that wholesome states that have not yet arisen might arise... [He arouses ardor so that wholesome states that have already arisen might endure... “...that they do not decline... “...that they may increase, reach fulfillment, and be cultivated to perfection. [He arouses ardor so that evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen might not arise... “...so that evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen might be abandoned... “...so that wholesome states that have not yet arisen might arise... “...so that wholesome states that have already arisen might endure... “...that they do not decline... “...that they may increase, reach fulfillment, and be cultivated to perfection. These, friends, are the four right endeavors. Thus it was said by the Blessed One, and in this regard, the following has been said: “He who, for the sake of abandoning evil, unwholesome states that have arisen, And for the sake of arising wholesome states that have not yet arisen, Exerts himself with diligence and right application— Such a person is called one who strives rightly. Thus it was said by the Blessed One, and having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to the monastery. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the four right endeavors were taught by the Blessed One as the path leading to the cessation of suffering. What are the four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, stirs up energy, applies his mind, and exerts himself. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, stirs up energy, applies his mind, and exerts himself. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, stirs up energy, applies his mind, and exerts himself. He generates desire for the endurance, non-decline, increase, fulfillment, cultivation, and perfection of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, stirs up energy, applies his mind, and exerts himself. Friends, these four right endeavors were taught by the Blessed One as the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said: “Friend Sāriputta, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the four right endeavors were taught by the Blessed One as the path leading to the cessation of suffering? “Friend Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has developed and cultivated the four right endeavors, he is capable of realizing any state realizable by direct knowledge to which he might turn his mind, should he so wish. That is why the four right endeavors were taught by the Blessed One as the path leading to the cessation of suffering. [The Venerable Ānanda said: “It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta, it is marvelous, friend Sāriputta! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘When a bhikkhu has developed and cultivated the four right endeavors, he is capable of realizing any state realizable by direct knowledge to which he might turn his mind, should he so wish. [The Venerable Sāriputta said: “Friend Ānanda, suppose a king or a royal minister had a frontier city with strong ramparts, walls, and foundations, and a single gate. There would be a gatekeeper there, wise, skilled, and prudent, who would not allow those inside to go out, nor those outside to enter, but would keep those inside in and those outside out. In the same way, friend Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has developed and cultivated the four right endeavors, he is capable of realizing any state realizable by direct knowledge to which he might turn his mind, should he so wish. [The Venerable Sāriputta said: “Friend Ānanda, suppose a man had a well-covered jar filled with water and placed on a stand. If he were to open the jar’s mouth, dip his hand in, and feel around, he would know whatever was in it. In the same way, friend Ānanda, when a bhikkhu has developed and cultivated the four right endeavors, he is capable of realizing any state realizable by direct knowledge to which he might turn his mind, should he so wish. “‘If unarisen wholesome states do not arise, they would lead to my harm,’ thus he exerts himself.
‘If arisen wholesome states cease, they would lead to my harm,’ thus he exerts himself.
And here, “evil unwholesome states” should be understood as greed and so forth; “unarisen wholesome states” refers to serenity and insight.

The path and the arisen wholesome states refer specifically to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). However, once the path has arisen and is ceasing, there is nothing that leads to what is unbeneficial;
for it ceases only after having provided the condition for the fruit.
Alternatively, it was stated that in the previous case as well, only serenity and insight should be understood [as the wholesome states], but that is not correct.
In this context, the following story is told to clarify the meaning of the statement: "When serenity and insight have arisen, they lead to harm as they cease.

It is said that a certain elder whose taints were destroyed, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Great Cetiya and the Great Bodhi," came from the countryside to the Mahāvihāra with a novice attendant who was an attainer of meditative absorptions; having arrived, he entered a courtyard of the monastery.
At the time of evening, while the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus was worshipping the Cetiya, he did not go out to worship the Cetiya.
Why? Because those whose taints were destroyed possessed great reverence for the Three Jewels.

Therefore, when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had finished their worship and was withdrawing, at the time when people were eating their evening meal, [the Elder] went without even informing a novice, thinking, "I shall worship the Cetiya."
He went out alone. The novice thought, "Why is the Elder going out alone at an unusual hour?

I shall find out," and he followed right behind his preceptor's footsteps. Since the Elder had not directed his attention to it, he was unaware of the novice's arrival and ascended to the courtyard of the shrine by the southern gate.
The novice also ascended immediately after him, following step for step.

The Great Elder, having looked up at the Great Cetiya and experienced rapture directed toward the Buddha, focused his entire mind upon it and paid homage to the Cetiya with a heart overflowing with joy.
Seeing the Elder’s manner of worship, the novice thought, "My preceptor pays homage with an exceedingly serene mind; perhaps he has obtained flowers and is performing an offering?"
The Elder, having paid homage and stood up, placed his hands in añjali at his head and stood gazing at the Mahācetiya.
The novice, having coughed, made known his arrival. The Elder, turning around and looking about, asked, "When did you arrive?
"At the time of paying homage to your cetiya, venerable sir. "Did you pay homage to the cetiya with great faith?"
"Shall we, having obtained flowers, pay homage? "Yes, novice; apart from this cetiya, there is no other repository for relics such as this.
Who would not pay homage with flowers to such an incomparable Great Thūpa?
"In that case, venerable sir, please consent; we shall bring them. Having said this, he immediately entered into meditative absorption (jhāna).
Having gone to the Himālaya by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), he filled a water-strainer with flowers endowed with excellent color and fragrance.

Before the Great Elder had even reached the western gate from the southern gate, he returned, placed the flower-strainer in the Elder’s hand, and said, "Venerate them, venerable sir. The Elder said, "The flowers are too small for us, novice."
"Go, venerable sir, and having brought to mind the virtues of the Blessed One, offer worship.
The Elder ascended by the staircase facing west and began to make an offering of flowers on the floor of the inner railing.
Flowers fell in full abundance upon the railing floor and reached knee-deep on the second floor.
They filled it by means of their supernormal power (*iddhi*). Then, having descended, he made an offering upon the footprints. Those too were completely filled.
Knowing they were full, he proceeded scattering [the flowers] on the lower level. The entire courtyard of the shrine (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) was completely filled.
When that was full, he said, "Novice, the flowers are not being exhausted. [The novice replied,] "Venerable sir, turn the water-strainer upside down."
Having turned it face down, he shook it, and then the flowers were exhausted.
Giving the strainer to the novice, he circumambulated the Cetiya three times along the elephant wall, paid homage at four places, and as he was going toward his own cell, he thought:
"How great indeed is this novice's psychic power! Will he be able to maintain this supernatural majesty?"
"Protect him. Then, seeing that he would not be able [to do so], he said to the novice: "Novice, you are now possessed of great psychic power;
yet, having destroyed such power, in your final days you will drink conjey crushed by the hand of a blind weaver-woman.
This is indeed the fault of youthfulness; stirred by his preceptor's words, he—
He did not request, saying, “Venerable sir, please explain a meditation subject to me”;
rather, he went along as if not hearing what our preceptor was saying.
After the Elder had paid homage to the Mahācetiya and the Mahābodhi tree, and had the novice take his bowl and robes, he proceeded by stages.
He went to the Kuṭeḷitissa Mahāvihāra. The novice did not go on alms-round following his preceptor step by step;
instead, having asked, "To which village are you entering, venerable sir?
and realizing, "My preceptor will now have reached the village gate," he took hold of both his own bowl and robe and those of his preceptor.
Having traveled through the air, he gave the elder his bowl and robes and entered the village for alms. The elder constantly exhorted him:

"Sāmaṇera, do not act in this way! The supernatural power of an ordinary person is indeed unstable and unsteady; having encountered an unsuitable object such as a form, it is broken by even the slightest [distraction].
When one has fallen away from a peaceful meditative attainment, the life of the holy life (brahmacariya)..."
“He cannot steady himself. The novice did not wish to hear what his preceptor was saying, and he continued to act in that very same way.
As the elder proceeded by stages, performing worship at the cetiyas, he arrived at the monastery named Kammabinduvihāra.
While the elder was staying there, the novice continued to act in that same manner.

Now one day, a weaver’s daughter—beautiful and in the prime of her youth—having departed from the village of Kammabindu, descended into a lotus pond and was gathering flowers while singing. At that moment, a novice monk was passing by the edge of the lotus pond;
as he went along, he became captivated by the sound of her song, like a blind fish caught in a net. Immediately, his...
His supernatural power vanished, and he became like a crow with clipped wings.

However, by the power of his peaceful meditative attainments (*santasamāpatti*), he did not fall into the water there, but descended like a *simbali* cotton-wool and gradually came to rest on the bank of the lotus pond.
He went quickly, gave the bowl and robes to his preceptor, and returned. The Great Elder said, "This was already foreseen by me..."
"Having seen him, even if he is restrained, he will not turn back. Saying this, she entered for alms without saying anything further.
The novice went and stood on the bank of the lotus pond, waiting for her to come back across.
She too, seeing the novice first traveling through the air and then returning and standing there, thought: "Surely he is distressed because of me."
Having understood this, he said, "Step back, novice. He stepped back.
The other one climbed out, put on her garment, approached him, and asked, "What is it, venerable sir? He explained the matter to her.
Although she instructed him by showing, through many reasons, the disadvantage of the household life and the benefit of living the holy life (*brahmacariya*), his weariness with the world—
Being unable to dissuade him, she said, "Because of me, he has fallen away from such supernatural power;
it is no longer right for you to abandon him," and having said this, she went home and reported the matter to her parents.
They too came and, though they exhorted him in various ways, when he would not accept their words, they said: "We are of high birth..."
He observed them and said, "We are weavers. Will you be able to perform the work of a weaver?
The novice replied, "Lay follower, once one has become a householder, one might indeed do the work of a weaver or the work of a basket-maker;
why do you feel such greed for this mere robe? The weaver, having given him a robe tied around his waist, led him home and gave him his daughter.
Having thus learned the craft of weaving, he worked at the loom in the workshop together with other weavers.
While the wives of the others had prepared and brought food early in the morning, his wife had not yet arrived.
As the others set aside their work and sat down to eat, he remained sitting there spinning his shuttle. She arrived later, and then he—
“You have arrived far too late! she rebuked him. Now, a woman—even one who knows that a universal monarch (cakravartin) has his heart bound to her—regards him as if he were a slave.
Therefore, she spoke thus: “In the houses of others, wood, leaves, salt, and so forth are stored;
there are also messengers and servants who bring things from outside to give them away. But I am all alone.”
“You too do not know whether this exists or that does not exist in my house. If you wish, eat;

if you do not wish, do not eat. He, becoming angry—thinking, “Not only do you bring me food after the sun has set, but you even provoke me with your words”—seeing no other weapon, tore a thread from the cotton-roller and hurled it at him.
Seeing him approaching, she turned her head slightly. Now, the tip of a shuttle-handle is sharp;
as she turned, it entered the corner of her eye and remained there.
She seized the eye with both hands with great force, and blood flowed from the punctured spot. At that time, [he went] to the preceptor...
He recalled these words: "It was with reference to this that my preceptor said to me, 'In the future, you will drink conjey kneaded by the hands of a blind weaver-woman.
This must have been seen by the Elder; oh, what a man of far-reaching vision this noble one is!
And he began to weep with a loud cry. Then others said to him, "Enough, friend, do not weep; the eye, indeed..."
"It is not possible to restore what has been broken by weeping," they said. He replied, "I am not weeping for this reason;
rather, it is on account of this that I weep," and he related everything in its proper sequence. Thus, serenity and insight that have arisen lead to harm when they cease.

There is another story: About thirty bhikkhus, having paid homage at the Kalyāṇi Mahācetiya, were descending from the forest path onto the main road when they saw a man coming along the way who had returned from working in a burnt field.
His body was as if smeared with soot; he was wearing a single saffron robe that appeared as though it too were smeared with soot, tucked under his armpit.
Clad in his robes, when looked upon, he appeared like a charred log.
Having performed his work during the day, he lifted a bundle of half-burnt firewood, came along a by-path with his hair disheveled over his back, and stood before the bhikkhus.
Upon seeing him, the novices looked at one another and said, "Friend, your father—your..."
“Your great father was my maternal uncle,” they said, laughing, and as they went on, they asked, “What is your name, lay follower?
Being thus questioned about his name, he became filled with remorse;
he cast aside the bundle of wood, adjusted his cloth, put it on, paid homage to the Great Elders, and said, “Wait a moment, venerable sirs. The Great Elders waited.
The young novices came and even mocked the great elders in their presence. A lay devotee said: "Venerable sirs, you laugh at me upon seeing me;
do not think that you have reached the pinnacle by this alone.
In the past, I too was a recluse just like you. Yet, you possess not even a mere measure of one-pointedness of mind."
"In this teaching, I was one of great psychic power and great majesty; taking up the sky, I made it earth, and taking up the earth, I made it sky.
Taking what was far, I brought it near, and taking what was near, I made it far. I could pierce through a hundred thousand world-systems in an instant.
Look at my hands; they are now like the hands of a monkey. By these very [hands]..."
"Seated right here, I touched the moon and sun with my hands. Using these very feet as footstools, I sat upon the moon and sun.
Such supernatural power of mine has vanished through negligence; do not be negligent yourselves.
For through negligence, people encounter such calamity. By dwelling heedfully, you will reach the end of birth, aging, and death."
"Therefore, venerable sirs, being heedful, take me alone as your object," he said, and after thus admonishing them with a warning, he gave them instruction.
While he was still speaking, those thirty men were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and, practicing insight (*vipassanā*), attained Arahantship right there.
Thus it should be understood that even serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), when they arise and then cease, lead to what is disadvantageous.

And here, regarding the phrase "of evil states that have not yet arisen," the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in such passages as: "The unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise.

Regarding "of evil states that have arisen," there are four kinds of arising: arising as currently occurring (*vattamānuppanna*), arising as having been and passed away (*bhutvāvigatuppanna*), arising by way of providing an opportunity (*okāsakatuppanna*), and arising by reaching its plane (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*). Among these, those defilements which are presently existing...
That which belongs to one possessing [a state] such as arising (*uppāda*) is called "presently arisen" (*vattamānuppanna*).

However, when a kamma has impelled and the resultant (*vipāka*), having experienced the flavor of the object, has ceased, it is called "vanished" (*vigata*). When the kamma itself, having arisen and ceased, has vanished, it is also called "vanished.
Both of these are designated by the term "arisen after having been experienced and vanished" (*bhūtvāvigatuppanna*). Wholesome or unwholesome kamma [is related] to another...
Having obstructed the ripening of another karma, one creates an opportunity for one’s own ripening;
when that ripening arises once such an opportunity has been created, it is reckoned as "arisen from the creation of an opportunity. This is what is called *okāsakatuppanna*.
Furthermore, the five aggregates are called the "ground" for insight (*vipassanā*); they are divided into past, present, and future. Within these, the latent defilements (*anusaya*) reside.
However, they cannot be described as past, future, or present.
For even when latent in past aggregates, they remain unabandoned; likewise, even when latent in future or present aggregates, they remain unabandoned.
This is what is called "arisen by way of having acquired the plane. Therefore, the ancients said: "The defilements that have not been eradicated in those respective planes..."
...are reckoned as "arisen having attained the plane.

Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of what is arisen: arisen as manifestation (*samudācāruppanna*), arisen by way of apprehending an object (*ārammaṇādhigahituppanna*), arisen without being suppressed (*avikkhambhituppanna*), and arisen without being eradicated (*asamugghātituppanna*).
Among these, that which is occurring at this very moment is called "arisen as manifestation. Once—

It cannot be said that defilements will not arise at every moment of recollecting once the eyes have been opened and the sign as an object has been grasped. Why? Because the object has been apprehended.
How so? Just as it cannot be said that milk will not flow from a milky tree at the very spot where it is struck by an axe, so it is here. This is what arises from the apprehension of the object.
As for the name: it cannot be said that the defilements which have not been suppressed by attainment will not arise in this particular place.

Why? Because they have not been suppressed. How so? Just as if one were to strike a milky tree with an axe, it cannot be said that the milk will not flow out from this particular spot; such is the case here. This is what is meant by "arisen without being suppressed."

[This is] called "arisen. However, for one who has been reborn even in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), defilements that have not been eradicated by the Path still arise; this should be explained in detail according to the previous method.
This is what is called "arisen without having been eradicated" (*asamugghātituppanna*).

Among these types of arisen states, there are: arisen as currently occurring (*vattamānuppanna*), arisen as having occurred and passed away (*bhūtvāvigatuppanna*), arisen as providing the opportunity (*okāsakatuppanna*), and arisen as manifest activity (*samudācāruppanna*).

There are four kinds of arisen [defilements] that are not to be abandoned by the path: those arisen by way of having acquired a plane, those arisen by way of having grasped an object, those arisen without being suppressed, and those arisen without being eradicated. There are four kinds of arisen [defilements] that are to be abandoned by the path:
for when the path arises, it abandons these defilements. As for the defilements it abandons, are they past, future, or present?
It should not be so stated. For this has also been said:

"If one abandons past defilements, then one must be exhausting what is already exhausted, ceasing what is already ceased, making what is already vanished vanish, and making what has already set go to its setting. One abandons that which is past and non-existent. If [one abandons] the future..."
If one abandons defilements, then one abandons what is unborn, unarisen, unproduced, and unmanifested.

One abandons that which is future and non-existent. Now, if one abandons defilements in the present, then one who is lustful abandons lust, one who is hateful abandons hatred, one who is deluded abandons delusion, one who is bound up abandons conceit, and one who is misapprehending abandons wrong view.
One abandons restlessness when it has reached distraction, doubt when it has reached the undesirable, and underlying tendencies when they have become firmly established.
Dark and bright phenomena proceed together in a state of union and equilibrium. There is a path-cultivation that leads to defilement... [etc.
...Therefore, there is no cultivation of the path, no realization of the fruit, no abandoning of defilements, and no breakthrough to the Dhamma. There is.
“There is the development of the path... there is the realization of the Dhamma. How so? Just as, for example, a young tree that has not yet borne fruit...
[and so on] ...they do not become manifest because they have not yet become manifest.
Thus, although a tree with unproduced fruit appears in the Pāḷi, it should be illustrated by means of a tree with produced fruit. For just as when it has fruit...
Suppose there were a young mango tree, and people were to enjoy its fruits, filling their baskets by dropping the remainder to the ground.
Then another person were to cut that tree down with an axe; by doing so, he would not have destroyed the fruits already past, nor would he have destroyed those yet to come or those present.
For the past fruits have already been enjoyed by people, and the future ones have not yet been produced.
It is not possible to destroy [the fruit]. However, at the moment when that [tree] is cut down, since there are no fruits at all, even those in the present are not destroyed.

But if the tree were not cut down, then those fruits which would have been produced through the earth-essence and water-essence would have been destroyed; for they would simply not have arisen, being unproduced.

They do not arise; being unmanifested, they simply do not become manifest. In the same way, the Path does not abandon the defilements (kilesa) categorized as past and so forth, nor does it fail to abandon them.

For those defilements whose arising might have occurred had the aggregates (khandha) not been fully understood by means of the Path—since the aggregates have been fully understood by means of the Path’s arising—those defilements do not arise even though they were not yet born, and they do not come into existence even though they were not yet produced.

They do not arise; they do not become manifest because they were previously unmanifest. This point should be clarified by the example of a woman who has recently given birth and does not conceive again, or by the medicines drunk by those afflicted with disease for the purpose of pacifying their illness.
Thus, when the Path abandons defilements, it cannot be said whether those defilements are past, future, or present; nor...

And yet, the path does not abandon all defilements. However, it is with reference to those defilements which the path does abandon that the passage beginning, "of arisen evil [states]," and so forth, was spoken.
Furthermore, the path does not abandon only defilements; rather, because of the non-abandonment of certain defilements, those [states] which might otherwise arise—
He abandons even those aggregates that have been grasped. And this has been said:

"By means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, through the cessation of volitional consciousness, name-and-form—which would otherwise arise in the beginningless round of existence, setting aside the seven [remaining] births—cease right here.
This is the detailed explanation. Thus, the path emerges from both the grasped and the ungrasped. By way of becoming (*bhava*):
However, the path of stream-entry emerges from the existence of the woeful states; the path of once-returning, from a portion of the existence of happy destinies;

the path of non-returning, from the existence of sensual-sphere happy destinies; and the path of Arahantship, from the existence of the fine-material and immaterial realms. Some even say that it emerges from all existences whatsoever.
Now, at the moment of the path, how is there development for the arising of those [factors] not yet arisen, or how is there development for those already arisen?
"By way of stability": this refers precisely to the occurrence of the Path. For when the Path occurs, because it has never arisen before, it is called "unarisen.

Indeed, having come to a place not previously reached, or having experienced an object not previously experienced, people say: "We have come to a place not yet reached; we are experiencing an object not previously experienced. That which...
Its occurrence is itself called its "stability" (*ṭhiti*); thus, it is also appropriate to say that one "develops [the path] for the sake of stability.

Regarding the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the brief exposition is stated in the *Cetokhila Sutta*. It "goes toward tranquility," or "goes for the purpose of the pacification of defilements," thus it is "leading to tranquility" (*upasamagāmī*).
It "goes toward full awakening," or "goes for the sake of the full awakening of the Path," thus it is "leading to full awakening" (*sambodhagāmī*).

The sections beginning with "living detached" have been explained in the *Saṃvara* chapter on the curbing of all taints (*āsava*). This is the summary here; however, this discourse on the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*) has been set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
248. In the discourse on liberation (*vimokkha*), in what sense are they called "liberations"? They are so called in the sense of "resolving" (*adhimuccana*). What, then, is this sense of resolving?
It is the sense of being thoroughly released from opposing states (*paccanīka-dhamma*), and by way of delighting in the object (*ārammaṇa*).

The meaning of "well-liberated" (*suṭṭhu-muccanaṭṭha*) is that it occurs upon the object without restriction and with freedom from apprehension, like a child lying on his father’s lap with all his limbs relaxed;
this is what is meant. This meaning, however, does not exist in the final liberation (*pacchima-vimokkha*), but exists in all the preceding ones.
Regarding the phrase "one possessing form sees forms," herein [the meditator contemplates] internal hair and so forth by way of the blue kasiṇa and the rest.
The fine-material jhāna that has been produced is "form" (*rūpa*); because he possesses that, he is "possessed of form" (*rūpī*).
"He sees forms externally" means that he also sees external forms, such as the blue kasiṇa and so forth, with the eye of jhāna.
By this, all four fine-material-sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna upon kasiṇas based both internally and externally are shown.

"Not percipient of internal forms" (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī*) means not being percipient of forms internally; the meaning is that one has not produced fine-material-sphere jhāna regarding one's own head-hairs and so forth.
By this, the fine-material-sphere jhānas produced externally after performing the preliminary work externally are shown.
"He is intent only on the beautiful" (*subhanteva adhimutto hoti*): by this, [the text refers to] the color-kasinas, such as blue and so forth, which are perfectly purified.

The meditations (jhānas) have been shown. In this regard, although there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) toward "the beautiful" (*subha*) within the actual absorption (*appanā*), nevertheless, one who dwells having made the perfectly pure kasiṇa of the beautiful his object comes to be described as "intent upon the beautiful.
It is for this reason that the teaching was given in this way. However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it is asked: "How is it that he is intent upon the beautiful?"
It is called liberation because beings become non-repulsive through the cultivation of loving-kindness. Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness...

[and so on] ...because loving-kindness has been cultivated, beings become non-repulsive. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and with equanimity... [and so on] ...because equanimity has been cultivated, beings become non-repulsive.
"Thus, being resolutely intent upon the beautiful, it is called 'liberation,'" so it is said.
Regarding the phrases "entirely transcending perceptions of form," and so forth, everything that needs to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"This is the eighth liberation": this is the eighth because of the complete relinquishing and liberation from the four aggregates.
This is called the supreme liberation.
249. Regarding the discourse on the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), "bases of mastery" refers to the causes for mastering.
What do they master? Both adverse phenomena and objects of perception. For they master adverse phenomena by way of being their opposites.
These are the objects for a person’s excellence in knowledge.
In the case of the passage beginning with “perceiving forms internally,” one is said to “perceive forms internally” by means of preliminary work (*parikamma*) on internal forms.
When performing preliminary work on blue, one does so either on the hair, the bile, or the pupil of the eye; when performing preliminary work on yellow, one does so on the fat or the skin.
Or he applies it to the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes;
when performing the treatment for redness (*lohitaparikamma*), he applies it to the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes;

when performing the treatment for whiteness (*odātaparikamma*), he applies it to the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. That [color] is indeed very blue, very yellow... [and so on].
It is not very red or very white; it is simply not quite pure.
"One sees forms externally": this refers to one for whom the preliminary work (*parikamma*) has arisen internally, while the sign (*nimitta*) is external.
Such a person, by way of the preliminary work being internal and the absorption (*appanā*) being external, [thinks]: "Internally..."
"One percipient of forms sees forms externally" is what is said. "Limited" means unextended.
Whether they be beautiful or ugly—whether they be of good color or bad color—it should be understood that this base of mastery is spoken of specifically by way of their limited nature.
"Having mastered them" means, for example, as one who has a full stomach, having received only a spoonful of food, thinks: "What is there here..."

Just as one who has gathered food together makes it into a single mouthful with the thought, "There is something to be eaten," even so, a person preeminent in knowledge, possessing clear wisdom, thinks:
"What need is there to attain [jhāna] upon such a limited object? This is no burden for me.
Thus, having mastered those forms, he attains absorption; he reaches absorption right along with the arising of the sign (nimitta).

This is the meaning. By the phrase "I know, I see," his mental application (*ābhoga*) is indicated; however, this applies only to one who has emerged from attainment, not while within the attainment itself.
"He perceives thus" means that he perceives thus both by way of the perception of mental application and by way of the perception of the jhāna.
For while the perception of mastery exists for him within the attainment, the perception of mental application belongs only to one who has emerged from the attainment.
"Infinite" (*appamāṇāni*) means having increased measure; the meaning is "vast. Regarding the word "having overcome" (*abhibhuyya*):
here, just as a gluttonous man, upon receiving one large portion of food, thinks, "Let there be more, let there be more;
what will this do for me? and does not perceive it as something great, even so is the person supreme in knowledge, possessing clear wisdom.
Thinking, "What is there to attain here? This is not immeasurable; I have no burden in achieving one-pointedness of mind," he attains it by overcoming those [hindrances];
the meaning is that he reaches absorption (appanā) right along with the arising of the sign (nimitta).
"Perceiving the formless internally" means being devoid of the preliminary perception (parikamma-saññā) regarding internal form, either due to non-attainment or due to lack of interest.

"One sees forms externally": one for whom even the preliminary work (*parikamma*) and the sign (*nimitta*) have arisen only externally is thus called "one who, being percipient of the formless internally, sees forms externally" by way of both the external preliminary work and absorption (*appanā*).
The rest here is exactly according to the method stated for the fourth base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).
Among these four, however, the limited [meditation subject] is presented for those of a discursive temperament; the immeasurable for those of a deluded temperament;
the beautiful for those of a hating temperament; and the ugly for those of a lustful temperament. For these subjects are suitable for them.
And their suitability has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the description of the temperaments (*caritaniddesa*).
In the context of the five bases of mastery (*pañcama-abhibhāyatana*) and so forth, the term "blue" (*nīla*) is stated in a comprehensive sense;

"blue-colored" (*nīlavaṇṇa*) is by way of color; and "blue-appearing" (*nīlanidassana*) is by way of appearance. What is meant is that they are seen as being entirely blue, with no visible gaps and with undiluted color.
The phrase "blue-luminous" (*nīlanibhāsa*), however, is stated by way of radiance; it means "blue-radiant."
The meaning is "endowed with blue radiance. By this, he shows their extreme purity;
for it is precisely by way of their pure color that these four bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) are described. As for the *umā* flower:
this flower is glossy and soft, and even when being seen, it remains purely blue. However, flowers such as the *girikaṇṇikā* possess a white constituent when being seen.
Therefore, this alone was taken [as the example], not those others. "Bārāṇaseyyaka" means produced in Bārāṇasī.
It is said that there the cotton is soft, the spinners and weavers are skilled, and the water is pure and smooth;
therefore, the cloth is smooth on both sides, appearing soft and smooth on both surfaces.

The meaning of the passages beginning with "yellow" (*pītāni*) should be understood in this same manner. Furthermore, regarding the acquisition of the blue kasiṇa— where one grasps the sign in something blue,
whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color-element— all details concerning the preparation of the kasiṇa, the preliminary work (*parikamma*),
and the method for absorption (*appanā*) have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Attaining the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge": having previously developed those states such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, they indeed attain the state of an Arahant and are thus called "those who have attained the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge.
However, it is only by having gained mastery over these eight bases of mastery that they are called "those who have attained the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge."

250. In the discourse on the *kasiṇas*, they are called *kasiṇas* in the sense of being "entire. They are called *āyatanas* (bases) in the sense of being a field for the states that have them as their object, or in the sense of being a foundation.
"Upwards" means directed toward the surface of the sky above. "Downwards" means directed toward the surface of the earth below.
"Across" means delimiting it all around like a circular field. For some [meditators]...
One expands the kasiṇa upwards, another downwards, and another all around.
For such reasons as these, one extends it just as one desiring to see forms extends light. Therefore it is said: "One perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across.
"Non-dual" means non-dual in the cardinal and intermediate directions; this, however, is stated for the purpose of showing that it does not become anything other than itself.
For just as for one who has entered water, there is only water in all directions and nothing else, even so the earth-kasiṇa is only the earth-kasiṇa;
there is no other breach of the kasiṇa for it. This same method applies everywhere.
"Immeasurable" (appamāṇa) is said with reference to the measure of its pervasion; for when one pervades it with the mind, one pervades it entirely.
"He grasps a measure, thinking, 'This is its beginning,' and 'This is its middle.

Here, "consciousness-kasiṇa" refers to the consciousness occurring in the space cleared by the kasiṇa. In this context, the directions—above, below, and across—should be understood with respect to the space cleared by the kasiṇa, and with respect to the consciousness occurring therein.
This is the summary here regarding the method for developing the meditation subject.
These earth-kasiṇa and other objects have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

It should be understood that here too, they reach the perfection of mastery in direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) only by one who has already attained mastery (*vasibhāva*). The same applies to the four jhānas immediately following these.
Whatever else needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the *Mahā-Assapura Sutta*.
252. Regarding the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), however, the meaning of "material" (*rūpī*) and so forth has already been stated.
Here, "sitam" means dependent upon, and "paṭibaddham" means bound to, this body composed of the four great elements. "Subho" means beautiful. "Jātimā" means produced from a perfectly pure mine.
"Suparikammakato" means well-worked, with stones and gravel removed. "Accho" means clear.
"Vippasanna" means perfectly clear. "Sabbākārasampanna" means endowed with all qualities such as being well-washed, well-pierced, and so forth.
By the words "blue," etc., he shows the perfection of its color; for when threaded [on a string], such a gem becomes clearly visible.
Regarding the phrase "even so," the application of the simile should be understood as follows: the body born of karma is like the gem, and the thread that has been threaded through it is...
The knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is like the jewel. The bhikkhu who has attained insight is like the man with eyes.

Just as the moment the jewel becomes manifest to one who has taken it in his hand and reflects, thinking, "This indeed is the jewel," so too is the moment the body composed of the four great elements becomes manifest to the bhikkhu who sits having directed his attention toward the knowledge of insight. "In this, this thread is woven."

Just as the time when a sutta becomes manifest, so too for a bhikkhu sitting after having directed his insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), it is the time when the contact and its four concomitants (the "contact-pentad") that have that as their object, or all consciousness and mental factors, or even the insight-knowledge itself, become manifest.

But is this manifestation of knowledge [a property] of the knowledge or of the person? It is of the knowledge; however, because of the manifestation of that [knowledge], it is [attributed] to the person.

These become manifest. And although this knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) occurs immediately after the path, nevertheless, because there is no occasion for it in between when the section on the direct knowledges (abhiññā) is undertaken, it is shown here.

Furthermore, for one who has not yet performed the comprehension of formations as impermanent and so forth, while hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear-element, or through the recollection of past lives...
When one recollects the "terrible shoulders" and sees a terrifying form with the divine eye, fear and terror arise;

this does not happen to one who has practiced insight (sammasana) by way of impermanence and so forth. Therefore, this is shown right here for the purpose of fulfilling the causes that dispel fear for one who has attained direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Here too, the attainment of the perfection that is the culmination of direct knowledge should be understood as occurring specifically through Arahantship.
253. Regarding "mastery in the mind-made psychic power" (*manomayiddhi*): herein, "mind-made" (*manomaya*) means produced by the mind.

"Complete in all limbs and minor parts" (*sabbaṅgapaccaṅga*) means endowed with all major and minor limbs. "With unimpaired faculties" (*ahīnindriya*) means having faculties that are not deficient in terms of their configuration.
For if the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) is fair-skinned, the form created by him is also fair; if he has unpierced ears, that [form] is also [unpierced].

"Unpierced ear" means that in every respect it is exactly like that [ear]. The triad of similes beginning with "the shaft from the *muñja* grass" is stated solely for the purpose of demonstrating its similarity.
For its internal shaft is indeed similar to the *muñja* grass; the sword is indeed similar to its sheath:
they insert a round sword into a round sheath, and a broad one into a broad one.
*Karaṇḍa*—this too is a name for a snake’s slough, not for a basket or a small box. For a snake’s slough is indeed similar to a snake itself.

In this context, although it is shown as if a man were lifting a snake out of a *karaṇḍa* with his hand—as in the phrase “a man might lift a snake from its *karaṇḍa*”—nevertheless, its extraction should be understood as occurring by means of the mind alone. For this so-called snake [remains] within its own kind...
Standing there, leaning against a space between logs or between trees, it casts off its own skin by itself through four causes:
through the power known as the effort of pulling the body out from the skin; through loathing the old skin as if it were devouring the body; and through these [other] two reasons.
It cannot be removed from there by anyone else. Therefore, its removal is by means of the mind.

It should be understood that this was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). Thus, the body of this bhikkhu is like the *muñja* grass and so forth, while the created form (*nimmitarūpa*) is like the *īsikā* reed and so forth;

this is the correlation of the simile here. Furthermore, the method of creation here and the discussion on the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), beginning with the power of supernormal success (*iddhividhā*), have been explained in detail in all their aspects in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, they should be understood according to the method stated there. For it is only the mere simile that is additional here.
In this context, the monk who has attained the knowledge of the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*) should be seen as being like a skilled potter and others;

the knowledge of the various kinds of supernormal power should be seen as being like well-prepared clay and so forth; and the transformation performed by that monk should be seen as being like the making of various vessels and other objects according to his desire.
Here too, it is precisely through mastery gained by practice that one reaches the perfection of the culmination of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
[This] should be understood. Likewise for the four higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) that follow. 255.
In that context, regarding the simile of the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*), "saṅkhadhamo" means a conch-blower. "Appakasireneva" means without difficulty.
"Viññāpeyya" means he would make [them] understand. In that case, when the conch-blower makes [the sound] known in the four directions in this way...

Just as the time when the sound of a conch becomes manifest to beings who discern it, thinking, “This is the sound of a conch,” so too should the time when sounds—both divine and human, whether distant or near—become manifest to the yogin be understood. 256.
In the simile for the knowledge of others’ minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), “young” means tender; “youthful” means endowed with the bloom of youth; “of a decorative nature” means...
"Though young, he is not indolent, nor does he have soiled clothes or body; rather, he is habituated to adornment.
This means that he has the custom of bathing two or three times a day, putting on clean clothes, and wearing ornaments.
"With a blemish" means having some defect such as a black mole, a wrinkle, a facial blemish, a pimple, or the like. In that regard, as for his facial appearance—

Just as a blemish on the face becomes evident to one who looks at it, so too it should be understood that for a bhikkhu who sits having directed his mind toward the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), the sixteenfold types of consciousness of others become evident.
Whatever needs to be said regarding the similes for past lives (*pubbenivāsa*) and so forth, all of that has already been stated in the section on Mahā-assapura.
259. “This, Udāyi, is the fifth quality”: having made the nineteen sections into a single quality by way of the practice, it is called “the fifth quality.

For just as in the *Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta* eleven sections were made into one quality by way of questions, so here it should be understood that the nineteen sections have been made into one quality by way of the practice.

Furthermore, among these nineteen stages, it should be understood that in the eight successive sections, the attainment of the perfection of mastery in direct knowledge culminates in the knowledge of insight and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints by way of Arahantship; in the remaining sections, it is by way of having attained mastery.
The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyisutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhimanikāya, is completed. 8.
The commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍikasutta.
260. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Samaṇamuṇḍika-sutta. Therein, Uggāhamāna is the name of that wanderer;
Sumanā is his natural (given) name. However, because of his capacity to grasp and master various things, people know him as Uggāhamāna.
It is called *samayappavādaka* because they proclaim their doctrines (*samaya*) therein. It is said that at that place, Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, and others—

Brahmins, Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, Paribbājakas, and other renunciants gathered together and proclaimed, discussed, and expounded their respective doctrines; therefore, that monastery was called Samayappavāda.
Because it was surrounded by a row of *timbarūsaka* trees known as *tindukācīra*, it was called Tindukācīra. Furthermore, because at first there was one...
Originally it was a single *sāla* tree; later, many *sāla* trees were planted there by means of the great merit of the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda.
Therefore, because its name was derived from that one original *sāla*, it is called "Ekasālaka" (The Single *Sāla*).
However, since that grove—covered with flowers and fruits—was the pleasure garden of Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Pasenadi, it became known as "Mallikā’s Grove."
He had gone. At that time, he was dwelling in the Mallikā Park, which had a single sal tree and was surrounded by *tinduka* and *acīra* trees, in the place called Samappavādaka.
"Dwells" (*paṭivasati*) means he dwells with the ease of a settled residence. "During the day of the day" (*divā divassa*): "midday" (*divā*) refers to the passing of noon;
the meaning is that he went forth as soon as it had become midday, even during the day. "Secluded" (*paṭisallīno*).

Having withdrawn the mind from here and there—from the range of visible forms and so forth—it becomes "withdrawn," having entered a state of one-pointedness through the practice of delighting in jhāna.
"Of those who are to be developed by the mind" means of those who increase the mind; those for whom, when they advert and attend, the mind becomes free from hindrances, uplifted, and grows.
"As many as" means however many there are. "This one is among them" means this one is included within them.
"A single disciple. He spoke thus while aspiring to approach him; the reason for this aspiration has already been stated in the Sandaka Sutta. "He said this":
this householder Dandapañña, having won him over with a discourse on the Dhamma, [made him] his own disciple.
Thinking, "I shall do it," he spoke these words beginning with, "Indeed, by four... In this context, *paññapemi* means "I show," "I establish.
*Sampannakusalaṃ* means "perfectly wholesome. *Paramakusalaṃ* means "supremely wholesome.
*Ayojjaṃ* means that which cannot be moved or shaken after having engaged in a battle of debate; it is immovable, unshakable, firm. *Na karoti* means...
He speaks only of non-doing; herein, however, he does not speak of either abandonment through restraint or abandonment through practice.
The same method applies to the remaining phrases.
"Neither rejoicing" means that the sectarians, whether knowing or not knowing, speak thus, thinking [it to be so].
"He does not rejoice, nor does he reject" means that, thinking "he speaks as if in conformity with the Teaching and as if with a clear conviction," he does not oppose him.
"Just as for Uggāhamāna" means: "If his word were true, then this child lying on its back would become an invincible ascetic, a steadfast ascetic;
however, we do not say such a thing. "Even his own body does not exist" refers to his own body.

There is no supernormal knowledge (*visesañāṇa*) regarding another's body either. Apart from mere movement, there is only what is called the movement of the body through contact with a fold in a bedspread or by being bitten by a bug; other than that, there is no other action performed by the body.
And even that occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements (*kilesasahagatacitta*). There is also no such thing as "speech," meaning wrong speech (*micchāvācā*).
There is no difference even in what is called right speech. "Merely weeping" means that for one overcome by hunger and thirst, there is merely weeping;

yet even that is with a mind accompanied by defilements. There is no difference even in what is called wrong intention or right intention. "Merely wailing" means there is merely wailing, the measure of weeping and laughing. For young children...
The mind functions with a past object: those who have come from hell weep, remembering the suffering of hell; those who have come from the deva-world laugh.
That too occurs only through a mind accompanied by defilements (*kilesa*). There is no distinction between "livelihood" as wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*) and right livelihood (*sammājīva*).
"Except for mother’s milk": there are indeed children who steal their mother’s milk; [the phrase] "milk in the mother" refers to that.
Having not yet drunk from their mother’s breast, they come from behind and drink milk.
Apart from this, there is no other wrong livelihood; he shows that even this occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilement.
263. Having thus rejected the doctrine of the wanderers, he now establishes the matrix for his own stage of training (*sekhabhūmi*).
He said, "By four [factors] indeed," and so forth. In that context, "standing having attained" means standing having distinguished [oneself].

Regarding the passage beginning with "no evil deed by body," it is not merely the non-performance [of such deeds] that is intended; rather, the Blessed One here prescribes restraint, abandonment, and reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhā*).

It is with reference to this that he spoke thus. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "and not perfected in skillful [states]" was spoken with reference to one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
Now, establishing the matrix (mātikā) for the stage of one beyond training (asekkhabhūmi), he says, "By ten indeed, I am," and so forth.
Therein, two initial tetrads are established based on three terms, and two final tetrads are established based on one term.
This is the matrix for the stage of one in training (sekkhabhūmi).
264. Now, analyzing that, he said: "And what, master carpenter, are unwholesome virtues? and so forth.

Therein, "with lust" (*sarāga*) refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (*lobha*). "With hatred" (*sadosa*) refers to the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).

"With delusion" (*samoha*) may include the two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*), or indeed all unwholesome states of consciousness; for delusion exists in all unwholesome [states].
For it is said, "it arises. "Arising from this" means those whose arising or origin is from this mind characterized by lust and so forth;

thus they are "arising from this. "Where" means having reached which place do they cease without remainder? "In this" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), which is used here as a locative case.
For the morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha becomes complete in the fruit of stream-entry; having reached that state—
Unwholesome virtue ceases without remainder. It should be understood that "unwholesome virtue" is a designation for immorality (*dussīlya*).

Regarding the phrase "one who has entered upon the practice for the cessation of unwholesome virtues": here, one is said to have "entered upon the practice for cessation" up until the path of stream-entry; however, once the fruit is attained, those [virtues] are said to have been ceased. 265.

By the terms "free from lust" (*vītarāga*) and so forth, only the eightfold wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is expressed. For it is by means of this that wholesome virtue (*kusalasīla*) arises.
"Virtuous" means he is endowed with virtue and endowed with qualities. "But not consisting of virtue" means: "Enough with this much;
there is nothing further to be done beyond this"—thus he does not consist of virtue. "In that [fruit] for him" refers to the fruit of arahantship (the locative case).
For upon attaining the fruit of arahantship, unwholesome conduct ceases without remainder.

"One who has entered upon the way to cessation": here, one is said to have "entered upon the way to cessation" up until the path of Arahantship; however, when the fruit is attained, those [mental states] are said to be "ceased. Regarding the perceptions of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) and so forth:
the perception of sensual desire is co-nascent with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed;

the other two are co-nascent with the two types of consciousness accompanied by grief. "The first jhāna": this refers to the first jhāna of the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). "In this case" (*ettha*) is used in the locative sense, meaning "in the fruit of Non-returning. For when one has attained the fruit of Non-returning, unwholesome intentions cease without remainder.
"Practicing for cessation": here, one is said to be "practicing for cessation" up until the path of non-returning; however, once the fruit is attained, those [states] are called "ceased.
For the three perceptions beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*) are simply the eight wholesome co-nascent perceptions (*sahajātasaññā*) of the sense-sphere.
267. "In this case": this is the locative case referring to the fruit of arahantship. For having reached the fruit of arahantship associated with the second jhāna—
Wholesome intentions cease without remainder. Regarding the phrase "one who has entered upon the way for cessation":
here, one is said to have "entered upon the way for cessation" up until the path of Arahantship; however, once the fruit is attained, they are said to be "ceased. The rest is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta is finished.
9. The commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta:

"Thus have I heard" refers to the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta. Therein, the words "But when, venerable sir, the Blessed One... were spoken by the wanderer wishing to hear a discourse on the Dhamma, demonstrating his longing for the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma.
271. "Let that very thing appear to you here" means: if you desire to hear the Dhamma, let one question and one reason present themselves to you alone.

"In such a way that it might appear to me" means: by whatever reason my teaching of the Dhamma might manifest, for by that reason, when the discourse has arisen, it is easy to teach the Dhamma—this is what he indicates. To me, therefore...

"Venerable Sir," he thought upon seeing him: "If the Blessed One were here, he would illuminate the meaning of this speech for me today, making it clear as if lighting up a thousand lamps. Thus, he recollected the Ten-Powered One alone and said to him, "Venerable Sir, for me...
and so forth. In that context, *aho* and *nūna* are two particles used in the sense of recollection.
As he was thus recollecting the Blessed One, this thought occurred to him: "Oh, how wonderful it would be if the Blessed One were here!
Oh, how wonderful it would be if the Sugata were here! "Of these" means of these phenomena (*dhammā*). "Well-skilled" means thoroughly skilled, subtle, and clever.
"He, the Blessed One, would surely speak; he, the Sugata, would surely speak. For that Blessed One possesses the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).
“Many thousands of millions of aeons [are] open and manifest as a single courtyard”—this is the intended meaning here.

Regarding the phrase “I know his past,” one who is a recipient of such knowledge, when told, “In the past you were a khattiya, you were a brahmin,” understands it and listens with due respect. But one who is not a recipient [thinks], “It will be thus.”
"It will be thus"—by this he shows merely the movement of his head. Therefore he said:
"I might satisfy his mind with an answer concerning his past. Or else, "He [might ask] me about the future";
for the knowledge of the future belongs to one who has attained the divine eye, and therefore he spoke thus. The other [part of the passage] is exactly as explained previously.
"I shall teach you the Dhamma"—it is said that even when taught in the past, he would not have understood it, and even when taught in the future, he would not have understood it.
Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to teach him the subtle and delicate mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*), spoke thus. But how could he understand that?
He would certainly not have understood it even before; however, in the future, it will serve as a condition for his latent predisposition (*vāsanā*).
Having seen that it would happen, the Blessed One spoke thus.
"A dust-demon" (*paṃsupisācaka*) refers to a demon born in an unclean place; for such a one, having grasped a single root, becomes invisible.
Here is the story: it is said that a certain female spirit (*yakkhinī*), having seated two children at the gate of the Thūpārāma, went out in search of food.
They went into the city. Seeing a certain elder monk who lived on alms-food, the children said, "Venerable sir, our mother has entered the city; please tell her:
'Whatever you may obtain, take it and go quickly, for the children cannot endure their hunger. "How shall I find her? he asked.
"Venerable sir, please take this," they said, and gave him a single piece of radish root. The elder perceived thousands of *yakkhas*;
by means of the sign given by the children, he saw that *yakkhinī*—ugly and hideous, nothing but a mass of womb-impurities clinging to the street.
Having seen her, he explained the matter to them, saying: "In what way do you see me?"
When this was said, he showed him a root-section; she cut it off and took it.
In this way, having taken a single root, the dust-demons (paṃsupisācakā) become invisible in body. Referring to them, he said, "I do not even see a dust-demon.
"It does not appear" means it is not seen, it does not manifest.
"Even though this speech of yours is long, Udāyin"—even if one were to speak for a hundred years or a thousand years, it would not illuminate the meaning;
this is the intended sense. "It becomes unconvincing" means it turns out to be non-leading, baseless, and purposeless.
Now, showing that color, he said, "Just as if, venerable sir," and so forth. Therein, "placed upon a yellow cloth" means set upon a red cloth of a different color.
"The self is of such a color" refers to the aggregates produced in the Subhakiṇha deva-world;
he says this thinking, "At the time of our death, the self shines like the aggregates in the Subhakiṇha deva-world."
273. "Of these two"— it is said that he spoke thus because the light of the gem does not radiate outward at all,
whereas the light of a firefly radiates only for a distance of two, three, or four finger-breadths, while the light of a great firefly radiates even as far as the circumference of a threshing floor.

“Viddhe” means pierced; the meaning is that it has become distant due to the clearing away of clouds. “Vigatavalāhake” means cloudless. “Deve” means in the sky. “Osadhitārakā” means the white star (the morning star).
For because people take and drink medicinal herbs starting from its rising, using it as a sign, it is therefore called the “herb-star. “Abhido aḍḍharattasamayaṃ” means at the time of midnight.

"At the time when the night was undivided" means at midnight; by this, he indicates the moon situated in the middle of the sky. The same principle applies to "after midnight," which refers to the time of midday as well.

"Than those who experience it" means there are more than those who experience it; the sense is that they are both numerous and even more numerous. "The radiance does not reach them" means they do not partake of the light; rather, they dwell having pervaded the surroundings with the radiance of their own bodies. 274.
Now, since he sat down thinking, "I shall ask about the world of absolute happiness," yet he was confused regarding his question—
Because he was born [of such a lineage], the Blessed One, reminding him of that past, said: "But, Udāyin, is there a world of absolute happiness?

and so forth. In this context, "possessing form" (*ākāravatī*) means possessing a cause (*kāraṇavatī*). Or else, "a certain quality of asceticism" (*tapoguṇa*) is said with reference to the practice of the naked ascetics (*acelaka*);
the meaning is "abstinence from drinking fermented liquor" (*surāpānavirati*).
275. But why, venerable sir, does he ask, "What then is that method with its specific modes that leads exclusively to happiness"?
It was because it occurred to him: "We speak of absolute happiness for beings, yet we describe the method as being pleasant at times and painful at times.
However, for one who possesses absolute happiness, even the method leading to it should be exclusively happy."
"It must be so. Our discourse is not leading to liberation; only the Teacher’s discourse leads to liberation.
Thinking, "Now I shall find out by asking the Teacher himself," he therefore asks.
"In this matter we have been ruined" means: for this reason we have been ruined. But why did they say this? It is said that they...

In the past, having established themselves in the five qualities, performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, and produced the third jhāna, they passed away without falling away from that jhāna and were reborn among the Subhakiṇha devas; thus they knew [this].
But as time went on, they no longer even knew the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, nor were they able to produce the third jhāna.

Having learned that the five preliminary states constitute "the method possessing formal characteristics," they then grasped the third jhāna as "an exclusively blissful world. Therefore, they spoke thus. "Superior" means:
we do not know any practice superior to these five states, nor any exclusively blissful world superior to the third jhāna; this is what is meant.
...there is. "Having made it silent" means having silenced them when they had begun to make a great noise all at once. 276.

Regarding "for the sake of realization," there are two kinds of realization here: realization as acquisition (*paṭilābha-sacchikiriyā*) and realization through direct experience (*paccakkha-sacchikiriyā*).
In that regard, having produced the third jhāna and passed away without falling away from that jhāna, [one is reborn] in the Subhakiṇha world among them...
Having become equal in lifespan and appearance to the gods, one is reborn; this is called the realization through acquisition (*paṭilābha-sacchikiriyā*).

Having attained the fourth jhāna, one goes to the Subhakiṇha world by means of the transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*) and stands together with those gods, converses with them, and engages in discussion;
this is called the realization through direct experience (*paccakkha-sacchikiriyā*). For both of these, the third jhāna is...
This is called the "path with specific modes. For indeed, without producing that [path], it is impossible both to be reborn in the Subhakiṇha world and to produce the fourth jhāna.
Thus, referring to these two kinds of realization, he said:
"Surely, venerable sir, it is for the sake of realizing this world of absolute happiness..."
277. *Udañcanikā* means a water-drawer. "He created an obstacle" means he caused such an affliction that he did not obtain the going-forth (pabbajjā), because his supporting conditions had failed.
It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, this man went forth and practiced the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma).
Then, a certain fellow monk who was dissatisfied with the Teaching said, "Friend, let us disrobe."
He reported this. [The other] conceived a longing for his bowl and robes and praised the state of a householder.
The first gave him his bowl and robes and left the order. Because of that karma, an obstacle has now arisen to his going forth in the presence of the Blessed One.
However, for him, the previous discourse was only the length of one *bhāṇavāra*, while this one is only a single *bhāṇavāra*.

The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma thinking, "Though the Dhamma has been taught through such an extent of scripture, the penetration of the path and its fruit has not yet arisen even from a single portion of the teaching; however, it will become a condition for him in the future.

Having seen that this will be a condition for him in the future, the Blessed One, while still living, did not place even a single bhikkhu in the foremost position among those dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*). For he perceives—
The Blessed One said: "In the future, having gone forth in my dispensation, this one will become the foremost of those who dwell in loving-kindness.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, during the time of King Dhammāsoka, he was reborn in Pāṭaliputta.

Having gone forth and attained Arahantship, he became known as the Elder Assagutta and was the foremost of those who dwell in loving-kindness. By the power of that elder’s loving-kindness, even animals—

They attained a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā-citta*). The Elder, having become the preceptor and teacher for the community of monks throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, resided in his dwelling place;
a forest extending about thirty *yojanas* became a single meditation hall.
The Elder spread out a piece of leather in the air and, sitting upon it, taught the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*). As time passed...

Even when he did not go out for alms at the proper time but remained in the monastery, he would discourse on the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); consequently, people went to the monastery itself and gave offerings.
When King Dhammāsoka heard of the Elder’s virtues and desired to see him, he sent messengers three times;
yet the Elder did not go even once, saying, "I am giving exhortation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
The commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 10.
Commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta.
278. Thus have I heard: this is the Vekhanassa Sutta. Regarding that, "Vekhanassa" was, it is said, the teacher of Sakuludāyī.
Having heard that "the wanderer Sakuludāyī has been defeated in the 'Question on the Highest Praise'," he thought, "I have taught him thoroughly, and he too has learned it thoroughly;
how then could he have been defeated? Come now, I shall go there myself."
“Having asked the ascetic Gotama a question concerning supreme praise, I shall know [the answer].
Having traveled from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī, a distance of forty-five yojanas, he approached the Blessed One.

Upon arriving, he stood right there in the presence of the Blessed One and uttered an inspired utterance (*udāna*). In this regard, it should be understood as being identical to what was previously stated according to the same method.
