280. Why was this fivefold set undertaken? Because among householders, some are heavy with sensual desire and intent upon sensual desire, while others are heavy with renunciation and intent upon renunciation.
And among those who have gone forth, some are heavy with sensual desire and intent upon sensual desire, while others are heavy with renunciation and intent upon renunciation.
Now, this one who is heavy with sensual desire and intent upon sensual desire—
[He] is present. Thinking, "As this discourse is being told, he will perceive his own inclination toward sensual pleasures;
thus this teaching will be suitable for him," [the Buddha] began this teaching. "The supreme bliss of sensual pleasures" refers here to Nibbāna.
"Will be led astray" means he will be led into a state of ignorance. "It turns out to be merely a name" means...
It becomes nothing more than a mere meaningless statement. "Let the past be, let the future be":

because you lack the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) appropriate for discourse on the past, and you lack the divine eye knowledge (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) appropriate for discourse on the future, he said, "let both of these be. "By means of cord-fastenings" means by means of fastenings made of thread.
Indeed, for the sake of protection, strings are tied to his hands, feet, and neck;
it is with reference to these that this was said. However, in his old age, those strings either become rotten and fall off by themselves, or they are cut and removed.
By the phrase "even so," he shows this: the time when a young boy does not yet understand the binding of strings.
The non-knowing of ignorance regarding its prior limit is like [the darkness] before dawn; for it is not possible to know the prior limit of ignorance.
However, at the time of liberation, there is a knowing similar to that [dawn], in that the release from the bond of ignorance has occurred through the path of Arahantship.
The rest is entirely clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta of the Papañcasūdanī,
the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Chapter on Kings (Rājavagga) 1.
The Discourse to Ghaṭīkāra (Ghaṭikārasuttavaṇṇanā) 282.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Discourse to Ghaṭīkāra. Therein, "he manifested a smile" while traveling along the Great Highway (Mahāmaggam).
Looking at a certain spot on the ground and reflecting, "Did I ever dwell in this place while practicing the holy life?
he saw: "In the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a market town called Vebhāra in this very place;
at that time, I was a young brahmin named Jotipāla, and Ghaṭīkāra was my companion."
“There was once a potter by the name of Nāma; with him I performed a certain virtuous deed here that remains unknown and hidden from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Come, let me make it known to the Saṅgha.
Having stepped down from the path, he stood in a certain spot and manifested a smile; showing his very white teeth, he gave a gentle laugh.
They laugh. For just as worldly people, slapping their chests, laugh saying "kuhaṃ kuhaṃ," so it is not with the Buddhas;
rather, the laughter of the Buddhas is merely an expression of being joyful and exultant.
And this laughter occurs through thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by mental joy (*somanassa*). In that regard, the worldlings [regard] it as unwholesome...

By means of eight consciousnesses—four from the wholesome of the sense sphere and four from the wholesome of the fine-material sphere—one laughs. Learners (sekkhā) laugh by means of six consciousnesses, having excluded the two associated with wrong view from among the unwholesome.
Those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) laugh by means of five consciousnesses: four functional consciousnesses accompanied by roots and one rootless functional consciousness.
Even among these, when a powerful object enters the range of perception, they laugh by means of two.

They laugh with consciousnesses associated with knowledge; they laugh with three types of consciousness: the two types of double-rooted consciousness and the rootless consciousness when the object is weak.

However, in this instance, it was the functional, rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy that produced the Blessed One’s smile, which was merely an expression of being exceedingly joyful.
Yet even such a trifling thing as this smile became manifest to the Elder.

How so? For at such a time, from the four tusks of the Tathāgata, there arose three times from the mouth of the great cloud that pervades the four continents—like flashes of white lightning—circular rays of light the size of the trunk of a great palm tree, which shone brilliantly upon his noble head.

Having performed a circumambulation, they vanished right at the tips of the fangs. By that sign, even as the Venerable Ānanda was walking behind the Blessed One, he recognized the manifestation of the smile.
He said this to the Blessed One: "It is said that here the Blessed Kassapa exhorted the community of monks, proclaiming the Four Noble Truths."
Thinking, "I shall inspire the Blessed One’s desire to sit here as well; thus this spot of ground will have been used by two Buddhas,
and the great multitude, having honored it with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and having made it a site for a cetiya,
will become intent upon the path to heaven," he spoke these words beginning with, "Then indeed, venerable sir."
283. Regarding the phrase "by the shaven-headed ascetic" (*muṇḍakena samaṇakena*): it is permissible to say "shaven-headed one" (*muṇḍo*) or "ascetic" (*samaṇo*).
However, because his knowledge was not yet mature, he spoke thus out of contempt, using only the terminology he had learned while in the brahmin family.

"A bathing-cloth" (*sottisinānaṃ*) refers to a cloth made for the purpose of bathing. A "bathing-cloth" (*sotti*) consists of bundles of small balls made by binding powdered *kuruvinda* stones with lac.
It is said with reference to this that it was stated: "At that time, the group-of-six monks were bathing with *kuruvindaka* thread.

Holding it at both ends, they rub their bodies with it. "Thus, 'it is right'" means just as even nowadays people, when told, "We are going to pay homage to the cetiya," or "We are going for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma," [do so].
They did not show enthusiasm; however, when told, "Let us go to see a theatrical performance and the like," they accepted with a single voice.
Likewise, when it was said, "Let us bathe," he who accepted with a single voice spoke thus. 284.
He addressed the young brahmin Jotipāla: having bathed first on one side according to the custom of the noble ones.

Having stepped out and stood there, while the Bodhisatta—who possessed the strength of a nāga—was waiting for the conclusion of his bath as he was bathing with great royal pomp, [the other] addressed him as he was wringing out his lower and upper garments and his hair in the water. He spoke thus, pointing him out because of his proximity.
"Having untied the waist-band," means that the Bodhisatta, who had the strength of a nāga, said, "Move aside, good sir," while turning slightly.
The meaning is: "having caused him to release what he had grasped. Having touched him by the hair, he said this;

for it is said that he thought: "This Jotipāla is wise; if he obtains even a single sight of the Tathāgata, he will gain confidence upon seeing Him, and he will also gain confidence through the discourse on the Dhamma; and being confident, he will be able to manifest his confidence."
"Friends indeed exist for this purpose: having done whatever is necessary, let us take my companion and go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
Therefore, seizing him by the hair, he said this:
"Ittarajacco" means one of another birth, one not of the same birth as myself, one of inferior birth; such is the meaning. "Na vatidan" [means...]
"This journey of ours will surely not be insignificant nor small; it will be great.
For he did not take hold [of the burden] by his own power, but took hold of it by the power of the Teacher; thus he reached his conclusion even at the very moment of taking it up.
Regarding the phrase "yāvatādohipi": here the letters *do*, *hi*, and *pi* are particles; the meaning is "as far as the limit" (*yāvatuparima*). This is what was said.
There is [this view]: “Having gone beyond mere verbal address and grasping by the waist, one must make an effort to go there even as far as seizing the hair. 285.
Regarding “a talk on the Dhamma”: here, it is a talk on the Dhamma connected with past lives for the sake of attaining mindfulness.
It should be understood. For the Blessed One spoke to him in this manner for the sake of his recovery of mindfulness: “Jotipāla, you have not descended into an inferior state;
rather, you have descended after aspiring for omniscience upon the seat of Great Enlightenment.
For one such as you, an abiding in negligence is not fitting,” and so forth. However, the Elders dwelling beyond the sea say: “Jotipāla...”

"Just as I, having fulfilled the ten perfections and realized omniscient knowledge, now wander the world with a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, so too shall you, having fulfilled the ten perfections and realized omniscient knowledge,
wander the world surrounded by a host of recluses. It is not fitting for one such as you to fall into negligence."
He spoke of the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation in such a way that his mind inclined toward the going-forth.
286. Ānanda, he obtained... [the formula continues] ...he obtained the going-forth and the full ordination.
Having gone forth, what did he do? He did what must be done by Bodhisattvas. For Bodhisattvas go forth in the presence of the Buddhas. Having gone forth—

Furthermore, they do not fall like ordinary beings whose horns have dropped; rather, having become well-established in the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), having mastered the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Pitakas, and having undertaken the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), they enter the forest and, fulfilling the conduct of coming and going, practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Increasing their insight (*vipassanā*), they stand firm until they reach the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*).
They do not exert effort for the sake of attaining the fruits of the path. Jotipāla did exactly the same.
287. Regarding "ordained for half a month": for when a youth from a noble family has been ordained and departs after staying for even half a month, his parents' grief does not subside;
moreover, he himself does not know how to handle the bowl and robes, being [surrounded] by young bhikkhus and novices.
Confidence does not arise with them, affection for the elders is not established, and dissatisfaction arises wherever they go.
However, if he lives [nearby] for such a time, his parents are able to see him;
consequently, their grief diminishes, and he learns how to take up the bowl and robes from the novice monks and young bhikkhus.
Confidence arose with them, affection for the elders was established, he took delight wherever he went, and he felt no weariness.
Therefore, thinking, "It is fitting to stay for this long," he stayed for half a month and then departed.
"Red rice in a *paṇḍu* husk" refers to red rice that had been placed in a husk and dried. It is said that of that rice...
From the time of sowing onwards, this was the method of care: the fields were well-tilled;
having established the seeds there, they sprinkled them with scented water. At the time of sowing, they tied cloth and palm-leaf mats over them like canopies.
When the grain was ripe, they cut off the heads of the rice, placed them in handfuls within small bags, and bound them with cords.
Having dried them right there in the open air, they spread out fragrant powders, filled the storehouses with them, and opened them in the third year.

Thus, having taken the fragrant, red-husked rice that had been stored for three years—free from black grains and perfectly pure—they prepared various kinds of snacks and meals. It was with reference to this that it was said: "exquisite."
“Hard food and soft food... [and so on] ... he announced that it was time.

(288) “I have consented”—with reference to what does he say this? At the time of departing from Vegaḷiṅga, Ghaṭīkāra had taken a promise from him to dwell the rains retreat in his presence; it is with reference to that that he says it. Indeed, a change occurred.
"I had grief" means that for three months he was unable to give alms, listen to the Dhamma, and attend upon the twenty thousand bhikkhus according to this routine;
thus, regarding this failure, there arose a change of mind and mental dejection, but not with respect to the Tathāgata. Why?
Because he was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). It is said that previously he had been devoted to brahmins. Then, on one occasion—
While going to pacify a rebellion in the border regions, he said to his daughter named Urañchada, "Mother, do not neglect our deity.
When the brahmins saw that princess, they lost consciousness. When asked, "Who are these?
she replied, "They are your 'earth-gods' (bhūmideva). Thinking, "Such are indeed the earth-gods," they spat in contempt.
She ascended the palace. One day, while standing and looking down at the street, she saw the foremost disciple of the Blessed One Kassapa;
having summoned him and given him almsfood, she became a stream-enterer even as she was listening to his expression of thanks.
She then asked, "Are there other bhikkhus as well? and was told, "The Teacher resides at Isipatana with twenty thousand bhikkhus."
Having heard this, he invited them and gave a gift.
The king returned after having pacified the border regions. Then, the brahmins arrived even earlier than him and disparaged the daughter, speaking ill of her.
However, the king had already granted her a boon at the very time of her birth: "Seven..."
They chose as their boon that she should be granted the sovereignty for seven days. Then the king handed over the kingdom to her for seven days.
While she was feeding the Teacher, she summoned the king and had him sit outside the enclosure.

Upon hearing the Teacher’s expression of thanksgiving, the king attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotāpanna*). And it is impossible for one who has attained stream-entry to harbor resentment toward the Tathāgata.
It does not exist. Therefore it was said: “Not concerning the Tathāgata.
[The phrase] “let him take whatever he wishes” means that, it is said, he did not engage in the buying and selling of vessels after having baked them;
rather, having spoken thus, he would go into the forest for the sake of wood, or clay, or straw. The great multitude [said]: “By Ghaṭīkāra...”
Having heard, "The vessels are cooked," they come bringing pure rice, salt, curds, oil, molasses, and so forth.
If the vessel is expensive while the price is low, thinking, "We will take it by paying whatever [is required]," they do not take it.
This righteous merchant looks after his parents and attends upon the Perfectly Enlightened One; much unwholesome [kamma] has been done by us.
Thinking, "It will be so," they go back again and fetch the capital.
But if the vessel is of little value while the capital brought in is great, the merchant acts righteously;

thinking, "There will be merit for us," they carefully secure the goods as they were brought and depart, just like householders. Yet, why does one with such qualities not go forth into homelessness? [This was] the course of the King's speech.
"He supports his blind, aged mother and father by cutting [the food] for them," he said.
289. "Where indeed? means "In what place indeed? "From the pot" means from the cooking vessel. "From the saucepan" means from the vessel for curry.
"Eat" means consume. But why do they speak thus? It is said that Ghaṭikāra, having cooked the rice and prepared the curry...
Having fed his mother and father, and having eaten himself, he sets out the Blessed One’s portion of rice and curry, prepares a seat, provides a stand, and presents water;
then, having given the signal to his parents, he goes to the forest. Therefore they say: "abhivissattho" means "excessively confident. "Pītisukhaṃ" (bliss of rapture).
"He does not abandon" means he does not abandon it continuously; rather, whether during the night or the day, in the village or in the forest, at whatever moment he recollects:
"In this world with its devas, the Supreme Person has entered my house, taken material food with his own hands, and consumed it; what a gain for me!"—at each such moment...
In that moment, five-colored rapture arises; it is with reference to this that it was said. 290.
"From a basket" means from what has been cooked. But why did the Blessed One do so? Because it was a legitimate provision, similar to the meal [placed] in the bowls of the monks;
therefore, he did so. Furthermore, the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) applies only to the disciples.
For the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a fixed time for the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). It is just as when flowers and fruits are found in a king’s garden:
they restrain others who would take them, yet the king himself enjoys them as he pleases; this case is exactly like that.
However, the elders dwelling beyond the sea say, "It is said that the deities received [the fruit] and gave it [to the Buddha]."

"Take him away, venerable sirs! Take him away, good men! they said, their hearts filled with joy at the thought of seizing their son, who—when asked, "Where have you gone?"—replied, "To the presence of the One of Ten Powers. "Where indeed is he going?
Does he not even know that the Teacher’s dwelling place is subject to rain? thinking thus, they spoke these words, perceiving a transgression in their son.
"He stood for three months under the open sky" means that the Blessed One, it is said, had the grass brought after three of the four months of the rainy season had passed;
therefore he spoke thus. As for the meaning of the words here: "that which has the sky as its covering" is *ākāsacchadana*.
"The god did not rain excessively" means that he did not merely fail to rain, but rather, just as in this case, by nature, even when the rim [of a vessel] is turned downward...
Not even a single drop of water fell within the area where the water had fallen [before];
thus, like being inside a house with a thick roof, neither wind nor sun caused any affliction, and there was only the natural pervasion of the seasons.
Later, even after that townsite had been abandoned, that place remained rain-proof. When people were working there while it was raining, [they would take shelter].
There they perform their work after placing a cloth over it; until the end of the eon, that place shall remain exactly as it is.
And this is not through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, but rather through the perfection of their own virtues.
For it was said of them: "Where could the Perfectly Enlightened One not find [a place]? Even our own dwelling, we two blind men—" [and so on].
He did not give rise to dejection on account of that, thinking, "The Supreme Person in the world with its devas has had grass brought from our residence and had the fragrant chamber roofed over.
Rather, a no small and powerful joy arose in them, thinking, "The Supreme Person in the world with its devas has had grass brought from our residence and had the fragrant chamber roofed over.
Thus, it should be understood that this miracle occurred solely because of their own excellence of virtue.
292. Regarding the phrase "two hundred cartloads of rice": here, it should be understood that two carts constitute one *vāha*.
And "suitable curry" refers to oil, molasses, and so forth, appropriate for the soup.

It is said that the King sent this much, under the impression that there would be food for twenty thousand bhikkhus for three months. Why did he refuse, saying, "It is enough; let it remain with the King himself"?
Because he had attained fewness of wishes, this thought occurred to him: "I have never been seen by the king;
how then has he sent [this message]? Then he reflected: "The Teacher has gone to Bārāṇasī;

surely, when he was requested for the rainy-season residence by the king, he informed him that he had given me his promise and spoke words of praise regarding my virtues. It is through these words of praise that he has received this gain."
Rather, it is like what is gained by an actor after dancing, or like what is gained by a singer after singing. [He thinks:
"What use have I for this? Having performed my duty, I am able to provide service even to my parents and to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The rest is clear in all respects.
The commentary on the Ghaṭikāra Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 2.
The commentary on the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta.
293. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta. In this context, *Thullakoṭṭhika* means a large granary, a full storehouse.
It is said that this district always had abundant crops; seed-grain was constantly being exported, while harvested grain was constantly being imported.
Because of this, the granaries in that town were always full. Therefore, it became known by the name Thullakoṭṭhika.
294. Why is he called Raṭṭhapāla? He is called Raṭṭhapāla because he was capable of holding together and protecting a divided kingdom.
But when did this name arise for him? It arose during the time of the Sammasambuddha Padumuttara.
For a hundred thousand eons prior to this, when the lifespan of human beings was one hundred thousand years, there appeared [the Buddha] named Padumuttara.
The Teacher, having arisen, wandered for the benefit of the world accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus. With reference to this, it was said:
"The city was named Haṃsavatī; the kṣatriya was named Ānanda;
Sujātā was the mother of the Teacher Padumuttara."
But even before Padumuttara had appeared, two householders in Haṃsavatī, full of faith and confidence, established an almsgiving for the poor, the destitute, beggars, and others.
At that time, five hundred ascetics living on the mountains arrived at Haṃsavatī.
Those two men attended upon them, having divided the company of ascetics into two groups. After staying there for some time, the ascetics returned to the foot of the mountain.
They departed. Two senior elders of the Saṅgha were left behind. Then, they served as their attendants for the rest of their lives.
While the ascetics were eating and offering words of thanksgiving, one praised the abode of Sakka, and the other praised the abode of the Nāga King Bhūmindhara.
Among the householders, one made an aspiration for the abode of Sakka and was reborn as Sakka; another [made an aspiration] for the Nāga realm.
There was a king of the nāgas named Pālita. When Sakka saw him come to his own assembly hall, he asked him, "Do you take delight in the nāga realm?
He replied, "I do not take delight in it. [Sakka said,] "In that case, give an offering to the Blessed One Padumuttara and make a resolution at this spot;
then we both shall dwell in happiness. The nāga king invited the Teacher, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, [to his abode].
While the Blessed One was giving a great almsgiving for seven days, he saw a novice named Uparevata, the son of the Ten-Powered Padumuttara Buddha.
On the seventh day, having given divine robes to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he made an aspiration for that novice’s future status.
The Blessed One, looking into the future, said: "In the future, [to the disciple] of Gotama..."
Having seen that the son of the Buddha would become Prince Rāhula, he said, "Your aspiration will be fulfilled.
The Nāga king told this matter to Sakka. Having heard his words, Sakka likewise gave alms for seven days;
then, having been reborn into a family capable of sustaining and protecting a divided kingdom, [he saw] one who had gone forth out of faith.

Upon seeing the noble son named Raṭṭhapāla, he made this aspiration: "In a future world, when Buddhas like you have arisen, may I be born into a family capable of restoring and protecting a divided kingdom;
and having gone forth out of faith, may I become one named Raṭṭhapāla, just like this noble son. The Teacher [declared] that it would come to fruition.
Having understood this, he spoke this verse:
"There shall be born here one who will be able to support the four castes together with the king;
he shall belong to the family known as Raṭṭhapāla."
Thus it should be understood that this name of his arose during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara.
"This thought occurred to him"—what was it? "In whatever way," and so forth. Herein, this is the summary of the account:
"In whatever manner I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as I examine it in that very way, it occurs to me thus:"
There is this thought: "This holy life of the three trainings must be practiced for even a single day so that it reaches the final consciousness as entirely fulfilled by being kept unbroken;

and it must be practiced for even a single day so that it reaches the final consciousness as entirely purified by not being stained with the defilements, like a conch shell that has been polished smooth."

One should conduct oneself having made oneself resemble a cleansed conch shell; it is not easy for one living in a household, dwelling in the midst of a home, to conduct oneself in this way—perfectly complete...

[and so on]—therefore, what if I were to shave off my hair and beard, and, having donned saffron-colored robes dyed with yellow dye, which are suitable for those leading the holy life, were to go forth from the household life?
“...should go forth into homelessness.
Not long after the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika had departed, Raṭṭhapāla approached the Blessed One;
he did not request the going-forth while they were still present. Why? Because there were many [people] there.
There are kinsmen and blood relatives, friends and companions, who might seize him by the arm and drag him back, saying, "You are the only son of your mother and father;

you must not go forth. Fearing that this would create an obstacle to his renunciation, he rose up together with the assembly, walked a short distance, and then returned, under some pretext of attending to bodily needs.
Having approached the Blessed One, he requested the going forth. Thus it was said:
"Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, not long after the inhabitants of Thullakoṭṭhika had departed... 'May the Blessed One let me go forth.
But since the Blessed One, from the time of the going forth of the young Rāhula onwards, did not allow the going forth of a son who had not been permitted by his mother and father, therefore—"
He asked him: "But have you been permitted by your mother and father, Raṭṭhapāla, for the going forth?
[The Buddha said: "Mother and Father. Here, "Mother" is an address to the mother, and "Father" is an address to the father.
"Only son" means there is only one son; there is no other elder or younger brother. And here, although it should be said "only son," the term is used out of compassion.
"An only son" is what was said. "Dear" means one who generates joy. "Beloved" means one who increases the mind's affection.
"Nurtured with happiness" means grown up in happiness; the meaning is "raised in comfort. "Brought up in comfort" means nurtured in ease;
from the time of birth, being carried from lap to lap by nurses and provided with horse-carts and other such children’s toys.
"Playing and feeding you delicious food, we have raised you in comfort.
You, dear Raṭṭhapāla, do not know anything of suffering"—the meaning is that you, dear Raṭṭhapāla, do not know or remember even a small fraction, a mere part, of suffering.
"Even by death we shall be separated from you against our will"—even if...

"While we are still living, your death might occur; even by that death of yours, we shall not exist against our will or without desire—that is, we shall not be able to avoid it—but rather we shall come to experience separation from you.
"But what [reason] do we have?"—this being so, what indeed is that reason by which we would permit you to live?
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "But what [is the rule] for us? For what reason shall we permit him while he is still living? 296.
"In that very place" means in the very spot where his parents did not grant him permission. "Without having been removed" means...
Because of the lack of any covering. "Paricārehi" means:

having presented musicians, actors, dancers, and so forth, you should move your sense faculties there as you please together with your companions; that is to say, you should direct them hither and thither.
Alternatively, "paricārehi" means: having presented musicians, actors, dancers, and so forth, [you should do so] with your companions...
"Play, sport, and enjoy yourself"—this is also what is meant by "let him play. "Enjoying sensual pleasures" means enjoying wealth together with his own children and wife.

"Performing meritorious deeds" means performing wholesome actions such as giving gifts and so forth, directed toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, which clear the path to a happy destination. "He became silent" was for the purpose of interrupting the continuity of the conversation.
There was no conversation or dialogue between them.

Then his parents, having spoken to him three times and receiving no reply, summoned his companions and said, "This companion of yours wishes to go forth; restrain him. They too approached him and [spoke] three times.
They spoke, but even they remained silent. Therefore it is said: "Then the companions of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla...
[as above] ...remained silent. Then, after his companions had spoken to him three times, this thought occurred to them:
"If he dies because he does not obtain the going-forth, no merit will be gained. But if he has gone forth, then his mother and father will at some time..."
"They will see the time [of his return], and we too shall see it. Furthermore, this going-forth (pabbajjā) is indeed burdensome:
day after day one must take an earthen bowl and wander for alms; living alone, eating but one meal a day, and the holy life (brahmacariya) are exceedingly difficult to practice.
Moreover, he is delicate and of a city-dwelling breed; being unable to practice that way of life, he will return here once again."

“We will obtain permission from Raṭṭhapāla’s parents. They did so. His parents, having made this agreement—that “once you have gone forth, you must inform your parents”—gave him their permission. Thus it is said:
“Then the companions of the young man Raṭṭhapāla went to the parents of the young man Raṭṭhapāla... [and so on].
"You have been permitted by your parents... [etc. ...you should show yourself. In this context, "should show yourself" means you should show yourself upward;
that is, having come, you should show yourself in such a way that they see you from time to time.
"Having taken strength" means eating suitable foods and maintaining the body with ointments and other such treatments.
Having generated bodily strength, he paid homage to his parents, and casting aside his circle of kinsmen with tearful faces, he approached the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and said, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One ordain me. The Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu standing nearby:
"In that case, bhikkhu, ordain Raṭṭhapāla and grant him full admission."
“Very well, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One.
Having obtained the noble son Raṭṭhapāla with Jinadattiya as his co-resident pupil, he caused him to go forth and conferred full ordination upon him. Thus it was said:
“The noble son Raṭṭhapāla received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.”
"Living with resolute self-exertion" means living in this manner for twelve years. For this venerable one was a person yet to be guided;

therefore, although he possessed merit and was endowed with a firm resolve, and though he practiced the duties of a recluse thinking, "Right now, this very day, may I attain Arahantship," he reached Arahantship only in the twelfth year.
“I approached where the Blessed One was”: my parents, granting me permission to go forth, said, “You must come from time to time to grant us your presence,” and thus they gave their consent.
My parents have indeed undergone great hardship, and that aspiration for which I went forth has now reached its fulfillment; now, [I shall approach] the Blessed One...
Thinking, "I will take leave of him and show myself to my parents," he approached with the desire to seek permission.
[The Blessed One] turned his attention, thinking, "What trouble might arise now that Raṭṭhapāla has gone?
Then, knowing that there would indeed be trouble, he looked to see whether Raṭṭhapāla would be able to overcome it, and beheld his attainment of Arahatship.
Having seen him, he knew, "He will be able. Therefore it was said: "Just as the Blessed One knew... [omission] ...you consider the time right. In the Migacīra park, which is so named.
For that park had indeed been authorized by the King with the words, "This is given to those who have gone forth at an improper time;
let them enjoy it as they please"; therefore the Elder—[knowing] "the fact of my arrival"—
Without even giving rise to the thought, "I will inform my parents;
they will send me water for washing the feet, warm water, oil for anointing the feet, and so forth," he entered the park itself. "He entered for alms" means he entered on the second day.
"In the middle one" means in the middle door-tower of a house that has seven door-towers. "He had it scraped" means...
He had the barber shave his hair. He said this: “These ascetics, having ordained my dear son, do not let him be seen for even a single day, as if they had placed him in the hands of thieves;
these cruel-doers think they may approach this place again, so they must be driven away from here. Having thought thus, he spoke.
He spoke these words beginning with, “By these shavelings. *Ñātidāsī* means a slave belonging to one’s kinsmen.

*Ābhidosikaṃ* means stale, having remained overnight and become putrid after exceeding one night. Herein, this is the word-meaning: it is *abhidoso* because it is overcome by the defect of putrefaction;
that which is *abhidoso* is *ābhidosiko*. This is a designation for that which has exceeded one night, namely, *ābhidosiko*.
"That which was kept overnight. "Barley-gruel" means barley-porridge.
"Wishing to discard it" means that since it is unfit for consumption even by slaves, laborers, or cattle, she wishes to throw it outside like refuse. "If this" means if this [gruel].
"Sister" is a term of noble address used to speak to her own nursemaid, who was a slave of her kinsmen. "Fit to be discarded" means...
It has the nature of something that must be discarded. This is what is meant: "Sister, if this is something to be discarded outside, free from ownership, then pour it here into my bowl.
But is it permissible to speak thus? Is it not an act of requesting (*viññatti*) or an instigated speech (*payuttavācā*)?
It is not. Why? Because it is free from ownership (*nissaṭṭhapariggaha*). For that which is to be discarded...
Regarding property that has been relinquished, where the owners have no attachment, it is permissible to say, "Give it, bring it, pour it out.
For this reason, even though this venerable one belongs to the foremost lineage of the Noble Ones, he spoke thus.
Regarding "from the hands": for one who extends the bowl for the purpose of receiving alms, [the area] from the wrist upwards belongs to both.
"Of the hands. "Of the feet" means of both feet starting from the edge of the lower garment.
"Of the voice" means of the voice as he uttered the words, "If you are my sister. She took the sign means that, while looking at the backs of his hands and so forth, she thought:
"The backs of these hands and feet are like those of my son Raṭṭhapāla, resembling the back of a golden tortoise."
"His fingers are as well-rounded as haritāla sticks, and his voice is sweet"—thus she grasped, recognized, and observed the features she had previously noted during his time as a householder.

As that venerable one had spent twelve years living in the forest and subsisting on alms-food, his physical appearance had become different; because of this, that female slave of his kinsmen [recognized him].
"Having seen him, she did not recognize him, yet she took up the sign.

[The Blessed One] said this to Raṭṭhapāla’s mother: "Even though she was the nurse who had raised her by adjusting his limbs and feeding him milk, my son—having gone forth and attained the state of one whose taints are utterly destroyed—[did not recognize her]."

Unable to utter words such as, "Venerable sir, are you indeed my son Raṭṭhapāla?", she entered the house in haste and said this to Raṭṭhapāla’s mother: "Yaggha" is a particle used for the purpose of announcing something.
"Sace je saccaṃ": here, "je" is a particle used in addressing; for in that region, they address female slaves in this manner.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: “For you, madam, are a slave; if you speak the truth. Why did she approach?
Women from noble families incur reproach when they go outside, yet this was an urgent matter;
she thought, “I shall inform the merchant,” and so she approached. [She approached] a certain...
"Kuṭṭamūla" means that, it is said, in that region there were halls in the houses of donors where seats were prepared and water and gruel were set out.
There, renunciants, having gone for alms, would sit down and eat.
If they so desired, they would also take what belonged to the donors. Therefore, in such a place belonging to a certain family...
It should be understood that "a certain wall-base in the hall" is meant. For renunciants do not sit and eat in unsuitable places like destitute people.

Regarding the phrase "Is there, dear sir?": here *atthi* is used in the sense of existence (*vijjamānatthe*), while *nāma* is used in the sense of questioning (*pucchanatthe*) or in the sense of supposition (*maññanatthe*).

This is an elliptical expression (*nipāta*). For this is what is meant: "Is there indeed, dear Raṭṭhapāla, any wealth for us, that we should not be called destitute, since you, sitting in such a place, will consume yesterday’s sour gruel?
Likewise, is there indeed, dear Raṭṭhapāla, any life for us... [that we should not be called dead].
"You should be called 'one who has lost his mind,' since you sit in such a place as this to eat yesterday's sour gruel.
It seems, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that there is indeed within you a quality of a recluse acquired by relying on the Teaching,
since even though you were raised on the flavors of fine food, you regard this loathsome, yesterday's sour gruel as if it were the Deathless."
“Will you eat it without being affected [by its taste]? However, because that householder was overwhelmed by suffering, he was unable to state the matter fully and said only this:
“My dear Raṭṭhapāla, you will indeed eat yesterday’s sour gruel.
Regarding this, grammarians state the following characteristic: this [use of the future tense] is employed in the sense of non-acceptance and disregard.
With the word *atthi* used as a prefix, the future tense was employed in the phrase “*paribhuñjissasi*” (“will you eat”). Its meaning is this:
“That there is [food]... will you eat? Even though this is before my very eyes, I do not believe it, nor do I trust it.
The householder spoke these words while standing right there, holding the Elder’s bowl by its rim. The Elder, too—

While his father stood by holding the bowl and cloth, the elder ate that putrid gruel—which was like a dog’s vomit, or like a rotten chicken egg oozing from its broken shell—standing firm in noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*) and consuming it as divine food and the taste of the Deathless (*amatarasa*).
Indeed, it is said that an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) would not have been able to eat such gruel.
But the elder, established in noble psychic power, consumed it as divine sustenance and the flavor of immortality.
Having eaten as if [it were ordinary food], he took water with a water-vessel (*dhamakaraṇa*), washed his bowl, his face, and his hands and feet, and said, "From where, householder?

and so forth. In that context, "from where" (*kuto*) means "from where indeed" (*kuto nu*). "Neither gift" (*neva dānaṃ*) means that we did not receive any gift by way of the objects to be given. Nor...
“Refusal” means that we did not even receive a polite greeting such as, “What is it, dear Raṭṭhapāla?
Are you well? Have you come without much fatigue? Has food not yet been prepared at home?
Why did the Elder speak thus? It was out of consideration for his father. For he thought: “Just as... [text continues]”
"He speaks thus to me; I suppose he speaks likewise to other renunciants as well.

And in the Buddha’s teaching, there are monks like me whose virtues are concealed—like a lotus within a leaf-cup, like fire covered by ashes, like the heartwood of sandalwood hidden by sapwood, like a precious gem wrapped in thread, and like the moon veiled by clouds."
"There is no end [to his merit]; even toward them he will not utter such words, but will remain established in restraint"—it was with this encouragement that he spoke thus.
"Come, dear one," he said, meaning, "Dear one, let there be no home for you; come, we shall go to a home.

"Enough," the Elder replied, speaking thus while rejecting the offer on account of his practice of the strict *ukkaṭṭha-ekāsanika* (the practice of sitting alone in a high place). However, the Elder consented because he was by nature one who practiced the strict *sapadāna-cārika* (the practice of wandering for alms from house to house in regular order).
He did not consent to alms from his own kinsmen, but he consented out of consideration for his mother.
It is said that as she remembered the Elder, great sorrow arose within her; through her weeping alone, her eyes became as if they were cooked.
Therefore, the Elder thought, "If I depart without seeing her, her heart will surely break," and so he consented out of compassion.
"Having had it made" means having had two heaps made—one of silver and one of gold. But how large were those heaps?
They were so large that a man standing on this side could not see a man of medium stature standing on the other side. Such was their size.
301. Saying, “This for you, dear child,” he presented him with a heap of kahāpaṇas and a heap of gold.
*Mattikaṃ* means that which has come from the mother; the meaning is: “This is the wealth given for the sake of perfumes, garlands, and so forth, to your grandmother when she came to this house.
Regarding *aññaṃ pettikaṃ aññaṃ pitāmahaṃ*: [he gave] that which belonged to your father and that which belonged to your grandfather.
It is his own property, yet it is quite different; moreover, what is stored away and what is invested is exceedingly vast.
And here, it should be understood that the term "pitāmaha" is stated by means of the elision of a *taddhita* suffix. Alternatively, the reading is "petāmaha.
"Sakkā tatonidānaṃ" means on account of wealth, with wealth as the cause. For one who guards such and such wealth, there is the depletion of wealth due to kings and others.
He spoke thus with reference to those who, upon reaching [the state of non-returning], experience the arising of sorrow and so forth.
When this was said, the householder Seṭṭhi thought, "I brought him here thinking, 'I will cause him to leave the monastic life,' but now he has begun to give me a Dhamma talk;
he will not do as I say. Having risen and gone away, he had the door to his harem opened and said: "This one..."
"He is your master; go, make whatever effort is necessary to capture him," he commanded.
The female dancers standing at the gateway came out and surrounded the Elder. Regarding those two chief women among them, it is said: "the former second wife," and so forth.
"Each seizing him by the feet" means grasping him by one foot each.
“Of what sort, O noble son, are those celestial nymphs?”—why did they speak thus?

It is said that at that time, seeing many young kṣatriyas, young brahmins, and sons of wealthy merchants renouncing the world after abandoning great prosperity, those who did not understand the virtues of renunciation asked, “Why are these people going forth?
Then others said, “They are celestial nymphs and divine dancers...”
"...because of this reason. That talk spread widely. Taking up that [story], they all said thus.
Then the Elder, rejecting it, said, "We are not, sister," and so forth. "He addresses" means he speaks or converses.
"They fell down right there, swooning" means that upon seeing him addressing her with the word "sister," [they thought], "She will come today; she will come today."
"For twelve years we have not gone outside; it was by depending on him that our children were not lost, and through whose power we might live.
Now we have fallen away from him and from others as well. This world thinks only of itself;
therefore, they too, thinking 'Now we have become destitute,' thought only of themselves: 'He now has no need of us.'"
"Being our co-wives, she regards us as if we were daughters lying in the same mother’s womb.
Having thus fallen into intense grief, they fainted and fell down right there—that is, they collapsed. "Do not harm us" means:
do not harm us by showing off wealth and then sending away the women; such is "harm" (*viheṭhā*).
“Of those who have gone forth. Why did he speak thus? Out of consideration for his parents. It is said that the merchant, thinking—“The marks of one who has gone forth are defiled;
having removed the robes of one who has gone forth, let us bathe and the three of us eat together”—did not give alms to the Elder.
The Elder [thought]: “By creating an obstacle to the food of one like me, whose taints are destroyed, these...”
“...they would produce much demerit”; he spoke thus out of compassion for them.
“He uttered verses” means he recited verses. Therein, “behold” (*passa*) is said with reference to the people standing nearby.
“Mind” (*citta*) refers to the variegated mind. “Form” (*bimba*) refers to the physical body (*attabhāva*). “A mass of sores” (*arukāya*) is said by way of the nine openings of wounds.
The body of skin. "Erected" means it is raised up all around, having been bound together by three hundred bones with nine hundred sinews and smeared over with nine hundred pieces of flesh.
"Afflicted" means it is constantly afflicted by the affliction of old age, the affliction of disease, and the affliction of the defilements.
"Full of many thoughts" means it is full of many thoughts due to the hopes and aspirations arising in others; for [in the case] of women...
Thoughts of men arise regarding the body, and thoughts of women regarding their own bodies.
Even when this body has become a corpse discarded in a charnel ground, crows, hawks, and other scavengers still crave it; thus, it is said to be "full of many thoughts.

Regarding the phrase "for which there is no lasting stability": for that body, there is absolutely no stability whatsoever, just as with an illusion, a mirage, a mass of foam, or a bubble on the water.
There is no such thing; its very nature as something subject to breaking is certain.
"Covered with hide" means covered with the raw hide of a human being. "It shines together with clothes":
even a form that is decorated with perfumes and the like, as well as with jewels and earrings, shines only together with clothes; without clothes, it is loathsome.
It is not fit to be looked upon.

"Stained with lac" means dyed with lac. "Smeared with powder" means that after removing facial pimples and the like with mustard-paste, one has caused the diseased blood to dissolve with salt-clay and cleared the blood with sesame flour.
Having prepared a turmeric-colored paste, they apply it to the face with a ball of powder; because of this, it shines exceedingly.
It is with reference to this that it was said.
"Aṭṭhāpadakatā" means having applied scented water and fashioned a pattern of eight squares by making circular turns around the edge of the forehead. "Añjanī" means an ointment tube.
"Odahīti" means he placed [it]. "Pāsanti" means a net of snares. "Nāsadāti" means he did not strike.
"Nivāpan" refers to food similar to the bait-grass mentioned in the *Nivāpa-sutta*. "Kandante" means while crying out and lamenting.
For with this verse, the Elder showed his parents as being like deer-trappers, and the rest of his kinsmen as being like the retinue of deer-trappers.
He showed himself like a heap of gold and silver, like a net of precious gems,
like the food he had eaten spread out as a bait-trap, and like a great deer. For just as a great deer, having eaten its fill of the bait-trap grass and drunk water,
lifts its neck, surveys the directions, and [thinks], "May it be well for me when I have gone to such-and-such a place," [so did he show himself].
"Will it be so?"— even as the deer-hunters were thus lamenting,
the Elder, without even clashing against his snare, leapt up, entered the forest, and stood beneath a dense-thatched thicket like a parasol,
fanning himself with a very gentle breeze while looking back along the path he had come; in this very manner, having spoken these verses, the Elder [vanished] through the air.
Having gone, he presented himself at Migacīra.
But why did the Elder go through the air? It is said that his father, the merchant, had bolts fastened upon the seven gate-towers and commanded the Mallas:
"If he goes out, seize him by his hands and feet and [strip] the saffron robes..."

“Go and have them take off their householder’s dress. Therefore, the Elder—thinking, “May these men not commit demerit by seizing such a one as I, who am a great destroyer of the taints, by the hand or by the foot”—went through the air.
As for the elders dwelling beyond the sea, [he said]: “While standing right here, recite these verses and then ascend into the sky.”
"He attended upon King Koravya at Migacīra"—this is the very path of the recitation. 303.

*Migava* is the name of that park-keeper. "Clearing" means: having had the park paths made level, having had the places within the park suitable for carving cleared, or having had the places suitable for sweeping swept;
[and] the scattering of sand, the strewing of flowers, the placing of full water-jars, the setting up of plantain trunks, and so forth.
And the meaning is "while doing so. As for the phrase "he approached where King Koravya was": our king constantly spoke in praise of this son of good family;
he desired to see him but did not know that he had arrived. Thinking, "This is indeed a great gift;
having gone, I shall inform the king," he approached where King Koravya was.
"He was praising him" means that, it is said, the king, recollecting the Elder, spoke of his virtues even in the midst of his army and in the midst of his theatrical troupe, saying:
"A difficult deed has been performed by this son of good family, who, having abandoned such great prosperity and gone forth, has now returned and does not seek permission [to leave again].
Having grasped that, he spoke thus. "Let him go," he said.
The meaning is: having caused each person to be given that which is appropriate for them among the harem, the high ministers, the army, and so forth.

"Ussaṭāya ussaṭāya" means "having risen up, having risen up"; the meaning is that he approached taking along a retinue that had risen to the highest ranks by way of the high ministers, great provincial lords, and others.
"Let the venerable Raṭṭhapāla sit here on the elephant-back rug" refers to the *hatthatthara* (elephant-back rug).
Having made the quality of the flowers—whether thin or thick—and so forth, he becomes distinguished in meaning;
thinking that it is not proper to sit down in such a place without having asked permission, he spoke thus.
304. *Pārijuññāni* means states of loss or exhaustion. *Jiṇṇo* means decayed by old age. *Vuḍḍho* means advanced in years.
"An old man" means one who is advanced in age. "One who has reached a stage of life" means one who has passed beyond the prime of life.
"One who has arrived at the final stage" means one who has entered the last period of life. "He goes forth" means that having gone to the main monastery and paid homage to the monks, he says:
"Venerable sirs, in my youth I performed much wholesome merit; now I am an old man, and for an old man this is indeed called 'going forth. [He goes] to the courtyard of the shrine..."
“Having swept [the grounds] and cleared away the weeds, I shall live; let me go forth, venerable sirs,” he requested, evoking compassion.

Out of pity, the elders granted him the going-forth. It was with reference to this that it was said. The same method applies to the second instance as well. “Free from illness” (*appābādha*) means healthy.
“Free from affliction” (*appātaṅka*) means free from suffering. “With a balanced digestive fire” (*samavepākiniyā*) means with a properly functioning digestion. “Of the stomach” (*gahaṇiyā*)...

Regarding the fire element born of karma (*kammaja-tejodhātu*): therein, one for whom food that has been eaten is digested, or one for whom it remains exactly as it was, like a meal in a covered vessel—both of these are not endowed with a balanced digestive heat (*samavepākini*).
However, one for whom a desire for food arises even while eating is endowed with balanced digestive heat. It is neither too cold...
"Neither too cold nor too hot" means neither too cold for that reason nor too hot. "Successively" means in the sequence beginning with "kings carry them off," and so forth.
In the second instance, it refers to the sequence beginning with "fear of kings, fear of thieves, fear of drought," and so forth. 305.
"The summaries of the Dhamma have been recited" means the expositions of the Dhamma have been recited. "It is led away" means it is led toward old age and death.
He goes, or he is led away from there by the exhaustion of his lifespan. "Unstable" (*addhuva*) means devoid of a stable state.

"Without protection" (*atāṇa*) means devoid of one capable of protecting him. "Without refuge" (*anabhissara*) means without a resort; it is devoid of one capable of providing comfort by approaching and coming to his aid.
"Ownerless" (*assaka*) means without an owner, devoid of one's own property. "Everything must be abandoned and departed from" refers to one's own belongings.
Having abandoned everything observed [as dear], one must depart from the world. "A slave to craving" means a servant of craving. 306.

"In the elephant-lore" means in the art of elephant-training. "Skilled" means one who has performed his duties; the meaning is that he is one who has trained in the training and is proficient in the craft.
This same method applies everywhere. "Strong of thigh" means endowed with the strength of the thighs. For him whose shield and weapon—

One who, having seized the enemy army and entered it, breaks what is unbroken and holds together what is broken, possesses the strength of the thighs (*ūrubala*) to recover a kingdom fallen into the hands of others;
such a person is called "one with the strength of the thighs. "One with the strength of the arms" (*bāhubalī*) means one endowed with the strength of the arms.
The rest is exactly as before. "Adequate" (*alamatta*) means one whose personal existence (*attabhāva*) is capable.
“They will proceed after having cleared away [the obstacles]”: this was said with the observation that they will proceed by clearing away—that is, by stepping over—any calamity that has arisen.
“Indeed, Master Raṭṭhapāla, there exists in this royal family abundant gold and bullion”: this the king spoke while bringing forward the reason for the subsequent exposition of the Dhamma.
Then he further said this: he uttered the verse in accordance with the four expositions of the Dhamma, beginning with the words “I see in the world.”

307. “There they desire even more sense pleasures” means that having obtained one, they desire two; having obtained two, they desire four—in this way, they continue to desire ever higher and higher both sense pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sense pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*).

“Having overcome” means having conquered the host of enemies. “Together with the ocean’s edge” means including the limit of the sea. “On this side of the ocean” means that which is on this side of the sea, namely their own country; the meaning is that they are not satisfied with that. “Not elephants” means that there are none.
"Aho vatā no" means "O, alas for us! or "Aho vata nu"; this is the reading. They also say "amaraṃ.
This is what is meant: that which the relatives surround and weep over, they speak of it as "O, alas, our brother is dead," "our son is dead," and so forth.
"They touch, they feel; they touch the touch of death. "Likewise touched" means that just as the fool is, so too is the wise man touched by the touch of death;
there is no one who is not touched. However, this is the distinction: "The fool lies down as if slain by his own foolishness.
This means that the fool, having encountered the touch of death, lies down as if slain, as if struck down, by his state of folly.
He says: "Alas, what a good deed I have not done! and so forth; through such remorse (*vippaṭisāra*), he wavers, trembles, and struggles.
But "the wise man does not tremble" means that the wise man, seeing the sign of a happy rebirth, does not tremble and does not waver.
"By which one attains completion here" means by which wisdom one attains in this world the completion of all duties, namely, *arahantship*.
One attains that which is far superior to wealth. "Because it is unfinished" means because it is not yet completed; the sense is: because of the non-attainment of *arahantship*.
"In various states of existence" means in inferior and superior states of existence.
"He enters the womb and the next world": among those who commit evil, any being whatsoever [enters] the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) by way of succession.
Having entered [the womb], he goes to another world. "Another of little wisdom" means that another person of little wisdom has faith in such a person of little wisdom.

"Is slain by his own karma" means that, by virtue of the actions he himself has committed, he is punished with such judicial tortures as being flogged with whips and so forth. "And having passed away, in the other world" means having gone from here, in the other world of the states of woe (apāya).

"By means of various forms" (*virūparūpena*) means by means of diverse forms; the sense is "by means of various natures. "Regarding the strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇesu*) means having seen the danger in all the strands of sensual pleasure pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.
"The young" (*daharā*) refers to those who are tender, starting from even the stage of the *kalala* (the embryo in its first week).

"The old" (*vuḍḍhā*) refers to those who have exceeded a hundred years. "The ascetic life alone is better" (*apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo*) means that which is non-contradictory and leads to the unerring goal.
“Having reflected, O Great King, that the ascetic life alone leads exclusively to liberation—and is thus better, higher, and more sublime—I have gone forth.
Therefore, regarding what you asked—“What did you see or hear?”—you should remember me as one who went forth having both seen and heard;
with these words, he brought his teaching to a conclusion.
The commentary on the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 3.
The commentary on the Maghadeva Sutta.
308. “Thus have I heard” refers to the Maghadeva Sutta. Regarding the phrase “in the mango grove of Maghadeva”:
formerly, a king named Maghadeva planted that mango grove. When those trees were decaying, other kings subsequently planted [new ones] as well.
Nevertheless, it came to be known by its original designation as the “Mango Grove of Maghadeva. He smiled...
Thinking, "May he protect me," and wandering for alms in the evening, the Blessed One saw a delightful spot of ground and reflected:
"Have I dwelt in this place before? As he pondered, he recalled: "Formerly, when I was King Maghadeva, I planted this mango grove;
it was right here that I went forth, developed the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), and was reborn in the Brahma-world."
"However, this matter is not known to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; I shall make it known.
Saying this, he displayed his smile, showing his upper and lower teeth.

"One who possesses the Dhamma is *dhammika*. One who has become a king through the Dhamma is a *dhammarāja*. One who stands firm in the Dhamma means one who stands firm in the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*)."
"Established. "He practices the Dhamma" means he conducts himself with equanimity.

"There, among the brahmins and householders" refers to the fact that he did not diminish even that maintenance which had been granted to the brahmins by previous kings, but gave it according to the established custom;

the same applies to the householders. This was said with reference to that. By the word "of the fortnight," the fortnight of miracles (*pāṭihārika-pakkha*) is also included. [This refers to] the eighth-day *uposatha*.
Indeed, by way of both the retrograde and the progressive sequence, the seventh and ninth days;

and by way of the retrograde and progressive sequence of the fourteenth and fifteenth, the thirteenth and the first (pāṭipada)—these days should be understood as the "miracle fortnights" (pāṭihārika-pakkha). On those days as well, he observed the Uposatha. 309.

Regarding the term "messengers of the gods" (devadūtā): "god" (deva) here refers to Death (maccu), and their "messengers" (dūtā) are thus the messengers of the gods. For when grey hairs have appeared upon the head...
He stands as if in the presence of King Death; therefore, grey hairs are called "messengers of the god of death" (*maccudeva*).
They are also called "divine messengers" (*devadūtā*) because they are like messengers from the gods.

For just as when a goddess, adorned and prepared, standing in the sky says, "On such-and-such a day you will die," it happens exactly so, even so, when grey hairs have appeared on the head, it is just like a prophecy by a deity.
Therefore, the grey hairs are called "messengers like the gods" (*devasadisa-dūta*).

They are also called "messengers of the pure gods" (*visuddhideva-dūta*) because all Bodhisattvas, upon seeing an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and one who has gone forth into homelessness, experience a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), renounce the world, and go forth. As it is said:
Having seen one who is aged and one who is suffering from illness,
having seen one who is dead with the span of life exhausted,
and having seen one who has gone forth clad in saffron robes—
"Therefore, O King, I have gone forth.
By this method, the grey hairs are called "messengers of the gods" (*devadūta*) because they act as messengers for the deities of purification.
"Having given a choice village to the barber" means having given a preeminent village worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Why did he give it?
"His mind was filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃviggamānasa*). For upon seeing the grey hairs placed in his joined palms, spiritual urgency arose within him.

Although he still had eighty-four thousand years of life remaining, nevertheless, perceiving himself as if standing in the presence of the King of Death, he felt such urgency that he took delight in going forth. Thus it is said:
“Having seen his grey hair, Maghadeva, the lord of Disā,
the wise one, was moved by a sense of urgency and resolved upon the going-forth.
Furthermore, it is said:
“Grown upon my head, these hairs have taken away my youth;
they have appeared as messengers from the gods.

It is time for me to go forth. Regarding “in a generation of men”: this refers to men born into a lineage. “Having shaved off hair and beard”: even those going forth into the ascetic life shave them off.
For indeed, those who go forth first shave off their hair and beard; from that time on, as their hair grows, they wander about wearing it bound up in matted locks.
The Bodhisatta likewise went forth into the ascetic life.
Having gone forth, however, he did not devote himself to wrong means of livelihood, but sustained himself on alms brought from royal palaces while cultivating the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
Therefore, it was said: "Accompanied by loving-kindness," and so forth.
He played the games of childhood; that is, he played while being carried from lap to lap. For they moved about carrying him up as if he were a bouquet of flowers.
"The son of King Makhādeva... went forth"—on the day of his going forth, five auspicious events occurred.

There were five auspicious ceremonies at one and the same time: King Maghadeva’s funeral feast, the auspicious occasion of that king’s renunciation, the auspicious occasion of his son’s coronation, the auspicious occasion of his son’s appointment as viceroy, and the auspicious occasion of his son’s naming ceremony; the entire surface of Jambudīpa was filled with joy.
311. "Puttapaputtakā" means sons and grandsons; such was the succession that proceeded from him. "He was the last one" means he was the last of those who went forth into the religious life.

It is said that when the Bodhisatta had been reborn in the Brahma-world, he reflected, "Is that noble practice which I established in the human world still being carried out? and he saw that it continued for so long—
“The lineage continues; now it shall no longer continue.

However, thinking, “I will not allow my lineage to be cut off,” he took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of the very king born in his own family, being conceived as if to join the axle-pin of his own dynasty. For that reason, his name was Nimi. Thus he...
Having become the very last of those who had gone forth as kings, he was thus the "last in renunciation.
Yet, in terms of virtues, he was far superior. For he possessed two virtues that surpassed all other kings:
he gave a daily alms-giving by distributing a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at each of the four gates, and he granted audiences on every Uposatha day.
He turned them back. For when those who did not observe the Uposatha went there thinking, "We shall see the king," the gatekeeper asked, "Are you observing the Uposatha or not?
Those who were not observing the Uposatha he turned away, saying, "The king does not grant an audience to those who do not observe the Uposatha.
There was even no opportunity for them to say, "We are inhabitants of the countryside; where shall we get food at this time?"
There was none. For at the four gates and in the royal courtyard, many thousands of prepared meals were already set out.

Therefore, the great multitude, having had their hair and beards shaved at whichever place they desired, bathed, changed their clothes, and eaten whatever food they pleased, would resolve upon the factors of the Uposatha and proceed to the gate of the king’s palace.
The doorkeeper asked them repeatedly, “Are you observing the Uposatha? and they replied, “Yes, indeed.
He said, “In that case, come in,” and having ushered them in, he presented them to the king. Thus, he was superior by these two qualities. 312.
*Devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ* means of the gods reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. It is said that those gods [were born] in the kingdom of Videha.
The inhabitants of Mithilā city, having abided by the King’s advice, observed the five precepts, performed the Uposatha rites, and were reborn there;
they spoke in praise of the King’s virtues. It is with reference to them that it is said, “of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
He was seated means that he sat upon the upper floor of the excellent palace, reflecting upon generosity and virtue.
It occurred to him thus: "Is it giving that is great, or is it virtue?
If giving is great, I shall give gifts in abundance; if virtue is great, I shall fulfill virtue alone.
While he was still unable to decide, "This is great, this is great," Sakka went and appeared before him. Therefore it was said: "Then, Ānanda,... [as above]..."
"He appeared before him. It occurred to him thus: "A doubt has arisen in the king;
for the sake of cutting through that doubt, I shall answer his question and take a promise from him to come here. Therefore, having gone there, he appeared before him.
When the king saw a form never seen before, he became terrified, his hair standing on end. Then Sakka—
“Do not fear, Great King; ask your question with confidence, and I shall dispel your doubt,” he said.
The king replied: “I ask you, O Great King, Lord of all beings:”
"Between giving and the holy life, which is of greater fruit?
Thus he asked the question. Sakka replied: "What is called 'giving'? It is indeed virtue that is great by reason of its distinguished qualities.
For formerly, O Great King, after I had given alms for ten thousand years to ten thousand matted-hair ascetics, from the realm of the hungry ghosts..."
“I am not liberated, but those who were virtuous, having partaken of my gift, have been reborn in the Brahma-world,” he said, and spoke these verses:
“By an inferior holy life one is reborn among the Khattiyas;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one is purified.”
"Bodies such as these are not easily obtained by anyone through mere begging;
those who are homeless ascetics are reborn in such bodies.
Having thus dispelled the king's doubt, he said, "A great gain for you, O Great King," and so forth, in order to receive his promise to go to the world of the devas.
Therein, "unwavering" means not fearing. "He consented" means: "I am exhorting the great multitude toward wholesome deeds;
moreover, having seen the dwelling place of those possessed of merit, it is easy to converse with them when they have come onto the path of men"—thus he consented.
"Very well, venerable sir" means: "So be it; may your words be auspicious," having said this. "Having joined" means: in one [place] alone.
Having yoked a thousand noble thoroughbred horses to it, they have no need for individual yoking;
rather, by the power of his mind, they become yoked of their own accord. That divine chariot is one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length:
from the felloe to the front of the chariot it is fifty *yojanas*, and from the felloe to the rear of the chariot it is fifty *yojanas*.

It is fifty *yojanas* in extent, and its entirety is made of the *sattavaṇṇa* jewel. One should not assume that he sent the chariot facing downward because the world of the gods is above and the world of humans is below;
rather, just as he would send it along its natural path, he sent it yoked together with the moon once the people’s evening meal was finished.
They appeared as if two moons had risen simultaneously. When the great multitude saw them, they cried out, "Two moons have appeared! But as they drew closer and closer, it was no longer two moons;
it was not two celestial palaces (vimānas), but a single palace, and not two palaces, but a single chariot.
As the chariot approached, it became the size of an ordinary chariot, and the horses likewise became the size of ordinary horses. Having thus brought forward the chariot,
Having circumambulated the king’s palace, he turned the chariot at the location of the eastern lion-window, facing it toward the path by which they had come;
standing right there at the lion-window, he made it ready for mounting.
When [the charioteer] said, "Ascend, Great King," the king—thinking, "I have obtained a celestial vehicle"—did not ascend immediately, [waiting] for the citizens...
Then he gave this advice: "Behold, dear ones, that divine chariot which has been sent to me by Sakka, King of the Devas.
It was not sent on account of my birth, lineage, or family background; rather, it was sent because he was pleased with my virtue, conduct, and qualities.
If you too shall guard your virtue, he will send one for you as well. Thus [you must] guard it."
"This conduct is indeed fitting. I shall not remain long after going to the world of the gods; be heedful!
Having thus exhorted the great multitude and established them in the five precepts, he mounted his chariot.
Then the charioteer Mātali, thinking, "I too shall do what is suitable for the Great King," showed two paths in the sky and said, "Moreover, O Great King," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by which," O Great King: among these paths, one leads to hell and another to the world of the devas;

by which of these two shall I lead you? "By which" means by whichever path, having gone along it, one is able to see that place where those of evil deeds experience the result of their evil deeds—this is the meaning. The same method applies to the second phrase as well. It is also said in the *Jātaka*:
“By which path, O best of kings, Disampati, shall I lead you—by that of those who perform evil deeds, or by that of those men who perform meritorious deeds?
This is the meaning of this verse. Therefore he said:
“First, let me see the hells, the dwellings of those who have committed evil deeds;
the places of those who perform cruel acts, and the destiny of the immoral.
“By both paths, Mātali, lead me!”—Mātali, lead me by way of both routes, for I wish to see the hells.
"Even the world of the gods. First, by which path? "First, lead by way of hell.
Then Mātali, through his own supernatural power, showed the king the fifteen great hells. Herein is the detailed account:
"Mātali showed the king the difficult-to-cross River Vetaraṇī..."
"Boiling, mixed with caustic liquid, hot like a crest of fire"—
this should be understood according to the method stated in the *Jātaka*. Having shown the hell and turned the chariot back,
he proceeded toward the world of the gods, showing the celestial mansions (*vimāna*) of the goddess Bīraṇī, the devaputta Soṇadinna, and the host of devaputtas.
He led her to the world of the gods. Regarding that, there is this detailed account:
“O Hero, if you have heard of Bīraṇī in the world of the living, she was formerly the slave Āmāyadāsī of a brahmin.”
When she recognized that the guest had arrived at the proper time,
she rejoiced at him just as a mother does at her son;
she was self-restrained and practiced sharing.
"She rejoices in the celestial mansion"—
this is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Jātaka*.
As he was thus proceeding, however, the rim of his chariot wheel struck only against the threshold of the gateway at Cittakūṭa.
A great clamor arose in Devanagara. Leaving Sakka, the king of the gods, all alone behind, the host of deities went out to meet the Great Being.

Seeing that honor shown by the deities, Sakka was unable to restrain his heart and said, "Enjoy yourself, O Great King, among the gods by means of your divine power. It occurred to him thus: "This king..."
"Having arrived today, he has brought the host of gods face-to-face with himself in a single day. If he were to stay for one or two days, the gods would not look upon me.
Being envious, he spoke thus with this intention: "Great King, you have no merit to dwell in this world of the gods;
dwell there by means of the merit of others. Thus spoke the Bodhisatta.
—“Jarasakka was unable to maintain his composure; for what is obtained by depending on another is like goods acquired through begging.
Thus he spoke, beginning with the words “Enough, dear sir,” while rejecting [the offer]. It is also said in the Jātaka:
“As a borrowed carriage, as borrowed wealth;”
"Exactly so it is with that which comes from another by way of a gift;
yet I do not desire that which comes from another by way of a gift."—All this should be recited.
But how many times did the Bodhisatta, while in a human existence, go to the world of the devas? Four.
—during the time of King Mandhātu, during the time of King Sādhina, during the time of the lute-player Guttila, and during the time of King Nimi.
During the time of King Mandhātu, he dwelt in the world of the devas for an incalculable period; while dwelling there, thirty-six Sakka-devas passed away.
During the time of King Sādhina, he dwelt for seven days, which by human reckoning amounts to seven hundred years. During the time of the lute-player Guttila...
And during the time of King Nimi, he resided there for only a brief moment, which amounts to seven days by human calculation.
314. "Right there he sent back Mithilā" means that having sent it back, he re-established it exactly in its natural, original chamber.

315. "Kaḷārajanaka" was his name; however, he was called Kaḷārajanaka because of his black teeth (*kaḷāradanta*). "He did not go forth from the home life into homelessness"—he did not do only this much; everything else remained exactly as it was before.

316. Regarding the phrase "there is a cutting off": here one should understand this distinction—what cuts off the noble practice, by what is it cut off, who sets it in motion, and by what is it said to be set in motion?
In that regard, a virtuous bhikkhu who fails to exert energy, thinking, "I am not able to attain arahantship," cuts it off. It is cut off by one who is immoral.

It is so called. The seven trainees (sekha) set it in motion. That which is set in motion by one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is said to be "set in motion. The rest is clear in all respects.
Thus ends the commentary on the Maghadeva Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
4. Commentary on the Madhura Sutta 317.
“Thus have I heard” introduces the Madhura Sutta. Therein, “Mahākaccāna” refers to one who, during his time as a householder, was the son of the royal chaplain to the King of Ujjeni;
he was handsome, pleasing to behold, gracious, and golden-hued. “In Madhurā” means in the city of that name. “In Gundavana” [means...]
In the Kaṇhakagunda forest. "The son of the King of Avanti" means the son of the daughter of the king of the kingdom of Avanti. "Both grown old and an arahant":
they do not honor even a young arahant in the same way as they do one who is elderly;
however, this elder was both grown old and an arahant. "O Master Kaccāna, the brahmins," [the king said]; it is said that the king was one who held the brahmins in high esteem, and therefore...
Thus he spoke. In such passages as "The brahmin alone is the best caste," he shows that among the bases for designating birth, lineage, and so forth, the brahmins alone are the best.
"Other castes are inferior" means he says that the other three castes are inferior and base.
"Fair" means white. "Dark" means black. "They are purified" means they are purified in the bases for designating birth, lineage, and so forth. [Of] Brahmā...
"Sons" means sons of Mahābrahmā. "Legitimate, born from his own breast" means they were born from his mouth after dwelling in his breast;
or alternatively, they are "legitimate" because he nurtured them while holding them to his breast. "Born of the Brahmā-nature" means produced from Brahmā.
"Created by Brahmā" means fashioned by Brahmā. "Heirs of Brahmā" means the successors of Brahmā. "This is merely a sound" means this is nothing more than a conventional designation.
