318. "Ijjheyya" means he would succeed; the meaning is that whatever wealth and so forth he might desire, his heart's wish would be fulfilled to that extent.
"Khattiyopissāssa" means even a khattiya would be one who rises before him, [that is,] one who rises before him as he possesses the perfection of sovereignty.
"Nesaṃ ettha kiñci" means there is nothing whatsoever belonging to them here.
322. "We might invite him to a seat" means: having cleared away the seat where he is sitting, we would say, "Sit here.
"We might also offer [something] to him" means: having brought it forward, we would invite him to it. In this context, there are two kinds of offering: by word and by body. [By word:
"At whatever time you desire, you may tell me what you need, such as robes and so forth."
For when one speaks with words and, having brought something forward, invites [someone], that is called "inviting by speech.
When, however, perceiving a deficiency in robes or other requisites, one gives them while saying, "Take this," that is called "inviting by body" after having brought it forward.

It is with reference to both of these that he said, "We would not even invite [them]. "Protection, defense, and guard" refers to that which is termed protection as well as that which is termed defense.
Guarding. However, that protection which is provided by stationing men with weapons in hand is not called a "legitimate" arrangement.

But when one arranges it such that wood-gatherers, leaf-gatherers, and the like do not enter the monastery at improper times, and hunters and the like do not catch deer or fish within the monastery boundary, then it is indeed called a "legitimate" arrangement.
It exists. It is with reference to this that he said, "righteous" (*dhammika*).
"While it is thus" means while there is equality and sameness in the honoring of those who have gone forth among all four castes. The rest is entirely clear everywhere.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Madhura Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta 324.

“Thus have I heard” refers to the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta. In that context, *kokanada* means a red lotus (*paduma*). That auspicious palace was constructed so as to display a lotus for viewing; therefore, it received the designation “Kokanada.”
325. Regarding the phrase "as far as the final step of the staircase," here "the final step of the staircase" refers to the first step of the stairway.

"He saw" means that while standing at the gatehouse for the purpose of looking out, he saw [him]. "The Blessed One remained silent" means that while reflecting, "For what purpose has this great honor been performed by the prince? he [saw it was] for the sake of a desire for a son.
He understood the state of affairs. For that prince was childless, and he had heard it said:
"It is said that by performing service for the Buddhas, one obtains whatever is desired in the mind.
Having made this aspiration—"If I shall obtain a son, the Perfectly Enlightened One will step upon my cloth; if not, He will not step upon it"—he [performed service].
He had [the seat] spread out. Then the Blessed One, having reflected, "Will a son be born to him? saw that "one will not be born.
It is said that formerly, while living on a certain island, he had eaten a young bird together with Samacchanda.
Had his wife been someone else, he might have obtained a son; however, since they both committed the evil deed with one accord, [no son was born].
He knew that therefore no son would be born to him. However, when the cloth was stepped upon, [the king] might have fallen into a wrong view, thinking:
"There is a worldly tradition that whatever is prayed for by those who have rendered service to the Buddhas is obtained;
yet I have made a great aspiration and do not obtain a son—this saying is empty. The sectarians too [might think]: "There is..."
“They will criticize them, saying, ‘This is something not to be done by recluses; they wander about crushing their own robes.
And at present, there are many monks who tread upon others and are able to read the minds of others; knowing who is capable, they will tread upon them, and knowing who is incapable, they will not.
But in the future, the underlying predisposition will be weak, and they will not know the future.”
As they stepped into those [footprints], if their wish were to be fulfilled, that would be well; but if it were not to be fulfilled, [they thought]:
“Formerly, by making a formal resolution before the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, they obtained whatever they desired; now they do not obtain it.
It seems those very same bhikkhus were fulfillers of the practice, while these are unable to fulfill the practice.”
Thinking, "People will feel remorse," for these reasons the Blessed One, being unwilling to step on it, remained silent.

He laid down a training rule: "Monks, a cloth mat must not be stepped upon. However, regarding those who did not step on what had been prepared for the sake of an auspicious ceremony, he established a supplementary rule for the purpose of stepping on it: "Monks, householders..."
“Bhikkhus, I allow auspicious ceremonies for the sake of the welfare of householders.
(326) “The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations”—this the Elder spoke with reference to the third of the reasons already mentioned.
Why did he say, “Not indeed from pleasure comes pleasure”? Because [he was] perceiving it as the pursuit of sensual pleasure.

Having made the offering, the Perfectly Enlightened One did not step upon it; therefore, thinking, "I too shall have the same aspiration as the Teacher," he spoke thus. 327. From the words "As for me...

up to "...in the last watch of the night," it should be understood according to the method explained in the Mahāsaccaka Sutta. Thereafter, up to the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) of the group of five, it should be understood according to the method explained in the Pāsarāsi Sutta.
343. "In the craft of handling the hook" means in the craft of grasping the hook. "I am skilled" means I am proficient. But whose [craft] is this?
"Did he learn his craft from his father? "From his father; his father, too, had learned it from his own father.
It is said that in Kosambī, a king named Parantaparāja reigned.

The queen-consort, heavy with child, was sitting on the palace roof basking in the morning sun together with the king, wrapped in a red woolen blanket. A certain bird, a *hatthiliṅga*, [mistook her for] a "strip of meat..."
Thinking thus, he seized her and leapt into the air. Fearing that he might abandon her, she became silent;
he placed her on the branch of a tree at the foot of a mountain. She let out a great cry, making a loud noise with her hands.
The bird fled, and right there she gave birth to her offspring. While it was raining throughout the three watches of the night, [she wrapped] the blanket...

She sat down after having put on her robe. Not far from there lived an ascetic; hearing her voice, he came to the foot of the tree at daybreak, asked about her birth, and having constructed a ladder and helped her down, led her to his own dwelling and gave her rice-gruel to drink.
Because the child had been conceived and born during the rains and on a mountain, he gave him the name Udena.
The ascetic, having gathered various fruits, supported both people.
One day, as the ascetic was returning, she went out to meet him, displayed feminine charms, and caused his breach of virtue.
As time passed while they were living together, the King of Pāranta died.
The ascetic, having observed the constellations during the latter part of the night and learned that the king was dead, asked: "Your father the king is dead;
does your son wish to dwell here, or would he raise the royal parasol over his ancestral kingdom?
She then related the entire sequence of events to him from the beginning, including her son's desire to raise the royal parasol.
Having learned this, he informed the ascetic. The ascetic knew the art of binding elephants; from where had he obtained it? From Sakka.
It is said that in the past, Sakka came to attend upon him and asked, "By what means do you dispel fatigue?
He replied, "There is a danger from elephants. Then Sakka gave him both an elephant-binding spell and a lute, saying, "Out of a desire to drive them away..."
"If you wish to summon them, play this lute and recite this verse;
if you wish to call them forth, recite this verse," he said. The ascetic gave that craft to the prince.
He climbed a banyan tree, and when the elephants arrived, he played the lute and recited the verse; the elephants, terrified, fled away.
Thus, having recognized the power of his craft, on the following day he employed the art of summoning.
The eldest elephant came and presented its shoulder. Having mounted its shoulder, he selected a young elephant capable of fighting;
then, taking a blanket and a seal-ring, and having paid homage to his parents, he set out. Proceeding by stages, he entered various villages one after another.
Saying, “I am the king’s son; let those who desire prosperity come,” he gathered a crowd of people and surrounded the city.
To those who did not believe him when he said, “I am the king’s son; give me my royal parasol,” he showed them his blanket and his signet ring, and then raised the parasol.
Having become a keeper of elephants, he would say, “In such-and-such a place there is a beautiful elephant.”
When this was said, he went and took it. Caṇḍapajjota, thinking, "I will learn the craft from him," employed a wooden elephant;
having seated warriors inside it, he seized the man who had come to take the elephant, and sent his daughter to learn the craft from him. He then entered into a life of cohabitation with her.
Having taken him, he went back to his own city. This Prince Bodhi, who had been conceived in her womb, learned his craft in the presence of his father. 344.
Regarding "the factors of striving" (*padhāniyaṅgāni*): "striving" (*padhāna*) refers to the state of exerting effort; one who possesses such striving is called "one who strives" (*padhāniyo*).
"The factors of one who strives" (*padhāniyaṅgāni*) means the factors belonging to a monk who is striving. "Faithful" (*saddho*) means endowed with faith.
Now, that faith is fourfold: faith as arrival (*āgamanasaddhā*), faith as attainment (*adhigamasaddhā*), faith as conviction (*okappanasaddhā*), and faith as clarity (*pasādasaddhā*).
Among these, the faith of the omniscient Bodhisattvas is called "faith as arrival" because it has arrived starting from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*). [The faith] of the noble disciples...

Faith through realization (*adhigama-saddhā*) is so called because it is attained through personal penetration. Faith through conviction (*okappana-saddhā*) is the firm settling of the mind characterized by immovability when the words "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha" are uttered.
Faith through clarity (*pasāda-saddhā*) is the arising of serene confidence; however, in this context, faith through conviction is intended.
"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to the knowledge of the four paths. One has faith that "this was well-penetrated by the Tathāgata"; this is merely the starting point of the teaching.
Furthermore, by this factor, faith in the Three Jewels is intended.
For one who possesses strong confidence in the Buddha and the others, their exertion and energy succeed.

"Free from illness" means healthy. "Free from affliction" means free from suffering. "With a well-balanced digestion" means with a properly functioning digestive process. "Of the stomach... [The text continues:]...of the stomach.
Of the fire element born of karma. "Neither too cold nor too hot" means that one who is accustomed to extreme cold is afraid of cold, while one accustomed to extreme heat is afraid of heat;
for such people, striving does not succeed. It succeeds for one accustomed to the middle [temperature]. Therefore it is said: "of a moderate degree, capable of enduring striving.
"One who reveals oneself as one really is" means one who makes manifest one's own lack of virtue as it truly is.

"Leading to arising and passing away" means capable of discerning—that is, delimiting—both arising and passing away; by this, the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*), which grasps the thirty-two characteristics, is stated.
"Noble" means purified. "Penetrative" means capable of penetrating those aggregates of greed and so forth that have not been penetrated before.
"Leading rightly to the destruction of suffering" is said because the defilements are abandoned by way of their specific counteractive function (*tadaṅga*).
"That suffering which is being exhausted" refers to that which leads to the exhaustion of suffering. Thus, by all these terms, it is specifically insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) that is spoken of;
for the striving of one who lacks wisdom does not succeed. These five factors of striving (*padhāniyaṅga*) should be understood as purely mundane.
"He, having been instructed this evening, will attain distinction tomorrow morning" means that he was instructed when the sun had set, [and will attain it] at the rising of the dawn.
He will attain distinction. One instructed in the morning [attains it] at sunset; one instructed at sunrise [attains it] at the time of the sun's setting.
Furthermore, this teaching was spoken with reference to a person of guidable capacity (*neyya-puggala*).
For a person of guidable capacity with dull wisdom attains *arahantship* in seven days, one with sharp wisdom in a single day, and those with middling wisdom in the remaining days.
It should be understood as follows: "O, the Buddha! O, the Dhamma! O, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma!

Because, due to the loftiness of the Buddha’s qualities and the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, one might attain Arahatship in the evening after having been given a meditation subject in the morning, he spoke thus in praise.
The phrase *yatra hi nāma* is an indeclinable particle used in the sense of wonder.
346. "Pregnant" means one who has conceived a being. When it is said, "Venerable Sir, this which is in my womb," is it then the case that such a being has taken refuge?
It is not so. There is no such thing as taking refuge without consciousness; however, protection is indeed present for it.
Then, when the parents [say] to it at the time of its maturity, "Dear child, take refuge in that very same [refuge] while still in the womb..."

If they remind him, saying, "We had you take them," and he, having reflected, arouses mindfulness, thinking, "I am a lay follower who has gone for refuge," then it is said that the refuges have been taken. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.

The commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta is finished. 6. Commentary on the Aṅgulimāla Sutta 347. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Aṅgulimāla Sutta. Regarding the phrase "he wears a garland of fingers": why does he wear it? It is by the command of his teacher. Herein, this is the sequential account: [The story of Aṅgulimāla follows.]... [omitted] ...Thus far is the sequential account. Therefore, he wears it by the command of his teacher. Furthermore, he wears it for the purpose of inspiring fear in those who are hostile toward the Blessed One. For they will think: "This man has been ordained by the Blessed One; surely he must be a powerful personage. And thinking thus, they will not act with hostility toward the Blessed One. Moreover, he wears it so that people might know him as "Aṅgulimāla," and so that he may be distinguished from others. This is the reason he wears it. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the Vedic tradition (*brahmajāla*).

For in the Vedic tradition, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the Vedic tradition. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *mātaṅga* outcasts. For among the *mātaṅga* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *mātaṅga* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *caṇḍāla* outcasts. For among the *caṇḍāla* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *caṇḍāla* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *nigama* outcasts. For among the *nigama* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *mātanga* outcasts. For among the *mātanga* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *mātanga* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *caṇḍāla* outcasts. For among the *caṇḍāla* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *caṇḍāla* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *nigama* outcasts. For among the *nigama* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *nigama* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *pukkusa* outcasts. For among the *pukkusa* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *pukkusa* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *venakula* outcasts. For among the *venakula* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *venakula* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *dog-cookers*. For among the dog-cookers, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the dog-cookers.

Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *necca-bhara* outcasts. For among the *necca-bhara* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *necca-bhara* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *pulinda* outcasts. For among the *pulinda* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *pulinda* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *mātanga* outcasts. For among the *mātanga* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *mātanga* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *caṇḍāla* outcasts. For among the *pukkusa* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *pukkusa* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *venakula* outcasts. For among the *venakula* outcasts, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *venakula* outcasts. Furthermore, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the *dog-cookers*. For among the dog-cookers, it is said: "One should wear a garland of human fingers. Thus, he wears it because he is a follower of the custom of the dog-cookers. It is said that he took conception in the womb of a brahmin woman named Mantāṇī, the chaplain’s wife of the King of Kosala.
The birth of the child from the brahmin woman occurred during the night.
At the moment of his emergence from his mother’s womb, all the weapons in the entire city burst into flames, as did the king’s auspicious spear and the sword-blade kept upon his royal couch.

It burst into flames. The brahmin went out, observed the constellations, and realizing that [the prince] had been born under an unlucky star, he went into the presence of the king and asked whether he had slept well.
The king replied, "How could I have slept well, teacher? My auspicious weapon has burst into flames; it portends either the loss of my kingdom or my life."
“...or else some obstacle will arise, I think. “Do not fear, Great King; a boy has been born in my house.
By his power, not only in your residence but throughout the entire city, weapons have burst into flame.
“What will happen, Teacher? “A thief, Great King. “Is he a lone robber, or a thief who plunders the kingdom? “A lone robber.”
"Your Majesty," he said. Having spoken thus, and wishing to win the king's favor, he added: "Slay him, Your Majesty! Being but a single thief, what can he do?
He is like a single head of rice in a field of a thousand cartloads of husked grain. Look after him!
As they were taking his name, they saw the auspicious stone staff placed upon his bed and the arrows placed upon the roof.
A tool for making palm-leaf fans had been placed upon a cottonseed pod; though these [fires] were blazing, they did not harm it in the least.
Therefore, they gave him the name Ahiṃsaka (The Harmless One). When it was time for him to learn his craft, they sent him to Takkasilā.
There, becoming a pupil of the Dhamma, he applied himself to his craft. He was perfect in his duties, obedient in responding to commands, and pleasing in his conduct.
He was one who spoke kindly. The other resident pupils were outsiders. They thought, "Ever since the time the young man Ahiṃsaka arrived, we have not been able to distinguish ourselves;
how can we undermine him? Sitting down, they consulted together: "We cannot say he is 'of little wisdom,' for he excels all of us in wisdom.
We cannot say he is 'of bad conduct,' for he is perfect in his duties. They could find no fault with him.
"It cannot be said that he is ill-born because he is well-born; what shall we do?
Then they deliberated upon a harsh plot, saying, "We will split him by creating a rift between him and his teacher.
Dividing themselves into three groups, some first approached the teacher, paid homage, and stood before him. "What is it, dear ones? [he asked]. "In this house..."
"A single story is being told. "What is it, father? "I think the young brahmin Ahiṃsaka is causing dissension among you.
The teacher, rebuking them, spat out, saying, "Go away, you wretches! Do not cause division between my son and me!
Then the others came, and then the other three groups came, and having spoken in the same way, they said, "As for us..."
"Do not believe them; examine it and then know for yourselves," they said.
Seeing them speaking out of affection, the teacher thought, "I suspect there is some intimacy here," and he broke his composure, thinking, "I shall have him killed.
Then he reflected: "If I have him killed, people will say, 'The world-renowned teacher had his own pupil killed for the sake of learning a craft from him.'"
‘When a young man arrives, he will harbor ill-will and deprive him of life.
Then no one at all will come to learn a craft, and my income will diminish.
Therefore, I shall say, ‘This is the final stage of the craft,’ and tell him, ‘Kill a thousand people with your bare hands! Surely someone here will rise up and have him killed.”
Then he said to him, "Come, dear son, kill a thousand deer; in this way, the practice of your craft will have been performed.

[The son replied,] "We are born into a family of non-violence, Teacher; it is not possible [to do so]. [The teacher said,] "My son, a craft whose practice has not been performed does not yield its fruit.
Taking his five weapons and bowing to his teacher, he entered the forest. Even at the place where he entered the forest—
Even in the middle of a forest, or standing at the exit from the forest, he would kill people.
He did not take clothing or head-dress. He went along merely counting "one, two," yet he did not even learn the numbers.
By nature he was wise; however, his mind did not settle upon the taking of life, and therefore, gradually—
He could not even keep count; he would cut off one finger at a time and set it aside. Wherever he placed them, those fingers would disappear.
Thereupon, he pierced [the remaining fingers] together and made a garland of them, which he wore; thus the designation "Aṅgulimāla" (Finger-Garland) arose for him.
He rendered the entire forest uninhabitable, so that people could no longer go into the forest for the sake of wood and other resources.
There was no one capable [of stopping him].
Even coming into the village during the night, he would kick it open with his foot and, having killed those who were sleeping right there, he would take them away one by one.
The village retreated and settled in a market town; the market town [retreated] to a city.
People, starting from a distance of three leagues, abandoned their homes and came with their children in their arms;

they surrounded Sāvatthī, established a camp, and gathered in the royal courtyard, wailing and crying out, “Your Majesty, there is a bandit in your kingdom named Aṅgulimāla! When Bhaggava realized, “This will be my son,” he—
He said to the brahmin woman: "Madam, a bandit named Aṅgulimāla has appeared; he is none other than your son, Prince Ahiṃsaka.
Now the king will set out to capture him; what should be done? [She replied: "Go, sir, take my son and come back. [He said:
"I cannot venture to do so, noble lady, for there is no such thing as trust among four types of people: 'The bandit was my old companion.'"
"One should not be trusted; 'my old rug is on the branch'—one should not be trusted; 'the king honors me'—one should not be trusted;
'the woman has fallen under my power'—one should not be trusted. But a mother's heart is tender.
Therefore, thinking, "I shall go and bring back my son," she set out.
On that very day, as the Blessed One surveyed the world at the time of dawn, he saw Aṅgulimāla and thought:

“If I go, his safety will be secured. Standing in a forest where there is no village, upon hearing a four-line verse, he will go forth in my presence and realize the six supernormal powers. If I do not go, having offended his mother, he will be beyond rescue.”
Thinking, "He will become one; I shall show him favor," the Blessed One dressed in the morning, entered for alms, and having finished his meal, departed from the monastery desiring to show him favor.
To demonstrate this matter, the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One" was spoken.
"Having formed groups, having formed groups" means having made a pact and being divided into factions.
"They go to their destruction in their own hands" means they go to ruin (atthaṃ) within their own hands. But did they say this because they recognized the Blessed One, or without recognizing him?
Without recognizing him. For the Blessed One had gone alone in an unrecognized guise. And the thief—[in that regard]...
At that time, he had long been distressed by poor food and painful sleep.
"How many people has he killed? [The answer was: "One less than a thousand.
Thinking, "Now, having obtained one more, I shall complete the thousand," he killed whoever he saw first, and having completed the count, [he began] the practice of his craft.
Having shaved off his hair and beard, bathed, and changed his clothes, thinking, "I shall see my mother and father," he came from the middle of the forest toward the entrance of the forest;
while standing to one side, he saw the Blessed One.
To show this matter, the passage beginning with "He saw" was spoken.
"He performed a feat of supernormal power (*iddhābhisaṅkhāra*)," [meaning] he drew back the great earth as if raising up waves and then stepped forward;
on the near side, folds appeared, and Aṅgulimāla went along after letting out a space only the width of an arrow.
The Blessed One showed a vast open space in front, with himself in the middle and the robber at the edge. Then—"

"Having reached him, I will seize him," he thought, and ran with all his might. The Blessed One was at the far edge of the courtyard while the robber was in the middle. Thinking, "I will seize him here," the robber ran with great speed.
The Blessed One showed him either a stream or dry land ahead; by this means, he led the robber for three *yojanas*. The robber—
He grew weary; the saliva dried in his mouth, and sweat poured from his armpits.
Then it occurred to him: "How wonderful this is! Why did he take the deer? For the sake of food at a time when he was hungry. It is said that by striking a thicket, he would startle the deer;
then, pursuing whichever deer pleased his mind, he would capture it, cook it, and eat it.
"Should ask": the meaning is, "By what reason is this one called 'standing' even while walking, and why am I called 'not standing' even while standing?
What if I were now to ask this ascetic about that reason?
(349) "Having laid aside": having set aside and removed that staff which might otherwise be wielded against living beings for the purpose of harming them.
The meaning is: "I am established in loving-kindness, patience, reflection, non-violence, and the qualities conducive to harmony. As for the phrase "you are not so established":

because you are unrestrained toward living beings, killing as many as these thousands of creatures, you possess neither loving-kindness, nor patience, nor reflection, nor non-violence, nor the qualities conducive to harmony; therefore, you are not established.
"Now, even while standing in this posture, you will run toward hell; you will run toward the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras"—this is what was said.
Then the thief thought: "This is a great lion's roar, a mighty thundering; this cannot belong to anyone else; it must be Mahāmāyā."
"This is the thundering of my son Siddhattha, the king of ascetics;

surely I have been seen by the Perfectly Enlightened One with his sharp eye, and the Blessed One has come for the sake of gathering me under his care. Having thought this, he said, "After such a long time indeed," and so forth.
In that context, *mahito* means honored with the four requisites by gods, humans, and others. *Paccupādī* means after a long period of time.
He entered this Great Forest for the purpose of gathering me after my transgression. "Having abandoned evil" means having relinquished evil.
"Itveva" means having spoken thus. "Weapons" refers to the five weapons. "Pits" refers to those cut off on all sides. "Precipices" refers to those cut off on one side.
"Chasms" refers to places where fruit has fallen; however, here by these three terms, the forest itself is meant.
"Akirīti" means he threw it away and discarded it.
"Tadā avoca 'tamehi bhikkhu'" means that when the Blessed One was ordaining him, [the youth] thought, "Where shall I find a razor?
Where shall I find a bowl and robes? and thus had no need to search for them; however, he did look toward his past karma. Then, for him...
Knowing that he had given the eight requisites to those who were virtuous, he extended his right hand and said:
"Come, bhikkhu; well-proclaimed is the Dhamma. Lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
At the very moment these words were spoken, he obtained a set of bowl and robes produced by supernormal power. At that same instant, his lay appearance vanished.
The mark of a recluse appeared:
"The three robes, the bowl, the razor, the needle, the girdle,
and the water-strainer— these eight belong to a bhikkhu devoted to yoga."
When he had spoken thus, the eight requisites arose as if already attached to his body.

"This indeed was his state of being a bhikkhu" means that this very state of being a "Come, bhikkhu" (ehibhikkhu) became his state of full admission as a bhikkhu; for there is no separate formal act of admission (upasampadā) for those who are "Come, bhikkhu."
350. "With a junior monk as attendant" means with a junior monk who carries his belongings;
the meaning is that he went having had his own bowl and robes taken by him and having made him his attendant. His mother was separated from him by a distance of eight usabhas, [thinking]:
"Dear Ahiṃsaka, where are you standing? Where are you sitting? Where have you gone? By me..."
“Father, she did not speak with me,” she said; and wandering about, not seeing him, she went away from that very spot.
“With about five hundred horsemen,” [he thought]: “If the thief is defeated, I will pursue and capture him;
if I am defeated, I will flee with speed. Thus he set out with a healthy force.
Why did he go to the monastery (*ārāma*)? It is said that he was afraid of the thief;
though his mind desired to go, he did not go [at first] out of fear of censure. Then he thought: “I shall pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One and sit down.
He will ask, ‘Why have you come out with an army? Then I shall explain. For the Blessed One...”
He does not sustain me only with matters pertaining to the future life, but he sustains me even with matters pertaining to the present life. If victory should be mine, he will consent;
but if defeat should be mine, he will say, "Great King, what is the use of your going on account of a single thief? Then people will perceive me in this way:
—“The king set out to seize the thief, but he was turned back by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Seeing this as a release from blame, he departed.
But why did he say, “Where indeed is he”? It was because the Blessed One, having observed his underlying potential (*upanissaya*), intended to bring him [to the Buddha].
"He should ordain him" was said for the sake of the Blessed One’s protection.
As for "of the king," it was not only the king who was afraid; the rest of the populace also became terrified.
Casting aside their shields and weapons, they fled right before his eyes, entered the city, closed the gates, and stood watching from atop the watchtowers. And so...
He said: “Aṅgulimāla, knowing that the king was coming to him, arrived first and sat down in Jeta’s Grove;
the king was seized by him, but we escaped and were released.
“There is no fear for you from him” means: he will not now deprive even a tiny ant of its life; the meaning is, “there is no fear for you from his presence.”

"How is his clan?"—why does he ask this? He asks thinking: "It is not proper to address one who has gone forth by the name given due to a cruel deed; rather, I shall address him by way of his mother and father's clan.
"Requisites" means: "I shall make an effort for their sake. And even as he was speaking, [he saw] the cloth tied around the belly.
Having released it, he placed it at the feet of the Elder.
351. The four ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) beginning with "forest-dweller" are those mentioned in the Canon. However, since the Elder had actually undertaken all thirteen, he said, "Enough.
With reference to what did he say, "Venerable sir, as for what we..."? [He meant: "Even a running elephant..."
Having pursued him, he thought, "I shall seize him," and at the place where he had come, he seized those elephants and other animals sent by the king in this manner.
The king also, thinking, "Surround and seize him with elephants alone, with horses alone, or with chariots alone," sent many elephants and other animals on numerous occasions.
But when they had thus departed, [Aṅgulimāla] rose up and said to him, "Hey! I am Aṅgulimāla!"
Not even one among them was able to turn his weapon while making a sound; he crushed them all and killed them.
"The elephants were wild forest elephants, the horses were wild forest horses, and even the chariots broke apart right there"—it is with reference to this that the king speaks thus.
"He entered for alms" does not mean that he entered for the first time; rather, this was said with reference to the day of the women's viewing.
Moreover, he would enter even during the day; and when people saw him, they were terrified and fled, or bolted their doors.
Some, upon merely hearing "Aṅgulimāla," would flee and enter the forest, or having entered their houses, would bolt the doors.
Those unable to escape stood with their backs turned. The Elder [even] offered a ladleful of rice...
He did not receive even a spoonful of alms; he was exhausted by his lack of food. Not obtaining anything outside, he entered the city, thinking it was common property for all.
Through whichever gate he entered, there arose the cause for the collapse of a thousand fraudulent schemes, as word spread that Aṅgulimāla had arrived there.
"This thought occurred to him" refers to the state of having reached compassion. There were one thousand people minus one.
"Even for a single day, there was no compassion in him as he was killing; how did it arise merely by seeing a woman with child?
It is through the power of renunciation (*pabbajjā*); for this is the power of renunciation.
'Because of that' means: because compassion arose in you, therefore—O Aṅgulimāla, [it is] by noble birth."
"Do not take this; it is not your birth. This was the time of being a householder, and as householders they even kill living beings and commit acts such as taking what is not given.
But now you have attained what is called the birth of the Noble Ones (ariya).
Therefore, if you feel scruples about saying, 'Sister, since I was born,' then say it by qualifying it thus: 'born into the birth of the Noble Ones. Thus he exhorted her.
He said this to that woman: "It is not possible for a man to approach the place where women give birth.
"What are you doing, Elder? she asked. The Elder Āḷavaka had them announce: "The Elder Aṅgulimāla has come to ensure safety by performing an act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
Then, having enclosed the area with a curtain, they prepared a seat for the Elder outside the curtain.
The Elder sat there and performed an Act of Truth, saying: "Sister, since I was born into the noble lineage of the Omniscient Buddha.
Simultaneously with that truthful utterance, the child emerged from the water-vessel like water poured out from a vessel.
Mother and son were safe. And this protective chant (paritta) crushes no danger whatsoever; it is a great protection.
Thus it was said. When the Elder had sat down and performed the *saccakiriya* (act of truth), they prepared a seat at that spot.
Even a female animal whose womb was obstructed would be brought there and made to sit; immediately, the delivery of the fetus occurred with ease.
As for one who was weak and unable to be brought there, they would bring water used for washing the seat and sprinkle it on her head.
At that very moment, the fetus was expelled, and it also cured another disease. This is said to be a miracle that lasts for an entire eon.
But did the Blessed One have the Elder perform medical treatment? He did not. For when people saw the Elder, they were terrified and fled.
The Elder grew weary from eating almsfood and was unable to practice the duties of a recluse. To him—
Out of compassion, he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*). It occurred to him thus:
"Now, people will hear that the Elder Aṅgulimāla has regained a mind of loving-kindness and is ensuring the safety of humans through an act of truth;
they will think to approach the Elder. Consequently, being untired by the search for alms-food, he will be able to practice the duty of a recluse."
Out of favor, he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*). For an act of truth is not a medical practice.

Furthermore, although the Elder had taken up his fundamental meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) thinking, "I shall perform the duty of a recluse," as he sat in his night-quarters and day-quarters, his mind would not turn toward the meditation subject;
it went only to the place in the forest where people had been slaughtered.
It becomes manifest. The manner of speech and the gestures of hands and feet of those terrified of death—saying, "I am wretched, I have but one young son;
give me my life, Master!"—come into his field of vision. Becoming remorseful, he rises from that very spot and departs.
Then the Blessed One, having rendered that birth irrelevant, [instructed him] to increase his insight here.

Thinking, "He will attain arahantship," he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) by means of his noble birth. The passage beginning with "One who is secluded" is explained in detail in the Vattha Sutta.

352. "Thrown by another as a clod": this refers to a clod thrown from any direction whatsoever into a space just large enough for a stone to pass, intended to cause crows, dogs, pigs, and the like to retreat;
yet, having come back, it falls upon the Elder’s body itself. To what extent [does this occur]?
"Is it thus? [The Blessed One replied: "It remains so until one has tied the waist-belt, wandered for alms, returned, and reached the place where the waist-belt was first tied.
'With a split head' means with a head split down to the bone after the thick skin has been cut away.
'O Brahmin,' he said, referring to the state of one whose taints are exhausted. 'By the ripening of that karma of yours, O Brahmin...'"
This was said with reference to *sabhāga-dṛṣṭadharmanvedanīya-karma* (karma to be experienced in the present life that is homogeneous).

For while the karma is being performed, it fulfills three categories. Among the seven moments of consciousness, the first impulsion volition—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is called *dṛṣṭadharmanvedanīya-karma*.
It yields its result in this very existence. That which is unable to do so is *ahosi-karma* (karma that has become past).
"Ahosikamma" (karma that has been) is so called by way of this triad: "there was no ripening of karma," "there will be no ripening of karma," and "there is no ripening of karma.
The seventh javana-consciousness, which accomplishes the purpose, is called "upapajjavedanīya-kamma" (karma to be experienced upon rebirth).
It yields its result in the immediately following existence. That which is unable to do so in that manner is, according to the method already stated, "ahosikamma."
It is called [kamma] to be experienced in this very life. Between the two, the five impulsive moments of volition are called kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives;
when it finds an opportunity in the future, it then yields its result. As long as the round of existence continues, there is no such thing as "kamma that has already been exhausted.
However, for the Elder, there were these two: kamma to be experienced upon rebirth and kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives.

Kamma that was to be experienced in future lives has been eradicated by the path of Arahantship, which brings about the destruction of kamma; however, there is kamma to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
Even for one who has attained Arahantship, that [kamma] still yields its result. With reference to this, the Blessed One said, "For whom indeed you... and so forth.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "for whom indeed," the meaning should be understood as: "O Brahmin, for whatever kind of kamma it may be, through the ripening of that kamma... you have come to this state.
"Released from clouds" is merely the heading of the teaching; what is intended here is the moon released from these defilements, namely: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu.

For just as the moon, when thus free from defilements, illuminates the world, so too the diligent bhikkhu, liberated from the defilement of negligence, illuminates this world of his own aggregates, bases, and elements.
It dispels the darkness of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"It is covered by the wholesome" means it is covered by skill in the Path (*magga-kusala*); it is rendered such that there is no further rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*).
"He exerts himself in the Buddha’s teaching" means he dwells fully engaged in the Buddha’s teaching through body, speech, and mind. These are the three *udāna* verses of the Elder.
“*Disā hi me*”: it is said that the Elder spoke this while performing a protective rite for himself. In this context, “*disā hi me*” means “my enemies.
Those who revile him thus—“Just as we experience suffering because of our kinsmen killed by Aṅgulimāla, so too let Aṅgulimāla experience [suffering]”—to them he says:
“*Me disā*,” meaning the discourse on the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
"Let them hear"—this is the meaning. "Let them apply themselves"—let them dwell engaged and intent with body, speech, and mind.
"Those who truly enjoin the Dhamma, being peaceful"—those peaceful, virtuous persons who truly enjoin, incite, and cause others to take up the Dhamma;
let those men be my companions, let them serve and attend upon me—this is the meaning.
"Those who praise non-conflict": "non-conflict" is said to be loving-kindness (*mettā*); thus the meaning is "those who praise loving-kindness.
"May they hear the Dhamma at the proper time": may they, from moment to moment, hear the Dhamma that consists of patience, loving-kindness, reflection, and consolation.
"And may they practice accordingly": and may they emulate and fulfill that Dhamma.
For he who has seen me will never harm me; indeed, he would not harm me at all.
Furthermore, let them not kill or injure anyone else—not only me, but no other person whatsoever.
Having attained supreme peace—that is, having reached Nibbāna, which is the state of supreme peace—one should protect both the timid and the steadfast.
"The moving" refers to those with craving; "the stationary" refers to those without craving. This is what is meant:
whoever attains Nibbāna is capable of protecting all that is moving and stationary. Therefore, [he says]: "May the quarters reach Nibbāna for me as well;
thus they will not harm me at all. He spoke these three verses in order to perform a protective chant (*paritta*) for himself.
Now, illustrating his own practice, he said: "For those who lead water are channel-makers.

In this context, "channel-makers" refers to those who, having cleared a main channel (*mātikā*), bind it at the places where it must be bound and thus lead the water. "Fletchers" refers to those who work with arrows.
"They straighten" means that after smearing [the wood] with oil and heating it in hot ashes, they bend it down at the high points until it becomes straight.
They "make straight" (*tejana*); *tejana* means an arrow. For the archer makes it straight, and he also urges on the enemy;

therefore it is called "making straight. "They tame themselves": just as channel-makers lead water by a direct path, fletchers [straighten] an arrow, and carpenters make wood straight, even so do the wise tame themselves—they make themselves straight and free from crookedness.

"Tādinā" means by the Teacher who has attained the characteristic of being "such" (tādi), remaining unshaken amidst the desirable and undesirable; for it is said: "The Blessed One is 'such' in five ways:

he is such toward the desirable and the undesirable; he is such because he has vomited out [defilements]; he is such because he has abandoned [them]; he is such because he has crossed over [the flood];
he is such because of the designation of that. "Bhavanettī" means the rope of existence; this is a name for craving. For by means of it, beings are bound like oxen by a rope around their necks.
Beings are bound by existence in the heart and are led to this or that state of becoming; therefore, it is called "the lead to becoming" (*bhavanetti*).

"Touched by the ripening of karma" means touched by the volition of the Path. For since karma is cooked, ripened, burnt, and brought to total exhaustion by the volition of the Path, it is for that reason called "the ripening of karma.
Because he has been touched by that [volition], he has become free from debt and stainless.

One is not free from debt regarding painful feeling. Furthermore, in this context, four kinds of enjoyment should be understood: enjoyment by theft, enjoyment as a debt, enjoyment as an inheritance, and enjoyment as an owner.

Among these, the enjoyment of one who is immoral is called "enjoyment by theft," for he enjoys the four requisites having stolen them. And it has been said: "O bhikkhus, [you have enjoyed] by theft..."
“The alms of the country have been eaten. However, for one who is virtuous, consumption without reflection is called “consumption as a debt.
For the seven types of trainees (sekkha), consumption is called “consumption as an inheritance. For one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), consumption is called “consumption as a master’s.
Here, with reference to the absence of the debts of defilements, it is said “debtless” (aṇaṇo). There is also the reading “indebted” (aniṇo). [This refers to] consumption as a master’s.
Having intended this, it was said: "I eat my food.
"Intimacy with sensual delight" means: do not indulge in, do not practice, intimacy with craving for either of the two kinds of sensual pleasures.
"This was not ill-considered by me" refers to that which I considered when I thought: "Having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One, I shall go forth."
That which was my counsel was not ill-counselled. Regarding the phrase "among the distributed phenomena":

when it is said "I am the Teacher," whatever phenomena have arisen in the world and been distributed, among those phenomena, I have approached—that is, I have attained—the very best, which is Nibbāna;
therefore, this coming of mine is called a "welcome arrival. Thus [said] Tissa.
"Knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the wisdom consisting of the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).

"The Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished" means that whatever duty remains to be done in the Buddha’s dispensation, all of that has been completed by me. Thus, he brought the teaching to its ultimate perfection through the three knowledges and the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
The commentary on the Aṅgulimāla Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 7.
The commentary on the Piyajātika Sutta.
353. Thus have I heard: this is the *Piyajātika-sutta*. Therein, "even one's own works do not appear" means they do not appear at all;
however, they do not appear according to their usual course. The same method applies to the second phrase as well. And here, "does not appear" means it does not please.
"A cremation ground" (*āḷāhana*) means a charnel ground. "Alteration" (*aññathatta*) is a state of being otherwise due to disfigurement.
The "faculties" (indriyāni) are phenomena cognizable by the mind; however, this was said with reference to a fixed location.
"Born of the beloved" means they arise from what is beloved. "Originating from the beloved" means they have their source in what is beloved.
"If that, O Great King," [was said] even though he did not perceive its meaning, solely out of faith in the Teacher.
He says: "Go away, depart from us, you who are not of our own kin"—this is the meaning. Alternatively, "go away, depart" means "go elsewhere; do not stay here. 356.
"Having cut in two" means having severed, making two portions with a sword. "He tore himself apart" means by that very [sword]...
He slit his own belly with a sword. For if she had been unloved by him, he would not have killed himself thinking, "Now I shall take another woman.
But because she was beloved by him, he did this, desiring to be united with her even in the next world.

357. "Piyā te vajirī" (The Vajirī you love): thus she thought to herself—"If I were to speak of this matter beginning with 'Once upon a time, Great King, in this very Sāvatthī, a certain woman...', he would rebuff me, saying, 'Who did this for you? Go away, there is no such thing!
Therefore, I shall convince him by means of what is currently happening. Having reflected thus, she spoke as follows. "Vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā" (Because of change and alteration).
In this context, *vipariṇāma* (change) should be understood as occurring through death, and *aññathābhāva* (alteration) as occurring by fleeing and going away with someone else.
Regarding the phrase "Vāsabhā," there was a queen of the king named Vāsabhā; he spoke referring to her.
Why did he say "You were dear to me" last of all? It is said that she thought: "This king is angry with me..."
"If I were to ask first of all, 'Are you dear to me? he would say, 'You are not dear to me; go away!
In that case, the conversation would find no foothold. Thus, for the sake of providing a foothold for the conversation, he asked last of all.

By the fact of being abandoned in Kāsi and Kosala, its transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is to be understood; by its falling into the hands of rival kings, its alteration (*aññathābhāva*) is to be understood.

"Ācamehī" means "give water for rinsing the mouth. Having rinsed his mouth, washed his hands and feet, and cleansed his face, he spoke thus because he desired to pay homage to the Teacher. The rest is self-evident everywhere.
The commentary on the *Piyajātika-sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, is finished.
8. Commentary on the Bāhitika Sutta 358.
"Thus have I heard" introduces the Bāhitika Sutta. In this context, *ekapuṇḍarīkaṃ nāgaṃ* refers to an elephant of that name.
It is said that upon its flanks there was a white spot the size of a palm fruit; for that reason, it was called "Single White Lotus" (*Ekapuṇḍarīka*).

They gave him the name Sirivaḍḍha. [The phrase] "the minister Sirivaḍḍha" refers to a high official of that name who was traveling together with [the king] for the sake of pleasant conversation, having mounted his own private elephant.
Regarding the word *no* in the phrase *āyasmā no*: here *no* is a particle used for inquiry.
Having observed the Elder’s manner of carrying his outer robe and bowl, the minister said, "Yes, Great King."
359. "Opārambho" means one who is worthy of being reproached for the fault of being censurable. "What do I ask? asks the King.
He asks, "I ask this because it arose in the case of Sundarī.
"For that which we, O Bhante..."—having taken up this phrase, "O Bhante, that which we [could not understand] by the wise," the Venerable One was unable to fulfill the question with a reason.
By speaking thus, [the meaning] is fulfilled.

(360) "Unwholesome" (*akusala*) means produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*). "Blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) means accompanied by defilement (*sadosa*). "Afflictive" (*sabyābajjha*) means accompanied by suffering (*sadukkha*).

"Resulting in suffering" (*dukkhavipāka*) refers here to the outflow-result (*nissanda-vipāka*). "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to one whose bodily conduct proceeds for the sake of such things as self-affliction.
"Great King, when it is said, 'The Tathāgata has abandoned all unwholesome states and is endowed with wholesome states,' this praises the abandonment of every single unwholesome state.

"Yes, it does praise them. When this was said, the meaning would have been stated according to the question. However, such an answer is not difficult; for even one who has not abandoned the unwholesome...
The Blessed One might have praised abandoning; however, he explained it in this way to show that because of his own abandonment of unwholesome states, he is "one who acts as he speaks.
The same method applies to the bright side (the wholesome side) as well.

362. *Bāhitika*: This is the name for cloth produced in the country of Bāhitika. "Sixteen cubits in length" means equal to sixteen cubits in length. "Eight cubits in width" means equal to eight cubits in width.
363. “They are for the Blessed One’s feet,” he said, and offered them to the Blessed One. Having given them, he fashioned a canopy over the Perfumed Chamber and fastened it there.
From that time forth, the Perfumed Chamber shone with even greater splendor. The rest is clear throughout.
This teaching, however, was concluded by way of the person to be guided.
The commentary on the Bāhitika Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 9.
The commentary on the Dhammacetiya Sutta.
364. Thus have I heard: this is the *Dhammacetiyasutta*. Therein, "Medāḷupa" is its name;
for it is said that at that town there were many stones the color of fat (*meda*), and thus it became known as Medāḷupa.
As for the lodging place (*senāsana*) there, it was not fixed, and therefore it is not mentioned. "Nagaraka" is its specific name.
To the town of the Sakyans. "On some business" means not on any other business;
rather, he commanded, "Seize Bandhula the general together with his thirty-two sons this very day.
On that same day, the Blessed One had been invited by his wife Mallikā along with five hundred bhikkhus, and [was present] with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
As soon as she had returned home and sat down, they brought a message to Mallikā, saying, "The General has passed away," and gave it to her.
She took the letter and asked for the oral message. They reported, "Noble Lady, the King has had the General executed along with his thirty-two sons all at once.
She said, "Do not let this become common knowledge among the people," and placed the letter in the fold of her garment.
Having done so, he served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. At that time, a certain oil-jar was brought out; it struck against the door-sill and broke.
Having removed it and had another brought, he served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
When the Teacher had finished his meal, for the purpose of initiating a discourse, he said: "One should not worry over the cause of a broken oil-jar."
He said: At that time, Mallikā took out a leaf, placed it before the Blessed One, and said:
"Blessed One, this news of the death of the general, along with his thirty-two sons—the Blessed One himself does not even consider this;
what then should I worry about, on account of a mere ghee-pot? The Blessed One said: "Mallikā, do not worry; [this cycle] is without a known beginning."
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma concerning impermanence and other such themes, saying, "This is what happens to those wandering in saṃsāra," he departed.
Mallikā summoned her thirty-two daughters-in-law and gave them instruction.
The King summoned Mallikā and asked, "Is there any cause for estrangement between the commander-in-chief and us? She replied, "There is none, my Lord. He [then questioned] her...
Having understood his innocence from his words, he became remorseful and experienced intense mental distress.

Thinking, "I have destroyed a companion who came to me as a friend, believing him to be one who would do no harm," he thereafter found no pleasure in his palace, nor in theatrical performances, nor in the joys of sovereignty; he began to wander here and there.
This was precisely what had to be done. It is with reference to this that it was said:
"On account of some business. Regarding the phrase *dīghaṃ kārāyanaṃ*: Dīgha Kārāyana was the nephew of the general Bandhula;
because [Bandhula] had been executed by the king without cause and without fault, he was appointed to the position of general by the king. It is with reference to him that this was said.
It was said: "With great royal majesty" means with great royal power;

the meaning is: with a great military force, possessing the splendor of various costumes, as if splitting the surface of the earth or overturning the ocean. "Pleasing" (*pāsādika*) means causing delight even upon being seen.
"Inspiring confidence" (*pasādanīya*) is a synonym for that same term. Alternatively, "pleasing" means...
"Producing confidence. "Quiet" means soundless. "Without noise" means devoid of noise because the meaning [of the sounds] is not manifested.
"Free from the breath of people" means devoid of the movement of people. "Suitable for human seclusion" means appropriate for secret human activities;
the meaning is that they are suitable for those deliberating on secrets. "Conducive to retreat" means conducive to the state of being hidden away.
They are suitable for becoming one. Regarding the phrase "where indeed I have been," it does not mean that the Blessed One had previously attended upon him there;
rather, he had previously attended upon those of such a kind. Therefore, the meaning here is: "where indeed I have been" refers to those of such a nature.
"There is, Great King," [said the general]—the wise general knew, "The king holds the Blessed One in high regard. If he...
The king might ask, "Where is the Blessed One? and it would be appropriate to point him out without hesitation;
therefore, having dispatched scouts and learned the Blessed One’s place of residence, he remained there. For this reason he spoke thus.
"He entered the monastery" means that, having established his camp outside the town, he entered together with Kārāyaṇa.
366. "Vihāra" refers to the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), so they say. "Āḷinda" means the porch. "Having coughed" means having made the sound of a cough.
"Aggaḷa" means the door-panel. "Strike" means strike slightly with the tip of your fingernail near the keyhole; this is what is meant.
It is said that non-humans strike the door too high, while long-tailed creatures (dīghajātikā) strike it too low. Likewise...
Having struck [the door], one should strike near the hole in the middle; thus they speak, explaining that this is the duty regarding the door-keeper.
"Right there" means in the very place mentioned by the monks. "The sword and the turban"—this is merely a figurative expression for:
the fly-whisk, the fan, the turban, the sword, the parasol, and the sandals.
Having descended from his vehicle, King Uruvela removed his royal insignia.
He then presented the five regalia of royalty that had arrived with him. But why did he give them?

It was because it would have been improper to approach the Exalted One, the Fully Enlightened One, who is so exceedingly venerable, in an ostentatious manner; rather, he wished to approach alone according to his own preference.
"And I shall converse with him. For when the five royal insignia have been turned back, it is not necessary to say "you turn back";
they all turn back of their own accord. Thus, for these two reasons, he gave [the bowl]. *Rahāyati* means he makes it secret; he conceals it.
This, it is said, was his intention: "Previously, this king also [was together] with the ascetic Gotama..."
"Having recited the four-cornered spell, he had my maternal uncle seized along with his thirty-two sons;
now, desiring to recite the four-cornered spell once more, will he perhaps have me seized as well? Thus did this thought arise in him through the power of anger.
"The Blessed One opened the door": it was not that the Blessed One rose up and opened the door himself, but rather [he extended his hand] thinking, "Let it be opened."
He opened it. Then, thinking, “For many millions of eons, while you were giving gifts, the Blessed One has never performed the task of opening a door with his own hand,” the door opened by itself.
However, because it was opened by the mind of the Blessed One, it is appropriate to say, “The Blessed One opened the door. Having entered the vihāra means having entered the Gandhakuṭī.
Having entered, as soon as he had stepped inside, Kārāyaṇa took the five royal insignia, went to the military camp, and addressed Viṭaṭūbha:
"Friend, raise up the parasol! "Why has my father gone? "Do not ask about your father; if you do not raise it yourself, I shall take it and raise it. "I shall raise it."
“Very well,” he consented. Kārāyaṇa, leaving behind for the king one horse, one sword, and one female attendant,
raised Viṭaṭūbha’s royal parasol and took it, saying, “If the king desires to live,
let him not come,” and departed for Sāvatthī itself.
367. *Dhammanvaya* means the following from, the inference from, or the subsequent understanding of the Dhamma, which is to say, direct knowledge (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*).
Now, in order to show by what sequence of Dhamma one arrives at the realization that "the Blessed One is perfectly enlightened," etc., he said:
"But here, venerable sir," and so forth. In that context, *āpāṇakoṭika* means "until the limit of life"; *pāṇa* is life, and that constitutes the boundary.
Having made it their limit, they continue to practice even at the time of death; that is to say, they do not transgress it.

There is also a reading, "apāṇakoṭikaṃ," meaning "until the end of life. The sense is: "It is not as some who, for the sake of life, transgress [the precepts] and practice having made a limit of living beings (pāṇakoṭikaṃ).
"This too, venerable sir, is mine" refers to the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment and the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma.
"And this occurs because of the Saṅgha’s being well-practiced; for thus, venerable sir, do I perceive this underlying principle of the Dhamma regarding the Blessed One," he demonstrates.
This same method applies everywhere.
"As if not fixing his gaze" means as if not binding his gaze. For having seen something unpleasing, [he does so].
There is no further need for looking [at them], therefore they do not "bind" the eye. Having seen what is pleasing, there is a need to look again and again, therefore that is said to "bind" the eye.
These, however, are unpleasing; therefore he spoke thus.
"Bandhukaroga" means a family disease. They say, "Those born in our family are like this. "Uḷāra" means of great influence.

"Later than before" (*pubbenāparaṃ*) means a distinction subsequent to what preceded. In this context, one who, having performed the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, brings forth meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), is said to perceive a sublime distinction later than before.
One who, having made that attainment the proximate cause, develops insight (*vipassanā*) and attains *arahantship*, is said to perceive a sublime distinction later than before.
370. "He should have him killed" means he should have someone fit to be killed killed.
"He should have him fined" means he should have someone fit to be fined fined, that is, made penniless by means of wealth.
"He should have him banished" means he should have someone fit to be banished from the kingdom banished.
373. *Isidatta-purāṇā* means Isidatta and Purāṇa. Among them, one was a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), and the other was content with his own wife.
*Mamabhattā* means those whose food belongs to me; they are my food-recipients.

*Mamayānā* means those whose vehicle belongs to me; they are my vehicle-recipients. *Jīvikāya dātā* means a giver of a livelihood, one who provides the means of subsistence. *Vīmaṃsamāno* means examining or investigating.
At that time, it is said, the king lay down as if he had fallen asleep, though he had not actually entered sleep.
Then those architects asked, "In which direction is the Blessed One? and having heard, "In such-and-such a place," they deliberated:

"If we place our heads toward where the Perfectly Enlightened One is, the king will have his feet [toward him]. If we place our heads toward where the king is, the Teacher will have his feet [toward him]. What [should we do]?"
"Shall we do so? Then this thought occurred to them: "If the king becomes angry, he might take away what he has given us.
Yet, we cannot knowingly treat the Teacher with our feet. Having thus placed the king at their feet, they lay down.
It was with reference to this that the king spoke thus.
374. "He departed" means that having emerged from the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), he went to the place where Kārāyaṇa was stationed;
not seeing him there, he went to the location of the army camp (khandhāvāra); not seeing anyone else there either, he questioned that woman.
She related the entire occurrence. The King said: "I must not go there now alone; having gone to Rājagaha..."
Thinking, "I will come with my nephew and seize my kingdom," he set out for Rājagaha.
On the way, he ate only coarse grain porridge and drank plenty of water. Because his constitution was so delicate, the food did not digest properly.
Even as he reached Rājagaha, he arrived at an inopportune time when the gates were already closed. "Today..."
Thinking, “Having slept in the hall, I shall see my own nephew tomorrow,” he lay down in a hall outside the city.
During the night, his end-of-life symptoms manifested; several times he went outside.
From that point on, unable to walk even a step, he lay in the lap of that woman and passed away at the break of dawn. She [then] took him...

Having perceived his state, she began to lament with a loud voice, saying: "My lord, the King of Kosala, who once ruled over two kingdoms, now lies here in the shelter for the destitute outside another's city, having met his end as one who is helpless.
When the people heard this, they informed the king. The king came, saw him, recognized him, and [asked] the reason for his arrival.
Having learned this, he performed the funeral rites for the body with great ceremony and, sounding the drum to assemble his forces, thought, "I shall seize Viṭaṭūbha," and mustered his army.
The ministers fell at his feet and said, "O King, if your maternal uncle were healthy, it would have been appropriate for you to go;
however, now that Viṭaṭūbha himself depends upon you for his sovereignty..."
Having thus persuaded him, saying, “He truly deserves to be raised up,” they restrained him.
*Dhammacetiyāni* means words expressing veneration for the Dhamma. For when veneration is paid to any one of the Three Jewels, it is as if it were paid to all;
therefore, when veneration is paid to the Blessed One, the Dhamma is also thereby venerated.
The Blessed One said, "They are shrines of the Dhamma. "Pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" means they constitute the beginning of the holy life of the Path;
the meaning is that they consist of the preliminary practice. The rest is clear everywhere.
[End of] the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the *Dhammacetiyasutta* is finished.
10. The commentary on the *Kaṇṇakatthalasutta*:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Kaṇṇakatthalasutta*. Therein, "at Uruññā" means at Uruññā; [it is the name] of that kingdom as well.
The city had this very same name, and the Blessed One was dwelling in dependence upon the city of Uruññā. Regarding the phrase "in the deer park at Kaṇṇakatthala":
not far from that city there was a certain delightful area of land named Kaṇṇakatthala;
because it was given as a sanctuary for deer, it was called a "deer park" (migadāya), and [he was staying] in that deer park at Kaṇṇakatthala.
"By some business or other" means not by anything else, but specifically by the business mentioned in the immediately preceding sutta.
"The sisters Soma and Sakulā" refers to these two sisters who were the king’s consorts. "Bringing food" means bringing food to the place where it is served;
for at the king’s dining place, all the female attendants go to serve the king, taking spoons and other utensils.
They likewise departed in that same manner.
But why, Great King, did he speak thus? It was for the sake of clearing the king of reproach. For the assembly might have thought:
"This king, even as he was coming, announced the message of the women; we [acted] according to our own nature."
"We thought he had come to see the Blessed One, but this man has come bearing a message from women;
I suspect he is a slave to women, for previously too he came for this very reason. However, when questioned, he will explain the reason for his own arrival;
thus, in order to free him from this reproach, he spoke as follows.

378. He said, "It has been well-spoken. "One who can see all at once" means that there is no one who, by means of a single advertence (*āvajjana*) or a single consciousness (*citta*), can either see or know everything—past, future, and present.
For even if one adverts with the thought, "I shall know all the past by means of a single consciousness," it is impossible to know all the past.
It knows only a single part. However, with that entire mind, one does not know the future and the present in their entirety.
This same method applies to the others. Thus, this question has been explained by way of a single consciousness.

"Having the nature of a cause" means having the intrinsic nature of a cause, being of the class of a cause. "Together with the nature of a cause" means together with the class of a cause. "I am concerned with the future life, venerable sir," refers to the quality of the future life.
“I ask you, venerable sir.
(379) Regarding the phrase “these five,” in this sutta the five factors of striving (*padhāniyaṅga*) are explained as being mixed with the supramundane.
However, when it was asked, “Venerable sir, what do you prefer? the Elder Cūḷa Samudda, who dwelt in the Kaṭhina Aṅgaṇa, replied: “For me—”
"Only supramundane [states] are intended," he said. "Difference in striving" means diversity of striving.

For the striving of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is of one kind, that of a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) is another, that of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) is another, that of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is another, that of an *arahant* is another, that of the eighty great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*) is another, and that of the two chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*) is another.

The striving of the Paccekabuddhas is of one kind; the striving of the Omniscient Buddhas is of another kind. The striving of an ordinary person does not reach the level of the striving of a stream-enterer...
[and so on] ...the striving of a Paccekabuddha does not reach the level of the striving of an Omniscient Buddha.
It was with reference to this meaning that he said, "I speak of a difference in striving. "They might go for the purpose of being tamed" means:
The meaning is that they would undergo that treatment which is seen as a procedure for the tusks—namely, not making them crooked, not cutting them off, and not shortening the tip.
"The ground of the tusks" means the ground to be traversed by the tusks.

Regarding the terms "lacking faith" (*assaddha*) and so forth, all four—the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*)—are called "lacking faith. For the worldling [is inferior] to the stream-enterer.

One who has not attained faith is faithless; a stream-enterer is faithless in relation to a once-returner, a once-returner in relation to a non-returner, and a non-returner is faithless in relation to an arahant because he has not attained their faith.
Since affliction arises even for an arahant, all five are said to be "subject to much affliction.
However, for a noble disciple, there is no such thing as being "crafty" or "deceitful. For this very reason, the Elder said: "The five..."
"I prefer the view that the factors of exertion (padhāniyaṅga) are described as supramundane," he said.

However, in the *Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta*, where it says, "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you about three kinds of wild colts and three kinds of wild men," the name "enlightenment" (sambodhi) occurs even in reference to a noble disciple;
therefore, it is stated that [the factors] are described there as being mixed with the supramundane.
But the worldling who has not yet attained the energy of the stream-entry path—[and so on]...
up to—the non-returner who has not yet attained the energy of the path to arahantship, is likewise fourfold, being either lazy or faithless; the same applies to one who lacks wisdom.
Herein, the correlation with the simile should be understood as follows: for one who is devoid of exertion toward the paths is like the untamed elephant and the others.
The person is like a tamed elephant and so forth who possesses the exertion of the path.

Just as untamed elephants and the like cannot go to the state of being tamed or reach the ground of taming without first making a firm resolve, without breaking through [resistance], and without casting off the yoke,
even so, one devoid of the exertion of the path cannot reach what is to be reached or accomplish what is to be accomplished by one possessing the exertion of the path.

It is not able to produce a quality (*guṇa*). However, just as tusked elephants and the like are able to proceed with their tusks or reach the stage of tusks without making a false step, without breaking off, and without failing in their exertion, even so, one who exerts themselves on the path and possesses such exertion on the path is able to reach what is to be reached and to produce the quality that is to be produced. This...
It is said: “One who possesses the striving for the path of stream-entry, by virtue of possessing the striving for the path of stream-entry,

is able to reach the stage that has been attained and to produce the qualities that ought to be produced… [and so on] … one who possesses the striving for the path of arahantship, by virtue of possessing the striving for the path of arahantship,
is able to reach the stage that has been attained and to produce the qualities that ought to be produced.”
380. "Right efforts" (*sammappadhāna*) means right efforts by way of the effort of the path. "I do not say there is any difference whatsoever between liberation and liberation":

the meaning is that I do not say there is any difference to be stated regarding the liberation of fruition (*phalavimutti*) of one [stream-enterer] compared to the liberation of fruition of the other.
"By light, or in light" (*acciyā vā accimhi*): "by light" means in light.
The same method applies to the other two lines as well; for here, this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.
When [the Buddha asks], "What do you think, Great King?"—that is, "Great King, what do you think?"—[if the king replies], "There are gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings;

there are gods of the Thirty-three... [and so on]... there are gods who wield power over the creations of others; there are gods even higher than those," [the Buddha would say]: "Do you not thus know the existence of these gods?"

"By what means do you speak thus? [The Elder replied: "From that, I know their existence; but as for whether they come to the human world or not, asking this, he said, 'If so, venerable sir,' and so forth.
"With affliction" (*sabyābajjha*) means accompanied by suffering—that is, those whose mental suffering has not been abandoned through its complete eradication.
"Comers" (*āgantāro*) means those who come by way of rebirth. "Without affliction" (*abyābajjha*) means those whose suffering has been eradicated.
"Anāgantā" means one who does not return by way of rebirth.

"Pahoti" means he is able. For a king, even if someone is meritorious and endowed with gain and honor, if the king acts in such a way that no one approaches him, he is able to displace that person from that position. Even if that person lacks merit, [he can do so for] the entire village...
If one who has gone for alms does not obtain enough to sustain himself, by acting in such a way that he becomes endowed with gain and honor, one is able to cause him to be removed from that position.

Even one who possesses the holy life, by associating him with women and causing the destruction of his virtue, or by forcibly disrobing him, one is able to cause him to be removed from that position. And even one who lacks the holy life...
Having cast a minister endowed with all sensual pleasures into prison and not even allowing him to see the faces of women, one is said to "deprive him of that position.
