Furthermore, regarding the kingdom, whatever one desires, one causes that person to be banished.

"Not even sufficient for a mere look" means that, within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), gods who are subject to affliction (*sabyābajjha*) [cannot even see] those gods who are free from affliction (*abyābajjha*) by means of visual consciousness.

They are not capable [of seeing]. Why? Because for an Arahant, there is no occasion for such a state. However, in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), they stand and sit within a single celestial mansion; thus, they are capable of seeing by means of visual consciousness.

Yet, they are unable to see, observe, or penetrate the characteristic that has been seen, observed, and penetrated by these [beings], because [the Arahant] possesses the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu).
"They are not able to see [them], nor even the higher deities by means of visual consciousness.
(382) "Who is this, venerable sir?"—the King asks as if he did not know, although he knows the Elder. Why?
Out of a desire to offer praise. "Ānandarūpa" means having the nature of joy. The "Brahma-question" should also be understood according to the method already stated.
"Now, a certain man..."—this story was indeed told by Viṭaṭūbha himself. Thinking, "It was told by you! It was told by you!
they became angry and, having each raised their own troops right there in that very place, might have engaged in a quarrel;
therefore, for the sake of preventing this, that royal official spoke thus. The rest is clear everywhere.
This teaching, however, is concluded by way of the person who is to be guided (*neyya-puggala*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
5. The Chapter on Brahmins. 1.
Commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta.

383. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Brahmāyu Sutta. In that context, "together with a great community of bhikkhus" means "great" both in terms of greatness of virtue and in terms of greatness of number.

For that community of bhikkhus was great in virtue because it was endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires, and it was also great in number because it consisted of five hundred members. Of the bhikkhus...
"By the Saṅgha" means by the community of monks, that is, by the group of ascetics designated as a "Saṅgha" due to its commonality of view and virtue;
this is the meaning. "Together with" (*saddhim*) means in one place. "With about five hundred monks": those of whom five is the measure (*matta*) are "about five" (*pañcamattāni*).
"Measure" (*matta*) is said to mean a limit; therefore, just as when it is said "one who knows the measure in food," it means one who knows the measure in food.

The meaning is "he knows the measure"; likewise here, the meaning should be understood as "about five" (pañcamatta) means "five as a measure" regarding those hundreds of bhikkhus. "Hundreds of bhikkhus" (bhikkhusatāni) means [the word] bhikkhusatāni. "By those about five hundred bhikkhus" (tehi pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi).

"One who is one hundred and twenty years old" (vīsasatavassiko) means one who is over a hundred years old by twenty. "Of the three Vedas" (tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ) refers to the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda.

One who has gone to the further shore by means of the practice of striking with the lips (*oṭṭhapahata*) is a "pāragū" (one who has reached the further shore). Regarding the term *sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ*: together with the *nighaṇḍu* and the *keṭubha*.

*Nighaṇḍu* refers to a treatise that elucidates synonyms for names, trees, and so forth. *Keṭubha* refers to a treatise consisting of various rules of composition for poets, intended as an aid to them.
Together with the *akkharappabheda* (analysis of syllables) are the *sakkharappabhedānaṃ* (those possessing the analysis of syllables). *Akkharappabheda* is...

"Training and grammar. Regarding the phrase "with history as the fifth": having made the *Atharvaveda* the fourth, those for whom history—consisting of ancient tales associated with such expressions as "Thus it was, thus it was"—is the fifth are called "those for whom history is the fifth" (*itihāsapañcamā*);
[he studies] their [scriptures], those for whom history is the fifth. He studies both the words and the remainder, which is grammar (*byākaraṇa*).
And he who expounds [this] is a master of grammar. *Lokāyata* refers to the science of caviling debate (*vitaṇḍavāda*).
The *Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa* is a treatise twelve thousand units in length that elucidates the characteristics of Great Beings such as the Buddhas;
therein were the so-called "Buddha-mantras" consisting of sixteen thousand verses, by means of which—“by this characteristic... [and so forth].
It is known that by being endowed with this [quality] one is called a Buddha; by this, one is called a Paccekabuddha;

by this, the two Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, the Mother of the Buddha, the Father of the Buddha, the Chief Attendant, the Chief Female Attendant, and the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) [are so designated].
Thus is the distinction understood. "Without deficiency" means not lacking in these worldly arts and the marks of a Great Man, but rather making them complete.
"It does not exist" is what is meant. One who is "weak" (avaya) is one who is unable to sustain those [teachings] either in meaning or in text.
Regarding such passages as "He heard," etc., whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the Sāleyyaka Sutta. 384.
"This one, dear," he said thus after addressing the young man, being himself unable to go because of his old age. Furthermore—
This brahmin thought: "In this world, many people wander about taking the name of one who has risen to fame, saying, 'I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha.
Therefore, it is not proper for me to approach him based on mere hearsay alone.
For when approaching someone, even the departure may be burdensome, and misfortune may arise. What if I were to send my own pupil..."
"Having sent him, I shall approach him only after knowing whether he is a Buddha or not"—it was for this reason that he addressed the young man, saying, "This one, dear sir," and so forth.
"Tassa bhavato" means "of that venerable one. "Tathā santameva" means "while he is truly such [a person].
For this is the accusative case used in the sense of describing a state of being (*itthambhūta-ākhyāna*). As for the phrase "But how, sir, do I say...": here, "how" (*kathaṃ*)—
"But, sir, please explain to me how that Master Gotama may be known, in such a way that he can be known;
this is the meaning. Or, 'yathā' (how) is merely a particle. 'Kathaṃ' (how) is a question regarding manner:
the meaning is, 'In what manner shall I know the Master Gotama?'"

When this was said, his preceptor replied to him: "My dear son, do you say that while standing on the earth you do not see the earth, or that while standing in the radiance of the moon and sun you do not see the moon and sun?

Having spoken these words, he spoke the passage beginning with "But they have come, my dear," in order to demonstrate the manner of his knowledge. In that context, "in the mantras" means in the Vedas. "The Tathāgata... [and so forth].

It is said that, thinking "he will arise," the gods of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) inserted the marks of a Great Man into the Vedas beforehand and, in the guise of brahmins, taught the Vedas, saying, "These are called the Buddha-mantras.
[They did this] thinking, "By following them, beings of great power will come to know the Tathāgata.
For that reason, the marks of a Great Man appear in the Vedas from of old. However, after he has attained final Nibbāna...
As the Tathāgata gradually passed away, they disappeared; therefore, they do not exist at present.

"Of the Great Man" (mahāpurisassa) means of that person who is great through qualities such as his vow, the knowledge of undertaking that vow, and his compassion. "Only two destinations" (dve eva gatiyo) means only two final ends.

Now, although this word *gati* occurs in the sense of a division of existence—as in "Sāriputta, there are these five destinations"—and in the sense of a dwelling place—as in "the forest is the destination of wild animals"—it is used here in the sense of a final end.
In such passages as “thus possessing supreme range,” it refers to wisdom;
in such passages as “that which has gone to its destination,” it refers to the state of being spread out; but here it should be understood as referring to the ultimate goal (niṭṭhā).

In that regard, although one does not become a Buddha merely by possessing those qualities by which one becomes a king, they are nevertheless said to be the very same because of their commonality of birth. Therefore it was said: “of one who is possessed of these.”
"If he dwells in a house" means: if he lives in a household, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī*).

He is a "king" (*rājā*) because he gladdens (*rañjati*) the world through four wonderful qualities and the bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*). He causes the wheel-treasure to turn; he causes it to turn by means of the four wheels of prosperity, and through them he governs others.
Furthermore, he is so called because in him there is the turning of the wheels of postures for the benefit of others.

A wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī*). Here, "king" (*rājā*) is the general term, while "wheel-turner" (*cakkavattī*) is the specific qualification. One who acts according to the Dhamma is "righteous" (*dhammiko*); the meaning is that he conducts himself by way of justice and equity.

Having obtained the kingdom through the Dhamma, he has become a king; thus, he is a "Dhamma-king" (*dhammarājā*). Alternatively, he is righteous by virtue of performing deeds for the welfare of others, and a Dhamma-king by virtue of performing deeds for his own welfare.
One who is sovereign over the four quarters is "lord of the four quarters" (*cāturanto*), [referring to the realm] bounded by the four oceans.
The meaning is: he is the lord of the earth adorned with the four lights.
He is a conqueror (*vijitāvī*) because he has triumphed over internal adversaries such as anger and over all kings externally.

"Having attained stability in his realm" means he has reached a state of steadiness and permanence in his kingdom such that it cannot be shaken by anyone; or else, the realm has attained stability under him, being free from anxiety.
“Delighting in his own work, unshakable, and imperturbable” means he has attained the steadiness of the realm. “Seyyathidaṃ” is a particle;
its meaning is, “What are those [things]? Regarding the phrases beginning with “the wheel-treasure” (*cakkaratana*), it is a wheel and, in the sense of producing delight, it is a treasure;
thus, it is the “wheel-treasure. This same method applies everywhere.
Among these treasures, however, this wheel-turning monarch conquers what is unconquered by means of the wheel-treasure;

he traverses at his pleasure the conquered realm by means of the elephant and horse treasures; he protects the conquered territory by means of the counselor-treasure; and he enjoys the pleasure of luxury by means of the remaining [seven] treasures.

Furthermore, the first [treasure] provides him with the application of energy, while the elephant, horse, and householder treasures provide him with the application of lordship, and the last [the counselor-treasure] provides him with the application of wisdom.

The application of the power of counsel is perfectly fulfilled; this is the fruit of the threefold application of power through the gems of women and jewels. He experiences the pleasure of wealth through the gems of women and jewels, and the pleasure of sovereignty through the remaining ones.
Specifically, for him, the first three succeed through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa*);

the middle ones through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*); and the final one through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
This should be understood. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the teaching on the Ratana Sutta in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta.
Furthermore, a commentary on these treasures, together with the sequence of their arising, will follow in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta.
"More than a thousand" means exceeding one thousand. "Brave" means those of a fearless nature. "Heroic in form" means having bodies like those of the sons of gods.
Thus, first of all, some explain it; however, this is the true nature [of the term]: "Vīra" refers to supreme heroes.

The "vīraṅga" (hero-limb) is the limb of heroes; what is meant is that it is the cause of heroism, namely vigor (*vīriya*). Those whose form (*rūpa*) consists of the "vīraṅga" are called "vīraṅgarūpā";
what is meant is that they are as if their bodies were made of vigor. "Crushers of enemy armies" means that even if [the enemy] should stand facing them...
The intention is that he is capable of crushing the enemy army. "By means of the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with "No living being shall be killed.
Regarding the phrase "He is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, whose veil is removed from the world":

here, in this world of defilement-darkness covered by the seven veils—namely, lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, ignorance, and misconduct—he has removed those veils, and thus light has arisen all around him.

"Having sacrificed, he stands"—this refers to one whose covering is removed (*vivaṭṭacchado*). In this regard, it should be understood that by the first word, his worthiness of worship is expressed; by the second, the reason for that, namely that he is a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*); and by the third, the state of having the covering removed, which is the cause of his Buddhahood, is stated.

Alternatively, *vivaṭṭacchado* means "one who has turned away from the cycle and is free from covering," that is to say, one who is devoid of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and devoid of concealment (*chadana*).

Thus, by that [second confidence], he is an *arhat* due to the absence of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) due to the absence of concealment (*chadana*).

In this way, two causes have been stated for the first two terms. Furthermore, here the first accomplishment is achieved by the second confidence, the second accomplishment by the first, and the third accomplishment by the third and fourth.
The first is the Eye of Dhamma (*dhammacakkhu*), and the second is the Buddha-Eye (*buddhacakkhu*).
It should also be understood that he accomplishes the third [eye], the all-seeing eye (*samantacakkhu*). By saying, "You are a receiver of mantras," he produces in him a sense of courage.

385. He too, through that discourse of the teacher, being free from delusion regarding the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and perceiving the Buddha-mantras as if they had become a single radiance, said, "Sir, so be it.
The meaning of this is: "Sir, I shall do exactly as you tell me."
"Samannesī" means he sought; counting them one by two, he gathered them together. "Addasā kho" (he saw): how did he see?
For no one is able to seek out the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of Buddhas when they are sitting or lying down, but they are able to do so when they are standing or walking.
Therefore, having seen him who had come for the purpose of seeking the marks, the Buddhas...
"Having risen from their seats, they stand or engage in walking meditation. Thus he saw him engaged in postures corresponding to the display of the marks.
"For the most part" means generally; the sense is that he saw many [marks] and did not see few.
Then, for the purpose of illustrating those which he did not see, it is said: "except for two. He doubts: "O, alas!"... [text continues].
He generates the aspiration: "May I see him. He is perplexed (*vicikicchati*): searching here and there for those [marks], he is distressed and unable to see them.
He does not resolve (*nādhimuccati*): through that perplexity, he does not reach a definitive conclusion. He does not become confident (*na sampasīdati*):
because of that, he does not attain serene confidence in the Blessed One, thinking, "This one possesses the complete marks. Through doubt (*kaṅkhāya*)...
Or, "weak" refers to doubt (vimati); "middling" refers to perplexity (vicikicchā); and "strong" refers to the state of non-resolution.
Through these three factors, there is a state of turbidity in the mind due to lack of confidence. "Enveloped in a sheath" means covered by the sheath of the prepuce.
"The private parts" refers to the organ of generation. For the Blessed One’s private parts were like those of an elephant, enveloped in a sheath and golden-hued.

It was like the interior of a lotus; because it was covered by his garment, and because he did not perceive its great extent with his tongue placed inside his mouth, he remained doubtful and perplexed regarding those two marks.
Then the Blessed One thought: "If I do not [reveal] these two marks to him..."
"I shall show him, so that he will become free from doubt. If there were doubt in him, his teacher would also not be free from doubt;
then he would not come to see me, and not coming, he would not hear the Dhamma.
Not hearing the Dhamma, he would not realize the three fruits of asceticism. But when he is free from doubt, his teacher—
"Free from doubt, having approached me and heard the Dhamma, he will realize the three fruits of asceticism.
It was for this very purpose that the perfections were fulfilled by me. I shall show him those marks.
He performed such a feat of supernormal power. Of what nature was it? What more need be said here? This has been stated by the Elder Nāgasena himself when questioned by King Milinda:
He said: "It was difficult, venerable Nāgasena, that was performed by the Blessed One. "What was it, Great King?

"It was, venerable sir, that he showed the place where a sense of shame was produced in the great multitude; and he showed it to the Brahmin Brahmāyu, to his pupil Uttara, to the sixteen Brahmins who were pupils of Bāvari, and to the three hundred young men who were pupils of the Brahmin Sela. "No, Great King."
"The Blessed One shows what is hidden; the Blessed One shows a shadow.

Having fashioned it through psychic power (*iddhi*), he showed the Great King merely a shadow-form, clothed in an undergarment, girt with a waist-band, and draped in a robe. "If a shadow is seen, is it not indeed seen?
'Wait, Great King! A being who awakens upon seeing the heart-form (*hadayarūpa*)..."
"The Perfectly Enlightened One would have extracted his heart-flesh and shown it. "Well said, venerable Nāgasena! "Having stretched out" means having drawn forth.
"He rubbed" means he stroked it, making it like a stiff needle. By that action, its softness was demonstrated;
by the rubbing of the ear-cavities, its length; and by the rubbing of the nostril-cavities, its thinness.
It should be understood that the broadness [of the face] is indicated by the covering of the forehead.
Regarding the phrases "both ear-canals," and so forth: here, there is no dirt or grime in the ear-canals of the Buddhas;
they are like silver tubes that have been washed and set in place. Likewise with the nostrils; for they too are like well-polished golden tubes.
They were like jeweled tubes. Therefore, having extended his tongue and made it like a stiff needle, he brought it to the edge of his mouth;
inserting it into the right ear canal, he withdrew it and inserted it into the left ear canal.
Withdrawing it from there, he inserted it into the right nostril, and withdrawing it from there, he inserted it into the left nostril.

Then, having drawn it out and displaying its broadness, he covered his entire forehead with his tongue—which was like a flash of lightning, like a red cloud, like a half-moon, and like a golden plate—using a fold of red woolen cloth. Why did he think, "What if I were to..."?
[He thought this because] "I went there to examine the marks of a Great Man, and they have been seen."
"Those, dear one, are the marks of a Great Man. When asked by my teacher thus, I will be able to say, "Yes, teacher.
But if he asks me, "What is the performance and non-performance of these like? I shall not be able to say that;
and if I say, "I do not know," the teacher will become angry, thinking, "Did I not teach you all of this so that you might know it?"
“Since you have been sent, why have you come without knowing [the reason]? Thinking, “What if I were to follow him,” he pursued him.

The Blessed One, having set aside these four places—the bathing place, the place for washing the face, the place for attending to the body, and the place where he sat surrounded by the wives of kings, royal ministers, and others—remained in all other locations.
He even allowed him as much space as a single fragrant chamber.

As time passed, people said: "It is said that this young Brahmin Uttara, the pupil of the Brahmin Brahmāyu, is wandering about testing whether the Tathāgata is truly a Buddha or not; he is known as 'the tester of a Buddha'."
He became well-known. In whatever place the Buddhas dwell, five duties are invariably performed, as has already been shown below.

There, after the meal, while the Blessed One sat upon the decorated Dharma-throne and, taking up his ivory-inlaid fan, was teaching the Dharma to the great multitude, Uttara also sat down not far away.
At the conclusion of the discourse on the Dhamma, the faithful people invited the Blessed One for the following day’s meal.
They also approached the young brahmin and said to him: “Dear son, we have invited the Blessed One;
you too should come with the Blessed One and partake of a meal at our house. On the following day, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, [went there].
When he enters the village, Uttara follows step by step, keeping him in sight at every stride.
When they enter a family home, he sits watching everything from the moment the water for the guest-offering is received until the meal is finished.
At the conclusion of the meal, when the Tathāgata has placed his bowl on the ground and is seated, [Uttara watches] the young man’s breakfast meal.

They prepare the meal. Having eaten while sitting to one side, he returns again, stands before the Teacher, and after hearing the expression of gratitude for the meal (*bhattānumodanā*), he goes to the monastery together with the Blessed One.
There, the Blessed One sits in the fragrant pavilion (*gandhamaṇḍalamāḷa*), summoning the monks once their meal is finished.
When the bhikkhus had finished their meal, put away their bowls and robes, and returned to pay homage, the Blessed One would enter the fragrant chamber once the time had been announced;

the young brahmin also went along with the Blessed One. Standing at the entrance of the fragrant chamber, the Blessed One would instruct the Saṅgha of bhikkhus who had arrived surrounding him, and having dismissed them, he would enter the fragrant chamber.
The young man also entered. The Blessed One sat for a short while on a small couch, and the young man sat nearby, watching him.
After sitting for a moment, the Blessed One indicated that it was time to retire;
thinking, "It will now be time for Master Gotama to go into his dwelling," the young man closed the door of the fragrant chamber and departed to one side.

He sits down. People, having given alms before the meal and finished their breakfast, having undertaken the precepts of the Uposatha, with their upper robes purified and garlands and perfumes in hand, come to the monastery thinking, "We shall hear the Dhamma"; it becomes like the camp of a wheel-turning monarch.
The Blessed One, having spent a short time in the lion’s posture, arose and, having delimited the morning period, [entered] meditative attainment.

He enters [meditation]. Emerging from that attainment and perceiving that the great multitude had arrived, he departed from the fragrant chamber and, surrounded by the great multitude, went to the perfumed pavilion.
Seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared there, he taught the Dhamma to the assembly.
The young brahmin, sitting not far away, thought: "What now will the ascetic Gotama say to the assembly regarding his attachment to the household life?"
“Does he teach the Dhamma while exalting or disparaging, or not? Thus he scrutinized every syllable and every word.
Without delivering such a discourse, the Blessed One, perceiving the time, brought his teaching to a conclusion.
Scrutinizing in this manner for seven months, the young brahmin wandered about alone until he reached the Blessed One’s doors of body and so forth.
He did not see even the slightest lapse. This is not surprising, that a human youth should not have seen one who had become a Buddha;

for when he was still a Bodhisatta, Māra the son of a deity—though a non-human being—followed him for six years on the ground of striving without seeing even a single thought connected with household life, and having followed him for one year after he had become a Buddha, saw nothing at all.
“For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step, yet I could find no opening in the mindful Sambuddha.
Having spoken these initial verses, he departed. Then the young man thought: “I have followed the venerable Gotama for seven months...”

As I followed him, I did not see any fault in him. Even if I were to follow him for another seven months, or seven years, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, I would still not see any fault in him.
Moreover, his teacher is now old; it is impossible to know the "security from bondage" [the goal of yoga]. It is by the very nature and qualities of the ascetic Gotama himself—
"Having declared the state of Buddhahood, I shall inform my teacher," he said. Having taken leave of the Blessed One and paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he departed.
Upon arriving in the presence of his teacher, he was asked: "Dear Uttara, is it true that such a report has arisen concerning the venerable Gotama?
He replied: "Teacher, what are you saying? The world-system is too narrow; the summit of existence..."
"Indeed, he is exceedingly lowly; for the multitude of virtues of that venerable Gotama is as boundless as space.

It is exactly so, sir, with that venerable Gotama," and having said these things, he described the thirty-two marks of a Great Man in their proper order as he had seen them, and then he explained his conduct and behavior.
Thus it is said: "Then the young brahmin Uttara... [etc.]..."
“Such and such is Master Gotama, and even more than that.

386. Therein, “with well-placed feet” means that when others place their feet on the ground, either the ball of the foot, the heel, or the side touches first, or else the middle is hollow; but when he lifts [his feet], it is not so.
In the case of those such as the one with level feet, only a single part of the sole rises first; it is not so for him.
Rather, his entire foot-sole touches the ground and rises from the ground all at once, like the surface of a golden sandal.
Therefore, they say: "That venerable Gotama has well-placed feet."

In this regard, concerning the Blessed One’s well-placed feet: even if the Blessed One extends his foot with the thought, "I shall step upon a hell many hundreds of fathoms deep," at that very moment the sunken place rises up like a blacksmith's bellows filled with wind until it becomes level with the earth;
and even a raised place sinks down as he steps upon it. This occurs when he extends his foot thinking, "I shall step far away."
Even a mountain as large as Mount Sineru bends down like a steamed bamboo sprout and approaches near his feet.
For instance, when he performed the Twin Miracle and extended his foot with the thought, "I shall step upon Mount Yugandhara," the mountain bent down and came near his foot;
having stepped upon it, he [then] stepped with his second foot onto the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
He stepped [upon it]. Indeed, a place marked by the Wheel-Treasure cannot become uneven.
Whether it be a stump, a thorn, gravel or pebbles, excrement or urine, or even saliva, mucus, and the like, they vanish before [his foot] reaches them and sink right there into the earth.
This is because of the power of the Tathāgata’s virtue and the power of his wisdom.
Through the splendor of the Dhamma and by the power of the ten perfections (pāramī), this great earth becomes level, soft, and strewn with flowers.
Therein, the Tathāgata places his foot evenly and lifts it evenly; he touches the ground with the entire surface of both soles.
"Wheels" refers to the two wheels on the two feet. Their spokes, rim, and hub are already described in the Discourse (pāḷi).
Regarding the phrase "perfect in all their aspects," this distinction should be understood as follows:
it is said that in the center of those wheels, a hub (*nābhi*) is visible; a circular rim (*vaṭṭalekhā*) demarcated by the hub is visible;

a band encircling the face of the hub is visible; the opening of the axle-hole (*panāḷimukha*) is visible; spokes (*ara*) are visible; circular rims on the spokes are visible; and the outer felloe (*nemī*) is visible.
The jewel on the wheel-rim is seen. This much, for now, is what has actually come down in the text (*pāḷi*).
However, the section on the many [auspicious signs] has not yet been included; it should be understood as follows:

a spear, a glory (*siri*), a calf, a *nandi* [lotus], a *sovattika* [garland], an ear-ornament (*vaṭaṃsaka*), a *vaḍḍhamānaka* [vase], a pair of fish, a throne (*bhaddapīṭha*), a hook (*aṅkusa*), a javelin (*tomara*), a palace (*pāsāda*), and an archway (*toraṇa*).
A white parasol, a sword, a palm-leaf fan, a peacock-feather fan, a yak-tail fan, a turban, an alms-bowl, a jewel, a garland of flowers,
a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white lotus, a pink lotus, a red lotus, a full water-jar, a full bowl, the ocean, the world-system, the Himālaya mountains,
Sineru, the moon and sun, the constellations, the four great continents, and two thousand minor islands.
Even including the retinue of a wheel-turning monarch, everything is merely an attendant feature of the wheel-mark itself.
"Long heels" means having long heels; the meaning is that the heels are full.
For while the forefeet of others are long such that the shank rests upon the top of the heel, as if the heel had been cut off and set aside, it is not so [in this case].
Of the Tathāgata. Of the Tathāgata, however, among the four parts [of the foot], two parts constitute the forefoot;
in the third part the shank is established; and in the fourth part the heel is like a ball on a red blanket, as if it had been turned on a lathe with an awl.
"Long-fingered" means that while for others some fingers are long and some are short, it is not so for the Tathāgata.
For the Tathāgata, however, the fingers and toes of his hands and feet are long like those of a monkey;
they are thick at the base and gradually taper toward the tips, becoming slender like a haritāla-stick rolled in resin-oil. Therefore, it is said: "long-fingered."

"Soft and tender hands and feet": they are soft like a layer of cotton that has been beaten a hundred times and set aside after being soaked in the cream of ghee; and his hands and feet are always tender, like those of a newborn infant—thus he is "one with soft and tender hands and feet.
"Webbed hands and feet": this means the spaces between the fingers and toes are not bound by skin.

For one such as Phana-hatthaka, being marred by human defects, does not even receive the going forth into homelessness. But in the case of the Tathāgata, the four fingers of each hand and the five fingers of each foot [are thus joined].
They are of equal measure; because they are of equal measure, the mark of the *yava* stands having pierced through one another.
Then his hands and feet are like latticed windows constructed by a skilled carpenter. Therefore it is said: "with webbed hands and feet" (*jālahatthapādo*).
Because his ankles are positioned high, he has elevated feet (*ussaṅkhapādo*). For in others, the back of the foot—
Their ankles are positioned such that their feet become stiff as if bound by pins; they cannot turn them at will, and when walking, the soles of their feet do not appear.
But for the Tathāgata, having ascended [the body], his ankles are established above [the knees].
Therefore, from the navel upward, his upper body is like a golden statue placed upon a ship.
He is motionless; only his lower body moves. His feet turn with ease.
When people stand in front, behind, or at both sides and look, his soles are visible, not only from behind as is the case with elephants.
"Enijaṅgha" means having shanks like those of the eni deer, with shanks full of flesh, not with the mass of flesh of the calves bound together on one side.
The meaning is that he is endowed with shanks that are well-rounded, resembling the interior of a rice husk, and encircled by flesh that is evenly distributed all around.
"Anonamanto" means not bending;
by this, his state of being neither hunchbacked nor dwarfed is indicated. For the rest of people are hunchbacked.
Or there are those who are dwarfish; the upper body of the hunchbacked is incomplete, and the lower body of the dwarfish is incomplete.
Because their bodies are incomplete, they are unable to rub their knees without bending over. But the Tathāgata, because both parts of his body are complete, is able to do so.

He is one whose private parts (*vatthaguyha*) are hidden and concealed within a sheath (*kosa*), like that of a bull or an elephant; thus he is "one whose private parts are hidden in a sheath" (*kosohitavatthaguyha*). "Private parts" refers to the organ of generation (*aṅgajāta*) which ought to be covered by a cloth.

"Golden-colored" means he resembles a solid golden image that has been rubbed with natural vermilion, polished with leopard fangs, and finished with a coating of red ochre. By this, his body’s density, glossiness, and smoothness are shown.
It is said that "the skin is like gold" for the purpose of showing the color of the complexion; or rather, this is merely a synonym for the preceding term.
"Dust and dirt" means either dust or grime. "Is not smeared" means it does not adhere; it rolls off just like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
However, washing the hands, washing the feet, and so forth, are for the purpose of observing the proper time and for the sake of the donors.
The Buddhas perform these acts for the sake of the fruit of merit, yet they do so even as a matter of formal duty.
For it has been stated that a monk entering a dwelling should enter after washing his feet.
Regarding the term *uddhaggaloma*: at the end of the curling [of the hair], the hairs stand upright as if looking up toward the beauty of the face; thus he is one whose body hairs are *uddhaggaloma*.
"Brahmujugatto" means having a body straight like that of Brahmā; his body is indeed upright, tall, and long.
For most beings, the body bends at three places: the shoulders, the waist, and the knees.
Those who bend at the waist bend backward, while those who bend at the other two places bend forward. Furthermore, some with long bodies are crooked on one side, and some hold their faces upturned.
They move about as if counting the constellations; some, with little flesh and blood, become like spikes and go along quivering.
But the Tathāgata, having risen straight up, becomes long in stature like a golden archway erected in a city of the gods.
Regarding "seven protuberances": the two backs of the hands, the two backs of the feet, the two shoulders, and the head—these seven [are the protuberances].

"He has flesh full in seven places" means he is well-fleshed in seven locations. In others, however, the network of sinews is visible on the backs of their hands and feet, and the ends of the bones are prominent on the shoulders and the trunk;
they thus appear like hungry ghosts (manussapeta), but not so the Tathāgata.
For the Tathāgata, because his flesh is full in those seven places, the backs of his hands and other parts have hidden networks of sinews.
With a torso resembling a golden-colored linga that has been turned and set upright, he appears like a stone statue or a work of painting.
"Sīhapubbaddhakāyo" means one whose body is like the forepart of a lion;
for while the forebody of a lion is fully developed, its hindquarters are not, whereas the Tathāgata’s body is like the forepart of a lion.
The entire body is complete. Like that of a lion, it is not ill-formed or distorted by being bent or raised here and there;
rather, it is long where length is appropriate, and in places requiring shortness, thinness, stoutness, or roundness, it is exactly as required. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, when a desirable result of kamma is manifested, he shines with whatever limbs are long..."
Those limbs by which it is beautiful when long take on a long shape; those limbs by which it is beautiful when short take on a short shape;
those limbs by which it is beautiful when thick take on a thick shape;
those limbs by which it is beautiful when thin take on a thin shape; those limbs by which it is beautiful when round—those [take on a round shape].
"The limbs are formed rounded.

Thus, the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of the Tathāgata is fashioned by a mind of various kinds, a meritorious mind, and adorned with the ten perfections (*pāramī*); even all the skilled craftsmen or those possessed of psychic power (*iddhimanta*) in the world are unable to produce even a likeness of it.
"With full shoulders" (*citantaraṃsa*): the space between the two shoulders is called *antaraṃsa*; he has that which is full and complete, thus [he is so called].
He has shoulders that are level. For in others, that area is depressed, and two distinct depressions at the base of the spine are apparent.
But in the Tathāgata, from the waist upwards, a layer of flesh rises up as far as the shoulders, covering the back like an elevated golden plank and remaining firmly established there.
"Symmetrical like a banyan tree" means being symmetrical like a banyan tree.

Just as a banyan tree—with its trunk and branches—whether it is fifty cubits or a hundred cubits [in height], is of one and the same proportion both in length and in breadth, so too [the Buddha] is of one and the same proportion both in body and in span.
Unlike others whose body is long but the span is short, or whose span is long but the body is short, his proportions are not uneven.
This is the meaning. For that very reason, it is said: “As far as his body extends,” and so forth. In this context, *yāvatako assa* means “as far as his [body] extends.

*Samavaṭṭakkhandho* means one whose trunk is well-rounded. Whereas some—like cranes, herons, or boars—have long necks, crooked necks, or broad necks, and when speaking, a network of veins is visible; such a person is dull-witted.
The sound does not issue forth in that way for him. For the Tathāgata, however, the neck is like a well-rounded golden pillar;
when he speaks, no network of veins is visible, and his voice is as great as the thundering of a cloud.
Regarding the term *rasaggasaggī*: here, they are called *rasaggasā* because they swallow (*gasanti*) the taste; this is a designation for the flavor-carrying channels (*rasaharaṇī*). These...

"Supreme among tastes" means he possesses the excellence of supreme taste (*rasaggasaggi*). For the Tathāgata, seven thousand channels for conveying flavors run upward and are fixed right at the neck.
Even a morsel of food the size of a sesame seed, when placed on the tip of the tongue, permeates the entire body;
it was by this very power that his body was sustained during the Great Struggle (*mahāpadhāna*) even by a single grain of rice or a ladleful of black bean soup.
[It] was so. But because others lack that [quality], the nutritive essence (*ojā*) does not pervade their entire body; therefore, they are subject to many ailments.
This characteristic becomes manifest by way of the outflow-result (*nissandaphala*) known as freedom from illness.
"Having a jaw like that of a lion" means having a jaw like a lion’s. In that regard, it is only the lower jaw of a lion that is fully developed.
Not the upper row. However, for the Tathāgata, like a lion, both rows are complete, resembling the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight.
Regarding the phrases "having forty teeth" and so forth: there are twenty teeth established in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower, making forty.
"He has teeth" means he has forty teeth. For while others, even those with a full set of teeth, have only thirty-two, the Tathāgata has forty.
Furthermore, while some of the teeth of others are high and some low—thus being uneven—the Tathāgata’s teeth are as level as a conch-shell surface cut by an iron blade.
The teeth of other crocodiles are sparse; when they consume fish, meat, and so forth, the gaps between their teeth become filled.
However, the Tathāgata’s teeth are without gaps, like a row of diamonds set upon a golden vine, or like a boundary marked by a measuring cord.
“With very white teeth”: in others, decayed teeth also emerge, whereby some teeth become black or discolored.
The Tathāgata has very white teeth; his teeth possess a radiance that shines even beyond the star Osadhi.
Therefore it is said, “with very white teeth.”
"Having a large tongue": while the tongues of others may be thick, thin, short, stiff, or uneven, the Tathāgata’s is soft, long, broad, and endowed with perfect color.
To dispel the doubts of those who have come seeking this mark, he rolls that tongue—because of its softness—like a stiff needle and [reaches] both nostrils.
Because it is long, it touches both ear canals; because it is broad, it covers the entire forehead up to the hairline.
Thus, by demonstrating its softness, length, and breadth, he dispels doubt.
It is with reference to such a tongue, endowed with these three characteristics, that the term "one with a large tongue" (*pahūtajivho*) is used.
Others have voices that are broken, cracked, or like the cawing of a crow; however, the Tathāgata is endowed with a voice resembling that of Mahābrahmā.
Indeed, because Mahābrahmā’s voice is not obstructed by bile or phlegm, it is pure.
Likewise, the Tathāgata’s voice purifies the basis for the action performed, and because that basis is pure...
The sound arising from the navel onwards arises as pure, endowed with all eight qualities.
"He speaks like a *karavika* bird" means he is a *karavikabhāṇī*; the meaning is that his sweet voice is like the song of a mature *karavika*.
Herein, this is the sweetness of the *karavika*'s song: it is said that when the *karavika* bird eats a ripe mango of sweet flavor...
Having struck with their snouts and tasted the dripping sap, they clap their wings and begin to frolic like intoxicated quadrupeds and other animals as they warble.
Even the quadrupeds intent on foraging cast aside the grass in their mouths to listen to that sound; and wild beasts, while pursuing small game, raise their feet—
They remain without even raising their heads; even the deer that follow them stand still, having cast aside the fear of death;
even the birds soaring in the sky remain with their wings spread out; and even the fish in the water remain listening for that sound, flapping their fins.
Such is the sweet voice of the cuckoo.

Asandhimittā, the queen of Dhammāsoka, asked the Saṅgha: "Venerable sir, is there any sound equal to the sound of the Buddha? "There is the sound of the karavika bird. "Where, venerable sir, is that bird? "In the Himalayas. She said to the king:
"Your Majesty, I wish to see the karavika bird. The king replied, "Having sat upon this cage..."
“Let the karavīka bird come! he said, and released a golden cage. The cage went and stood before one of the karavīkas.
Thinking, “The cage has arrived by the king’s command; it is not possible to go,” he sat right there.
The cage returned and stood directly in front of the king. They were unable to make the karavīka sound. Then the king—
“How is it, my friend, that these are making this sound? he asked. “They are gods, having seen their kinsmen,” he replied.

Then the king had him surrounded by mirrors. Seeing his own reflection, thinking, “My kinsmen have arrived,” he struck with his wing and cried out with a sweet voice, like one blowing a jeweled flute. All the people in the city were as if intoxicated.
They frolicked. Asandhimittā thought: "If even this animal’s voice is so sweet, what must the voice of the Blessed One have been like—He who has attained the glory of omniscient knowledge?

Having thus conceived a surge of joy and not letting that joy fade, she, together with seven hundred attendants, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. So sweet was the cry of the karavika bird.

The voice of the Tathāgata is sweeter than that by a hundredfold and a thousandfold; however, because there is nothing else so sweet in the world as the *karavika* bird, he is described as "one who speaks like the *karavika*.
Regarding the phrase "with deep-blue eyes," it does not mean that his eyes are entirely blue; rather, in those places where they are blue, they are like the *umā* flower, being exceedingly pure.
The eyes are endowed with various colors: in places where yellow is appropriate, they possess a yellow color like the *kaṇikāra* flower;

in places where red is appropriate, they possess a red color like the *bandhujīvaka* flower; in places where white is appropriate, they possess a white color like the star of healing herbs (*osadhitāraka*);
and in places where black is appropriate, they possess a black color like the *addāriṭṭhaka* fruit, all within this golden celestial mansion.
They appear like lion-cages with their jewels uncovered.
Regarding the term *gopakhuma*: here, "eye-lashes" (*pakhuma*) refers to the entire apparatus of the eye.

That [apparatus] has thick constituent elements (*dhātu*) in a black calf, whereas in a red calf it is clear; thus, it is said that his eye-apparatus is like that of a red calf born at that very moment.
This is the meaning. For the eyes of others are incomplete; they possess eyes that protrude like those of elephants, mice, crows, and the like, even if they are deep-set.
But the Tathāgata’s eyes are like polished and cleansed jewel-beads, covered with delicate, smooth, blue-black eyelashes.
*Uṇṇā* means woolly hair (*uṇṇaloma*). "Between the eyebrows" means it grows precisely at the top of the nose, in the middle between the two eyebrows;
having grown upward, it is situated in the center of the forehead. "White" means pure, with the color of the star Osadhī.

"Soft" means like a layer of cotton that has been beaten a hundred times and placed in clarified butter (*sappimaṇḍa*). "Resembling tula-cotton" means equal to the *simbali*-cotton, the *latā*-cotton, or *tūla*-cotton.
This is the simile for its whiteness. When grasped at the tip and pulled upward, it reaches the measure of half an arm;

when released, it curls to the right and stands upright, like a silver bud placed in the middle of a gold plate, or like a stream of milk issuing from a golden vessel, or like the radiance of the dawn.
On his forehead, he shines with a most enchanting splendor like the medicinal star (the moon).
Regarding the term "uṇhīsasīsa" (uṣṇīṣa-head), it is stated based on two reasons: the fullness of the forehead and the fullness of the head.
For from the right ear-lobule of the Tathāgata, a layer of flesh has arisen, covering the entire [head].
Covering the forehead and filling it out, it extends to rest upon the top of the left ear, shining like the turban-bound head of a king.
It is said that having recognized this mark of Bodhisattvas in their final existence, kings began to wear turbans;
this, then, is one interpretation. However, other people have incomplete heads, some having shaven heads.
Some have heads like a fruit, some like a bone, some like a gourd, and some like a mountain slope. But the Tathāgata’s head is perfectly complete, as if turned on a lathe, resembling a water-bubble;
therein, according to the first method, it is called "uṇhīsa-sīsa" because it is like a head wrapped in a turban (*uṇhīsa*). According to the second method, it is like a turban in every respect.
"Parimaṇḍala-sīsa" means a head with a protuberance (uṇhīsa).

Now, these marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) are well-explained when taught by showing these four categories—kamma, the deed corresponding to the mark, the mark itself, and the benefit of the mark—with respect to each individual mark. Therefore:
Having shown these actions and so forth as spoken by the Blessed One in the *Lakkhaṇa-sutta*, they should be explained.
For one unable to determine them according to the sutta itself, they should be understood by the method set forth in the commentary on that very sutta in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
"Indeed, sir, by these [marks], that venerable Gotama is endowed with them, O teacher—by these thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
He is like a golden archway set up in a city of the gods, variegated with jewels;
he is like a *pāricchattaka* tree a hundred leagues high in full bloom amidst the mountains; he is like a *sāla* tree in full flower between the peaks."

Having also illustrated the point that he moves about as if illuminating the world with his own splendor and majesty, like the vault of the sky adorned by a multitude of stars, he said "But as he was going... and so forth, in order to explain his mode of conduct.
(387) Regarding "to the right": for when Buddhas intend to undertake the act of walking—whether standing, sitting, or lying down—they do so by directing their movement toward the right.
The right foot alone is placed forward. This is indeed called the "constant miracle.

"He lifts the foot not too far" means he lifts it thinking, "I shall not place this right foot too far away. For if it were carried too far, the left foot would be dragged along by the right foot as it moved;
thus, the right foot would be unable to go far, remaining instead close to its original position.
If it were to set down [immediately], there would be what is called a "break in the stride.

However, when the right foot is raised by its full measure, the left foot is also raised by that same measure; and when the foot raised by its measure sets down, it sets down at that very same measure.
In this way, the function of the Tathāgata’s right foot is regulated by the left, and the function of the left foot is regulated by the right.
It should be understood as "restrained.
"Not too fast" means he does not walk too quickly, like a bhikkhu going during the day for the sake of a meal at a monastery.
"Not too slow" means he does not walk too slowly, such that one coming from behind finds no space.
"Knee to knee" means [he walks] with the knees together. "He does not raise the thigh" means that, as if walking in deep water, he does not lift the thigh.
"He does not bend it down" means that, like one cutting tree branches or using a staff or hook, he does not cause it to sag backward.
"He does not twist it" means that, like one rubbing the foot against places where it is bound or unbound, he does not make it rigid.
"He performs [the action]. He does not bend" means that, like one playing with a mechanical puppet, he does not move it here and there.
"Only the lower body moves" means that only the lower part of the body stirs, while the upper body remains motionless like a golden statue placed on a ship.
For one looking from a distance cannot discern whether the Buddhas are standing or moving. "By the power of the body" means...
Shaking his arms, with sweat pouring from his body, he does not go by means of bodily strength.
"With his whole body" means that without turning his neck, he looks back in the manner described in the *Rāhulovāda* as the "elephant’s backward glance.
Regarding the phrases "not upwards," and so forth: he does not look upward as if counting the constellations, nor [does he look] for a lost cowrie shell.
Like one seeking a mere *māsaka* coin, he does not look downward; nor does he walk looking here and there like one observing elephants, horses, and the like.
"The distance of a yoke" means that walking with his eyes fixed at a distance of nine spans (*navavidatthi*), he is said to "look the distance of a yoke.
The Blessed One likewise looks only this much, like a well-trained noble steed harnessed to a yoke.
He goes. Therefore, it should not be said that he does not see beyond a distance of a yoke’s length;
for neither a wall, nor a door, nor a thicket, nor a creeper can obstruct him. Rather, through his unobstructed knowledge, many thousands of world-systems become as if a single open space.
"Into the interior of a house" refers to what was stated below in the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta.
From the threshold of the gate to the interior of the house; here, it should be understood as starting from the threshold of the house itself.
The phrase "without [moving] the body," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of showing that he enters by means of his natural mode of deportment alone.
For even when entering the lowly dwellings of poor people, the roof would rise up or the earth would sink down for the Tathāgata; yet the Blessed One—
He walks at his natural pace. "Not too far away" means that if he turns while too far off, he must walk back one or two steps behind before sitting down.
"Not too close" means that if he turns while too close, he must walk forward one or two steps before sitting down.
Therefore, standing at whatever step [is appropriate] in front...
Or, not going forward or backward, one must sit; there he turns over.
"With the hand" means that one does not sit by grasping the seat with the hands, as one suffering from a waist-wind ailment might do.
"Throws down" refers to one who, having done some work and being at play, falls while still standing; or also one who, sitting leaning against a limb on this side, rubs [it].
From the far bank he goes to the near bank, or sitting by the far bank, he returns to the near bank exactly as he went;

all this is called "placing the body on the seat. But the Blessed One, not doing it in that way, sits down slowly, as if hanging a loop in the middle of the seat or placing a tuft of cotton wool there. "Hand-worry" refers to the rim of the bowl.
"Placing drops of water," "fanning with a fan made of leaves," and "tearing or splitting [leaves]" refers to acting without restraint with the hand.
"Fidgeting with the feet" refers to acting without restraint by rubbing the ground with the feet and so forth.
"He does not tremble" means he does not fear. "He does not shake" means he does not sink down. "He does not quiver" means he does not waver. "He does not become agitated" means...
He is not agitated by fear-agitation nor by craving-agitation.
For instance, when someone has come for the sake of a Dhamma talk or similar purpose, and people have stood up after paying homage, he does not worry:
"Will I be able to capture their minds while preaching the Dhamma? Or, if questioned, will I be able to answer? Or, will I be able to offer a blessing after the meal?"
He is agitated by agitation born of fear. Another person is agitated by the agitation of craving, thinking, "Will I receive agreeable rice-gruel?
Will I receive agreeable snacks? Since he has neither of these two, he is not agitated.
"Turning toward seclusion" means having a mind that turns toward seclusion, which is Nibbāna. It may also be called "turning toward seclusion."
"Reading" means being endowed with the practice of seclusion (*vivekavatta*).

The "practice of seclusion" refers to a bhikkhu who, having finished his meal, takes up his primary meditation subject (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*) by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) during the midday rest, sits down cross-legged, and settles.
For one sitting in this manner, the deportment (*iriyāpatha*) becomes tranquil.
Regarding the phrases "he does not lift up the bowl" and so forth: some lift up the bowl as if drawing water from the rim of the bowl's opening;
another lowers it as if placing it on the back of his foot; another takes hold of it by making a firm grip; another shakes it here and there.
Avoiding doing these things, one should take hold of it with both hands, tilt it slightly, and [pour] the water.
"Accepts" means [he receives it]. "Not turning it over" means he does not wash the back of the bowl immediately after turning it over.
"Not too far" means he does not discard it in such a way that it falls far from the seat where he is sitting.
"Not too near" means he does not discard it right at the base of his feet. "Scattering" means throwing it about so that the recipient gets wet; he does not discard it in such a manner.
"Not too little" means that one does not take only a mere handful, like some person of evil desires who, while pretending to have few desires, takes only that much.
"Not too much" means more than what is required for mere sustenance.
"A measure of curry" means that the measure of curry is one-fourth part of the rice. For some person, when the food is pleasing, takes a great deal of food; and when the curry is pleasing...
There is much sauce, yet the Teacher does not take it in that manner. "Not with the sauce" means:
setting aside unpalatable sauce and eating only the rice, or setting aside the rice and eating only the sauce—that is what is meant by "passing the mouthful with the sauce.
The Teacher takes the sauce at intervals; he takes both the rice and the sauce.

They are finished on one side. "Two or three times": for food brought to the Tathāgata’s teeth by the tongue touches the teeth only two or three times, like a paste of fine powder applied to the teeth; therefore he spoke thus.
"It does not remain in the mouth": it turns back and goes down the throat, like a drop of water fallen upon a lotus leaf.
It passes through; therefore, it does not remain. "Experiencing the taste" means he knows tastes such as sweet, bitter, and astringent.
For in the case of the Buddhas, even in their drinking water, divine herbs are always placed; thus, the taste is manifest to them in every instance, yet they have no craving for taste.
“Endowed with eight factors” means endowed with the eight factors stated as “not for sport,” and so forth.
Furthermore, its detailed exposition is given in the *Visuddhimagga*; this was stated in the *Sabbāsava Sutta*. “When his hands have been washed”: what does the Teacher do?
First, he washes the place where the bowl is to be held. Having taken the bowl there, [he places it] upon the fine-meshed hand.
Having sent it forth, he moves it back and forth two times. At this point, like water fallen upon a lotus leaf, it turns back and goes away.

He does not do so "without interest," as some might set their bowl down on a stand and fail to wipe the water from the bowl, remaining indifferent even as dust falls upon it. Nor does he do so "guarding against excess," as...

A certain person sets up a protective boundary that exceeds the proper measure; having eaten, he wipes the water from his bowl and places it between the folds of his robe, then takes hold of the bowl by stepping on it with his stomach. He does not do this.
Nor does he express approval (*anumodana*): for one who, immediately after eating, while children are crying for food and are famished and hungry...
Having partaken [of offerings] among humans, he begins the *anumodanā* (expression of thanks) even before they have arrived;
consequently, some abandon all their tasks and come, while others do not arrive at all, and thus he lets the time pass.

Furthermore, when those who have come from among humans sit after having paid homage for the sake of the *anumodanā*, he does not perform the *anumodanā* but instead asks, "How is Tissa? How is Phussa?"
"How is it with Sumanā? How is it with Tissā? How is it with Phussā? How is it with Sumana? Are you all healthy?
Has the harvest been successful?"—by initiating such individual conversations as these, he lets the time for the expression of thanks pass by.
However, when he acts after discerning the opportunity of the people and at the time they have requested him, he is said not to let the time pass; the Teacher acts in this manner.
"Regarding 'not that meal': he does not criticize it by saying things such as, 'What is this meal? Is it undercooked rice? or 'Is it too soggy? "Regarding 'not another meal':
when one offers a blessing with the thought, 'I shall provide another meal for tomorrow or the day after,' one is looking forward to another meal.
Or again, [he does not look forward to another meal] thinking: "As long as the meal for women is being cooked..."
"I shall offer a blessing; then, at the conclusion of my blessing, she will give me a little even from her own meal," thinking thus, he prolongs the blessing;
this too is called "expecting. The Teacher does not act in this way. Nor is he one who desires to escape:
for some, having turned back, go away, and must be pursued with speed; but the Teacher does not do so.
He goes; he goes even while standing in the midst of the assembly.

"Too high" (*accukkaṭṭha*) means: for one who wraps [the robe] up as far as the jawbone, that is called "too high. For one who wraps it on after lowering it down only as far as the ankles, that is "too high.
Even for one who wraps it up at both sides and goes about with the belly exposed, that too is "too high."
It happens that someone might go along having draped one shoulder and uncovered the breast; even for such a person, this would be an extreme exaggeration. The Teacher does not do any of these things.
"Adhering" means that while the sweat of others causes their robes to stick and adhere, it is not so with the Teacher.

"Slipping away" means that even though the robe is released from the body like a husk, it does not remain detached. "The wind" means that even if the Veramba wind were to arise, it would not be able to move it.
“Devotion to the adornment of the feet” means devotion to the beauty of the feet through rubbing them with brick-dust and so forth.

“Having washed” means having washed one foot with the other. He does not say “neither for his own affliction,” etc., because of the existence of the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of others’ minds;
rather, he speaks by inference after seeing the continuity of the postures. “The Dhamma” refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
“He does not exalt” means that he does not exalt by way of worldly attachment, saying things such as, “What a great official you are! What a great householder!
He does not disparage means that he does not say, “What is this, lay follower? How did you come to know the path to the monastery?
Why do you not come out of fear? For monks do not take anything away by force; do not be afraid,” or, “Why do you live such a miserly life?”
Having said such things as "your name," he does not discourage [the listener] out of attachment rooted in the household life.
"Lucid" (vissaṭṭha) means smooth and unobstructed. "Intelligible" (viññeyya) means that which can be understood, clear; and it is precisely because it is lucid that it is intelligible.
"Melodious" (mañju) means sweet. "Worthy of being heard" (savanīya) means pleasant to the ear; and it is precisely because it is sweet that it is worthy of being heard.
It is "a drop" (*bindu*) because it is condensed. It is "non-diffusive" (*avisārī*) because it does not spread; it is non-diffusive precisely because it is a drop.
It is "deep" (*gambhīra*) because it originates from a deep source. It is "resonant" (*ninnādī*) because it emits a resonance; it is resonant precisely because it is deep.

It makes itself understood as a single, unified assembly, extending even to the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) according to the size of the gathering. "Outside" means even by a finger's breadth beyond the assembly.
It does not go outside. Why? "Lest such a sweet-voiced one be lost for no reason. Thus the Blessed One’s voice moved right over the heads of the assembly.
"Looking back" means that while keeping their hands in *añjali* at their heads and gazing at the Blessed One, they withdrew until they reached the point where his sight was lost.

Having paid homage, they depart. Regarding "not abandoning": for one who, having heard a discourse, rises up and then departs while conversing about other matters such as what has been seen or heard, he is said to abandon his true nature (*sabhāva*).
However, one who departs while still speaking in praise of the discourse on the Dharma heard does not abandon it; thus they set out by way of this state of non-abandonment.
"It was moving" means it was moving like a golden pitcher seven *ratana*s in height suspended by ropes.
"We saw it standing" means we saw it standing like a towering mountain of gold.
"And even more than that"—being unable to describe its qualities in detail, he summarizes the remaining qualities and describes them as if they were a bundle tied with thread.
Having thus made it appear as if he were releasing [the answer], he spoke these words. This is the intended meaning here:

"The qualities not yet mentioned are far more numerous than those already spoken by me. For the qualities of that Blessed One are infinite and immeasurable like the great earth and the great ocean, and they are as vast as space.
390. *Appaṭisaṃvidito* means one whose arrival is unperceived. For when approaching a renunciant at a time such as when [the latter] is engaged in preparing his robes and so forth—
Or, having dressed in one robe, at the time of stretching his limbs, he approaches and must turn back right then and there;

not even a mere greeting arises. But when permission has been granted beforehand, the monk sweeps the daytime resting place, puts on his robes, and sits in a secluded spot; then, as people come and look upon him, by that very sight—
They become confident, hospitality arises, and one obtains either an answer to a question or a discourse on the Dhamma.
Therefore, the wise request an opportunity. And since he was one of them, this thought occurred to him:

"Why did he speak thus without mentioning his own advanced age, saying 'I am old and aged'? For Buddhas are indeed endowed with great compassion; [they take into account] the fact of his being elderly..."
"Knowing this, he will quickly grant me an opportunity"—thus he spoke.
"He made room for me immediately" means that, rising up with speed, he split himself in two and made way.
"Those who are called by the name 'Nārīsamāna'" means those who are to be addressed by the feminine gender-name "Nārīsamāna."
"Nārīsamānasavhayā" means she is to be designated by the feminine gender; he speaks thus out of skill in conventional usage (*vohārakusalatā*).
"Pahūtajivho" means one with a broad tongue. "Ninnāmaye" means "bring this forth.
"Kevalī" means one endowed with all virtues.
394. *Paccabhāsīti*: having been asked all at once, he replied while answering the eight questions.

*Yo vedīti*: he who knows, he who understands; for whom past lives (*pubbenivāsa*) are manifest. *Saggāpāyañca passatīti*: this refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). *Jātikkhayaṃ pattoti*:
one who has reached the destruction of birth, i.e., attained Arahantship. *Abhiññā vositoti*: having fully realized that Arahantship through direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*).
“Vosita” means one who has reached the goal. “Muni” means one endowed with the sagehood of the knowledge of arahantship.
“Visuddha” means pure, bright. “Muttaṃ rāgehi” means freed from the defilements of passion. “Pahīnajātimaraṇa” means one whose birth is abandoned because he has attained the destruction of birth;
by the very abandonment of birth, death is also abandoned. “Brahmacariyassa kevalī” refers to that which is the entirety of the holy life.
The *kevalī* is one who possesses all states; the meaning is that he is endowed with the entire dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the four paths.
"One who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena" means he has reached the further shore through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) of all mundane and supramundane phenomena;

the meaning is that he stands having fully understood all phenomena. Alternatively, "one who has gone to the further shore" refers here to one who has reached the further shore of full understanding (*pariññā-pāragū*) regarding the five aggregates.

The meaning stated is this: he has reached the further shore regarding the abandoning of all defilements, the further shore regarding the four paths through cultivation, the further shore regarding the realization of cessation, and the further shore regarding all meditative attainments.

Furthermore, by the phrase "of all phenomena," he is said to have reached the further shore through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). "The Buddha is called 'one who is such' (*tādī*)" means he has gone to the further shore in six ways.
"He is called a Buddha because he has awakened to the four truths in every aspect.
But have all the questions been answered by this much? Yes, they have been answered.
By the statement "He knows the mind to be purified, released from lusts," the first question—concerning why one is a brahmin because of having warded off evil—is answered.
"Is. By the term "one who has gone beyond" (*pāragū*), because he has gone by means of the knowledges (*veda*), the second question is answered as "one who has attained knowledge" (*vedagū*).

By the terms "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) and so forth, because these three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) exist, the third question is answered as "one possessed of the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjo*).
By the phrase "freed from all lusts" (*muttaṃ rāgehi sabbaso*), because he has emerged from evil states, the fourth question is answered as "one who has crossed over" (*sottio*).
"has attained the destruction of birth"—by this, the fifth question is answered, as it refers specifically to arahantship.
"He has reached the goal" and "he is perfected in the holy life"—by these, the sixth question is answered.
"The sage who has reached the goal through direct knowledge"—by this, the seventh question is answered. "One who has gone beyond all phenomena."
By the phrase "such a one is called a Buddha," the eighth question is answered.
(395) The discourses on giving (*dānakathā*) and so forth have already been explained in detail below in the Sutta. "He followed" (*paccapādī*) means he practiced.
In this Sutta, "Dhamma" refers to the path to Arhatship, and "Anudhamma" refers to the three lower paths and the three [fruits].
And he attained the fruits of recluseship; the meaning is that he obtained them in successive order.
"He did not trouble me with legal matters concerning the Dhamma" means he did not weary me for the sake of the Dhamma, nor did he make me speak about it again and again—this is what is intended.
The rest is clear everywhere. In this context, by the phrase "he attained final Nibbāna," the culmination of the teaching is grasped precisely through the attainment of Arahatship.
The commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. 2.
The commentary on the Sela Sutta.
396. Thus have I heard: this is the Sela Sutta. Therein, the passage beginning with "among the Aṅguttarāpas" has already been explained in detail in the Potaliya Sutta.
"With twelve hundred and fifty" means with twelve hundred and fifty; that is to say, together with one hundred and fifty monks.
Furthermore, all those monks who had assembled at the gathering of disciples were indeed ordained by the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) formula.
They were renunciants whose taints were exhausted. "Keṇiya" was his name; he was a matted-hair ascetic (*jaṭila*).
It is said that he was a wealthy brahmin who, for the sake of protecting his wealth, had undertaken the ascetic life of renunciation.
Having given a gift to the king and received a tract of land, he built a hermitage there and lived there, engaging in trade with five hundred carts and supporting a thousand families.
It is said that, acting as his support, a single palm tree in his hermitage dropped a golden palm fruit every day.
During the day he wore saffron robes and bound his matted hair, but at night he enjoyed the excellence of sensual pleasures.
"With a discourse on the Dhamma" refers to a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the benefits of the drink. For this—

Keṇiya, feeling ashamed to go to see the Blessed One with empty hands, thought, "Even for those who abstain from eating at improper times, a drink is permissible," and having had five hundred jars of well-prepared jujube juice prepared, he set out. As for the fact that he had departed in this manner, it is said:
"Then it occurred to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic: 'What now shall I give to the ascetic...'"
“...should have it brought to Gotama”—this is indeed recorded in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* of the Canon.
As for the second time, why did the Blessed One refuse again and again? It was because of the faith [of the people] resulting from his refusal of the sectarians (*titthiya*).
This is not the reason; there is no such deception on the part of the Buddhas for the sake of material requisites. However, these thirteen and a half...
"Seeing so many hundreds of bhikkhus, he will surely prepare almsfood for just this many; tomorrow Sela himself will go forth together with three hundred men.

It would be improper to send the novices elsewhere while going with these very ones, or to send these ones elsewhere while going with the novices. Or rather, I shall take them all and go; [for] the alms-food..."
"It will not suffice. Then, while the monks are wandering for alms, people will criticize him, saying:
'After inviting the ascetic Gotama so long ago, Keṇiya was unable to provide even enough for his sustenance,' and he himself will feel regret.
But if a refusal is made, [people will say]: 'The ascetic Gotama repeatedly said, "You have great faith in the brahmins..."'"
Thinking, “He is taking the names of the brahmins,” he will likely wish to invite the brahmins as well;
then he will invite the brahmins separately, and they, having been invited by him, will eat after becoming monks.
In this way, his faith will be preserved—thus he refused again and again. By saying, “Even though, sir,” he illustrates this.
—“Sir Gotama, what is gained if I have full confidence in the brahmins? May Master Gotama consent;
I am able to give both to the brahmins and to you.
*Kāyaveyyāvaṭikaṃ* means bodily service. *Maṇḍalamāḷaṃ* means a cloth pavilion.
397. *Āvāha* means the taking of a bride; *vivāha* means the giving away of a bride. "He has been invited by me" means he was invited by me.
Then the brahmin, because his underlying predisposition (*upanissaya*) had reached maturity, upon merely hearing the word "Buddha," felt as if he were sprinkled with the Deathless (*amata*).
Manifesting his serene confidence, he said, "O Keṇiya, do you say 'Buddha'? Keṇiya, explaining it as it truly is, replied, "Buddha."
"O Sela, I say so," he said. Then, in order to confirm this further, he questioned him again, and the other likewise reported it as it was.
(398) Then, perceiving that even in a hundred thousand eons the sound of the word "Buddha" is difficult to encounter, this thought occurred to him:
"Even the mere sound... and so forth. "A row of blue forests" means a line of trees of blue color. "Step by step."
"Step by step" means: for if one places the foot either too close or too far away, a noise arises;
preventing that, he spoke thus. "Like lions wandering alone": a lion living in a herd falls into negligence along with its cubs and others, but one who wanders alone is vigilant.
Thus, demonstrating a state of vigilance, he makes a comparison with a solitary lion.
“May there be no [interruption] for me,” he said while teaching the proper conduct. This is the intended meaning here:
“If you were to insert your own talk into the midst of my discourse without being granted the opportunity to speak, the reproach would arise against me that ‘I was unable to train my pupils.
Therefore, you should converse only after seeing an opening. And yet, “I do not know it.”
The Bodhisatta Vipassī also, accompanied by a retinue of eighty-four thousand elders who had gone forth as monks, practiced the conduct of a Bodhisatta for seven months;
it was just like the time of a Buddha’s appearance. Our Bodhisatta likewise practiced the conduct of a Bodhisatta for six years.
Thus, even though they were endowed with the full physical marks, they were not yet Buddhas. Therefore, the Brahmin...
"But I do not know him," he said.

399. "One with a complete body" means one whose physical frame is complete due to the perfection of the marks and the absence of any missing limbs. "Radiant" means possessing the splendor of a beautiful body.
"Well-born" means perfectly formed through the excellence of height and girth, as well as the excellence of proportions.
“Of beautiful appearance” (*cārudassana*) means that his appearance is captivating to the mind, producing no sense of satiety even for those who gaze upon him for a very long time.
“Golden-hued” (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇa*) means having a complexion similar to gold. “With very white teeth” (*susukkadāṭha*) means having teeth that are perfectly white.
By saying “the marks of a Great Man” (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇā*), he concludes with a different phrasing what were previously stated as the physical characteristics (*byañjana*).
Now, having selected from among those characteristics those that were pleasing to his own mind and praising them, he spoke the verse beginning with "With clear eyes.
For the Blessed One has "clear eyes" due to the perfection of the five-colored clarity; he is "fair-faced" because his face resembles the full moon;

he is "tall" due to the perfection of his height and proportions; he is "straight" because of the straightness of his limbs like those of Brahmā; and he is "majestic" because of his radiant splendor. Furthermore—
And what was stated previously is stated again by way of praising him with the phrase, "In the midst of the community of recluses.
For it is precisely such a one who shines in this manner. The same method applies to the following verse as well.

"Possessed of supreme beauty" means endowed with the highest physical excellence. "Chieftain of charioteers" means the most excellent driver. "Of Jambusaṇḍa" means of Jambudīpa. One becomes a lord through manifest sovereignty.
“Khattiyas” means those of the warrior-noble caste (*jātikhattiya*). “Bhōgis” means those who possess wealth. “Kings” refers to whoever exercises sovereignty.
“King of kings” means one worthy of honor by other kings; the intended meaning is that he becomes a supreme ruler, a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).

“Lord of men” means having become the sovereign lord over human beings. When this was said, the Blessed One [replied]: “Those who are Worthy Ones (*arahant*), Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*), when their own beauty is being described...”
Fulfilling this wish of Sela, the Blessed One said, "I am a king," and so forth. Herein, the intended meaning is as follows:
Regarding that which you, Sela, entreat me—"You ought to be a king"—be at ease in this matter; I am a king.
