And while being a king, just as another king might rule over a hundred leagues or a thousand leagues, [so am I] a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
"Even if one were to offer [sacrifices] as far as the four continents, my domain is not limited in such a way. For I am the unsurpassed King of Dhamma;
from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, and across immeasurable world-systems in the horizontal directions, I rule.
Indeed, among all beings—whether footless, two-footed, or otherwise—I am the foremost. For there is no one equal to me in virtue... [and so forth]."

Or there is a counterpart by means of the knowledge and vision of liberation; thus, I, as a peerless King of Dhamma, turn the wheel by means of the peerless Dhamma distinguished by the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth—the wheel of command, saying, "Abandon this;
enter upon and abide in this"—and by means of the Dhamma of the scriptures, beginning with, "Bhikkhus, this is the noble truth of suffering," and so on.
Or rather, it is the Wheel of Dhamma itself. "A wheel that cannot be turned back" means that wheel which cannot be turned back by any ascetic...
[or] by anyone in the world.
Having seen the Blessed One thus revealing himself, Sela was filled with rapture and joy; and in order to further strengthen his resolve, he said:
"You claim to be a perfectly awakened Buddha"—with these words he spoke two verses. Therein, "Who indeed is the general?
he asked: "Who indeed is the general who shall follow the wheel of our lord the King as it is set in motion by Dhamma?
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was seated on the Blessed One’s right side like a heap of gold.
Shining with glory as if [with] beauty, the Blessed One, demonstrating that, spoke the verse beginning with "pavattitaṃ" (set forth by me).

Therein, "anujāto tathāgataṃ" means born after the Tathāgata as a cause; the meaning is that he was born by means of the Tathāgata as the cause. Furthermore, three types are mentioned: the base-born (*avajāta*), the conformably-born (*anujāta*), and the surpassingly-born (*atijāta*).
Among these, the base-born is one of immoral conduct; he is not truly called a son of the Tathāgata.
[The word] *hoti* [is used]. One who is "born before" (*atijāta*) is one superior to his father; even such a person does not exist as a son of the Tathāgata.
However, the Tathāgata has only one son, who is "born after" (*anujāta*). Showing this, he spoke thus.
Having thus answered the question, "Who indeed is the commander?", regarding what Sela said, "Do you claim to be the Fully Awakened One?"—
Desiring to make him free from doubt in that regard, [the Blessed One] spoke the verse beginning with "That which is to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) in order to make it known:

"I do not claim to be a Buddha merely by way of my word; rather, for this reason I am a Buddha. Therein, "that which is to be directly known" refers to clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and liberation (*vimutti*).
That which is to be developed is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). That which is to be abandoned is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*). Furthermore, by the mention of the cause...
Because their fruits are established, their fruits—the truth of cessation and the truth of suffering—are indeed already stated.

Thus, by including here that which is to be realized has been realized and that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood, he demonstrates both the fruit of the cultivation of the Four Truths and liberation itself, establishing his state of Buddhahood through the appropriate reason:
"Having awakened to what was to be awakened to, I have become a Buddha."

Having thus revealed himself in a non-figurative sense, he spoke these three verses beginning with "In the discipline" (*vinaye*) while leading the brahmin toward the overcoming of doubt regarding his own self.
Therein, "sallakatta" means one who extracts the arrows of passion and the like.
"Anuttara" means that unlike a disease treated by an external physician—which may recur even within this very same existence—such is not the case for that which has been pacified by me.
Furthermore, there is no arising of disease even in another existence; therefore, the meaning is "I am unsurpassed. "Brahmabhūto" means having become supreme.
"Atitulo" means having transcended comparison; the meaning is "beyond compare. "Mārasenappamaddano" means the crusher of the army of Māra, which has come forth as it is said:

"Desires are your first army. "Sabbāmitte" refers to those known as the Māras of the aggregates (khandha), defilements (kilesa), formations (abhisaṅkhāra), death (maccu), and the son of the gods (devaputta).
"Having brought all adversaries under control" means having brought them into one's own power. "Fearless from every quarter" (*akutobhaya*) means being without fear from any source.
When this was said, the brahmin Sela, instantly conceiving faith in the Blessed One and desiring the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), spoke these three verses beginning with "So be it, sir.
In that context, "born of a dark lineage" (*kaṇhābhijātiko*) refers to one born into a low caste family such as the *caṇḍālas*. From that [lineage], even they...
The young brahmin students, desiring to go forth, spoke this verse, saying, "If it pleases you, sir.
Then Sela, with a joyful heart, showing them [the way] and requesting their own going-forth, spoke the verse beginning with "O Brahmins.
Thereafter, the Blessed One [considered] that in the past, under the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara, Sela had been among those very three hundred men...
Having become the leader of the group, he built a monastic cell (pariveṇa) together with them and performed meritorious deeds such as giving.
By that kamma, while experiencing the prosperity of gods and humans, he was reborn in his final existence as their very teacher.
Furthermore, that kamma of theirs had matured for the ripening of liberation and served as the necessary support (upanissaya) for their becoming "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) disciples.

Therefore, ordaining them all through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula, he spoke the verse beginning with "Well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*). Therein, "visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means it is to be seen by oneself, directly perceived.
"Timeless" (*akālika*) means that because the fruit arises immediately after the path, it is not a fruit to be attained at some other time.
"Wherein there is no waste" (*yattha amogha*) refers to that holy life of the path wherein, for one who is diligent, [there is no waste] through the fulfillment of the three trainings.
"For one who trains, the going-forth is not in vain; it is fruitful—this is the meaning. Having said this, the Blessed One spoke: "Come, monks!
All of them, having taken up their bowls and robes and arrived through the air, were as well-disciplined as elders of a hundred years' standing and paid homage to the Blessed One.
It was with reference to their attainment of the status of "come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) in this manner that it was said: "Sela indeed obtained [it]," and so forth.
400. *Imāhi*: by these verses that were in accordance with Keṇiya’s mind. Therein, because there is no sacrifice for brahmins without the tending of the fire, it is said:
“Sacrifices have the fire-oblation as their head. The meaning is: those in which the fire-oblation is supreme, or those in which the pouring of the fire is predominant.
Because it is the first thing to be recited by those studying the Vedas, the Sāvittī is called “the mouth of the meters.”
The king is called the "mouth" because he is the best among human beings. The ocean is called the "mouth" because it is the support and the refuge of rivers.

By virtue of its conjunction with the moon, because it serves as the marker for such perceptions as "Today is the full moon of Kattikā" or "Today is Rohiṇī," and because it creates light and possesses a gentle nature, it is said that "the moon is the mouth of the lunar mansions.
Because he is the foremost among those who give heat, the sun is [called the mouth] of those who give heat.

When it is said, "The mouth," it refers generally to the Saṅgha. However, because they are the foremost among those worthy of offerings, at that particular time it is said with special reference to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha:
"For those desiring merit, the Saṅgha alone is the mouth for those who sacrifice.
By this, he shows that the Saṅgha is the gateway for the influx of merit.
He spoke another verse of confession beginning with "That refuge. Its meaning is as follows:

Since we have come to that refuge on the eighth day from now, O Blessed One who possesses the eye through the five eyes, we have been tamed by your own unsurpassed taming within your teaching; oh, the power of your refuge!
After that, having praised the Blessed One with two verses, the three hundred bhikkhus spoke the words beginning with “These are we,” requesting a salutation with the third verse.
Thus ends the commentary on the Sela Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
3. Commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta 401.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Assalāyana Sutta.

In this context, *nānāverajjakānaṃ* means those who have come from various foreign kingdoms, such as Aṅga and Magadha; or alternatively, it means those born and raised in those various kingdoms. *Kenacideva* means...
By means of such undetermined duties as the performance of sacrifices and the like. "Common to the four castes" (*cātuvaṇṇi*) means shared by the four castes.

However, they thought thus, considering that even though the ascetic Gotama does what is improper, we say that only those who are purified by bathing and purified by meditation are true Brahmins. "Vuttasiro" means one whose head has been shorn.

“Dhammavādī” means one who speaks according to the true nature of things (*sabhāvavādī*). “Duppaṭimantiyā” means they are difficult for those like us, who speak what is not the Dhamma (*adhammavādī*), to refute in debate.
This shows that it is impossible to bring about the defeat of one who speaks according to the Dhamma. “Paribbājaka” refers to the method of going forth;
those who, having mastered the three Vedas, go forth last of all—both the mantras by which they go forth and those who have gone forth [are meant].
"Whatever mantras they recite, or whatever conduct they practice—all that has been practiced and learned by you.
Therefore, thinking 'there is no defeat for you; there will surely be victory,' they spoke thus. 402.
"But they are seen," and so forth, was said for the purpose of shattering their tenets. In that context, "brahmin women" refers to...
Brahmin women are seen who have been brought from their families through marriage for the sake of obtaining sons for the brahmins.
At another time, they become subject to the menses—the meaning being that they have reached puberty. They become pregnant, meaning they have conceived.
They give birth, meaning they are bringing forth sons and daughters. They nurse, meaning they are suckling milk for their infants.
"Born from the same womb" means being born from the urinary passage of Brahmin women. "They say thus" means they speak in this way.
How so? "The Brahmin alone is the highest caste... [and so on] ...the heirs of Brahmā.
If, however, their word were true, the wombs of Brahmin women would have to be the chest of Mahābrahmā, and the urinary passage of Brahmin women [would have to be his private parts].

"May he not have a face"—thinking, "Let them not be allowed to say, 'We lived in the breast of Mahābrahmā and emerged from his mouth'"—this is the "doctrine of being born from the mouth," which cuts off [that claim]. 403.
"Being a master, one becomes a slave; being a slave, one becomes a master": this refers to a Brahmin who, together with his wife, engages in trade.
Or, having gone to the land of the Yonakas or the land of Kamboja, he dies;
if there are no sons of marriageable age in his house, the Brahmin woman enters into a union with either a slave or a laborer.
When a son is born, that man remains a slave, yet the son born to him becomes the master of the inheritance. He is pure on the mother’s side.
One who is impure on the father’s side, having engaged in trade, goes to the Middle Country, takes a Brahmin girl, and begets a son in her womb;
that son is pure on the mother’s side but impure on the father’s side.
This was said for the purpose of showing that even within the Brahminical system itself, there is a confusion of castes. What is the proof? Who...

"Breathing" (*assāsa*) is explained as follows: "Where you were all slaves when you were slaves, and all masters when you were masters—what strength or support do you have here that you say, 'The Brahmin alone is the highest caste'?
This refers to those who hold views that disrupt the continuity of the Suttas, such as the statement, "Is it not the case that only the Khattiya... and so forth.
408. Now, demonstrating the purification of the four castes (*cātuvaṇṇisuddhi*), he said, "Here, O King," and so forth.
"In the dog-watering trough" means in the trough from which dogs drink. "The business of fire" refers to the functions of fire, such as dispelling cold, removing darkness, cooking food, and so on.
"In this, Assalāyana" means while performing all these functions of fire.
409. Now, regarding this which the brahmins call "purity through the four castes," there is no fixed rule here concerning the "four castes.
For there is also a fifth caste, the *pādasika*. Thus, in order to show the fault in their doctrine in brief, he says here, "the young khattiya," and so forth.
In that regard, "but in this and that case" means: but in that former method, there is no distinction whatsoever among these young men.
He says, "I do not see [any such distinction]. Yet, there is indeed a difference even between these two.
For the son born of a Kṣatriya youth and a Brāhmaṇa maiden is called a Kṣatriya-pādaśika, while the other is called a Brāhmaṇa-pādaśika; these are youths of inferior birth.
Thus, having shown the fault in their doctrine regarding the purity of the four castes (cātuvaṇṇisuddhi) on account of the existence of a fifth caste, [the author] now...
Furthermore, while instructing on the purification of the four castes, he said, "What do you think? and so forth. Therein, *saddhe* means at a funeral feast;
*thālipāke* means at a gift of food offered as a presentation; *yaññe* means at a sacrifice; *pāhune* means at a meal prepared for guests.
With the word *kiṃ hi*, he indicates whether it will be of great fruit or not.
410. "In the past, Assalāyana, although you were of superior birth while I was of inferior birth, when questioned by me regarding the doctrine of birth, you were unable to provide an answer.

Now that you are of inferior birth and I am of superior birth as a Buddha, what will you be able to accomplish when questioned by me regarding the Buddhas' own doctrine of birth? There is no [answer] here."
Thinking, "Anxious reflection must be made," he began this teaching while encouraging the young man. In that context, *asita* means black. *Devala* is his name;
at that time, it was the Blessed One himself. *Paṭaliya* refers to sandals with thick soles.
*Patthaṇḍile* means in the courtyard of the leaf-hut. *Ko nu kho* means "where indeed? *Gāmaṇḍalarūpo viya* means "like a village boy."
"Indeed, sir, I am he. "I am that very Asitadevala, sir," he said.
At that time, it is said, the Great Being was wandering about as a Koṇḍadamaka ascetic. "They began to pay homage" means they made an effort to worship him.
From that point on, even though the ascetic had been practicing for a hundred years, he remained a Koṇḍita by not bowing to the young Brahmin born on that very day.

411. "Janikā mātā" means she by whom you were begotten is your mother who gave birth. "Janikāmātu" means of the mother who gave birth. "Yo janako" means he who is the progenitor, the father; or the reading may be "yo janiko pitā.

"Asitena" means by the seer Asita Devala, who possessed the five supernormal powers (pañca-abhiññā); they will not be able to answer this question on the Gandhabba when asked. "Yesaṃ" means of those seven seers.
"Na puṇṇo dabbigāho" means [the ladle] was not filled for those seven seers.
Having taken leaves and cooked them, there was one named Puṇṇa who was a donor; he knew the craft of preparing curd-mixture (*dabbi*).
You, along with your teacher, were not even equal to that Puṇṇa; therefore it was known that you do not know even the mere craft of preparing curd-mixture.
The rest is clear everywhere.

But this Assalāyana was faithful and confident; he had a shrine built within his own residence. Even to this day, those born in the lineage of Assalāyana continue to build shrines within their residences after having constructed their dwellings.
The commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Ghoṭamukha Sutta 412.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Ghoṭamukha Sutta. Therein, "in the Khemiya mango grove" means in the mango grove named after that.
"A righteous going forth" means a righteous renunciation. "By not seeing" means by not seeing wise people such as yourselves.
"Or else, whatever is the Dhamma here" means either whatever is the Dhamma, that is, the intrinsic nature (sabhāva), or through the non-perception of that very [nature].
By this, he shows: "Our word is not the authority; the Dhamma alone is the authority.
Then the Elder, thinking, "There must be much work here, as if in a new Uposatha hall," descended from the walking path, entered the leaf-hut, and—
He sat down. To demonstrate this, it was said: "Thus it was spoken," and so forth. 413.
"These four [types of] brahmins"—it is said that this thought occurred to the Elder:
"This brahmin says, 'There is no ascetic or brahmin who has entered upon the legitimate going-forth. For him, there are these four persons and two assemblies."
“Having shown this, I will ask: ‘In which assembly do you most often see the fourth type of person?
Knowing the answer, he will say, ‘In the assembly of those who have gone forth from the household life. In this way, by his own mouth, I shall cause him to declare: ‘The religious life is righteous.
Thus he began this teaching.

414. Therein, *sārattarattā* means "thoroughly impassioned. Speech that is *sānuggahā* is speech spoken with a specific purpose; for this was said by me: "Our word is not the authority; the Dhamma alone is the authority. 421.
But as for "what then of them," he asked in order to distinguish whether a householder might speak of what is permissible (*kappiya*) or what is impermissible (*akappiya*).
"He had it built" means he had it constructed. And having had it built, he passed away and was reborn in heaven. Regarding his skill in the art of knowledge...
"Having slain both mother and father, one must slay oneself"—thus it is said. There is no one else who, knowing this craft, has been reborn in heaven except for him.
However, having performed meritorious deeds by relying on that elder and being reborn there, he reflected, "By what kamma have I been reborn here? and, knowing it as it truly is, [he understood].

One day, when the Saṅgha had assembled for the purpose of repairing a dilapidated dining hall, he approached in the guise of a layman and asked, "Venerable sirs, for what purpose has the Saṅgha assembled? "For the purpose of repairing the dining hall.
"By whom was it built? "By Ghoṭamukha. "Where is he now? "He has passed away. "Does anyone have anything belonging to him?"
"Is he a kinsman? "He is my sister. "Then summon her," he said. The monks summoned her.
He approached her and said, "I am your brother, Ghoṭamukha by name. Having built this hall, I have been reborn in heaven.
In such and such places there is wealth deposited by me; take that and build this dining hall."
Having said, “And support your children,” he paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, rose into the air, and departed for the world of the devas.
The remainder is clear throughout.
[End of] the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
The commentary on the Ghoṭamukhasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Caṅkīsutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Caṅkīsutta. Regarding the phrase "in the Devavana Sālavana," it is said that in that place there were deities.
A restorative rite (*balikamma*) is performed there; therefore, it is called both "Devavana" (The Grove of the Gods) and "Sālavana" (The Sal Grove).
"He dwells in Opāsāda" means he lives in the brahmin village named Opāsāda; or, having overcome [others], he dwells there;
being its master, he dwells within the boundaries by which one must live there. However, here, by virtue of the prefix, the locative sense is implied.
The application of the words should be understood; for the same reason, there is no further application regarding the remaining terms.

In this context, the definition should be sought from the science of grammar (*śabda-śāstra*). "Abounding in beings" (*sattussada*) means crowded with beings, full of beings—that is, densely populated by many people and filled with various creatures such as elephants, horses, peacocks, and deer suitable for breeding. Furthermore, because that village...
It was provided with fodder and grass for elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as grass for the roofing of houses;
likewise, it was supplied with firewood and timber for building materials.

Furthermore, within its interior were many lotus ponds of circular, square, and other shapes, adorned with various water-born flowers, while outside there were numerous ponds that were always filled with water.
Because these things exist, it is said: "with grass, firewood, and water.
"With grain" (*sadhañña*) means together with grain; the meaning is a vast accumulation of grain consisting of various kinds such as early and late rice.
Up to this point, it has been described in which village the brahmin dwells in royal splendor, having raised the white parasol—his abundant prosperity and success.
It is illuminated. "Royal domain" (*rājabhogga*) means property obtained from a king. If one asks by whom it was given, it was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
"Royal inheritance" (*rājadāya*) means that which has become the king's portion; the sense is "heritage. "Brahmadeyya" means a gift for the noble ones;
the sense is that it is to be enjoyed under the designation of "king" after the royal parasol has been raised. Alternatively, "royal domain" (*rājabhogga*) refers to everything...

By one who instructs [others] on what is to be cut and broken, and who collects taxes from river-crossings, mountains, and so forth, having raised the white parasol and become a king, one may enjoy [the realm].
In this context, that which was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala is called "a royal gift" (*rājadāya*).
Here, it is a "royal gift" because it was given by the king; however, for the purpose of indicating the donor, the king, it is said: "by King Pasenadi of Kosala..."
"Given" (dinna) is what was said. "Brahmadeyya" means a gift for a brahmin; the meaning is that it is given in such a way that it cannot be taken back again, being relinquished and abandoned. 423.
Those who have become many and are united are a *saṅgha*. Those who possess a *saṅgha* in each of the various directions are called *saṅghī*.
"Previously, having gone out from within the village as individuals (*agaṇā*) and having come together outside as a group (*gaṇā*), they have become a group (*gaṇībhūtā*).
"Facing north" means facing the northern direction. "He addressed the steward" (*khattaṃ āmantesi*): a steward (*khattā*) is called a high official capable of answering questions;
he addressed him. "Let them wait" means let them bide their time for a moment; it is said, "let them stay."
424. "From various kingdoms" means those born in, residing in, or arrived from various kinds of kingdoms, such as Kāsi, Kosala, and so forth;
thus they are "from various kingdoms," and [the phrase refers to] those from various kingdoms.
"For some purpose whatsoever" means for some unspecified task, such as attending a sacrifice or a festival. Having heard of his departure, they thought: "This Caṅkī is a prominent brahmin."
"Most other brahmins have gone for refuge to the ascetic Gotama, yet he alone has not gone.
If he were to go there, he would surely be converted by the ascetic Gotama’s captivating magic and go for refuge.
Consequently, there would be no more gathering of brahmins at his house door. Let us create an obstacle to his journey."
Having deliberated, "Let us go," they went there. With reference to this, it was said: "Then those brahmins... and so forth.
In that context, "on both sides" means from two lineages. "On the mother's side and on the father's side" means: the venerable one’s mother is a brahmin; his mother’s mother is a brahmin;
her mother also is a brahmin. His father is a brahmin; his father’s father is a brahmin; his [grandfather’s] father also is a brahmin.
Thus you, sir, are well-born on both sides, from the mother’s side and from the father’s side.
“Of pure descent” means that your mother’s *gahaṇī* (receptacle) is pure; the meaning is that your mother’s womb is pure. Regarding the phrase “as far as the seventh generation of ancestors”:

here, the father’s father is the grandfather (*pitāmaha*); the generation of the grandfather is the “grandfather-generation” (*pitāmahayuga*). “Generation” (*yuga*) refers to the measure of a lifespan.
This is merely a matter of terminology; in actual fact, however, "grandfather" refers to the grandfather’s generation.
All ancestors beyond that are included by the term "grandfather" itself. Thus, one who can trace his lineage back through seven generations is one of pure descent.
Alternatively, it shows that he is "uncensured and unreviled in regard to birth. "Uncensured" means: "Take this man away! What [use is he]?"
"By this" means: thus he is unreviled and not reviled; "unreproached" means not reproached, one who has never before been subjected to abuse or censure.
"For what reason? means: by way of birth—meaning by such speech as "he is of low birth.
"By this factor" means: for this reason as well.
"A wealthy one" means a lord. "Possessing great riches" means endowed with vast wealth;

for in your house, O sir, there is much wealth like the dust and sand upon the earth, whereas the ascetic Gotama is destitute, sustaining himself by filling his belly with alms—thus they show [the contrast].
"Of great enjoyment" means possessing great luxury by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Thus, whatever quality...
They say this, thinking that by means of each respective opposite, they are merely demonstrating the absence of qualities in the Blessed One.
"Abhirūpa" means having a form superior to other men. "Dassanīya" means worthy of being seen because one never tires of looking at him even for a whole day;
he is "pāsādika" because he generates clarity of mind through the mere sight of him. "Pokkharatā" refers to the state of being beautiful.
The beauty of the complexion is *vaṇṇapokkharatā*; by that *vaṇṇapokkharatā*, meaning by the perfection of complexion.
However, the ancients say that *pokkhara* refers to the body, while *vaṇṇa* is simply the complexion. According to their view, both the complexion and the body are *vaṇṇapokkharāni*;
the state of these two is *vaṇṇapokkharatā*. Thus, "by the supreme *vaṇṇapokkharatā*" [is the meaning].
The meaning is: by means of an exceedingly pure complexion and the perfection of bodily form.

"Possessing a divine complexion" (*brahmavaṇṇī*) means possessing the most excellent complexion; even among those with pure complexions, it means being endowed with the very best, which is the golden complexion.
"Possessing a divine grace" (*brahmavacchasī*) means being endowed with a body resembling that of a Great Brahmā. "One whose presence is not insignificant to behold" refers to your honor...
In his body, there is no small space for vision; he indicates that all his limbs and members are indeed beautiful to behold and that they are also large.
One who possesses virtue (*sīla*) is "virtuous" (*sīlavā*).
One whose virtue is grown and increased is "one of mature virtue" (*vuddhasīlī*). By means of mature virtue... (*vuddhasīlena*)... [is the meaning].
"Endowed with virtue increased by growth": "endowed" (*samannāgato*) means "joined" (*yutto*); this is a synonym for the term *vuddhasīlī*.
They say all of this with reference solely to the five precepts (*pañcasīla*).
Regarding the phrase "one of beautiful speech" (*kalyāṇavāco*) and so forth: one whose speech is beautiful, lovely, and composed of well-rounded words and syllables is "one of beautiful speech."
One who possesses speech that is auspicious and sweet is called "one of auspicious speech" (*kalyāṇavākkaraṇo*). "Speech" (*vākkaraṇa*) refers to the sound of utterance.
It is called "urban" (*porī*) because it exists in the city (*pure bhavā*), owing to its state of being perfected in quality; or, because it exists in the city, it is urban.

It is also called "urban" because it resembles a city woman (*nāgarikithiyā*) by virtue of its delicacy. By means of that urban [speech]. "Crisp" (*vissaṭṭhā*) means unobstructed, free from defects such as being slurred or drawn out.
"Anelagalāyāti" means "to one who is free from drooling. For when some people speak, saliva (ela) drips from their throat, or it flows out as spittle, or drops of phlegm issue forth;
thus their speech is called "drooling" (anelagalā). The meaning is "to one who is the opposite of that.
"Atthassa viññāpaniyā" means capable of making known the meaning of what has been spoken by making clear its beginning, middle, and end.
The rest here regarding the description of the brahmins is self-evident. 425.
When it was thus said by those brahmins, Caṅkī thought: "There is no being who, when his own praise is being spoken, does not become satisfied;
thinking, 'Having recited this praise, we shall stop,' [he spoke] my praise by way of birth and so forth."
“They say this, yet it is not fitting for me to take delight in my own praise.
Come now, I shall refute their argument, make known the greatness of the ascetic Gotama, and cause them to go there.
Having thought thus, he said, “In that case, sirs, listen to me as well,” and so forth. In this context, those [verses] beginning with “Well-born on both sides” refer to himself.

Qualities are similar to qualities; yet even those [who say], "Who am I, and what are the qualities such as the excellence of birth belonging to the ascetic Gotama?"—thinking thus, they consider themselves to be far surpassed by his qualities.

However, he proclaims [the others] solely for the purpose of illustrating the greatness of the Blessed One. By specifying, "We alone are worthy," he illustrates this here: if, on account of the greatness of their qualities...
He is indeed one who should be approached; for just as a mustard seed is negligible compared to Sineru,
a cow’s footprint compared to the great ocean, or a drop of dew compared to the water in the seven great lakes,
even so our own qualities are meager and inferior when compared to the qualities of the ascetic Gotama, such as his excellence of birth and the rest.
"Therefore, we ourselves ought to approach that venerable Gotama for the purpose of seeing him.

Regarding the phrase "that which is on the ground and that which is situated in the air": here, the ponds plastered with lime in the royal courtyard and the pleasure garden, having been filled with the seven precious gems, constitute wealth placed upon the ground, which is called "grounded wealth" (*bhūmigata*); [as well as] the turrets of the palaces and so forth.
Furthermore, that which is filled and placed [there] is called "situated in the air" (*vehāsaṭṭha*). Thus, first, it was obtained by way of family inheritance.
On the very day of the Tathāgata’s birth, however, four treasures—Saṅkha, Eḷa, Uppala, and Puṇḍarīka—came into being.
Among them, Saṅkha was one *gāvuta* in extent, Eḷa half a *yojana*, Uppala three *gāvutas*, and Puṇḍarīka one *yojana*. Even from among those, as each place was taken...
It is indeed full. Thus it should be understood that the Blessed One went forth into homelessness, having renounced abundant gold and silver.
"A youth," and so forth, have already been explained in detail below.
Regarding the phrase "one of no small scope," it should be understood here that the opportunity for seeing the Blessed One is truly immeasurable. In this regard, there is this:

The Background: It is said that in Rājagaha, a certain brahmin, having heard that "it is impossible to take the measure of the ascetic Gotama," took a sixty-cubit bamboo pole and stood outside the city gate at the time when the Blessed One was entering for alms.
When the Blessed One arrived, he took up the bamboo pole and stood nearby; the bamboo reached only as high as the Blessed One’s knees.
He reached [the Buddha]. On the following day, having joined two bamboos together, he stood nearby;
the Blessed One, appearing only as high as two bamboos above the two bamboos, asked, "Brahmin, what are you doing? "I am taking your measurement," he replied.
"Brahmin, even if you were to come after joining together bamboos that fill the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), [you would still not reach my height]."

“You will not be able to grasp my measure. Indeed, O Brahmin Atula, I have fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons in such a way that no one else could grasp my measure; the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Having said this, he spoke a verse from the Dhammapada. At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings drank of the Deathless.
There is another account: it is said that Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, is four thousand eight hundred yojanas in height;
his arm span is twelve hundred yojanas; the breadth of his palms and soles is three hundred yojanas;
his finger-joints are fifty yojanas; the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas; and his forehead is one hundred and twenty yojanas.
His head was nine hundred yojanas high. Thinking, "I am so tall that I will not be able to look at the Teacher by bowing down," he did not go.
One day, having heard the Blessed One’s praise, he came thinking, "By some means or other, I shall look upon him.
The Blessed One, knowing his intention, reflected: "In which of the four postures shall I show myself?"
“Standing,” he thought, “means that even one who is low appears as if high; I shall show myself to him while lying down.
Having said, “Ānanda, prepare a couch in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber,” he adopted the lion’s posture there.
When Rāhu arrived, he saw the Blessed One lying down and, raising his neck, gazed up at him like the full moon in the midst of the sky. What is this?
When he was addressed as "Lord of Asuras," the Blessed One said, "I will not go, thinking that I shall not be able to look down upon him by bowing.
"O Lord of Asuras, I did not fulfill the perfections with my face turned downward; rather, I gave gifts while holding my head high.
On that very day, Rāhu went for refuge. Thus, the Blessed One was no small person to behold.
He is virtuous by virtue of the fourfold purification. That virtue, moreover, is noble, supreme, and utterly pure; therefore he is called "one of noble virtue" (*ariyasīlī*).

That very same virtue is wholesome in the sense of being blameless; therefore he is called "one of wholesome virtue" (*kusalasīlī*). "By means of wholesome virtue" is a synonym for this. He is the teacher of many teachers:
for with each single teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One, eighty-four thousand living beings [attain realization].
Immeasurable gods and humans drink the nectar of the path and its fruits. Therefore, he is a teacher to many, and a master to those disciples who are to be trained by him.
Regarding the phrase "one whose sensual desire is destroyed": although all defilements have indeed been destroyed in the Blessed One, the brahmin does not know this;
rather, he speaks of the virtue only within the scope of his own knowledge. Regarding "free from deceit": [this refers to] "adornment with alms-bowls" and "adornment with robes."
He is free from the restlessness described as "adornments for the lodging" or "the grooming, massaging, and rubbing of this putrid body. He is one who has no evil as his priority;
that is, he conducts himself having placed before him the nine supramundane states which are devoid of evil.
"To the brahmin folk" means to the community of brahmins distinguished by such names as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others. For he is not at variance with them.
"Placed at the head of the people. This means that these people walk with the ascetic Gotama placed before them.
Furthermore, "having no evil placed at the head" means he does not have evil placed at the head; he does not walk having placed evil before him, for he does not desire evil.
Of what [people]? Of the brahminical people—even toward the brahminical people who are in opposition to himself, he is not opposed.
"What is meant is: 'only one desiring welfare and happiness.
"From another kingdom" means from a foreign kingdom. "From another province" means from a foreign province.
"They come to ask questions" means that wise kṣatriyas and others, as well as brahmins, gandhabbas, and so forth, having prepared their inquiries, come thinking, "We shall ask questions."
They come together. Therein, some, having observed either a fault in their question or their own inability to receive the answer, sit in silence without asking;
others ask questions; and for some, the Blessed One, having inspired them with the zeal to inquire, provides the answer.
Thus, when the doubts of all of them have reached the shore, it is like [the waters] of the great ocean.
Like waves, they break only upon reaching the Blessed One. The rest here regarding the praise of the Tathāgata is self-evident.
“They are our guests” means they are our newcomers, recent arrivals, and visitors. “I master” means I know.
“Of immeasurable praise” means that even by one such as the All-Knowing One his praise is immeasurable, let alone by someone like me.
This is shown. And it has been said:
"Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon, without speaking of anything else..."
“The eon might come to an end within this vast expanse of time, but the praise of the Tathāgata would never be exhausted.
Having heard this discourse on his virtues, those brahmins thought: “Just as Caṅkī says, regarding the ascetic Gotama...”
“He speaks in praise; that venerable Gotama possesses incomparable qualities. Since we know his virtues to be such, we have indeed waited too long;
come, let us follow him. As they followed, they said, “In that case, sirs,” and so forth.
426. *Opāpeti* means “he causes to enter. *Saṃpurekkharonti* means they move about having placed even their children and themselves before them.
427. *Mantapadaṃ*: "Mantra" itself is the "mantra-word"; the meaning is "Veda. *Itihitiha paramparāya*:
this indicates that it has come down by way of tradition, in the sense of "thus indeed, thus indeed. *Piṭakasampadāya*: by means of the excellence consisting of the sacred word (*pāvacana*).
This shows that it has been handed down having been composed through metrical structures such as the *Sāvitti* and so forth, as well as through the arrangement of sections (*vagga*). In that regard:
And "in that" refers to those mantra-words. "Proponents" means those who cause [them] to proceed. "Of whom" means belonging to whom.
"Mantra-word" refers specifically to the mantra known as Veda. "Chanted" means recited by the ten ancient Brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka and others, by way of perfection in the phrasing.
"Expounded" means spoken by others; the sense is "recited. "Collected" means thoroughly assembled.
The meaning is that it was established by being formed into a mass (*piṇḍa*). "Singing after that" means that nowadays the brahmins sing after what was previously sung by them;
they recite it in succession or chant it. "Repeating after that" means they repeat that;
this is a synonym for the preceding term. "Repeating what has been spoken" means they recite in succession what was spoken and recited by them.
"They recite what has been recited" means that they cause others to recite what has already been recited by them. "Seyyathidaṃ" means "such as these," which is the sense of the phrase.

"Aṭṭhaka" and so forth are their names; it is said that after they had looked with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*) and, without causing harm to others, had compared [the teachings] with the word of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, they composed the mantras, one after another.
But the brahmins, having added [practices such as] the taking of life and so forth, and having split the three Vedas, made them contradictory to the word of the Buddha.
"A blind file" (*andhaveṇī*) means a line of blind men. For one blind man grasps the end of a staff held by one who has sight;
another blind man grasps that blind man, and yet another grasps him—thus fifty or sixty blind men are linked together in succession.
...is called "blind. "Mutually entangled" means they are clinging to one another; the meaning is that they are even devoid of a sighted person to hold the staff.
It is said that a certain rogue, seeing a group of blind men, incited them by saying, "In such-and-such a village, food and drink are easily obtained.
When they replied, "Sir, lead us there; we will give you this," he [took a bribe].

Having taken them, he left the path midway, went around a large thicket, and having had the man in front seize the hem of the one behind by the hand, said, "There is some business; you must go on for now," and then fled.
Though they traveled for the whole day, being unable to find the way, they cried out, "Where, sir, is the man with eyes? Where is the path?"
Having lamented and being unable to find the path, they died right there. It is with reference to them that it was said: "clinging to one another.
"Even among the former" means even one among the ten brahmins mentioned previously. "Even among the middle" means even one among the teachers and their predecessors in the middle period.
"Even among the latter" means even one among the brahmins of the present day.
"Five indeed," he says, having added three other such [categories] to the two found in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
"Of two kinds of ripening" means either as a ripening of what is real or as a ripening of what is unreal. "'This is not enough here,' Bhāradvāja:

by one who has practiced with the thought 'I shall preserve the truth,' a wise person [should understand] that regarding the thought 'What I have grasped is alone the truth, all else is vain,' this must be held with absolute certainty."
He established [the position] by opening the way for the subsequent question, stating that it is neither possible nor appropriate to reach the ultimate goal.

430. Here, Bhāradvāja, "monks" refers to himself alone, as in the *Jīvaka-sutta* and the *Mahāvaccha-sutta*. "In things that provoke greed" means in states of greed. The same principle applies to the other two phrases as well. 432.
"He establishes faith" means he establishes the kind of faith that is fully settled. "He approaches" means he goes near. "He attends upon" means...
He sits nearby. He lends his ear, meaning he applies the faculty of hearing. He hears the Dhamma, meaning he listens to the Dhamma of the teaching.
He retains it, meaning he retains it by making it familiar. He examines it, meaning he investigates it according to its meaning and its underlying reasons.
They endure contemplation, meaning they endure being observed; they appear thus: "In this [passage] virtue is taught, in this concentration."
The meaning is as follows: "Desire" (chanda) refers to the desire to act. "Exerts" means he makes an effort. "Weighs" means he evaluates by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Strives" means he exerts himself in the striving for the Path. "With the body indeed realizes the supreme truth":
with the co-nascent mental body (nāmakāya), he realizes Nibbāna; and with wisdom, having pierced through the defilements, he sees that very same [Nibbāna] made manifest and evident.
433. "Awakening to the truths" means awakening to the path. "Attainment of the truths" means the realization of the fruit.
"Of those very same" refers to the twelve [factors] mentioned below; thus it conforms to the long exposition of the path, and therefore that is not the meaning here.
This, however, is the meaning: "Of those very same" means of those mental states associated with the path. "Exertion" means the exertion of the path.
For that [insight] is highly beneficial for the realization of the truths, which is termed the actualization of the fruit; because in the absence of the path, there is no fruit.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances. The remainder is plain everywhere.
Thus ends the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Caṅkī Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Esukārī Sutta: 437.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Esukārī Sutta. In that context, "they would hang it upon a hole" means they would cause it to be attached to a niche.

By this, he demonstrates what is called the "duty of the caravan leader" (*satthadhamma*). It is said that when a caravan leader traveling through a great wilderness encounters a dead ox on the road, he takes its meat and attaches portions for all the members of the caravan, saying, "Having eaten this, you must pay such-and-such a fee.
Thus, there are those who eat the ox-meat and those who do not, as well as those who are able to pay the fee and those who are not.
"Even though they were unable [to pay]. Just as a caravan leader, in order to make one who has taken an ox on credit pay the price,

forcibly gives out portions to everyone and then collects the debt— this is the nature of a caravan leader— it was to show that in the same way, the brahmins, without having received a promise from the world,
have prescribed the four types of service according to their own inherent nature, that he said, "In this very way," and so forth.
"May he be worse" means may he have evil. "May he be better" means may he have welfare. Alternatively, "worse" (*pāpiyo*) means his personal existence (*attabhāva*) may be wicked or base;
"better" (*seyyo*) means excellent or supreme. "Better than" (*seyyaṃso*) means more excellent. "By high birth" (*uccākulīnatā*) means one is better by virtue of being born into a high family.
"Worse than" (*pāpiyaṃso*) means more wicked. And high birth increases one's standing in two kinds of families: the Khattiya family and the Brāhmaṇa family.
And [there are] three [grounds for] noble appearance. For even a *vaiśya* may possess a noble appearance. Noble wealth exists in all four [castes].
For even a *śūdra*, and even a *caṇḍāla*, certainly possesses noble wealth.
440. Regarding "the practice of alms-gathering": even a Brahmin possessing a hundred million pieces of gold must indeed wander for alms; such was the case with the ancient Brahmins.

Even those possessing eighty million in wealth go on alms-round but once. Why? Thinking, "If we go on alms-round now, there will be no reproach such as, 'They used to go on alms-round when they were poor,'" [they do so].
"One who despises" refers to one who, having abandoned the lineage of going for alms, maintains his livelihood through farming, animal husbandry, trade, and so forth;
such a person is said to "despise. "Like a cowherd" means, as follows:
A cowherd who steals goods that ought to be protected by himself is one who does what should not be done; such is the meaning.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances. "The grass mat and the carrying-pole" refers to both the grass mat used for sitting and the yoke-pole.
"Recalling" means recalling the ancient family lineage of his mother and father, wherein he was born.
The remainder is clear in all respects.
Thus ends the commentary on the Esukārī Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
7. Commentary on the Dhanañjāni Sutta 445.
“Thus have I heard” introduces the Dhanañjāni Sutta. Therein, “in Dakkhiṇāgiri”: *giri* means a mountain;
this is the name of a district situated to the southern direction of the mountain that encircles Rājagaha. “At the gate of Taṇḍulapāli.”
It is said that Rājagaha had thirty-two great gates and sixty-four small gates;
among these, one was called the Taṇḍulapāli gate, and it was with reference to this that he spoke thus. Regarding the phrase "relying on the king":
having been sent by the king with the instruction, "Go and take a share of the crops without oppressing the people," he would go and take the entire crop, saying, "Do not destroy us, venerable sir!"
And when this was said, he replied: "What was said at the royal court was weak; I was commanded by the king at the very time of his arrival, 'Do not let her weep.
In this way, relying upon the king, he plunders the brahmins and householders.
Having brought in most of the grain into his own house, he brings only a small amount into the royal court. And did he not cause oppression to the brahmins and householders?
He replied: “Yes, Great King, in this year the crops in the fields were poor; therefore, since I took them without pressing [the farmers], not much was produced.
In this way, he plunders the king by relying on the brahmins and householders.
446. “Let milk be drunk” means let fresh milk be consumed. “Until you have eaten” means as long as you shall remain after having drunk the milk.
"Right now will be the time for the meal. This shows that they will bring our breakfast right here.

Regarding the words "mother and father," and so forth: one should seek out and support elderly parents with soft rugs and coverlets, fine garments, sweet food, fragrant scents, garlands, and the like.
[One should also perform] the naming ceremonies and other auspicious rites for sons and daughters.
One performing all duties must support one's wife and children; for if this is not done, censure arises—this is how the meaning should be understood. 447.

"One who acts contrary to the Dhamma": here, "unrighteousness" (adhamma) refers to the five or ten types of unwholesome actions. "They would drag him away" means they would drag him to various hells for the purpose of inflicting punishments such as the fivefold binding.
448. "One who walks according to the Dhamma" (*dhammacārī*) means one who performs righteous deeds such as agriculture, trade, and the like.

"They retreat" (*paṭikkamanti*) means they sink back or decline. "They advance" (*abhikkamanti*) means they move forward or increase. "Better" (*seyyo*) means more excellent. "Inferior" (*hīna*) means base or lowly.
"And Sāriputta has passed away" (*kālaṅkato ca sāriputto*): the Blessed One said this to the Elder with the intention, "Go there and teach him. The Elder, too—
Having gone there at that very moment, he taught the Dhamma to Mahābrahmā;
from then on, even when speaking a four-line stanza, he did not speak anything that was not liberated by the Four Truths.
(From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the Commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*)
The commentary on the Dhanañjāni Sutta is finished.
8. The commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Vāseṭṭha Sutta. Therein, "in the grove at Icchānaṅgala" refers to the village of Icchānaṅgala.
Not far away, in a grove of trees, were five men including Caṅki and others, who were the family priests of King Pasenadi of Kosala, as well as many other well-known brahmins.
It is said that they used to assemble at two places every sixth month; whenever they wished to verify their lineage, they would go to Pokkharasāti.
They assemble at Ukkaṭṭhā for the purpose of purifying their birth. When they wish to purify their mantras, they then assemble at Icchānaṅgala.
At this time, they assembled for the purpose of purifying their mantras. This is the "intermediate conversation":
that is, the conversation they engaged in as they roamed about, speaking in a manner appropriate to their state of friendship.
In the meantime, this other conversation arose: "Virtuous" means endowed with good qualities. "Perfect in conduct" means perfect in behavior.
"Authorized and acknowledged" means they have been authorized by their teachers in this way: "You are trained," and they themselves have acknowledged it, saying, "Yes, teacher, we are trained.
"We" means "we are. "I am Pokkharasāti’s [son], and this youth is Tārukkha’s."
"I am the eldest pupil and chief disciple of Pokkharasāti; this one [is the disciple] of Tārukkha," he declares.

"Those who possess the three Vedas" means those brahmins who know the three Vedas. "Whatever has been declared" means whatever has been taught, even a single word, both in its meaning and its phrasing.
"In that regard, we are complete masters" means because we know it entirely, we have reached the final conclusion therein.

The meaning [of this is as follows]. Now, revealing that state of perfection (*kevalibhāva*), he spoke the verse beginning with "padakassa. In that context, regarding the phrase "in recitation we are just like our teacher," it means that in the matter of speaking, we are indeed equal to our teacher.
Regarding the phrase "by action" (*kammunā*), it refers to the action of the ten paths of wholesome karma. For previously, this [teacher] was referring to the sevenfold bodily and verbal action.
When he said, "For one who is virtuous, sir," he was referring to the threefold mental action by saying "one who is perfected in conduct.
For one endowed with that is perfected in behavior. By saying "the one with eyes," he addresses the Blessed One by way of his possession of the five kinds of vision.

"Beyond deficiency" means having transcended a state of lack; the meaning is "perfect. "Having approached" (*pecca*) means having gone near. "They pay homage" means they perform an act of reverence. "The Eye arisen in the world":
in this world shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, he has arisen as the Eye for the world, having dispelled that darkness by showing the welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth.
456. Thus, having been praised and entreated by Vāseṭṭha, the Blessed One, encompassing both men, said to them: "I [shall explain] to you..."
He said, “I shall explain,” and so forth. In this context, “I shall explain” (*byakkhissanti*) means “I shall expound” (*byākarissāmi*).
“Successively” (*anupubbaṃ*) means: let alone the consideration of brahmins; I shall describe them in regular order starting from grass, trees, insects, and moths.

“The classification of birth” (*jātivibhaṅgaṃ*) means the detailed exposition of birth. For births are mutually distinct; that is, the births of those various living beings are different from one another.
"Mutually different" means of various kinds.

[The Buddha] began this teaching with the thought: "I shall first speak of the class of non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) grasses and trees, and afterwards I will speak of the class of clung-to (upādinnaka) things;
in this way, the distinction between their classes will become clear. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "Venerable sir, why..."

“Is it because of the diversity of seeds that what is not clung-to is diverse, and because of the diversity of karma that what is clung-to is diverse? When asked, [he replied], “No, it is not permissible to say so.
For it is karma that casts one into a womb. It is through the womb that these beings come to be of various colors.
Regarding the phrase “grasses and trees”: here, even those such as the palmyra and coconut palms, which have pith within and bark without, are indeed just grasses.

However, all trees are characterized by having pith within and bark without. Furthermore, they do not claim for themselves, "We are grass" or "We are trees," nor do they know, "I am grass" or "I am a tree.

Even though they do not know that their characteristic is born of their species, their shape—which is produced from their own roots—is indeed determined by their species, being just like the grass and other plants from which they originated. For what reason?

For species are mutually distinct. Since one species of grass is different from another species of tree, and even among grasses, one species of palm is different from another species of coconut—thus it should be expanded. By this he shows this:
that which is diverse by way of species is apprehended as distinct from other species even without one’s own acknowledgment or the instruction of others.
And if one were a brahmin by birth, he too would be perceived as distinct from a khattiya, a vessa, or a suddaka even without his own claim or the instruction of others;
yet he is not so perceived. Therefore, one is not a brahmin by birth.
Later, however, with the verse beginning "Just as among these births," he will reveal this very meaning through the distinction of words.
Having thus shown birth among non-appropriated beings, he says "Then insects... and so forth, in order to show it among appropriated beings.
The phrase "down to the *kunthakipillika*" means making the *kunthakipillika* the limit.
And here, those that go by flying are called *paṭaṅga*. For their species are likewise diverse according to their colors, such as blue, red, and so on.
The species are indeed of many kinds. "Small" refers to black snakes and the like;
"large" refers to mongooses, wild cats, and the like. "Bellied" (pādūdara) means those whose feet are their bellies;
it is said that for them, the belly itself is the foot. "Long-backed" (dīghapiṭṭhika): for snakes, from the head down to the tail-tip, there is only back; therefore, they are called "long-backed."
"Udakā" means in water; "born in water.
"Pakkhī" means birds. For they go by means of wings, thus they are "wing-goers" (pattayāna); they travel through the air, thus they are "air-travelers" (vihaṅgama).
Having thus shown the classification of beings according to their birth—those that move on land, in water, and in the sky—he now [explains] for what purpose this...
He shows this, and in order to reveal it, he spoke the verse beginning with "yathā etāsu. Its meaning has already been stated in brief.
However, showing what must be said here in detail, he himself spoke the passage beginning with "na kesehi. Therein, this is the construction:
that which was stated—"Among humans, there is no diversity consisting of gender or birth"—should be understood as being non-existent in this way.

For example: "Not by hair. For there is no fixed rule such as "the hair of brahmins is like this, and that of khattiyas is like this," as there is in the case of elephants, horses, deer, and so forth; in this manner, everything should be applied.
"The mark is not based on birth, as it is in other castes"—this, however, is the conclusion of the very point already stated.

This is to be understood. This is its application: since there is no distinct mark (*liṅga*) consisting of birth among humans by means of these [parts] beginning with hair, therefore it should be understood that "among humans divided into Brahmins and so forth, there is no mark consisting of birth, just as there is not in other species.
Now, even though such a distinction of birth does not exist, this diversity—namely, "Brahmin" and "Khattiya"—has arisen in the following way:

To demonstrate this, he spoke the verse beginning with *paccattaṃ*. In that context, *vokāraṃ* means diversity (*nānattaṃ*). This is the summarized meaning here: just as among animals there is a diversity established by their very nature through the specific arrangement of hair and so forth, such [diversity] does not exist within the bodies of brahmins and others themselves. Even though this is so, regarding this diversity—such as "brahmin" or "kshatriya"—[the Blessed One said: *paccattaṃ kho pana nidānaṃ brāhmaṇo khattiyo hoti,* *idha paccaññāya caranti brāhmaṇā khattiyāti vā.* "But it is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya; having recognized this here for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as 'brahmin' or 'kshatriya'. In this regard, *paccattaṃ* means "individually" (*ekaikaṃ*); *nidānaṃ* means "cause" (*kāraṇaṃ*); *paccaññāya* means "having known for oneself" (*sayaṃ ñatvā*); *caranti* means "they proceed" (*vattanti*). Thus, the meaning is: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya; having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as 'brahmin' or 'kshatriya'. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality (*paccattavācakaṃ*), and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause (*hetuvācakaṃ*). Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of wholesome deeds (*kusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing wholesome deeds that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of unwholesome deeds (*akusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing unwholesome deeds that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of both wholesome and unwholesome deeds (*kusalākusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing both wholesome and unwholesome deeds that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of neither wholesome nor unwholesome deeds (*nevakusalānākusala-kammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing neither wholesome nor unwholesome deeds that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of wholesome deeds accompanied by the defilements (*saṃkilesikakusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing wholesome deeds accompanied by the defilements that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of wholesome deeds free from the defilements (*asaṃkilesikakusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing wholesome deeds free from the defilements that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of unwholesome deeds accompanied by the defilements (*saṃkilesikākusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing unwholesome deeds accompanied by the defilements that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of unwholesome deeds free from the defilements (*asaṃkilesikākusalakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing unwholesome deeds free from the defilements that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of neither wholesome nor unwholesome deeds accompanied by the defilements (*nevakusalānākusala-saṃkilesikakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing neither wholesome nor unwholesome deeds accompanied by the defilements that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. Having known this for oneself, they proceed [in life], whether as "brahmin" or "kshatriya. This is what was intended. Furthermore, *paccattaṃ* is a term signifying individuality, and *nidānaṃ* is a term signifying cause. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is individually, according to its own cause, that one becomes a brahmin or a kshatriya. And what is that individual cause? It is the performance of neither wholesome nor unwholesome deeds free from the defilements (*nevakusalānākusala-asaṃkilesikakammakaraṇaṃ*). For it is by performing neither wholesome nor unwholesome deeds free
"That designation is spoken of among humans as a conventional expression; it is spoken of merely as a worldly convention.

Having thus refuted the argument of Bhāradvāja, the Blessed One now [proceeds]: "If one were a brahmin by birth alone, then even one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct would be a brahmin.
However, since the ancient brahmins [recognized] his status as a brahmin..."
Neither do they accept it, nor do other wise people in the world; therefore, supporting Vāseṭṭha’s argument, he spoke eight verses beginning with "Whoever among men...

In this context, "cattle-herding" means the protection of fields—that is, agricultural work—since "go" is a name for the earth, he spoke thus. "By various crafts" refers to diverse crafts such as weaving and so forth.
"Trade" (*vohāra*) means commerce. "By serving others" (*parapessa*) means by performing services for others. "The profession of an archer" (*issattha*) means living by weapons;
it is said to be the use of arrows and spears. "By the office of a domestic priest" (*porohicce*) means by the work of a chaplain.
Thus, according to both the Brahminical tradition and worldly convention, he demonstrates the non-Brahmin status of one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct.
"Having established this, it being so, one is not a brahmin by birth; rather, one becomes a brahmin through qualities.
Therefore, whoever possesses qualities, having been born in whatever family, he is a brahmin; this is the principle here.

Having thus brought forth this principle according to its meaning, he now explains it by means of a verbal distinction, saying "And I am no brahmin," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: I, indeed, who am this—
Born from any of the four modes of birth, and specifically born of a mother praised by the brahmins—

that is what is meant by "born of a womb" (*yonija*) or "born of a mother. Furthermore, this refers to the "womb" described by the brahmins as the pure path of origin for a brahmin, according to the method beginning with "well-born on both sides," meaning one who is of perfectly pure descent.
By this [term], one possesses the perfection of a mother; because he is born and produced from her, he is called "born of a womb" (*yonija*) and "arisen from a mother" (*mātisambhava*).
I do not call one a Brahmin merely by virtue of being "born of a womb and arisen from a mother. Why?
Because, O venerable sir, he is called a "Bhovādin" (one who says "bho") simply because of that mere word, as he is distinguished from others who possess worldly attachments.
If one possesses worldly possessions (*sakiñcana*) and obstacles (*sapalibodha*).

But he who, though born anywhere, is "without possessions" (*akiñcana*) due to the absence of the defilements such as lust, and is "without grasping" (*anādāna*) through the relinquishing of all attachments—him I call a brahmin. Why?
Because his evil has been banished (*bāhitapāpa*).
458. Furthermore, there are twenty-seven verses beginning with "Having severed all fetters" (*sabbasaṃyojanaṃ chetvā*). Therein, "all fetters" (*sabbasaṃyojana*) refers to the ten kinds of fetters.
"He does not tremble" (*na paritassati*) means he does not tremble through the trembling of craving (*taṇhā-paritassanā*).

"Transcending attachments" (*saṅgātiga*) means having transcended the attachments of passion (*rāga*) and so forth. "Dissociated" (*visaṃyutta*) means dissociated from the four modes of birth or from all defilements (*kilesa*).
"Straps" (*naddhi*) means resentment (*upanāha*). "Leather thongs" (*varatta*) means craving (*taṇhā*). "The tethering rope" (*sandāna*) refers to the snare of bondage;

this is a designation for the obsession of views (*diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna*). "Together with the hitch" (*sahanukkama*): here "the hitch" (*anukkama*) is said to be the knot used for inserting the snare; this is the name for the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*).

"With the crossbar lifted" (*ukkhitapaligha*): here "the crossbar" (*paligha*) is ignorance (*avijjā*). "Awakened" (*buddha*) means awakened to the Four Noble Truths. "Endures" (*titikkhati*) means he is patient.

"Power of patience" means the power of patience as endurance. However, that [patience], when it arises once, does not constitute an "army of powers"; rather, it becomes one when it arises repeatedly. Because of its presence, there is an "army of powers.

"Possessing the ascetic practices" (*vatavanta*) means possessing the *dhutaṅgas*. "Possessing virtue" (*sīlavanta*) means possessing good qualities. "Free from arrogance" (*anussada*) means devoid of the arrogance of passion and so forth. There is also a reading, "not heard" (*anussuta*), which has the meaning of "not lustful" (*anavassuta*). "Tamed" (*danta*) means free from wickedness. "It does not smear" (*na limpati*) means it does not adhere.
"To sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) means to the objects of sensual pleasure which are the basis for defilement-pleasures.
"He understands the destruction of suffering right here": by this, the fruit of arhatship (arahattaphala) is intended as the "destruction of suffering.

"He understands" means he knows by way of realization (adhigama). "One who has laid down the burden" (pannabhāra) means one who has set down the burden; one who stands having lowered the burdens of the aggregates (khandha), the defilements (kilesa), volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). The term "dissociated" (visaṃyutta) has the meaning already stated.
"Of profound wisdom" means one whose wisdom functions regarding profound objects. "Wise" means one endowed with natural wisdom.
"Detached from both householders" means detached from both; the meaning is that he is indeed detached from both of these.
"Not clinging to a home" means not adhering to what is called a "home," which is the abode of the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Desiring little" means having no desire.
"Tasesu" means among those with craving. "Thāvaresu" means among those free from craving.

"Attadaṇḍesu" means among those who have taken up the rod [of violence]. "Nibbutaṃ" means extinguished by the extinction of defilements (kilesa-nibbāna). "Sādānesu" means among those with clinging (sa-upādāna).
"Ohita" means fallen away.
459. "Gentle" (*akakkasa*) means faultless. For even a tree that has sap is called "rough.
"Communicative" (*viññāpani*) means that which makes the meaning known. "Truthful" (*sacca*) means non-deceptive. "Utter" (*udīraye*) means speak.
"By which one does not become provoked" means that by such speech one does not cause another to become agitated or attached; the meaning is that one speaks such gentle speech.
"Long" refers to goods that have been strung together. "Short" refers to scattered goods. "Minute" means small. "Coarse" means large.
"Beautiful and ugly" means attractive and unattractive. For indeed, a long article may be of little value or of great value;
the same principle applies to short articles and the rest. Thus, by this much, not everything has been included; [the remainder is covered] by the term "beautiful and ugly."
But it is completely exhausted.
"Free from longing" means devoid of craving.
"Bases" refers to the bases of craving. "Having known" means having understood. "Plunged into the Deathless" means entered within the Deathless. "Attained" means having entered therein.

"Both are attachments" means that both of these are attachments; for merit causes one to cling to heaven (*sagga*), while demerit causes one to cling to the states of woe (*apāya*). Therefore, he said, "both of these are attachments. "He has transcended" means he has gone beyond.

"Untroubled" means free from the defilements (*kilesa*) that cause turbidity. "With delight and existence utterly exhausted" means with delight completely destroyed and existence completely destroyed.
In the verse beginning with "Whoever this," ignorance itself is the "quagmire" in the sense of being deceptive, and it is the "difficult passage" because of its great depth and inaccessibility.
In the sense of wandering, it is called *saṃsāra*; in the sense of deluding, it is called *moha*. "Crossed over" means having crossed over the four floods.
"Gone to the further shore" means having reached Nibbāna. "A meditator" means one who meditates by way of contemplating both the object and its characteristics. "Unshaken" means free from craving.
"Extinguished through non-clinging" means that, without grasping at anything, one is extinguished through the extinction of all defilements.

*Kāme* means in both kinds of sensual pleasures (*kāma*). *Anāgāro* means having become homeless. *Paribbaje* means he wanders forth. *Kāmabhavaparikkhīṇaṃ* means one whose sensual pleasures are exhausted and whose existence is exhausted.
*Mānusakaṃ yogaṃ* means the human bond of the five strands of sensual pleasure. *Dibbaṃ yogaṃ* means the divine bond of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

*Sabbayogavisaṃyuttaṃ* means detached from the bond of all defilements. *Ratiṃ* means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. *Aratiṃ* means weariness with the cultivation of the wholesome. *Vīraṃ* means one who possesses energy.
"Sugata" means one who has gone to a beautiful state, or one who has gone by way of a beautiful practice.
"Gati" means rebirth. "Pure" means in the past. "Pacchā" means in the future. "Majjhe" means in the present. "Kiñcana" refers to the defilement that creates something (an impediment).
"Mahesi" means a great seer in the sense of seeking great qualities. "Vijitāvī" means one who has won victory.

460. Thus, having shown that only one whose taints are exhausted is a brahmin by virtue of his qualities, the Blessed One spoke these two verses beginning with "For this is a mere designation," in order to show that those who adhere to the notion that one is a brahmin by birth do so without knowing this, and that their view is a wrong view.
The meaning of this is as follows: regarding what is called a brahmin, a khattiya, a Bhāradvāja, or a Vāseṭṭha—this name and clan...
"Fabricated, made, and conditioned"—this is a conventional designation (*samaññā*) in the world; the meaning is that it is merely a worldly usage (*vohāramatta*).
Why? Because it has arisen from convention (*samuccā*), come down through common usage.
For indeed, at the very time of its birth, this [name] was fashioned and made for it by its relatives and kinsmen. If they were not to fashion it thus, no one would recognize anyone upon seeing them.
One might think, "This is a brahmin" or "This is a Bhāradvāja. Thus, this conceptualization has been long-cherished as a latent tendency for those who do not understand the sphere of views.

That conceptualized name and clan—[one should know] that "this is merely a name and clan, conceptualized for the sake of worldly convention"—is a sphere of views long-cherished as a latent tendency in the hearts of beings who do not understand it. Of that...

Because they are possessed by underlying tendencies, they do not speak out of ignorance of that name and clan; what is meant is that they say, "One is a brahmin by birth," while remaining ignorant of this very fact.
Thus, those who form the dogmatic adherence that "one is a brahmin by birth" are ignorant of this mere conventional designation.
Having thus shown that their view is a wrong view, he now spoke the verse beginning with "Not by birth...

(*na jaccā...*) in order to reject the doctrine of birth in its primary sense and to establish the doctrine of action (*kamma*). Therein, for the purpose of expanding upon the half-verse "By action" (*kammunā*), the passage beginning with "The farmer by action" was stated.
In that context, "by action" means by the volitional action (*cetanā-kamma*) produced in the present through such acts as plowing.
"Seers of dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppādadassā*) means those who see dependent origination thus: "By this condition, this comes to be.

"Skilled in the ripening of kamma" (*kammavipākakovidā*) means that birth occurs by way of kamma in families worthy of honor or contempt; furthermore, the distinction between the inferior and the sublime arises when inferior and sublime kamma ripens. Thus they are skilled in the ripening of kamma.

In the verse beginning with “By kamma the world revolves,” the terms *loka* (the world), *pajā* (the generation), and *satta* (beings) have one and the same meaning; there is only a difference in the wording.
Furthermore, in this context, the first line should be understood as a negation of the view that “there is a Brahmā, a Great Brahmā, the supreme, the creator.
For it is by kamma that the world revolves through various destinies; who then could be its creator? By the second line...
“Thus, even though produced by karma, one proceeds through the course of existence (pavatta) by means of karma, distinguished as past and present;
