experiencing pleasure and pain, one proceeds while undergoing various states such as inferior and superior,” so it is shown. By the third [verse], he concludes that very point:
“In this way, in every respect, beings are bound by the bond of karma and proceed only because they are bound by karma.”
"Not otherwise. With the fourth [simile], he clarifies this point by means of a simile:

Just as for a moving chariot, the axle-pin is the binding factor, and it does not move without being bound by it, so too, for the world’s arising and its continued occurrence, karma is the binding factor;
without being bound by it, the world neither arises nor proceeds.
Now, since the world is thus bound by karma, he spoke these two verses beginning with "By austerity" (*tapena*) in order to demonstrate the state of excellence through excellent karma.
Therein, "by austerity" (*tapena*) means by the austerity of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). "By the holy life" (*brahmacariyena*) means by abstaining from sexual intercourse.

"By restraint" (*saṃyamena*) means by virtue (*sīla*). "By self-control" (*damena*) means by the control of the sense faculties. "By this" (*etena*) refers to this excellent, utterly pure, and sublime state.
One becomes a brahmin through action. Why? Because this is the supreme brahminhood; what is meant is that this action is the supreme quality of a brahmin.
There is also the reading *brahmānaṃ*. Here, however, is the etymological derivation: it brings (*āneti*) one to the sublime (*brahma*), meaning it brings about the state of being a brahmin.
In the second verse, "peaceful" (*santa*) means one whose defilements are stilled. "Brahmā and Sakka" refers to one who is both a Brahmā and a Sakka;
such a person is not merely a brahmin, but rather is both a Brahmā and a Sakka among those who understand—the wise.
Thus it is said, "O Vāseṭṭha, know this. The rest is entirely clear.
The commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed. 9.
The commentary on the Subha Sutta.
462. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Subha Sutta. In this context, "the son of Todeyya" means the son of the brahmin Todeyya who lived in the village of Tudigāma.
"One who is successful" means one who accomplishes and fulfills [his aim]. "The methodical Dhamma" means the Dhamma of causal principles.
"Wholesome" means blameless.
463. "Wrong practice" means a practice that does not lead to liberation and is unwholesome. "Right practice" means a practice that leads to liberation and is wholesome.

Regarding the terms "of great purpose" (*mahaṭṭha*) and so forth: it is called "of great purpose" because there is much purpose (*attha*) here, whether by way of many attendants performing services or by way of many requisites.
It is called "of great function" (*mahākicca*) because there are great functions (*kicca*) here, such as the recitation of names and auspicious ceremonies. Today...
"Mahādhikaraṇaṃ" means "great legal cases," because great legal issues termed "matters of business" (*adhikāra*) are to be dealt with here.
"Mahāsamārambhaṃ" means "great undertaking," because there is a great effort consisting of affliction due to many people being engaged and occupied in the work.
"Gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānaṃ" means "the work of household life. Thus the meaning should be understood in all sections. Regarding agricultural work (*kasikamma*): [text continues]
And herein, the greatness [of the effort] should be understood as consisting in the seeking out of requisites, beginning with the tip of the plough;
while the smallness [of the effort] should be understood as consisting in the exchange of goods in trade by taking them exactly as they are found.
"Failing" refers to agricultural work through drought, excessive rain, and so forth, and commercial work through the imperfection of gems, gold, and so on.
When it fails, the result is meager, and it may even lead to the cutting off of the roots [of merit]. Conversely, when it succeeds, the result is great, as in the case of Cūḷantevāsika.
"Even so," means that just as the subject of farming, when it fails, yields little fruit, so too is the subject of the household life.
For one who has not performed what is wholesome, having passed away, is reborn in hell. It is said that there was once a certain general named Mahādatta who was supported by brahmins.
At the time of his death, hell appeared before him. When asked by the brahmins, "What do you see?", he replied, "A house of blood.
[They said,] "Sir, this is the Brahmā-world. [He asked,] "Sir, what is called the 'Brahmā-world'?

[They replied,] "It is above. [He said,] "To me, it appears below. [They said,] "Even though it appears below, nevertheless, having passed away while thinking it was 'above,' you will fall into hell."
[He] was reborn [in hell]. Thinking, "He has brought a fault upon our sacrifice," they took a thousand [pieces of gold] and gave it to him to take away.
However, when it succeeds, it yields great fruit; for one who has performed wholesome deeds is reborn in heaven after passing away.
This should be illustrated by the entire account of Guttila’s celestial mansion (*vimāna*). Just as that business of trading, when it fails, yields little fruit, so too...
For one who does not fulfill the precepts and is intent on improper search, even the meditation subject of renunciation yields no fruit;
such a person obtains neither the bliss of jhāna and so forth, nor the heavenly realms or liberation. However, when practiced successfully, it is of great fruit.
For by fulfilling the precepts and developing insight, one attains even arahantship.
“Brāhmaṇas, Master Gotama,” he asked, “what is it that I am asking here? The brāhmaṇas say:
“There is no one called a renunciant capable of fulfilling these five qualities; only a householder fulfills them.
But the ascetic Gotama says again and again, “Whether it be a householder, young man, or a renunciant,” yet he does not [distinguish] the renunciant...
"He releases [the question]," meaning: "I think he does not perceive my very own question," thus he asks under the heading of generosity, "I ask about five things.

"If it is not burdensome for you" means: if it is not difficult for you to speak here in accordance with how brahmins prescribe it, provided there is no state of discomfort on your part, then please speak; such is the meaning. "Indeed, sir, it is not [burdensome] for me..."
With what intention did he say this? For it is difficult to speak in the presence of those who merely resemble the wise;
at every word and every syllable, they point out only faults. But when the truly wise hear a discourse, they praise what is well-spoken;
yet if it is poorly spoken, they rectify whatever is inconsistent within the text, the words, the meaning, or the phrasing.
There is no one equal to the Blessed One who is called "absolutely wise"; therefore he said: "Indeed, Master Gotama, it is not a burden for me whether you, or one like you, are seated here.
*Sacca* means truthfulness of speech. *Tapa* means the practice of austerity.
*Brahmacariya* means abstention from sexual intercourse. *Ajjhena* means the acquisition of mantras. *Cāga* means the relinquishing of material goods.
"466. 'He will be brought low' means he will be brought low in his state of ignorance.

"He said this": having been refuted by the Blessed One with the simile of the blind man leading the blind, and being unable to offer a rebuttal, he—just as a weak dog, having raised up a deer and turned it toward its master, then retreats itself—likewise pointed to his teacher.
Thus he spoke these words beginning with “the brahmin. In that context, “Pokkharasāti” is his name;

he is also called “Pokkharasāyi. It is said that his body shone like a white lotus, resembling a silver archway erected in a city of the gods, while his head was black in color, as if made of sapphire, and his beard was like a streak of dark clouds across the moon’s disk.
He appeared radiant; his eyes were like blue lotuses; his nose was perfectly rounded and utterly pure, like a tube of silver;
and the palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and his face shone as if polished with lacquer.
The Brahmin’s physical form had reached the pinnacle of beauty. "It is fitting to appoint this Brahmin as king in a place that lacks a ruler; for he is thus—"
"Sassiriko" (possessing beauty); thus, because he resembles a lotus (*pokkhara*), they know him as "Pokkharasāti.
Furthermore, because he was born from a lotus and not from a mother's womb, they also know him as "Pokkharasāyī" (one who dwelt in a lotus) because he lay within a lotus.
"Opamañño" means one of the Upamañña clan. "Subhagavaniko" means the lord of the Subhagavana grove near Ukkaṭṭhā. "Hassakamevā" means... [only laughter].
It is merely something to be laughed at. "Merely a name" means it is merely base. That very thing is empty because of the absence of any real substance; and because it is empty, it is hollow.
Now, in order to refute that [view] along with its teacher, the Blessed One said, "But what, young man," and so forth.
467. In this context, "Which of these is better? means which speech is better for them, or more praiseworthy—that is the meaning. "Sammucca" means...
"By convention" means by worldly usage. "Mantras" means having weighed and considered. "Having reflected" means having understood.

"Beneficial" means based on a reason. "In this way being" means when there is the state of superiority because it has been spoken after not abandoning worldly usage, but having weighed, understood, and made it based on a reason. "Enveloped" (āvuta) means covered. "Shrouded" (nivuta) means obstructed.
*Ophuṭo* means covered. *Pariyonaddho* means enveloped. 468.

*Gadhitō* and the following terms have meanings already explained. "If that condition exists, Master Gotama"—that is, if this cause is present—"then that fire would indeed be possessed of flames, possessed of color, and radiant, due to the absence of smoke, embers, and so forth."
"And so it is, young man. "I am like that," he said; that is, I am similar to that. This is what is meant:

just as a fire burning in dependence on fuel such as grass and wood is considered "with impurity" due to the presence of smoke, ash, and embers, even so, the rapture (*pīti*) that arises in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure is "with impurity" due to the presence of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and so forth. Just as...

But just as fire that has abandoned its fuel of grass and wood is purified by the absence of smoke and so forth, even so, the rapture associated with the two supramundane jhānas is purified by the absence of birth and the other [defilements]; this is the meaning. 469.
Now, as for those five qualities designated by the brahmins under the heading of "generosity" (cāga), they too are exactly five.
Having offered the oblation, they do not remain motionless; they incur six offenses together with one who is compassionate by nature.
Therefore, in order to point out that fault, he said, "Those young brahmins," and so forth. In this context, "compassionate by nature" means having compassion as one's inherent disposition.
"Where do you frequently observe [this]?"—the Blessed One said this because: "This one, having gone forth, [possesses] these five qualities..."
He said, "There is no one capable of fulfilling [these perfections]; it is the householder who fulfills them. Therefore, he asks with that very same intent, in order to make him say:
"Only one who has gone forth fulfills these; there is indeed no householder capable of fulfilling them.
Regarding such passages as "one who speaks truth constantly and continuously," even a householder, when there is no other alternative, may speak a falsehood for the sake of social intercourse.
Indeed, they do so; even when their heads are being cut off with a sword, those who have gone forth do not utter two words.
A householder is unable to observe even a single training rule for the duration of a month, whereas one who has gone forth is always an ascetic, virtuous, and devoted to austerity.
A householder is unable to perform the Uposatha observance for even eight days of a month, whereas those who have gone forth...

They remain celibate for as long as they live. A householder might even write down the *Ratana Sutta* and the *Maṅgala Sutta* and place them in a book, whereas those who have gone forth recite them constantly.

A householder may not be able to give even a regular portion of alms-food (*salākabhatta*) without interruption, whereas those who have gone forth, when no one else is present, give alms even to crows, dogs, and the like—even to a young novice carrying their belongings.

"Placing them into the bowl"—this is how the meaning should be understood. "I call these for one whose mind is full of loving-kindness": the meaning is that I declare these five qualities to be the attendants of a mind imbued with *mettā*.
470. "Born and grown": both born and increased. For he who is merely born there [in that state] but not elsewhere...
"Having grown up," means that for him, the village roads in his vicinity are not entirely unfamiliar; therefore, he said "one who has grown up since birth.
For even one who has grown up since birth, if he has been away for a long time, those roads are not entirely familiar;
therefore, he said "having returned immediately," which means having departed at that very moment. "Hesitation" means: "This..."
“Is this indeed the path, or is it not?”—this refers to lingering due to doubt.
“Stiffness” (vitthāyitatta) means that just as the body of someone who is asked about a subtle matter suddenly becomes rigid, so too is there a seizing of rigidity.
By the phrase “not at all,” he demonstrates the unimpeded nature of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
For that man, there might be an obstruction to his knowledge due to the interference of Māra and others; because of this, he might falter or be distressed.
However, the knowledge of omniscience is unimpeded; it is shown that no one is able to create an obstacle for it.
"Just as, young man, a powerful conch-blower"—here, "powerful" means endowed with strength. "Conch-blower" means...
A conch-blower. "Without difficulty" means without trouble or suffering.
For a weak conch-blower, even while blowing the conch, is unable to make his voice known in the four directions, and the sound of his conch does not pervade everywhere.
But for one who is strong, it is far-reaching; therefore, he said "one who is strong. Regarding the phrase "by the liberation of mind through loving-kindness": here...

When "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) is mentioned, both access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*) are appropriate; however, when "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) is mentioned, only absorption is appropriate.

Regarding "action that is limited" (*pamāṇakataṃ kamma*): action that is limited is said to belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while action that is measureless (*appamāṇakataṃ kamma*) belongs to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*).
Of these, it is specifically the action of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) that is intended here. For that—
Because it has been performed by extending [the mind] beyond limits through the modes of limited, unlimited, and directional pervasion, it is called "immeasurably performed.

"It does not remain there, it does not persist there" means that this sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) karma neither lags behind nor persists within that fine-material and immaterial-sphere (*rūpārūpāvacara*) karma. What is meant? That sense-sphere karma...
Neither can it stop, remain, pervade, or exhaust the karma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres,
nor can it take up its own place within them; rather, it is the karma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres itself that pervades,
exhausts, and takes up its own place within sense-sphere karma, just as a great flood does with a small amount of water.
"He remains; having warded off its result, he himself leads [the person] to companionship with the Brahmās. The remainder is clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Subha Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
10. Commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta. 473.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Saṅgāravasutta. Therein, "Cañcalikappa" is the name of a village. "Abhippasannā" means she was serene by way of verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
It is said that she was a stream-enterer, a noble female disciple, [the daughter] of a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.
His wife. That brahmin had previously, from time to time, invited other brahmins and rendered them honor.

But after bringing this brahmin woman into the home, being unable to provoke the anger of that beautiful brahmin woman from a great family, he was no longer able to honor the brahmins. Then, wherever the brahmins saw him—
“Now you are no longer a recipient of the brahmins’ favor; you do not even offer hospitality to the brahmins for a single day,” they pressed him.

Having returned home, he informed his wife of this matter and said, “If you, madam, could manage to guard your mouth for one day, we would give alms to the brahmins for one day. [She replied,] “What gift do you have to give?”

"Give it to the place where you like it; what have I to do with this? He then invited the brahmins, had rice porridge cooked with little water, had the house cleaned, and having prepared seats, he had the brahmins sit down.
The brahmin’s wife, having put on a fine cloak and taken a ladle, was serving the food when she tripped over the hem of her garment and said, "I am serving the brahmins!"
Without even forming a perception [of the food], he spontaneously recollecting the Teacher alone through the power of habitual practice, uttered an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
When the brahmins heard the inspired utterance, they thought, "This man is a partisan of both sides, a friend of the ascetic Gotama;
we shall not accept his gift," and becoming angry, they threw away the food and departed. The brahmin—[thinking] "Was it not already said before?"—
I said to her, “Today, for one day, you should guard your mouth”; thus, you have caused me to lose this much milk, rice, and so forth.

Overcome by extreme anger, she said: “In that very same way, this outcaste woman praises that shaven-headed ascetic whenever or wherever she may; now, O outcaste, I shall [punish] her for that teacher!”
“I shall challenge him to a debate,” he said. Then the brahmin woman said to him, “Go, brahmin; having gone, you will find out.
She then spoke these words beginning with, “Indeed, brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas... who could challenge him to a debate.
He then approached the Teacher.
“What must one cut off to sleep in happiness? What must one cut off so as not to grieve?
Of what single thing, O Gotama, do you approve the destruction?”—thus he asked the question. The Teacher said:
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily; having cut off anger, one does not grieve.
O Brahmin, the Noble Ones praise the slaying of that which has a root of bitterness and a tip of sweetness; for having cut that off, one does not grieve.”
He spoke the question. Having gone forth, he attained arahantship.

His younger brother, named Akkosaka-Bhāradvāja, hearing that "my brother has gone forth," approached the Blessed One; after reviling him, he was disciplined by the Blessed One, went forth, and attained arahantship.
Another of his younger brothers was named Sundarika-Bhāradvāja. He too [approached] the Blessed One...
Having approached him, asked a question, and heard the answer, he went forth and attained arahantship.
His younger brother, named Piṅgalabhāradvāja, also asked a question;
at the conclusion of the explanation of that question, he too went forth and attained arahantship. The young brahmin Saṅgārava was the youngest of them all on that day.
He was seated at the head of the meal-row together with the brahmins. *Avabhūtāvā* means they have become diminished, that is, they have become unfortunate.
*Parabhūtāvā* means they have reached ruin. *Vijjamānānaṃ* means among those who exist. *Sīlapaññāṇaṃ* means you do not know both virtue and wisdom. 474.
*Diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattā* means having attained mastery and perfection in direct knowledge regarding the present life, that is, in this very individual existence.

Having recognized [the truth], having reached the end of their journey, they declare, "We have attained Nibbāna, the far shore of all phenomena known as the perfections (pāramī)," and thus they profess themselves to be those who have realized the beginning of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariya*).
This means they profess themselves to be the originators, the producers, and the generators of the holy life. *Takkī* means one who grasps by means of reasoning; *vīmaṃsī* means...
An investigator, having practiced the course of wisdom, speaks thus: "I am one of them"—that is, I am one among those Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
(485) *Aṭṭhitavataṃ* means possessing unwavering asceticism; this connects with the word *padhāna* (striving), as does the word *sappurisa* (true person).
For this is what is meant: for the venerable Gotama there was the practice of unwavering striving, the practice of the striving of a true person.
"Ahosi" means "it was. When asked, "Is there a deva?", the young brahmin spoke thus with the perception that the Perfectly Enlightened One was proclaiming something even though he did not know it.
"Evaṃ sante" means while your state of not knowing exists. "Tucchaṃ musā hoti" means your statement becomes empty and fruitless.
In this way, the young brahmin attempts to refute the Blessed One with a charge of falsehood. By one who is wise...
"By a man" means by a wise person. He indicates: "But you, because of your ignorance, do not even understand what has been declared by me.
"Elevatedly acclaimed" means acclaimed with a loud sound, well-known in the world. "Supreme deities" (adhidevā):

for even Susudārakas are called "deities" (devā), and females are called "divinities" (deviyo), but the males are "supreme deities" (adhidevā); this is said in contrast to those in the world who have acquired the names "deity" and "divinity."
The meaning is "superior to human beings. The remainder is entirely clear in every respect.
The commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
The commentary on the Middle Fifty [Suttas] is finished.
